chassis.verdict: Yes — this family is two variants of a single generator, and the same three-part recipe underlies all ten. Every asset is built as: a dark soil-shadow ellipse on the ground, one perfectly straight vertical stem of identical thickness and identical dark-green-to-olive gradient rising from its centre, leaves clipped onto that stem, and a single tiny flower emblem glued to the apex. Chassis A (Buttercup, Daisy, Foxglove, Goldenrod, Poppy, Sunflower) is a leaf-ladder: nine to eleven strictly opposite, strictly symmetric leaf pairs stacked at even intervals from just above the soil to the very top, each pair a little shorter than the one below so the silhouette is always the same tapered cypress ogive. Chassis B (Bromeliad, Clover, Dandelion, and Violet as a reduced case) is the same stem with the leaves collapsed to the base instead — a radial fan of roughly a dozen blades splayed from one ground point in the same symmetric arc, with the bare stalk running straight up through the middle of the fan. Nothing varies except (a) the leaf glyph swapped in — spiky strap, serrated triangle, smooth lance, round blob, compound pinnule — and (b) the apex flower token's hue and petal count. The apex token is the worst tell: it is the SAME diameter, roughly 8-10 percent of image height, on every single plant, so the Sunflower's head, the Violet's flower, the Daisy's flower and the Dandelion's head are all the same small badge in a different colour. Real inflorescence architecture — Foxglove's one-sided hanging spike, Goldenrod's arching pyramid plume, Clover's globe pompom, Poppy's four crumpled petals, Sunflower's huge dark spiral disc — is the identity of five of these species and none of it survives the generator. What the chassis actually reads as is a decorative stylised sprig or heraldic frond with a lapel-pin flower stuck on top, not a wildflower.

All three are the same drawing. There is one shared sigmoid 'S' cane that rises from a fixed point at bottom-centre, bows left, crosses back right and tips left again at the top, with the same taper and the same paint-stroke thickness in every asset; the same eight alternating nodes fall at the same heights, each carrying an identical small dark coiled-tendril ellipse in the same position and at the same angle; the same soft ground-shadow ellipse sits under the same spot. Ivy and Passionflower are pixel-siblings: both occupy the identical x-range 139-300 on a 440px canvas and reuse the SAME seven-lobed deeply-cut palmate fan leaf sprite at the SAME nodes, changed only in hue (mint-teal vs. mid-green) with three small star-flowers stamped on top for Passionflower. Rattan keeps the identical cane, node ladder, tendril spirals and shadow and only swaps the leaf sprite for a hatched one-sided frond blade. Declared aspects of 1.5, 1.2 and 0.6 have no visible effect: all three render at the same height and the same girth. What the chassis actually READS as is a single potted cannabis/hemp cutting on a wire - a generic seven-finger palmate vine - recoloured three times; nothing about it says ivy, nothing says passionflower, and only the leaf swap gestures at a palm.

Four of the five are one drawing. Agave, Aloe and Yucca are the identical construction: a bilaterally mirrored ground fan of about thirteen tapering blades radiating from a single point at the soil line, every tip landing on the same shallow arc, the same soft airbrushed midrib-plus-herringbone venation painted on every blade, and one perfectly straight hairline dark-green stalk rising from dead centre to roughly twice rosette height, capped by a tiny vertical stack of 6-9 identical round beads. Only two variables move across those three: blade width (broad in Agave, medium in Aloe, narrow in Yucca) and bead hue (yellow / orange / white). Prickly Pear is the SAME fan with the blade swapped for a rounded oval pad and the stalk made invisible - the giveaway is that its yellow flower is left floating unattached in mid-air exactly where the other three put their stalk-tip beads. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a generic potted fan-palm or dracaena rosette with a lollipop flower stick pushed into the middle of it - not a succulent at all, because nothing anywhere in the family reads as THICK: no blade has depth, a cut face, a fleshy cross-section, a marginal tooth or a terminal spine. Desert Rose is the only off-chassis asset in the batch, and it is off-chassis into the wrong plant entirely (a ribbed columnar cactus). The family therefore has one body plus one outlier, and the one body is the wrong body.

All three are built from one primitive: a single convergence point on the ground, a fan of perfectly straight, uniformly tapered rods radiating out of it, one terminal ornament stuck on the far end of each rod, and one soft elliptical drop shadow underneath. Sundew and Venus Flytrap are the same object twice — identical straight spoke, identical filled ovoid head at the tip, identical short straight bristles radiating from that ovoid's perimeter, identical single-point hub — with only the camera (top-down vs side-on), the stalk hue (orange vs green) and the bristle tip (white bead vs bare cream spike) changed. Pitcher Plant swaps the rod-plus-ball for a rod-that-IS-a-cone with a leaf cap, but keeps the same fan-from-one-point layout, the same dead-straight taper with zero curvature or gesture, the same one-ornament-per-element rule and the same shadow ellipse. Nothing in the family has a rhizome, soil line, ground-hugging rosette, petiole wing, curl, droop or asymmetry — the growth form is not observed, it is a lathe. The chassis reads as a bouquet: a handful of straight skewers jammed into one spot with a differently-coloured thing skewered on each tip, which is why the flytrap reads as fruit on sticks and the sundew reads as a pinwheel rather than as plants.

This family is not seven plants, it is TWO drawings. Chassis A, the 'fountain', carries Cattail, Papyrus and Wild Rice: an identical radial spray of strap blades erupting from a single point on the ground, the same outer blades whipping down almost to horizontal, the same short hatch-tick marks stippled along every blade, the same tiny stem-cluster at the base and the same flat black ellipse shadow underneath. The only differences between the three are hue (olive / khaki / bright green) and a single thin ornament glued to the top of the centre blade. Seagrass is the same fountain with the splay angle closed to near-zero, giving an upright bundle. Chassis B, the 'plate', carries Duckweed, Lotus and Water Lily: the same dark navy ellipse with a pale rim, the same three flat ovals arranged in the same two-back-one-front positions, the same specular sheen top-left on each oval, the same hairline scored across each oval. Lotus and Water Lily are the SAME picture with the pad green shifted and the star flower recoloured pink instead of white — which means the packet's explicit warning ('Lotus leaves stand above the water; water lily leaves float on it. Do not conflate') was violated by drawing the lotus with the water lily's own file. Chassis A reads as a generic ornamental grass clump in a garden centre; chassis B reads as three olives on a dinner plate. Neither reads as water. Nothing in this family is differentiated by growth form, leaf shape, height, stem, or root — only by colour and by one small trinket bolted on top.

These two are not merely a shared chassis, they are the same render with a hue/value shift. Overlay them and every part matches: the same low mound sitting on the same soft grey drop-shadow ellipse, the same crown point low and slightly right of centre, the same count and the same fan of fronds radiating from it, the same two near-horizontal fronds sweeping right with an identical downward hook at the tip, the same three broad paddle-shaped blades standing near-vertical in the middle, the same left-hand fronds curving down-left to the same terminal angles. Every frond is built the same way: a thick pale lance-shaped midrib blade with a row of small stiff triangular sawteeth combed along both edges, teeth pointing outward and forward, tooth size identical across both plants. Growth form in both is a squat spreading mound clearly wider than tall (contradicting the 1.1 aspect both rows call for), never an upright vase. What the chassis actually READS as is a sago palm or small cycad, or a bristly agave: stiff, thick-ribbed, radiating palm fronds, not fern fiddlehead-derived foliage at all. Neither fern's identity survives it. The Maidenhair, whose entire diagnostic is jet-black hair-fine wire stalks carrying fan-shaped scalloped leaflets in an airy open lacy spray, is drawn here as a dense stiff comb-leaved cycad with no black anywhere and no lace of any kind; it is only the Sword Fern lightened. The pair should differ in almost everything (wire-thin black branching stems and wedge leaflets versus long stiff single-plane fronds in a tight shuttlecock) and instead differ in exactly one thing: brightness.

These two do NOT share a growth form. Air Plant is a radially symmetrical rosette of straight lanceolate blades springing from a single ground point with a tall vertical inflorescence spike; Rafflesia is a flat five-lobed corolla disc with no stem, no leaves and no vertical axis at all. Nothing about topline, axis, or organ layout is reused between them. What IS shared is the rendering chassis rather than the body: both are dead-centred on the canvas, both sit over the identical soft dark ground-shadow ellipse, both are built from smooth flat-gradient blob shapes with a single soft rim-light and no surface texture whatsoever, and both keep the same blue-black vignette backdrop. That shared painting language is why both fail their texture must-reads in the same way - the air plant's leaves have no fine absorbent scale fuzz and Rafflesia's warts read as glossy bubbles - but the underlying plant architecture is genuinely distinct, so this is not a one-chassis family.

Four of the five (Cedar, Hemlock, Redwood, Yew) are the SAME drawing. Shared parts, part for part: an identical straight vertical trunk of flat mid-brown with a slight taper and a rounded lollipop-stick foot, unbranched from ground to crown, with no bark texture, no flare, no buttress and no fluting on any of them; the trunk meets the crown at the same height and the same width every time. On top sits one soft-edged elliptical green cloud of identical size and identical blurred airbrush shading, with the same two lighter green highlight lobes near its centre. Out of that cloud radiate the same straight single-pixel-width needle sticks, all the same length, all pointing outward from the blob centre like a sea urchin - never in rosette tufts (Cedar), never in flat two-ranked feather sprays (Redwood, Yew). The same black ellipse shadow sits under the same foot. The ONLY thing that changes between the four is the ornament scattered on the blob: brown screw-shaped cones (Cedar, Hemlock, Redwood) or red berry rosettes (Yew), plus a slight hue shift. Aspect is ignored entirely - Redwood is specified 0.3 (extremely tall narrow column) and Cedar 1.0, and they are the same wide ball on the same stick. What the chassis READS as is a child's lollipop tree - a generic broadleaf shade tree with a bristly hairdo - and it is not read as a conifer by anyone. Juniper is the one genuine departure (a multi-cane shrub fan), so the family is not 5/5 one chassis, but it is 4/5, and the fifth is broken in its own way: a bundle of bare brown sticks with token green ticks.

This batch contains a single asset, so there is no sibling to compare a shared chassis against — but the one growth form present is worth naming precisely, because it is the template the rest of the palm family will presumably inherit. The chassis is: one bare brown tapering pole rising through the empty lower two-thirds of the frame, splitting into a Y-fork near the top, with a flat semicircular rosette of pinnate blades fanned out above the fork like an opened hand, and a pea-sized clump of brown spheres tucked in the dead centre of that rosette. Read as a growth form it is a cycad or sago palm, not a date palm: the crown is a flat 180-degree disc pressed into the picture plane rather than an open three-dimensional shuttlecock of arching fronds, the trunk carries no surface information at all, and the fork is anatomically impossible for a palm, which is an unbranched monocot. If this same pole-plus-fan-disc gets reused for coconut, oil palm and sago with only leaflet hue and blade count changed, the family will be one cycad in several colours; the differentiators that must live in the chassis itself are trunk surface (leaf-base diamonds vs rings vs fibre), crown geometry (open arch vs flat fan), and the size and hang position of the fruit mass.

Twelve of the fourteen are literally the same drawing. The chassis is a lollipop: one untapered brown popsicle-stick trunk of constant width with a rounded-off bottom end, no root flare, no bark texture and no branching whatsoever, rising to roughly the same height in every card; a single soft airbrushed green ellipse for the crown, wider than tall, its interior an undifferentiated blur with the same pale-green hotspot smudged left of centre; a scatter of small identical leaf decals pinned around the rim of that ellipse (they never overlap the trunk and never hang from a twig, so the crown has no internal structure at all); three to five fruit spheres pasted flat onto the blur at mid-crown height, always in the same rough triangle, always the same diameter; and the same dark ground-shadow ellipse under the stick. What changes between species is the leaf decal (narrow lance vs broad round vs fern-frond), the fruit sphere's fill colour, and nothing else. So the chassis READS as a child's drawing of a generic fruit tree - specifically it reads as an apple tree, and Apple, Apricot, Avocado, Cherry, Guava and Jujube are that apple tree recoloured red, orange, black, red, yellow and maroon. Brazil Nut, Chestnut, Durian and Jackfruit are the same tree with brown or striped balls, which is why an emergent 50m rainforest giant, a chestnut, a durian and a jackfruit are indistinguishable from one another. Every distinguishing feature the reference asks for lives in the parts this chassis does not have: bark (Cherry's banded red-brown, Guava's flaking copper, Fig's smooth grey), crown architecture (Brazil Nut's bare bole and flat top crown, Jackfruit's cauliflorous limbs, Apple's low crooked spread), and stalks (Cherry's long dangles, Fig's sessile axil fruit, Cashew's nut hanging below the apple). Only two assets leave the chassis: Coconut, which is a real palm silhouette but with an impossible forked trunk and a one-sided fan crown, and Hazelnut, which is a rectangular slab of stacked circles with nuts on bare vertical wires above it.

Twelve of the fourteen are one drawing. Every tree stands on the same straight, un-tapered brown popsicle stick — identical width top to bottom, identical rounded cap where it meets the ground, identical flat elliptical drop-shadow, and in no image does that trunk fork, bend, taper or carry a single branch. On top sits the same soft airbrushed green cloud, wider than it is tall, with the same fuzzy glow halo bleeding off its right side, and the same ring of loose leaf decals scattered around the cloud's rim as though blown outward from the centre. Fruit is the same 3-5 identical spheres with the same top-left specular dot, dropped onto the cloud at the same radius. There is no branch architecture anywhere, so nothing can hang, droop, spray, cluster on a trunk or sit on a bare twig — which is precisely what half these mustReads ask for. What the chassis reads as is a generic nursery-catalogue lollipop orchard tree, and the ONLY variables that move between species are leaf silhouette (broad oval / narrow lance / feathery pinnate) and fruit hue. That is not enough: Mango, Orange, Persimmon and Peach are the same orange-sphere lollipop; Lemon, Lime and Pear are the same yellow-sphere lollipop; Pomegranate is Plum in red. Papaya and Plantain break away only to share a SECOND identical chassis with each other — the same forked brown trunk with the same swept fan of stiff pinnate feather fronds and the same tiny fruit nub wedged in the fork — a chassis that reads as a palm or cycad and is wrong for both, flatly contradicting Papaya's own note that the plant has no branches.

All four are the same drawing with the palette and the fruit-blob swapped. Every one has an identical trunk: a straight, essentially untapered flat-brown stick with a rounded lollipop top, no bark texture, no root flare, no fork, no branch leaving the silhouette anywhere — it simply vanishes into the crown at the same height in all four, and it sits on the same black elliptical ground-shadow smear. Above it sits one soft airbrushed green cloud of nearly identical size and outline in all four, and pinned around that cloud's rim is a radial spray of leaf sprigs all aimed outward from the crown centre like a starburst — the arrangement is identical from image to image, only the sprig glyph changes. Rambutan, Starfruit and Walnut use the very same pinnate ladder sprig at the very same scale, so their foliage is literally indistinguishable; only Soursop swaps in a single-ovate leaf. Fruit in every case is 3-4 small equal-sized spheres scattered on the face of the cloud with a soft glow halo behind them, never hanging, never clustered on old wood, never sized differently. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a generic cartoon fern-palm sapling — a broom handle with a bush of ferns glued on top — and the species name is carried only by the colour of four little balls.

Eleven of the twelve are literally the same drawing. The shared chassis is: a smooth tapered brown cone rooted at the ground (the 'trunk'), from which five to seven perfectly straight brown canes splay outward in a symmetric vase/fan, each cane the same length and the same taper, each carrying leaves at even intervals along its ENTIRE length in strict opposite pairs, each terminating in one small blob-cluster at the very tip, and all of it sitting on the identical black elliptical drop shadow at the identical scale. Nothing structural changes across the family: not the topline (always the same fan of tips at the same height), not the branching (always from one basal cone, never a second-order branch, never a crossing or a broken cane), not where the cane leaves the silhouette (always the basal cone, always at the same splay angles), not the leaf attachment (always evenly spaced pairs from base to tip, so no bare lower stem and no crowded tip). Only three things are swapped: the leaf glyph (fine fern frond / small oval / palmate star / narrow lance / silver willow sliver), the foliage hue (green, blue-green, silver), and the colour of the terminal blob (purple, blue, red, pale green, pink, cream). Blackberry, Elderberry and Raspberry are the SAME image three times with the tip blob recoloured purple/purple/red. Currant and Gooseberry are the same image twice with the tip blob recoloured red/green — which is exactly the pair the packet warns must be told apart. What the chassis reads as is a florist's bunch of cut stems jammed in a vase: a hand-tied bouquet, not a shrub. Aspect ratio is ignored entirely — Cranberry (aspect 2.5, a creeping bog mat), Blueberry (0.8, dense broad twiggy) and Raspberry (0.7) all come out as the same tall narrow vase. The only asset off the chassis is Mesquite, which uses a straight-pole trunk with a soft round green fog crown, and that is its own defect rather than real variety.

This batch has a single member, so there is no sibling to compare it against and no shared-chassis defect can be proven cross-asset. What can be said about the growth form on its own is that it is the engine's generic radial fan-tuft: a solid unarticulated green wedge at the base from which broad strap blades splay symmetrically left and right in an even fan, each blade a smooth tapering ribbon with a light central highlight, plus one bare vertical stick carrying the seed head. Nothing about that tuft is specifically Poa - it is the same fan a spider plant, a liriope, a daylily or a young agave would get, and the only thing distinguishing this render as a grass at all is the blade narrowness. The reproductive part, which is where grass genera actually differ from one another, is a single dense bead column with zero branching, so if this chassis is reused across the rest of the grass family the whole family will differ only by hue and blade count and every genus will carry the same spike.

This family is not one chassis but TWO, and ten of the fourteen assets are on one of them. CHASSIS A, the grass fountain (Barley, Millet, Oats, Rice, Rye, Sorghum — six assets): an identical radial spray of narrow blades erupting from a single ground point, same silhouette width, same outer blades drooping and whipping down at the same two angles, same inner blades standing vertical, same flat elliptical drop shadow, and one dead-centre vertical culm carrying the SAME seed head — a short ribbed cylinder capped by a flared trapezoid fan. That head does not read as any cereal ear; it reads as a countersunk screw or a bolt with a washer, and it is pixel-for-pixel the same object in all six, rotated not at all and scaled barely. The ONLY thing that changes across the six is hue: gold (Barley, Rye), yellow-green (Millet), green (Rice), olive with a rust head (Sorghum), cream (Oats). Every feature that actually separates these six grasses in life — barley's awns longer than the head, oats' open dangling panicle, rice's head nodding under its own weight in flooded ground, rye's tall thin leaning ear, sorghum's stout corn-like cane with white-midribbed blades — is discarded and replaced by the same upright screw. CHASSIS B, the leaf-ladder column (Amaranth, Buckwheat, Potato, Quinoa — four assets): one straight vertical stem with a bare stub at the bottom, densely stacked opposite leaflets in two ranks packing into a rectangular block with a domed top, an identical tiny terminal ornament (a bead thread or a single star flower), and the same elliptical shadow. Only the leaflet outline (lance / round / feathery / toothed) and the hue change; the column proportion, the leaflet pitch and the top dome are shared. Read together the ladder four are a fern frond or a fuzzy caterpillar, not four different broadleaf crops. Only Arrowroot (rosette), Cassava (cane bush), Corn (bamboo pole) and Sweet Potato (diagonal vine) escape both templates. Compounding it: this is a family of STAPLE CROPS and not one of the four root crops here (Arrowroot, Cassava, Potato, Sweet Potato) shows a single tuber or rhizome — the harvest organ that is the entire reason the plant is in the family is absent from all four.

Only two assets here and they look different at a glance, but they are drawn by the same generator with two parameters changed. Both are a RADIAL BLADE FAN: N near-identical blade primitives all emitted from one hidden point on the ground line, sorted by angle, each blade a tapered lens with a single centre-rib and a soft lit-edge gradient. Neither has any stem architecture between ground and blade — no petiole, no culm node, no sheath — so nothing in either picture ever leaves the silhouette anywhere except that one buried origin. Taro is the fan with blade-width cranked wide and hue set to green; Wheat is the same fan with blade-width cranked narrow, arc-curl raised and hue set to gold. The only structural difference is that Wheat gets one extra vertical prop stuck through the middle of the fan (the ear), and Taro gets nothing at all — its harvest organ is simply not drawn. What the shared chassis READS as is an ornamental fountain grass / hosta clump: a decorative radiating rosette, not a crop plant. Neither asset shows the thing that makes a staple crop legible — Taro's upright peltate stalks and ringed corm, Wheat's single jointed straw — because the chassis has no concept of a stem at all.

Not one chassis but five stock templates recoloured, which is the same defect at a slightly larger grain — 14 species resolve to 6 silhouettes and 4 of them are literally the same drawing. TEMPLATE A, the 'feather-ladder wand' (Chamomile, Echinacea, Mint, Oregano): one straight round green stem rising from a bare foot with a black ellipse shadow, identical pinnate rungs of lance leaflets leaving the stem at a fixed ~40 degrees and stepping up at a fixed pitch, the ladder stopping at the same height on all four, and a single pea-sized flower blob glued to the tip — the ONLY differences across the four are leaflet count/olive-vs-green hue and whether the tip blob is white, pink, lilac or white-lilac. TEMPLATE B, the 'stacked-whorl column' (Ginseng, Mustard): the same wand with the rungs replaced by stacked radiating whorls, giving a fat bottlebrush column with a tiny cap ornament. TEMPLATE C, the 'ground fan' (Cardamom, Ginger): an identical agave/fan-palm rosette of stiff spiked lance blades radiating from one ground point, differing only in whether a thin bare stalk with a bead spike rises from the centre. TEMPLATE D, the 'lollipop tree' (Cinnamon, Clove, Nutmeg): identical brown rounded-rectangle trunk of the same width and height planted on the same ellipse, the same soft airbrushed green cloud crown of the same radius, the same scattered leaf slivers, and 4-5 ornament dots pinned into the cloud — orange trunk plus pink dots is Cinnamon, brown trunk plus brown catkins is Clove, brown trunk plus yellow spheres is Nutmeg. TEMPLATE E, the 'woody broom' (Lavender, Rosemary): the same splayed fan of brown stalks from a common trumpet-shaped base, the same scattered sliver leaves, the same beaded terminal spikes — Rosemary is Lavender with the needles turned green and the spike turned pale blue, so it reads as a blue lavender rather than as rosemary. Only Black Pepper has a silhouette of its own. What the chassis reads as: a decorative wand/bottlebrush stem, a palm rosette, and a child's lollipop tree — three generic plant icons doing duty for a whole spice cabinet, with the harvest (the thing that IS the spice) reduced in almost every case to a coloured dot at the top.

Four of the five are the same plant. Valerian and Yarrow are literally the same asset with a hue nudge — identical dead-straight vertical taper stem, identical flat elliptical ground shadow, identical count and pitch of pinnate side-ribs, identical tiny white pill capping the apex; only the green is a shade cooler on Yarrow. Thyme is that same skeleton stripped to bare chevrons: same single ruler-straight stem from the same shadow ellipse, same symmetric fixed-pitch rungs, with a stamped daisy instead of the white pill. Sage is the same taper stem bundled five times and fanned. The shared chassis is a MAST-AND-RUNGS diagram: one rigid vertical spar, leaves clipped on as mirror-image pairs at mechanically even spacing, and one small ornament stuck on the top — it reads as a fern frond or a bottlebrush, not as any culinary herb. Nothing in the chassis carries growth habit: there is no low spreading mound, no basal rosette, no woody square stem, no branching, no leaf-size gradient up the stem, and no difference in leaf SHAPE between species (small oval blade everywhere). Turmeric is the only asset that escapes the chassis, and it escapes into a different wrong plant.

All four are one chassis with a hue swap. Every asset is the same vertical spindle: a bundle of roughly eight parallel unbranched rods pinched to a single point at the ground, swelling to maximum width at about two-thirds height, then closing to a blunt cluster of rounded tips at the top, all sitting on the same soft elliptical drop shadow. Kelp, Red Algae and Sargassum are very nearly the same rendered shape at the same size and same left-lean; Kelp and Sargassum differ only in that Kelp has webbing filled between some rods and three flat ellipse blobs stuck on the midline. Green Algae is the identical spindle with the gaps between the rods fully webbed over into a solid membrane and the top flared square. Shared parts read explicitly as: a single point-of-attachment base (no holdfast, no disc, no claw, no rock), a strand-bundle body, no fork or branch anywhere in the family, no toothed or strap blade, no free-floating element. What the chassis actually READS as is a closed umbrella or a bound sheaf of spaghetti stood on its tip — a furled parasol, not a seaweed and certainly not a microbial colony. Because the base never grips and nothing ever branches, none of the four identities can be told apart by silhouette; the entire family is distinguishable only by colour.

This batch holds a single asset, so cross-member chassis reuse cannot be observed — but the one chassis it IS built on is worth naming, because it is the generic three-sphere bug rig rather than an ant. Topline: three separate lumps in a rising-then-falling line (big ball head, plain ovoid thorax, striped beach-ball gaster) with NO pinched petiole anywhere; head and thorax simply overlap, and thorax-to-gaster is bridged by a thick straight brown BAR of exactly the same width and colour as a leg, so the abdomen reads as stuck on a stick rather than joined at a waist. Body depth is uniform sphere-of-revolution shading on every segment. Limb form is six identical straight tapered sticks with no femur/tibia elbow, no tarsi and no feet — they just end in points at, and in one case below, the ground plane. Crucially the limbs do NOT leave the silhouette from the thorax: two sprout from the underside of the HEAD and three from the GASTER, with only one from the thorax, which is anatomically impossible for an insect and is the single loudest tell that this is a generic blob-and-sticks builder, not an ant rig. The skull is a featureless ball carrying one oversized vertebrate eye (dark iris plus a white specular dot) and no mandibles at all; the antennae emerge from inside that eye and sweep back as smooth shepherd's-crook whiskers. There is no neck carriage and no tail. What the chassis READS as: a cartoon mascot bug — closer to a stylised termite or a children's-book beetle — assembled from three shaded spheres and six toothpicks.

These are the same drawing twice with a hue swap and a leg-length slider. Both are built from an identical two-sphere body: a smaller front ball carrying a 2x2 cluster of four black eye dots in exactly the same spot, butted against a larger rear ball carrying the same soft mottled blotches and the same specular highlight arc along its upper-left. Both use the identical limb model - thin two-segment tapered sticks with a single knee bend, drawn BEHIND the spheres so no coxa or attachment point is ever shown, radiating fore-and-aft in a symmetric fan rather than leaving the silhouette from a defined body segment. Both sit above the same soft elliptical drop shadow at the same offset, with no feet, no claws and no tarsi where the sticks end. The chassis reads as a generic cartoon two-ball spider - the kind of shape a child draws for 'spider' - and it is the wrong body for BOTH members: a tick is a flat unsegmented teardrop with no waist and no visible eyes, and a sea spider's body is a near-invisible stick whose bulk lives in the legs. The only variables the family actually exercises are colour (rust vs cream) and how far the legs sprawl; not one identity-bearing part - mouthparts, body plan, segmentation, eye arrangement - was redrawn.

Not one chassis at the skeleton level — the Armadillo is built on the standard long-barrel quadruped rig (flat topline, four straight pole legs dropping from the underline at even quarters, pale blob feet, up-curled tail) while the Sloth is a bespoke hanging oval with two flat straps to a branch and no legs at all. But they DO share one head module and one surfacing method, and that is where both fail: an identical small tapered muzzle-cone with a single black bead eye and white catchlight is stamped on the right end of each body, and in both cases the body is a soft airbrushed mass of the same cream-taupe fur with a wispy hair fringe on which the diagnostic feature is PAINTED rather than BUILT. The armadillo's carapace is flat vertical stripes on fur instead of overlapping raised plates; the sloth's claws are absent instead of hooked. The shared chassis therefore reads as a generic soft small mammal — a numbat or a guinea pig — with the species written on it in pigment.

These two are the same bat with a hat swap. A pixel diff of the two renders resolves to a single bat-shaped mask, not two overlapping outlines: the torso is the identical vertical teardrop (narrow shoulders, widest at the belly, blunt rounded rump), the head is the same ball socketed straight onto that teardrop with no neck at all, the same two dot-eyes-with-white-highlight sit at the same height, the same three-toe foot fringe dangles off the same rump point, and the same soft ellipse shadow floats at the same offset below. The wings are the load-bearing evidence: both are the identical folded-paper polygon - a straight leading spar out to a sharp elbow at the same relative span, one hard crease dropping to the body, a straight-cut chord for a trailing edge with no scalloping between digits, and the same little bundle of three straight strut lines fanning from the elbow that stop well short of the membrane edge so no hand skeleton actually reads. Even the small fur-tuft ticks along the left flank repeat in the same place. What the chassis READS as is a paper kite or a Halloween window decal of 'a bat' - a symmetrical hanging-glider silhouette pinned flat to camera - rather than either of two animals: it is one generic bat icon, and the only deltas are ear shape (small round vs tall pointed), two added fangs, and a few degrees of hue. Nothing about mass, wing loading, hand proportion, muzzle length or posture separates a 1.5kg flying fox from a 35g sanguivore that runs on its wrists.

Eight of the nine (Black, Brown, Grizzly, Panda, Polar, Sloth, Spectacled, Sun) are one single chassis with only hue and a marking swapped, and that chassis is not a bear - it is a HERDWICK SHEEP / RAM. Shared parts, part for part: a flat level topline running dead horizontal from a squared-off rump to the withers with no hump and no rump rise on ANY of them; a deep woolly barrel torso whose lower edge is a straight horizontal line; four thin cylindrical stilt limbs of even diameter that leave the silhouette at the extreme four corners of the barrel (never from a shoulder or haunch mass), with a single faint knee crease and no elbow, no wrist and no digits; feet that are tiny dark tapered nubs reading as cloven hooves with a couple of white hatch ticks where claws should be; an identical skull - a big round dark-masked head carried high and forward, brow bulging over a round pale eye ring, and a heavy blunt muzzle that turns DOWN and then curls FORWARD exactly like a ram's rolled horn or a sheep's roman nose; no neck at all, the head is welded straight onto the front of the barrel; and no tail anywhere in the family. The one deviation, Bear.png, is a different but equally broken chassis: an ellipse of body with a radiating spike halo that reads as porcupine quills, carried on two flat rectangular planks for legs. So the family is a flock of eight recoloured sheep plus one hedgehog-blob - the bear body plan (bulk over the forelimbs, plantigrade paws with visible digits and claws, low-slung heavy head, stub tail) is absent from all nine.

All three are literally the same drawing with a hue swap. Shared parts: an identical three-lobe silhouette (sphere head, slightly larger sphere thorax, ovoid abdomen) at the same size ratios; the same single glossy black eye dot placed high-forward on the head; the same two thin antennae leaving the crown and curving up-and-forward with the same arc; the same radial corona of short spikes ringing ONLY the thorax (never the abdomen, on any of the three, so 'fully furry' can never be true); the same six wire-thin straight legs of uniform thickness with no femur/tibia/tarsus articulation, no swelling and no basket, leaving the silhouette at the same three points and splaying to the same stance width; the same two pairs of translucent wings swept back-and-right at the identical angle, the identical length, and overlapping the abdomen so heavily that the abdomen is mostly or entirely occluded in every asset; the same 3/4-left flying pose; and the same soft elliptical ground shadow at the same offset. Not one of the three carries a band, stripe, tongue or pollen load. What the chassis actually READS as is a generic cartoon gnat or fruit fly - the wings are far too large and too long for any bee, the abdomen is a smooth featureless bean, and the only thing separating Bumblebee from Honeybee from Orchid Bee is that the fill is brown, amber or green.

All five are the same ladybug template with a hue swap and nothing else. Every asset shares: the identical top-down egg-shaped elytral oval (aspect ~1.3 regardless of the packet's 1.6/1.7/2.0/2.6), the identical vertical hairline elytral suture running from the shield to the abdomen tip, the identical mushroom-shaped pronotum+head lobe (a wide trapezoid shield with a small round head bump on top carrying two white pinprick eyes on the dorsal surface — anatomically a ladybug's shield, never a scarab's spade or a firefly's hidden head), the identical pair of pale crescent rim-strokes at the upper left and right shoulder of the elytra, the identical single glossy specular streak on the LEFT elytron only, and the identical six thin grey arcs — three per side — that radiate from the mid-abdomen margin instead of attaching at the thorax, all the same length, curvature and taper, with no tarsi, no femur/tibia joint, and no oar fringing. Even the drop shadow ellipse is the same size and offset in all five. NOT ONE asset has antennae, though three of the five reference rows make antennae a must-read. The chassis reads as: a ladybug seen from directly above. Carrion Beetle and Dung Beetle are effectively the same picture twice — dark grey-brown versus black. Diving Beetle is that ladybug in olive green, Firefly is that ladybug in brown with a lantern glow pasted over the abdomen tip, and Ladybug is the chassis in red with spots, which is the only one where the chassis happens to be correct. This is one pony in five colours.

All thirteen are the SAME drawing with the fill swapped. Shared topline: a shallow dip behind the withers rising into a pronounced shoulder/neck hump, then a flat croup — a pony's back, never a cat's low straight spine. Shared body depth: a deep round barrel with a tucked-up belly and a visible girth seam, the depth of a goat, not a cat's shallow flexible tube. Shared limb form: four straight columnar posts of even thickness with a single faint chevron joint band low down that appears at the same height on every one of the 13; they leave the silhouette at the extreme front corner and extreme rear corner of the barrel, so there is no shoulder blade, no tucked elbow, no angled stifle and no hock — front and rear legs are the same part mirrored. Shared foot: a small dark wedge-shaped block with a lighter top band, reading as a HOOF; there is not one paw, one toe pad, or one claw anywhere in the family. Shared skull: a long tapering wedge muzzle ending in a rounded nose blob, with a single flat round side-facing eye placed far back in prey position — a horse/deer profile, not a cat's short blunt face with forward-set binocular eyes. Shared ear: one small triangle or rolled shell pinned flat and far back on the crown; no cat has ears there. Shared neck carriage: thick, horizontal to slightly lifted, with a throatlatch line at its base — a grazing carriage, the opposite of a cat's head-below-shoulders stalk. Shared tail: a thin uniform tube hooked up and back like a donkey's. The chassis READS AS A SHETLAND PONY OR A GOAT KID, and the eleven non-Lion non-Tiger entries are that pony in eleven coat patterns; Jaguar, Leopard, Ocelot and Clouded Leopard even share one identical paw-print-shaped blotch stamp, so the rosette distinctions the packet asks for do not exist in the art at all.

All eight are the same bird with a recolour. Every one is a single fat egg-shaped ovoid with an unbroken domed topline running bill-to-tail and no waist, neck or breast keel; the head is the same small circle stuck onto the upper-left shoulder of that ovoid with effectively zero neck; the bill is the SAME small straight yellow-orange triangle in all eight, hooked in none of them, which is fatal because the hooked bill IS the identity of this whole family; the same dark C-shaped scapular arc sweeps across the flank of all eight; the same mottled speckle patch fills the back; the same two thin yellow sticks drop out of the bottom-centre of the ovoid (not from a feathered thigh at the rear third where a bird's leg actually leaves the body) ending in the same three splayed twig toes with no curved talon on any of them; and the same soft ellipse shadow sits under all eight. Wings are the only other variable: either a small pointed spur tucked at the rear (Condor, Falcon, Kestrel) or a straight flat plank stuck out sideways with a few finger slots (Eagle, Osprey, Vulture) — never a raptor's broad fingered hand or a falcon's scythe. The chassis reads as a PIGEON, or a plump ground-nesting galliform chick. Hawk is that pigeon with a fanned turkey tail, Vulture is that pigeon with a pink head painted on, Secretary Bird is that pigeon on stilts with a crest, and the three 'flying' entries are that pigeon standing on the ground with planks glued on.

Five of the six are the identical vector path with only the fill hue swapped: the same rounded-bowl outline with a near-flat slightly domed top rim, the same eleven hair-thin dark ribs radiating from a single point at BOTTOM-centre, the same two thread-thin whiskers poking diagonally out of each upper corner, the same pair of grey triangular flaps sitting under the bottom edge, and the same soft ground ellipse. Overlaying Clam, Giant Clam, Mussel, Oyster and Scallop the outlines coincide almost pixel-for-pixel; nothing about shell depth, hinge, valve count, margin texture or foot changes between them. Razor Clam is the SAME primitive squashed to a 4:1 lens and rotated 20 degrees - the ribs and the corner whiskers survive the squash and give it away. What the chassis actually reads as is an UPSIDE-DOWN scallop shell, or more plainly a cream soup bowl / paper fan standing on two little wedge feet: the fan converges downward instead of spreading from a hinge, so there is no hinge line, no valve seam, no gape, no mantle, no siphon and no growth rings anywhere in the family. Every species-defining structure in this family lives in the shell margin and the valve pair, and the chassis has neither, so the only thing distinguishing an oyster from a giant clam here is that one is bone and one is teal.

These are one chassis with the eccentricity dial turned and one accessory bolted on. Both are a single closed convex hull drawn as a smooth symmetric lens/ellipse with a light rim-stroke, filled with the identical warm tan-to-umber gradient and the identical fine crosshatch scale mesh — the mesh even runs at the same angle in both. Both toplines are a featureless unbroken arc from nose to tail with no skull break, no nape, no gill cover, no lateral line and no head/body boundary of any kind; the head is simply whichever end of the ellipse the eye sits on. Both eyes are the same tiny white ring with a black pupil, parked at the extreme right tip of the hull at the same height. Both tails are the same small dark paddle butted flat onto the left end of the ellipse with no caudal peduncle, no fin rays and no fork. Neither fish has a single pectoral fin — the defining limb of this entire family, the thing that props a bottom-dweller on the substrate, is absent from both silhouettes. Both float above the same soft grey ellipse drop-shadow, which is the only thing implying a bottom. The chassis reads as a generic aquarium pan-fish / tilapia in profile: a scaled almond with a dot eye and a stub tail. The only per-species work is that Monkfish's hull is inflated to a fat egg and given a bulb lure plus a row of teeth, while Sculpin's hull is stretched to a slim leaf and given a sawtooth dorsal comb. Neither of the two identities in this family — Lophius's enormous flattened pancake head, or the sculpin's huge fanned pectorals — has been drawn at all.

Yes — one chassis, and in two of the three cases literally one drawing. All three are built from the same three primitives: (a) a dead-straight vertical olive stalk of constant width running from the soil to the crown with no taper, no rib, no bend; (b) an identical crown primitive — a shallow crescent 'lid' with a fan of hairline rays tucked under it, recoloured yellow on Fennel, white on Garlic and pale lilac-white on Onion, but the same silhouette pixel-for-pixel; (c) the same flat black elliptical ground shadow, which every plant meets at a pinched point. Garlic and Onion go further and share the entire foliage generator: the same strap-blade rosette, the same arch curve with the outer blades flopping over near horizontal, the same pale midrib highlight down each blade, the same narrow V where the blades converge. Onion is Garlic with the fan opened a few degrees wider and the grey pushed toward green — swap the hues and no stranger could tell them apart. Fennel alone swaps the foliage generator (a rigid pinnate herringbone of discrete opaque leaflets) but keeps the stalk, the crown disc and the shadow. What the shared chassis READS as is a lollipop: a stick with a tiny parasol or mushroom cap on top, planted in a grass clump. Critically, nothing in this family has a bulb — the defining organ of two of the three species is simply not drawn; the stems vanish into the shadow at a point.

This family has exactly one member, so no colour-swap-across-siblings comparison is possible — but the single asset is visibly built on the generic quadruped chassis this project reuses everywhere rather than on a camel-specific one. The parts are all the stock kit: a single fat egg-shaped barrel with a smooth domed topline, a long tapering tube neck rising from the front of that barrel, a featureless blob skull carrying one oversized round cartoon eye and a flat brown ear smear, two straight cylindrical legs (the far-side pair is not drawn at all) that leave the silhouette from the very bottom edge of the barrel with no shoulder or haunch mass, and small dark cloven hoof stubs at the ground. What the chassis READS as is a generic sandy long-necked ungulate — a llama or a young giraffe-toy — with a woolly texture patch airbrushed over the whole back. The camel-specific reads are supplied by paint, not by structure: the 'hump' is the barrel itself plus a lighter fur oval, not a mass that separates from a lean torso, and the padded splayed feet and knobbly knee pads that are the other half of camel identity are simply not modelled.

Yes - all four are one chassis with paint swapped. Every head is the identical rounded-dome cranium with ONE huge forward-facing cartoon eye ringed in white, a grey teardrop lying FLAT INSIDE the skull outline where an ear should be (no ear breaks the silhouette on any of the four), a long tapering muzzle ending in a blunt rounded nose, one long horizontal grey mouth line and a small hooked nostril. Every neck is the same smooth tube leaving the chest at the same forward point and rising in one simple forward arc - no S-curve anywhere, no crest, no dewlap. Every torso is the same deep round barrel whose belly hangs to roughly two-thirds of standing height, so every animal is short-legged: the four legs are the same straight tubes with the same faint rear-hock kink, they leave the silhouette at the same fore and aft points tucked well inside the barrel, and they end in the same tiny dark stippled hoof cap. Topline is the same broad dome on all four. The Alpaca and the Llama are literally the same picture - same outline, same head, same hip flap, same feet - separated only by extra spiky hair strokes on the alpaca's neck and belly. The Camel and Bactrian are the same picture in tan, separated only by a shallow crease pressed into the top of the back dome, plus a bolt-on tasselled tail and a flat un-shaded tan hip plate. What the chassis actually READS as is a generic woolly barrel-bodied sheep on a giraffe neck with an ornithopod head - not a camelid skeleton at all.

All four are the same drawing with the hue swapped and nothing else. Shared topline: a level back that rises to a small withers bump behind the shoulder, then a THICK short neck that runs forward almost horizontally — a grazing carriage, not a canid's alert one. Shared body depth: a deep rounded barrel that is deepest at mid-belly with zero abdominal tuck; a canid's flank tuck is absent in every one. Shared limb form: four straight tapering posts with no shoulder blade, no elbow, no stifle and — critically — no hock on the hind leg, so front and rear legs are the same post mirrored; every limb leaves the silhouette at the very bottom edge of the barrel rather than from a shoulder or hip mass, giving the wide four-corner stance of a pony. Shared foot: a dark rounded cap with a faint vertical split — under 4x magnification these are HOOVES, not digitigrade paws; there is no toe pad, no visible toes, no pastern. Shared skull: an identical rounded braincase with a long tapered wedge snout ending in a dark round nose blob, a single large round googly eye set high and forward, and on top a dark triangular 'tent' with a pale centre ridge that reads as one folded hood or crest rather than a pair of erect ears set at the sides of the skull. Shared tail: the same low-set brush leaving the rump at the same low angle and hooking down-and-forward, identical curve in all four. The chassis reads as a shaggy Shetland pony or a hoofed foal with an anteater-ish snout — in sandy, cream, white and orange. Nothing in the silhouette distinguishes a dingo from a red fox; only the fill colour and a white tail-tip blob change.

Yes — all three are the same drawing. The topline is one symmetric lens/almond arc with a pointed snout wedge at the front and an equally pointed peduncle at the back; Carp and Goldfish are the SAME outline at the same depth, differing only in fill hue (olive-gold vs saturated orange) and a marginally wider tail wedge, and Minnow is that identical outline horizontally stretched and desaturated. Every appendage is shared and placed identically: one small triangular pectoral flag pasted low on the mid-flank, a vestigial dorsal NUB (a 6-8px bump, not a fin) at the same point on the back, a matching ventral nub below it, a single flat swept tail wedge with a few stray hair-strokes, and the same drop-shadow ellipse under the belly. The head is not modelled at all — no mouth, no jaw line, no lips, only a faint operculum smear and one white-ringed dot eye set high and far forward, in the same relative position on all three. The scale treatment is one hatched diagonal grid stamped over the whole flank in every case. What the chassis READS as is a generic clip-art aquarium fish — a coloured lens with a token fin — whose species is signalled to the viewer ONLY by fill colour and by how far the lens has been stretched. Nothing that separates a carp from a goldfish from a minnow in real life (barbels, dorsal-fin length, tail architecture, lateral stripe, body-depth profile) is drawn.

The batch holds a single member, so no within-family cloning can be measured — but the one asset is visibly built on the project's generic quadruped chassis rather than anything felid, and it is the SAME chassis the canid batch is drawn on. Named parts: a dead-level topline running flat from withers to croup with no shoulder-blade rise and no loin dip; a deep barrel body roughly as tall as it is long through the ribs; four straight column limbs of near-equal length with no hock angle, no stifle, no elbow, and no crouch; the limbs leave the silhouette vertically off the bottom edge of the barrel (front pair at the very front corner, rear pair at the very back corner) instead of tucking under the body the way a cat's do; the feet are dark blocky hoof-shaped blocks, not toed paws with a heel pad; the skull is a long tapering wedge that droops downward at the tip; the neck is a thick short ungulate column carried level with the spine, not the low forward-slung felid neck; the tail is a stubby blunt club carried low. What the chassis actually READS as is a pony or okapi — a small striped ungulate. Nothing about the build is cat; only the paint job attempts it, and the paint is zebra-vertical rather than tabby.

All fourteen are the same drawing with two thickness settings. Every one has the identical topline: a smooth convex arc that rises out of the neck, crests just behind the shoulder and falls in one unbroken curve to the rump — no species here has a hump, a withers ridge, or a sloping croup, so Bison, Gaur, Eland and Hartebeest carry the exact same back as Cow. The body is a single sagging barrel whose belly line bows below the elbow in all fourteen; only its depth varies (deep for Banteng/Bison/Buffalo/Bull/Cow/Gaur/Musk Ox, shallow for Antelope/Gazelle/Impala/Eland/Hartebeest/Kudu/Oryx), and the two depths are the same outline scaled, not two builds. The limb is one part reused: a straight tapering tube leaving the silhouette at the very bottom edge of the barrel — the foreleg emerges from a dark hard-edged shoulder patch that is present, identically shaped, on every heavy member — with a small faceted polygon standing in for the knee/hock and a blunt two-toe hoof with a dark tip. There is no hock angle, no cannon, no pastern anywhere in the batch; the hindleg is the foreleg mirrored, so nothing has a driving rear. The skull is one wedge on all fourteen: a rounded cranium, a straight bridge, a bulbous rounded muzzle plate and a short horizontal slit mouth, with a single large forward-facing eye ringed in white — Bison and Musk Ox, both specified 'small' eyes, wear the same cartoon eye as Cow. The neck is short, thick and level in every asset; nothing carries its head low (Bison, Musk Ox) or high on a long neck (Gazelle, Kudu). The tail is one asset too: set high, arcing out and down clear of the rump, ending in a splayed brush of straight tines — the same brush hangs off Cow, Bison, Buffalo, Bull, Gaur, Musk Ox, Hartebeest, Kudu and Oryx, and it is far too long and too separated from the body on all of them. What the chassis actually READS as is a shaggy, barrel-bodied pony-goat: a stocky farm animal standing square with a level neck, a fleecy hatched coat and a horse's brush tail. The ONLY things that change across the family are hue, a marking decal, and a horn pair pasted onto the same skull — and even the horns come from a tiny set (a plain upcurving crescent on Banteng/Buffalo/Bull/Gaur, a lyre pair on Antelope/Gazelle/Impala/Eland/Hartebeest). Antelope, Gazelle and Impala are the same file at three temperatures of tan, and Buffalo, Bull and Gaur are the same file at three shades of brown.

All four are the same drawing with a hue swap and a texture pass. The body is one deep barrel loaf with a flat level topline, a blunt square chest and a rounded rump, and it sits at the same height in the frame in every render. The limbs are four straight tapering pegs that leave the silhouette at the extreme bottom corners of that loaf with no shoulder, haunch, stifle or hock articulation anywhere; each ends in the identical tiny dark two-dot hoof. The neck is the same short thick wedge rising forward at about thirty degrees off the front-top corner, and the head is carried at or above back level in all four -- including the water buffalo and the yak, whose reference rows both demand a low-carried head. Three of the four (Water Buffalo, Wildebeest, Yak) wear the exact same horn element: a single pale curved tusk laid across the top of the skull, so a buffalo's swept-back crescents, a wildebeest's sideways hooks and a yak's upsweep are all one asset. Those same three also share an identical rump ornament -- a pale ovoid disc plus a splayed hair fan projecting horizontally backwards, pasted onto the rump rather than growing out of it. Only the Saiga escapes the shared horn and tail, and it is still the same barrel and the same pegs. The chassis reads as a stocky woolly sheep-goat loaf on stilts; the colour and stroke-length pass is doing all the species work, and it cannot carry it.

Four of the seven — Octopus, Giant Octopus, Squid and Giant Squid — are the same drawing in four hues. Shared parts: an identical front-facing balloon mantle filling the top ~40% of frame (a circle for the octopodes, the same circle stretched ~1.4 tall for the squids); the same two tiny black dot eyes with the same upper-left specular catchlight, set at the same height INSIDE the bulb on all four; the same pair of dark elliptical 'ear' lobes sliding out from behind the bulb at the same angle on both sides; the same limb set leaving the silhouette from one point directly beneath the eyes — two outer arms sweeping wide to the frame edge, two inner arms hanging straight down, one short crossing curl — all rendered as smooth hairline strokes with zero taper, zero suckers and zero mass; the squids add the identical knob-tipped long pair; and the same soft drop-shadow ellipse under all four. Nothing but colour and one vertical scale factor distinguishes an Octopus card from a Giant Squid card. What the chassis READS as is not a cephalopod at all: it is a balloon-headed, thread-legged puppet — a cartoon jellyfish or a daddy-longlegs — because it has no muscular arm, no sucker row, no funnel, and no mantle/head separation (the eyes are set into the bulb, which turns the mantle into a face, the exact error two of the packet notes warn against). Cuttlefish is a lighter variant of the same idea: front-on bulb, dot-fan of stub arms, plus a flat fin backdrop and the one genuinely observed feature in the batch, the W pupil. Only Vampire Squid and Nautilus are off this chassis, and Nautilus escapes it by having no animal on it at all.

These two are the same drawing in two colours. Both share an identical topline — a single smooth convex arc rising from a POINTED snout tip, cresting at about 30% of the length, then falling in one unbroken curve to a thin peduncle; identical body depth profile (deepest at ~35%, no shoulder mass, no caudal keel); identical single dark low-slung ellipse standing in for the pectoral, dropped below the belly line at the same station on both so it hangs off the silhouette as a floating blob rather than emerging from a shoulder; identical tail — a symmetric, VERTICALLY forked caudal fin with equal lobes above and below the body axis and a concave notch between them, which is a fish's caudal fin, not a cetacean fluke; identical pale hairline rim-light stroke running along the topline and overshooting past the snout into empty black; and identical small pale ellipse 'blowhole' floating detached ABOVE the topline instead of set into the head. Neither has a melon, a mandible line that separates from the rostrum, or a paddle-shaped flipper. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a generic torpedo-bodied FISH — a salmon or small tuna in side view — and the only real differences between the two assets are hue (salmon pink vs slate grey), head bluntness (the Whale's head is a bit deeper), an arched mouth line on the Whale, and a small dorsal blob on the Dolphin. Nothing in either silhouette says mammal.

Yes — all three are one almond/lens body with a hue swap. The topline is the same single symmetric convex arc running nose-to-peduncle with identical curvature in each; the ventral line is its mirror, so the fish is a pointed oval with no belly/back distinction. Body depth is the same ~1.5:1 deep lens in all three, including Tetra, whose packet aspect of 2.5 is simply ignored. There is no skull: the head is not separated from the trunk by any gill cover, opercular arc, cheek plane or jaw line — the 'snout' is just the point where the two body arcs meet, so no fish here has a forehead, a mouth line, or a lower jaw. The eye is the identical white ring with black pupil placed at the same relative spot in each. The caudal fin is one reused dark wedge with a concave trailing edge, hung off the same pinched peduncle at the same angle; the dorsal is the same faint low ridge (effectively invisible on Pacu and Tetra) and the pectoral the same short arc stroke leaving the silhouette at the same point. Even the drop-shadow ellipse under the body is the same shape and offset. The chassis reads as a generic silver bream/moonfish — or honestly as a leaf with a tail — and the only per-species work anywhere in the batch is Piranha's row of white triangles pasted onto the lower margin.

The family has exactly one member, so there is no repeated-chassis defect to catch here — but the single asset already exposes what the underlying fish chassis is: a perfectly symmetric pointed lens (almond) hull, identical taper at head and tail, with no head-end swelling, no caudal peduncle and no belly asymmetry, wrapped in a beaded scale texture. Every fin is a flat opaque grey cut-out laid over or beside that hull rather than a membrane growing out of it: a sawtooth 'crown' plate floating over the mid-back, a rounded fan tail stranded in open water off the rear point with a visible gap and a stray line running through and past it, and a chevron pectoral that reads as a stray arrow. If this hull is reused for other perciforms it will read as the same leaf in different colours, because the silhouette carries no species information at all — the only thing distinguishing it is the bolt-on grey plates.

All three are the same animal with the paint changed. They share one skull: a wedge cranium with a single rounded brown ear-blob set high on the back of the head, one small round eye with a pale blue-grey iris, an identical long tapered snout with a small black button nose at the very tip, and the same little upturned smile line beneath it - the Civet only differs by a black mask disc painted over that same skull. They share one neck carriage: short, thick, head carried level and thrust forward off a high shoulder. They share one topline: a straight, faintly arched back from tall withers to a high croup with no lumbar dip. They share one body: a deep slab-sided barrel with a flat belly line, drawn as a single rounded mass with no waist, no chest/hip articulation and no low-slung carnivore taper. They share one limb: a long straight columnar leg that leaves the silhouette high on the shoulder and hip, carries a visible upper-limb 'sleeve' segment, kinks slightly at the hock and terminates in a dark cloven-looking HOOF scored with two or three toe lines - not a paw with digits or claws. The Meerkat is provably the same chassis stood on end: same skull, same ear-blob, same hoofed foot, with the forelimbs and the second hind leg simply deleted so the torso is a featureless armless sack. What the chassis actually READS as is small hoofstock - a goat/deer/pony. The Civet is that pony in appaloosa spots with a ringed tail bolted on; the Mongoose is that pony in a shaggy white fleece with a squirrel plume bolted on; the Meerkat is that pony amputated and balanced upright. Nothing in the batch has the viverrid/herpestid body the family is defined by: a long, low, tubular, short-legged carnivore standing on paws.

Yes — these are one fish drawn at three depths. All three share the identical almond/leaf outline built from two mirrored arcs that meet at a single sharp point at the nose and taper to the same narrow caudal peduncle; the same topline (a smooth convex back with one soft dark wash over the shoulder and no distinct nape, forehead or occiput); the same caudal fin, a wedge with an identical shallow V notch at an identical splay angle, pasted at the same peduncle height in all three; the same flank treatment, a diamond scale mesh with a superimposed dot grid at identical density and identical scale regardless of species (so the Tarpon's silver-dollar plates and the Bonefish's plain mirror flank are literally the same texture); the same single flat dark triangle for a pectoral fin at the same mid-flank position; the same tiny white-ringed circular eye set high and jammed against the snout tip; and the same drop-shadow ellipse placed identically under each body. Nothing that distinguishes real fish is present on any of them: no operculum or gill line, no lateral line, no jaw articulation, no pelvic or anal fins, no caudal peduncle keel. What the chassis actually READS as is a generic supermarket sea bass silhouette, and each species is produced by squashing that silhouette to a different aspect ratio and, in two cases, gluing one prop onto the face — a wire spike on the Bonefish, a floating grey bubble on the Mullet.

This batch has only one member, so cross-member comparison is impossible — but the single asset is plainly not built on a sea-grape body at all; it is drawn on the generic stock 'flowering shrub' chassis this project reuses across herbs and small flowering plants. That chassis reads as: a tight bundle of five or six straight brown twigs fanning out from a single narrow basal trunk in a vase/broom outline, each twig carrying many small identical lance-shaped leaflets in near-opposite pairs held at a uniform 45-degree upward angle, every twig terminating in a mauve-pink pompom flower head, with a flat elliptical drop-shadow puddle beneath. Nothing in that growth form is coastal, leathery, or woody-spreading; swap the flower colour and it would serve equally as lavender, oregano, heather or a generic pink wildflower. The one specific thing the reference demands — dinner-plate round leaves with red veins and hanging strings of grape-like fruit — is absent from the chassis entirely, and no amount of recolouring would produce it.

This family has exactly one member, so there are no siblings to compare and no shared-chassis reuse can be detected by comparison — but the single asset is still visibly built from the engine's generic inflated-invertebrate primitive rather than from a roach silhouette. The parts are: a large smooth sphere at the front carrying a single bead eye (reads as a HEAD, exposed), two thick barrel segments behind it separated by pale outlined hoop seams, a tapering rear lobe, thin unarticulated straight-stick legs (three splayed in a parallel rake at the front, two at the back) that leave the silhouette from the underside midline with no coxa, no femur/tibia bend and no spines, plus a fan of pale radiating filaments off the rear. That chassis READS as a plump segmented grub or a bumblebee/shrimp abdomen with antennae — a soft, round, three-dimensional balloon body. A cockroach is the opposite shape: a single low, FLAT, glossy oval of overlapping tegmina covering the whole dorsum edge-to-edge, with a shield-shaped pronotum plate laid over the front and the head tucked underneath and invisible from above. None of the roach-defining flatness, tegmina seam or pronotal shield exists on this chassis; only the antennae survive, and they are short, straight, rigid and swept FORWARD rather than long, threadlike and backswept.

These three are one body with a hue swap and a tail swap. Every one is the same symmetric pointed oval: a single convex topline arc running from a needle-point snout to a needle-point tail, mirrored exactly along the belly, so the silhouette is a leaf/almond with no caudal peduncle at all - the flank tapers to a knife tip and the tail fin is bolted onto that tip. Body depth is identical in all three (roughly 2.6:1 as rendered) even though the packet asks for 3.9, 3.5 and 4.2, so the aspect field is not reaching the art. The fin kit is the same stamp three times: two low rounded ellipse lobes on the back drawn BEHIND the body so they are half occluded and read as shadows rather than fins, one matching ellipse under the belly, and one small triangular pectoral fan at mid-flank in the same place at the same size. The head is the same skull three times - no mouth line, no jaw, no lips, no barbel, just the same dark curved gill arc and the same white-ringed eye punched half outside the topline at the snout, straddling the outline instead of sitting inside the head. Surface is the same scale stipple plus the same straight pale lateral-line stroke. Only two things vary: colour (gold, grey, olive) and the caudal fin (Cod a squat rounded paddle, Haddock and Pollock forked). What the chassis actually READS as is a generic pointed-oval bait fish - a minnow or a small perch, the shape you would draw for a 'fish' icon. Not one of the four gadid signatures (three separate dorsals, two anals, a chin barbel, a chunky truncate tail on a real peduncle) is drawn on any of the three.

All four are the same drawing with the hue swapped. Every one is the identical flat spiral doughnut: the body enters at lower-left, makes one full loop clockwise, the tail tip crosses over the top-left of the coil as a small hooked stub, and the head emerges at the right at the same upward angle in every image. The head is the same smooth rounded lozenge in all four - no arrow wedge, no distinct neck break, no jaw mass - carrying the same single oversized white eye with a black vertical slit in the same spot, and the same red forked tongue at the same length and the same fork angle. The ventral scale banding is the same combed hatch stroked across the whole tube at the same pitch, the body tube is the same near-constant diameter with no taper toward the tail, and the same soft elliptical drop shadow sits at the same offset below each coil on the same canvas position and scale. Sand Boa is specified as crawling at aspect 3.5 and is still drawn on the coiled doughnut with nothing changed but a slightly fatter tube. What the chassis reads as is a generic cartoon coiled-snake pictogram - a rope doughnut with a lollipop eye and a party-blower tongue - so the four differ only as olive, brown, khaki and gold versions of one icon rather than as an anaconda, a boa, a python and a sand boa.

These are one bird drawn five times with a hue swap. Every asset shares the identical chassis: a fat egg/teardrop body whose topline is a single unbroken convex arc from bill-tip to tail with no shoulder, no wing-butt and no rump break; body depth is roughly two-thirds of body length in all five, so the bird is as deep as it is long. There is no neck carriage at all — a small round ball head is fused directly onto the front of the egg at the same 10-o'clock spot in all five, tilted the same few degrees down. Every skull carries the same short triangular cone bill leaving the head at the same angle, and in four of five it is the SAME YELLOW-OCHRE, which is fatal for a family whose every real member has a black bill (only Chough's is recoloured orange, and even that is the same straight cone, not a decurved one). The wing is not a wing: it is one identical comma-shaped swirl overlay stamped on the flank at the same scale and rotation in all five, so nothing has a folded primary, a wing tip, or a visible feather tract. The tail is the same narrow grey spike exiting the body at mid-right around the vertical centreline (Magpie's is simply that spike stretched into a fat grey banana) — no wedge, no square tip, no graduation, and never the body colour. The limbs are the worst of it: there are no legs. Two flat splayed three-toe yellow footprints float DETACHED in empty space below and forward of the belly in every single asset, at the same offset, connected to nothing — the limb never leaves the silhouette because the limb does not exist. What this chassis actually READS as is a kiwi or a dumpy day-old duckling: a legless bottom-heavy dumpling with a stubby cone bill. Not one of the five reads as a corvid, and stood side by side they are indistinguishable except for fill colour, one crest spike (Jay) and one lengthened tail (Magpie).

Yes — this family is one body in two postures, and even across those two postures most of the parts are literally the same. Every one of the four uses the identical deep, front-heavy egg for a torso, with the same convex topline that peaks over the shoulder and falls in an unbroken curve to the rump, the same body depth (torso is nearly as tall as it is long in all four), and the same painted wing device: a comma-shaped scallop swirled onto the flank with a lighter speckled ellipse inside it, positioned at the same relative spot on all four. The skull is the same small sphere in every asset, and in every asset it is fused DIRECTLY onto the shoulder — there is no neck anywhere in this family, which is fatal since neck carriage is the whole point of a crane. The bill is one part recoloured four times: the same straight tapering yellow spike, thick at the base, dead-straight to a point, drawn at the same slight downward angle on Coot, Moorhen, Crane and Rail alike; nothing is downcurved, nothing is short. Crane and Rail are the same drawing twice — same torso outline, same wing swirl, same two thin yellow stick legs leaving the silhouette at the same point under the mid-belly with the same forward splay and the same stubby three-nub foot, and the same solid dark triangular tail wedge stabbing horizontally out to the right at rump height. Only the fill hue (grey vs brown) and a white head-tuft on Crane differ. Coot and Moorhen are the other twin pair — the same torso sunk into the same waterline with the same three concentric ripple rings and the same soft ellipse shadow beneath, the same short forward-tilted head, differing only in the head marking (white blaze vs red patch) and body hue (sooty vs olive-grey). What the chassis actually READS as is a plump, neckless, egg-bodied gamebird — closest to a kiwi or a young partridge — with a spike bill glued to it; there is no long-necked, long-legged, long-toed, laterally-slim rail-or-crane anatomy anywhere in the batch.

All four are the same drawing with a snout swap and a hue swap. Every one shares: an identical wedge torso whose topline is a dead-straight line rising from the shoulder to a rear-high hump then falling to a point; an identical flank treated as a panel of evenly spaced vertical pinstripes that reads as corrugated card or a radiator grille rather than as scutes; an identical dark trim band with a white pinstripe laid along the dorsal edge that floats slightly clear of the body outline and juts forward past the shoulder into empty air; an identical short blunt triangular tail cone of roughly a quarter body length that stops abruptly instead of tapering; identical limbs -- exactly two visible tubes, a forelimb planted under the MIDDLE of the torso rather than at the shoulder and a hind tube bent once, both leaving the silhouette from the flat bottom edge of the belly and ending in the same tiny three-toe splay; and an identical head-to-torso junction that is a hard vertical butt seam with no neck at all, the skull plate simply abutting the ribbed flank block, with the jaw plate hanging below the belly line. Alligator and Caiman are indistinguishable: same rounded-rectangle head slab, same single nostril dot placed high on the cheek behind the snout tip, same upcurved smiley mouth line, same vertical-slit eye on a raised bump -- purple versus green is the only difference. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a stubby cartoon salamander or gecko toy: a smiling slab head, a corrugated box body and a nub tail. Only the snout varies across the family (blunt slab, blunt slab, tapered with one tooth, needle with a tooth row), and the snout is doing one hundred percent of the identification work.

This is not ten designs, it is TWO rubber stamps plus one odd-one-out. STAMP A (six of ten: Brine, Cave, Fairy, Freshwater, Tadpole and Vent Shrimp) is pixel-for-pixel the same body with a hue swap: the same egg-shaped cephalothorax oval tilted about 15 degrees to the left, the same three hair-thin antennae fanning to the lower-left at identical angles, the same FOUR featureless straight pin legs dropping vertically out of the underside of that oval with no joints, no taper and no feet, the same fat sausage abdomen built from about six stacked arcs that curls clockwise DOWN AND FORWARD, the same five-blade tail fan pointing down-left underneath the animal, the same little knob at the fan's base, and the same drop-shadow ellipse. The only per-species edits are colour, the scale of the head oval (Tadpole's is inflated, Brine's is detached from the body entirely) and nothing else. What that chassis actually READS as is a plump maggot or grub wearing a balloon head - not a shrimp: there is no laterally compressed carapace, no rostrum, no antennules, no pleopod fringe, no swimmerets, and the tail is tucked forward under the legs instead of trailing behind, so every one of these six is the same crawling grub in six colours. STAMP B (three of ten: Freshwater, Mud and Vent Crab) is equally rigid: the same round barrel-stave carapace (a rounded rectangle painted with vertical stave lines and soft blotches), the same two straight eye-pins with white dot tips rising from the TOP of the shell rather than from a front orbit, the same two flat oval claw paddles held UP at the shoulders like rabbit ears with a dark ring drawn on the outer face, the same dark bar arms that begin in the MIDDLE of the carapace and run outward across the shell, and the same two banded stick legs per side - four walking legs total, not eight. That chassis reads as a wooden barrel or a woven basket standing on spider legs with two ears; no pincer on any of the three is actually split into two fingers. Giant Isopod is the only species with its own body, and even it is painted in the family's shared grammar of a smooth balloon with flat stripes ruled across it rather than real overlapping armour. Across the whole batch the same three painting habits recur: bodies are smooth inflated capsules, segmentation is a set of ruled lines on top of a capsule instead of a stepped silhouette, and every limb is a plain pin or bar with no joint, no claw tip and no foot.

This batch holds a single asset, so there is no sibling to compare against and no shared-chassis defect can be demonstrated within it. What I can say is what the one chassis in front of me reads as, and it is not a cuckoo chassis: a fat, near-circular egg-shaped body with the deepest point at mid-belly, a topline that arcs continuously from bill-tip over a small non-existent neck to the tail root with no shoulder or breast break, stubby thin legs that leave the silhouette at the very bottom of the belly and give perhaps a tenth of the body height in exposed tarsus, small three-toe feet planted directly under the mass, a skull that is merely a small bump grafted onto the front of the body, and a horizontal head carriage. That is the generic plump ground-bird chassis — the kiwi/quail/thrush blank — not the lanky, long-shanked, horizontal-carriage cuckoo body the roadrunner needs. The tail is not part of the chassis at all: it is a separate flat banded plank bolted onto the rear at a droop, reading as a wooden slat rather than feathers. If other cuckoos get built later, this blank must not be the one they inherit.

Yes - all five are the same body with a paint swap and one antler swap.
