Shared: a flat, near-level topline that rises very slightly mid-back and ends in the same squared-off rump with the same tiny wedge tail nub; the same deep rectangular slab torso carrying an identical hard-edged faceted panel seam behind the shoulder and a second panel at the haunch; four straight equal-thickness cylinder legs with no hock, no stifle, no upper/lower segmentation, all four dropping out of the bottom corners of the body box rather than from any shoulder or hip mass - so no animal in this family has a cervid hind limb; the same small dark hoof cap on every foot, never cleft, never splayed; the same blunt rounded muzzle wedge in right profile with one oversized white circular eye and black pupil set high and far forward on the cheek, and ears reduced to a nub or absent in all five; the same short, thick, forward-slanting neck that merges into the chest with no throat line, holding the head at the same height and angle in every image. The only real per-species geometry in the batch is the antler decal, and even that is one shared pale-bone three-tine fork reused verbatim on Deer, Elk, Reindeer and Caribou - Moose alone gets a different shape. What the chassis reads as is a stiff wooden park ornament stag / carousel pony: one carved toy deer body issued in white, spotted tan, gold and grey-brown.

All eight are the same drawing with a hue swap. Shared topline: a cresty, arched, upward-swept neck rising off a pronounced withers hump to a small head carried forward and slightly downward - a horse's neck carriage, not a canid's low level neck. Shared body: a deep rounded barrel with a convex belly, a shoulder 'shawl' shading panel and a disc-shaped haunch, identical in outline on all eight. Shared limbs: four straight tubular columns of uniform thickness with no elbow, no stifle, no hock angle and no forward knee break; they leave the silhouette at the four extreme corners of the barrel like table legs, instead of the forelimb hanging under a deep chest and the hind set back under a sloping croup. Shared foot: a small dark rounded block capping each column, with no toes, no pads and no digitigrade wrist - it reads as a hoof on every single asset. Shared skull: one wedge - rounded cranium, a short blunt muzzle bar projecting horizontally with a nostril dot and one eye - reused verbatim on Wolf, Coyote, Jackal, Fox, Arctic Fox and Maned Wolf, with only the ear flap swapped. Shared tail: a horizontal striped cylinder that attaches at mid-back, well forward of the hip, and terminates in a flat unshaded circular cap that reads as a sawn-off pipe; on Fennec it detaches from the body entirely. What the chassis actually READS as is a Shetland pony or a foal - barrel, cresty neck, straight legs, hooves - with a feather duster stapled to its back. The only proportion that varies at all across the eight is leg length (Maned Wolf longer, Fennec shorter); every other structural part is identical, so the family is one pony in eight colours.

These are unmistakably one drawing with two small edits. Both are the same left-facing insect at the same pitch and the same scale on the same dark-navy vignette with the same soft black ground ellipse. Head: an identical glossy cyan sphere with a specular highlight and two tiny white-ringed dot eyes clustered high and forward — not a hammerhead in one and a globe-eyed helmet in the other, literally the same ball. Thorax: the same slightly larger blue sphere butted against the head at the same angle. Limbs: the same three tiny curled hook legs hanging under the thorax, all pointing forward-down, leaving the silhouette at the same point on the thorax underside in both. Abdomen: the same device in both — a repeating row of tapering teal spheres/segments trailing back and slightly down; in the Dragonfly they are fused into a banded sausage, in the Damselfly the identical beads are simply spaced apart and detached. Wings: the same pale grey feather-plume blade, anchored at the same spot on the thorax top and swept back at the same angle — the Dragonfly gets three copies of it, the Damselfly gets one. Nothing that distinguishes an odonate is doing any distinguishing work here: the chassis reads as a generic cartoon bumblebee or gnat with feathers for wings, and the only actual variation between the two species is wing count and whether the abdomen beads touch.

All three are the identical asset with a hue swap and two or three sprinkled ornaments. The silhouette is one flat lens/leaf spindle: a dead-straight horizontal lozenge, symmetrically double-tapered so the snout end and the tail end are the same shape, with no cylindrical mass, no sinuous curve, and no separately modelled head. Every one carries the same topline (a straight pale rim line with a second lateral-line stripe running the entire length), the same body depth (a constant ~1/9 of length that swells at midpoint and pinches identically at both ends), the same interior fill of short vertical tick marks reading as a segment ladder, the same tiny 2px translucent whisker at the far left standing in for a tail, and the same white-ringed black dot eye pegged at the same relative x near the right rim. The 'limb' in a fish family is the fin, and it too is shared: every animal gets the same translucent leaf-blade lobe leaving the silhouette at roughly 60-75% of body length, above the spine on one and below it on another, plus a matching soft ventral blade. The skull is the same blunt squared-off snout cap on all three; the mouth is the same straight horizontal line, closed, with the only variation being whether a row of tiny white tooth pegs is hung beneath it. What the chassis actually READS as is a flat leaf or a lancetfish blade - a rigid pointed ribbon of plant matter with an eye stuck near one tip - and crucially not an eel at all, since none of the three has the continuous head-to-tail fin fringe or the round-sectioned rope body that defines the group. The three eels are one leaf in olive, sage and navy.

Yes — both monotremes are the same smooth legless loaf with a different appliqué glued to the front. Shared topline: one unbroken convex arc that rises from the rump, peaks just behind mid-back and falls in a single continuous curve into the head, with no neck break, no shoulder, no withers and no head mass distinct from the body. Shared body depth: a flat-bottomed teardrop mound roughly one-third as deep as it is long, filled with a uniform flat brown and a faint speckle texture, sitting on a soft elliptical drop shadow. Shared limb form: none at all — neither animal has a single leg, ankle or foot; the belly line runs straight from nose to tail with only a tiny tan nub under the echidna's front quarter, so there is no place where a limb leaves the silhouette and no foot exists to judge. Shared skull: there is no skull, only the tapering right-hand end of the loaf, marked by one small white dot eye placed identically on both. Shared tail carriage: absent on the echidna, and on the platypus a separate rounded lobe pasted onto the left end rather than grown out of the rump. The only real differences are additive decals — a radial cream-and-black spine fan stuck along the echidna's back, a dark oval disc stuck on the platypus's face, and a rust-vs-grey hue shift. What the chassis actually READS as: a legless potato / guinea-pig-sized blob with a shadow under it, into which one distinguishing prop has been inserted per species.

This batch is a family of one, so there is no shared chassis to compare against and no colour-swap defect is possible here. Judged on its own, the single asset is not built from a generic quadruped blank: the head is a purpose-drawn oversized wedge, the trunk is a bespoke segmented tube, and the tusks are unique geometry, so the underlying body is at least elephant-specific rather than the pony chassis seen in the canid/felid families. Where it does show engine-generic habits is below the shoulder: the four limbs are the same slim tapered cylinder with a single mid-band and a small toe-nail plate, mirrored front and rear, which is the same limb primitive that shows up on other quadrupeds and is exactly wrong for an animal whose legs must read as load-bearing pillars. The topline is a shoulder hump falling to a shallow dip and a rounded rump, which is closer to a tapir than to the saddle-backed African profile the reference asks for. If more proboscideans (mammoth, forest elephant, mastodon) are added later, the thing to check is whether they inherit this same head-lobe-plus-hose-trunk assembly with only tusk curvature and hair changed.

The three elephants are one drawing. Identical deep barrel body with a high convex topline that rises from the rump into a rounded shoulder mound; identical rump curve; four columnar legs leaving the silhouette at the same four points with the same tapered ankle and the same small grey toenail-hoof cap; the same left-rear tail drawn as a thin rope ending in a wide black bristle broom that flares outward and hangs to the ground line; the same featureless rounded skull with one large forward-facing white-scleraed eye at the same coordinate; the same neck carriage, i.e. no neck at all, head fused straight onto the shoulder mass; and the same trunk, drawn in every case as a corrugated, horizontally banded tube that reads as a vacuum-cleaner hose or a bendy straw hooking into a J to the right of the body rather than as muscle. The ear is the same object three times: a dark grey rounded-rectangle slab with vertical ribbing, pasted flat across the neck-and-shoulder junction so it reads as a saddle blanket, a folded wing, or a boot-scraper mat rather than an ear membrane. What actually changes between African, Asian and Forest is the size of that slab, the length of the tusks, and a slight warmth shift in the hide. The chassis reads as one generic zoo-poster elephant with a hose for a trunk and a rug hung on its shoulder. The Hyrax is genuinely a different body -- but it is a lamb, not a hyrax.

This batch holds exactly one asset, so cross-asset chassis reuse cannot be measured here — there is no second body to compare against. What CAN be said about the single chassis is that it is not a purpose-drawn anguilliform: it is the generic fish spindle stretched to aspect 12. The topline and the belly line are mirror images of each other, forming a perfectly symmetrical almond/lens that is deepest at exact midbody and tapers evenly to both ends; the body axis is dead straight with zero undulation or S-curve. The 'limb' vocabulary is a single triangular fan pectoral tucked just behind the gill line plus a second yellow lobe riding the belly under it, both leaving the silhouette at the same station right behind the head. There is no skull mass at all — the head does not widen, deepen or separate from the trunk, it just tapers to a slightly upturned point carrying one oversized white-ring eye set high and forward, with a thin scratched line for the mouth. The tail is not a continuation of the body at all but a small separate dart-shaped spike with three stray dark hair strands trailing off it. Surface is a mechanical grid of evenly spaced dark dots and dashes in ruled rows, which reads as knitted fabric or a corn cob rather than an eel's wet, smooth, unscaled skin. Taken together the chassis reads as a needlefish or garfish blade, not an eel.

These two are the same drawing with a fur setting changed. Identical topline (flat back, a soft withers bump, rump sloping to the tail root), identical shallow oval barrel, identical thick low-set neck that rises at the same angle, and the identical skull: a rounded cranium blob with ONE dark brown triangle for an ear fused into a large triangular cheek facet, one oversized cartoon eyeball with a white sclera ring, a long pale muzzle wedge with a hooked nostril tick, and the same stray pale plank/bar laid across the lower jaw that pokes out past the nose. Limbs are the same four near-cylindrical tubes with no shoulder, no elbow, no stifle and no fetlock; they leave the silhouette from mid-belly rather than from a shoulder or haunch, and each ends in the same small flat dark rectangle cap where a hoof should be (the foot crops are pixel-identical between the two). The rear is the same assembly in both: a flat, opaque, pasted-on ellipse sitting over the hindquarter with a wide fan-brush plume fired out horizontally behind it. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a pale tan toy quadruped of no species -- a plush llama or a long-muzzled donkey doll -- and the only difference between the two assets is that the pony has a long-hair fleece overlay sprayed uniformly over the flanks and belly. Neither the horse's erect brush mane nor the pony's shaggy mane and forelock exists on either animal; both necks are bare-crested, so the one feature that would have separated them is missing from both.

Yes — all six are one fish chassis with three knobs turned: hue, aspect ratio, and which accessory fin is bolted on. The shared body is a symmetrical almond/lens built from two mirrored arcs that meet in a sharp point at the snout and an equally sharp point at the caudal peduncle, so every animal has the same pointed-at-both-ends topline and the same flat belly-line; the dorsal profile is a single unbroken curve with no nape break, no forehead, no occiput. Every one carries the identical full-length white lateral-line stripe running dead through the midline, the identical hexagonal scale-dot stipple, the identical curved gill-cover arc stroke in the same relative place, one identical triangular pectoral fin planted at the same coordinate on the flank, and the identical small white-ring-with-black-pupil eye set on the snout slope — drawn even on Blind Fish and Cave Fish, whose entire identity is having no eye. The skull is not modelled at all: there is no jaw, no lip, no mouth line on any of the six, just the point where the two body arcs cross, so a cod, a cichlid and a cave tetra all have the same face. Crucially, EVERY unpaired fin is painted BEHIND the body fill instead of attached to the outline, so on Arctic Cod and Small Fish the dorsal and anal read as half-occluded ghost lobes bulging out from under the silhouette, and on Cichlid and Reef Fish the tail is a rounded fan floating off the peduncle point with black sky between it and the body. Arctic Cod and Small Fish are literally the same drawing in olive and silver; Cichlid and Reef Fish are literally the same drawing in blue and pink, down to the same five-tooth sawtooth crown hovering over the back and the same detached fan tail. What the chassis reads as is a generic aquarium-clipart 'fish' pictogram — a scaled lens with a stripe, a dot eye and a stuck-on tail — stretched long for the slim species and squashed round for the deep ones.

These two are the same drawing at two aspect ratios. Both are a single closed ellipse with no head, no snout, no gill line, no jaw and no neck or body taper anywhere along the topline; the topline and the ventral line are the same mirrored arc. The fin fringe is identical on both: a hard-edged grey-taupe band of constant width laid around the whole ellipse and ticked with short evenly-spaced radial hatch marks, which reads as pie crust or the stitched rim of a leather coin purse rather than as soft dorsal and anal fin rays. Both carry the same two glossy black circles with the same upper-left specular dot, set at the same relative height and the same small separation, and the same single 3-4 px hooked mouth tick below and left of them. Both terminate in the same tiny trapezoidal tail fan stuck onto the outside of the rim at the extreme right, with the same notch and the same fill. The fill is the same beige-to-brown vertical gradient with the same soft round speckle brush, only denser on the Flounder. Nothing else changes: not the eye form, not the fringe, not the tail, not the mouth. The shared chassis reads as an oval wooden serving platter or a pebble with a cartoon face applied to it, and the two entries are that platter at 1.6 and at 2.1.

Six of the seven (Cassowary, Emu, Kakapo, Ostrich, Penguin, Rhea) are one chassis with a hue swap and at most one appliqué. All six are the identical upright egg — the same vertical ovoid with the same left-leaning tilt, the same topline arc, the same pale rim-lit crescent down the right edge of the egg, and the same body depth from a single silhouette. All six carry the SAME texture map baked into that egg: rows of scalloped chevron scale-marks over the upper half and stippled dots over the lower left, and all six carry the same circular ridged medallion disc parked dead-centre on the belly like a navel or a bottle cap. The wing is the same feature every time — a small mid-grey rounded blob stuck onto the lower-right rear of the egg, never articulated, never a wing; on the Ostrich and Penguin it is still there, unchanged, underneath the added tail fan and shoulder line. The neck is the same thin tapering tube leaving the ovoid at the upper-left shoulder and curving forward, and the skull is the same small circle with one black dot eye and the SAME short yellow-orange triangular beak on every single bird — cassowary, emu, kakapo, ostrich, rhea and penguin all wear that one identical wedge, so the kakapo has no parrot hook, the rhea has no broad blunt bill and the ostrich has no tiny flat head. The legs are the same pair of thin yellow drinking-straw sticks with a forward knuckle and three splayed toes, dropping vertically out of the bottom of the egg, simply scaled shorter for Kakapo and Penguin. What that chassis actually READS as is a plush cartoon quail or a Fabergé egg chick — a squat scaled egg on stick legs — and nothing in it says ratite, parrot or penguin. Only the Kiwi is off-chassis: a genuinely separate horizontal furry ovoid with real hair strokes, no medallion, no wing blob, and a long down-curved bill, which is exactly why it is the one asset in the batch a stranger names correctly.

These two are NOT one chassis - the two silhouettes disagree on every load-bearing part. Topline: the Flying Fish is a straight, gently tapering spindle from nape to peduncle; the Mudskipper is a high-shouldered convex hump that crests just behind the head and falls away to a short tail. Body depth: slim fusiform (roughly 1:5 deep-to-long) versus stocky goby (roughly 1:3), and the Mudskipper carries a flat belly line sitting on the ground while the Flying Fish belly is a symmetric curve. Tail: a deep symmetric fork with two pointed lobes versus a short rounded paddle. Skull/snout: a needle point with the eye ring on the outline versus a blunt dome with two domed turret eyes riding on top. Fin insertion also differs - the Flying Fish planes leave the silhouette high on the flank and sweep back past the tail, the Mudskipper's fan leaves low and hangs below the belly. What IS shared is the drawing kit, not the body: both are pure flat side profiles built as one soft-gradient lozenge with mottled blob spots, both sit on the same elliptical drop-shadow, and both fins are drawn with the identical translucent-membrane-plus-hatched-ray brush (the Flying Fish wings and the Mudskipper pectoral fan and dorsal spines are visibly the same renderer). That is a shared toolset, which is acceptable; the body plans themselves are genuinely distinct.

These two do NOT share a body with each other, and that is itself the problem: only one of them was built as a flying mammal at all. The Bat is a bespoke aerial build - front-on, no ground contact, a small furry fusiform torso with an oversized ear-dominant skull and two membrane panels leaving the shoulders. The Colugo is not on that chassis and is not on any gliding chassis; it is drawn on the project's generic broadside quadruped body - level dead-straight topline from withers to rump, deep barrel torso, four short columnar pillar legs leaving the silhouette vertically at the corners with rounded dark hoof-like feet, short thick neck carrying a small head, a tapering downward-hanging tail, and a hard ground-contact shadow ellipse. That chassis reads as a spotted lamb or calf. So the family shares nothing that makes it a family: there is no common patagium construction, no common wing-arm, no common flight posture. The one part they do share is the eye treatment (a small white-ringed dark bead), and in the Bat that treatment is at least scale-appropriate while in the Colugo it stands in for the huge forward-facing eyes that ARE the animal. Nothing about the Colugo would change if it were relabelled Sheep.

Yes — these are one drawing recoloured four times. All four share an identical featureless ball/ovoid body with NO head-body separation and no neck carriage at all: the topline is a single smooth unbroken dome from snout to rump, and the 'skull' is simply the top third of that same ball with two hemispherical eye domes bolted on at the same coordinates in every asset. Body depth is identical (a circle, aspect ~1.1 in the render regardless of the 1.4-1.6 the packet asks for). The limb model is identical and anatomically wrong in the same way each time: the forelimbs are two thin straight vertical props that drop from the front of the belly, ending in a small splayed hand; the hind limbs leave the silhouette at the MID-FLANK, at the widest point of the ball, and run horizontally outward as a flat leaf-shaped paddle to a hand-like foot with 4-5 separated pointed digits lying flat on the ground — the same limb at the same angle and the same length on every frog. No frog in the batch has the diagnostic anuran hind leg (knee folded up above the topline, ankle high, foot tucked under). The feet are hands, not webbed paddles, and no toe of any frog carries an adhesive disc. Even the closed smiling mouth curve, the teardrop crown highlight and the ground-shadow ellipse are pixel-for-pixel the same. Bullfrog, Glass Frog and Tree Frog differ ONLY in hue (olive / mint / lime) and blotch scatter; Poison Dart Frog is the same chassis squashed and recoloured red, with the face assembly slid off-centre. The shared chassis reads as a plush cartoon Kermit-style frog toy squatting frontally — a mascot sticker, not any real anuran, and unmistakably the same animal four times.

All four are one drawing with the hue swapped and nothing else. The chassis is a single smooth egg-shaped blob that serves as head AND body at once — there is no skull, no neck, no shoulder, no separation between cranium and torso, so the topline is one unbroken dome from foot to foot. Two identical hemispherical goggle eyes are bolted to the upper-front of that dome at exactly the same coordinates in all four, each with the same white sclera ring, same dark iris, same highlight dot at the same clock position. One identical curved smile arc crosses the lower dome at the same height in all four. The forelimbs are two short straight pale posts dropping vertically out of the blob's lower front, each ending in the same tiny splayed hand — same length, same spacing, same angle in every asset. The hind limbs are the giveaway: in all four a flat wedge leaves the flank at dead 3 and 9 o'clock, runs horizontally outward and slightly down, and terminates in the same flat splayed webbed foot aimed laterally. There is no raised knee above the back, no folded haunch, no thigh mass — the standard folded-jumping-leg read that defines the entire family is absent from every single one. Same elliptical ground shadow, same soft blurred dorsal blotches (identical blur radius and density) in all four; the Toad is drawn a few percent smaller and that is the whole of its differentiation. What the chassis actually READS as is a cartoon smiley-frog emoji or a rubber bath toy — a green one, a white one, a brown one and an orange one. The two assets whose identity lives entirely in markings and skin texture (Toad, Wood Frog) therefore have no identity at all.

The two growth forms do genuinely differ and that part is fine: the chili is an upright multi-stem shrub whose stems all radiate from a single basal clump, while the cucumber is a zigzag climbing vine with alternating nodes and real coiled tendrils, and the leaf primitives differ too (thin sliver lancets on the chili, broad star-lobed palmate blades on the cucumber). What IS shared is the one organ this family is named for. Both harvests are the identical rendered primitive: a perfect glossy sphere with the same top-left specular hotspot, the same soft terminator falling to the lower right, and the same dark rim, changed only by hue (red vs green) and, on the cucumber, a few added stripes. Nothing about either sphere is fruit-specific — no tapering, no calyx, no ridging, no warting. Both also share the same tapered stem tube with an identical vertical gradient, the same tiny dark nub where the fruit meets the stem, and the same soft ground-shadow ellipse. The result reads as one berry-ball prop dropped onto two different plants, and because the pod shape and the cucumber's elongation are the entire identity of these two species, the shared sphere fails both of them at once.

All ten are the same drawing with the hue swapped. The body is one near-circular ovoid, deepest at mid-belly, with a flat level topline that runs unbroken from nape to rump on every card; there is no neck at all — the small round skull is simply pushed onto the upper-left shoulder of that ovoid, carrying the same short straight conical bill and the same black eye with the catchlight in the same position on all ten. The wing is the identical dark comma/spiral stroke laid on the flank with the same interior taper streak, in the same place, at the same size, on all ten. The legs are the same pair of thin yellow bare rods leaving the silhouette at the same low-centre point, at the same splay, ending in the same three-forward-toe foot; nothing is feathered, thickened, or scaled differently anywhere in the family. The same drop-shadow ellipse sits under all ten. The ONLY things that vary are (a) hue, (b) an optional 3-spike tuft on the crown (chicken, quail, peacock, rooster), (c) a dot pattern (guineafowl), and (d) the tail, which is one of exactly three interchangeable parts: a drooping 5-6 lobe fan (chicken, grouse, turkey, peacock), a short pointed wedge (partridge, quail, guineafowl, ptarmigan), or two straight flat planks (pheasant, rooster). What the shared chassis actually READS as is a fat stylised baby chick — a quail, at best. It cannot carry a rooster, a turkey, a peacock or a pheasant, and the requested aspects (2.4 pheasant, 2.2 peacock, 1.0 upright rooster) are all ignored because the ovoid never changes proportion. Grouse and Turkey are, apart from a slight tone shift, the same picture.

This family is not eleven organisms, it is THREE rubber stamps recoloured. STAMP 1 - the flat planispiral disc shell on a lens foot - carries SIX of the eleven: Conch, Freshwater Snail, Land Snail, Sea Snail, Snail and Water Snail are pixel-for-pixel the same drawing at the same scale and the same rotation, with the same ridged coil wound the same direction to the same central knob, the same faint outer whorl outline crossing the upper right, the same flat lens-shaped foot whose front tip and rear tip both project the same amount past the shell, the same identical three-prong tentacle fork poking out at the right at the same angle, and the same elliptical drop shadow - only the hue changes (grey-green, tan, walnut, brass, old gold). Conch is that same stamp with the foot deleted and a stray brown nub dropped at the lower right. STAMP 2 - a domed ellipse with a row of exactly five black holes across its upper third and a soft mottled fill - carries THREE: Abalone, Cowrie and Limpet are the same egg at the same tilt with the same five holes in the same places, differing only in colour (mint, apricot, tan); the row of holes is the ABALONE's diagnostic feature and it has been left on the cowrie and the limpet, where it is anatomically wrong. STAMP 3 - a low flat-bottomed loaf with a tiny jagged crest at the right end standing in for a head - carries Banana Slug and Nudibranch; the nudibranch is that loaf with a comb of cerata added on top. Across all three stamps there is NO head, NO eye, NO eyestalk and NO neck anywhere in the family: the same 3-to-5 pixel fork or crest is the entire head token on eight assets. The shells never form a helical spire - every coil is a flat ammonite disc, so the shelled half of the family reads as fossil ammonites on a slipper sole rather than as snails, and the unshelled third reads as a yellow loaf and a pink loaf.

This trio is NOT one body in three colours - the silhouettes genuinely differ: Pyrosome is a single tall vertical cone, Salp is a diagonal chain of four small lemon-shaped barrels, Sea Squirt is a pair of upright sacs seated on a substrate mound. Composition (one / four / two), attachment (free-floating / free-floating / cemented) and surface treatment (scattered stipple dots / hard hoop bands / rectangular grid) are all separately authored. What IS recycled, and recycled very visibly, is a single aperture primitive: every opening in all three assets is the same ellipse with a bright thin lip ring, a lighter inner wall crescent and a dark throat - the Sea Squirt's two siphons are literally miniature copies of the Pyrosome's mouth, and the same ellipse caps both ends of every Salp barrel. The shared body wall shading is also one recipe: a soft vertical gradient, dark at the silhouette edges, with one broad specular band up the near face and a soft rounded shoulder into the mouth. Because all three are tunicates a shared barrel-with-openings plan is biologically correct, so the chassis reads as a legitimate 'gelatinous tube with a bright-lipped opening' rather than as a pony in fancy dress - but the aperture is currently identical down to the highlight, and that is the one element to differentiate (a pyrosome mouth is a wide soft slack rim, a salp's is a stiff thin hoop, a siphon is a short muscular nozzle).

These two are the same body with the neck telescoped and the paint swapped. Shared parts, part by part: the same barrel — a deep oval with a shallow belly tuck and a rounded, un-angular rump; the same topline, a low arch that crests mid-back and settles to a soft croup rather than ramping from a withers; the same limb model — four straight columns with no hock angulation on the hind pair (the rear legs are identical posts to the fronts), each leaving the silhouette at the same points, chest-front and croup-rear, with the near leg opaque and the far leg a thin grey-tinted sliver directly behind it, ending in the same tiny dark cloven hoof tip; the same tail — a thick tapering cream/brown tube that leaves the UPPER FLANK (not the top of the rump), arcs backward and down and terminates in the same straw-coloured splayed tuft at the same angle in both; the same skull — a wedge with a long blocky muzzle, one dot nostril, a dark folded ear on the cheek and two knobbed skin-covered ossicone stalks on the crown; the same big round highlight eye set high and forward; the same neck carriage, rising forward off the same withers point at the same angle. What the chassis actually READS as is a llama or a stock toy pony: no giraffid brisket, no giraffid stilt-leg proportion in the okapi, no hock. For THIS family that is only half a crime — giraffe and okapi really are one giraffid body plan — but the chassis is not a giraffid one, it is a generic camelid, and the okapi is the giraffe body shortened with markings dropped on in the wrong places. Both are also finished the same wrong way: the coat pattern is applied as a saddle blanket over the barrel with a hard vertical cut at the rump, leaving the entire hindquarter as a flat unpainted slab on both animals.

Yes — these are one insect chassis in three hues. All three share the identical two-lobe body: a rounded thorax oval overlapped from behind by a slightly larger abdomen oval, same humped topline, same body depth, same blunt untapered rear. All three carry the same small ball head socketed at the same forward-down angle with one large round white-highlit eye in the same spot, and the same pair of hairline thread antennae swept up-forward at the same angle and the same (short) length. All three sprout the same rear-mounted fan of long lanceolate radiating-veined wings from the same point at the top-rear of the thorax, overhanging the abdomen the same way. The limbs are the giveaway: in every one they are uniform hairline sticks of constant thickness, leaving the silhouette at the same three points along the flat underside, tapering to a bare point with no tarsus or foot, and NOT ONE of them has a thickened femur. All three sit on the same soft ellipse drop shadow. Only hue (dark brown / olive / gold) and wing size and spread vary. What the chassis reads as is a generic winged midge or mayfly — a soft-bodied thread-legged flier. That is the exact opposite of an orthopteran, whose whole identity is the cranked, hugely swollen hind femur; the family has been built without the one part that defines the family.

All three are the same drawing with a hue swap and one tail edit. The body is an identical pointed lens/almond that is mirror-symmetric fore-and-aft: it tapers to a needle point at the snout AND to a needle point at the tail root, so there is no forehead, no blunt head, no caudal peduncle and no head-to-tail asymmetry of any kind. The topline is one smooth unbroken arc from nose tip to tail root on every fish. Every fish carries the same detached sawtooth dorsal slab -- a dark rectangle with 4-5 identical triangular teeth on top -- floating above and behind the topline with visible background between its base and the back, spanning only the rear half; it reads as a pasted-on crown or comb, not a fin growing out of the back. Every fish has the same tiny triangular pectoral fan at the same body coordinate, the same rounded dark blob for an anal fin under the belly, the same single dead-centre lateral hairline, and the same scale-dot hatch. The head is identical on all three under 4x zoom: no mouth aperture at all, just a short faint stroke that never reaches the snout tip and a curved gill arc -- no jaw line, no lower jaw, no teeth, on any of them. The eye is the same white-ringed circle and on Grouper and Sea Bass it sits ON the upper contour with its top half over the background. Only three things vary: hue (brown / grey / red), tail (Grouper a rounded fan, Sea Bass and Snapper an identical deeply forked swallowtail), and Snapper being drawn slightly deeper. What the chassis actually READS as is a generic cartoon bream/sunfish decal -- a leaf-shaped lozenge with a comb on its back -- and since the whole point of this family is what the MOUTH does (grouper bucket, snapper canines, bass large gape), the one feature the chassis refuses to draw is the family's entire identity.

This is one bird drawn seven times with the hue swapped. Every asset shares an identical egg-shaped body with the long axis horizontal, a topline that rises from the tail in a single smooth dome and drops straight into the rump, and a body depth roughly 0.9x the body length — a heavy, ground-hugging mass. There is no neck on any of them: the ball-shaped skull is butted onto the front-top of the egg with at most a two-pixel gap, so nothing kinks, curves, folds or extends. The bill is the same short tapering yellow cone leaving the skull at the same left-and-slightly-down angle on six of seven (Spoonbill alone gets a spatula grafted onto that identical cone). The limb form is identical throughout: two thin yellow sticks leaving the silhouette from the underside at mid-belly, not from the rear third where a wader's leg attaches, with one short tibia segment, one shallow forward-angled bend, and a flat three-toed pad — total leg length about a quarter of body height on every bird, so no stilt, no backward-bending ankle, no trailing toes anywhere in the family. The wing is the same crescent overlay stroked across the flank, and the tail is the same short pointed wedge exiting stage right at the same height. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a plump ground gamebird — a quail, a partridge, or a kiwi with a shorter bill. Nothing in the batch reads as a wader. The family's entire identity lives in neck length, neck carriage and leg length, and this chassis has none of the three, so the colour changes are decorating a bird from a different order.

The family has only one member, so there is no internal colour-swap to catch — but the single asset is visibly drawn on the same generic quadruped chassis this project reuses everywhere else, and that is the whole defect. Topline: a flat, near-horizontal tube that runs the full length and then STEPS UP into a separately-stacked head block, producing a shoulder hump and a short neck a hippo does not have. Body depth: shallow and constant, a sausage of even thickness rather than a barrel that bulges deepest at the belly; the belly line is straight, not sagging. Limb form: four short tapering nubs that leave the silhouette from the very bottom edge of the tube (not from a shoulder or haunch mass), each ending in a small dark rounded foot-blob with a faint toe split — pig trotters, not the splayed four-toed pillars of a hippo. Skull: a wedge with a squared muzzle lump, the one part that gestures at the reference, but the eye is a big cartoon white-and-pupil orb on the SIDE of the head at mid-height, and there is no nostril bulge on the crown. Neck carriage: head held clear of and above the topline. Tail: absent. What the chassis actually READS as is a dachshund-proportioned pig — a long low tube body, stub legs, dusty pink hide, a friendly side-mounted eye. Nothing about the mass distribution says hippopotamus; the animal's entire identity (a head that is a third of the body and a torso like a fuel drum) has been flattened onto the standard tube.

All six are the same animal repainted. The topline is one shape in every image: a flat, very slightly domed back that rises a touch at the withers and drops without a croup, with no rump mass and no wither/hip landmarks anywhere. The body depth is identical - a deep egg-shaped barrel whose belly line hangs to roughly mid-leg and bulges lowest just behind the elbow, giving a woolly, pot-bellied read rather than the flat-sided, tucked-up girth of an equid. The limbs are the same four featureless tapered tubes on all six; they leave the silhouette at the extreme four corners of the barrel with no shoulder or thigh mass at all, so the leg looks pinned onto the outside of the body instead of growing out of it, and there is no stifle, hock or fetlock articulation - the rhino and tapir get the exact same tubes, just shortened. The foot is one asset everywhere: a tiny dark rounded cap, too small for the leg, that reads as a cloven sheep/goat toe rather than a single round equine hoof, and it is the same on the rhino where three toes were required. The skull is one blunt wedge with a rounded cranium and a muzzle that tilts down at about 30 degrees, plus the same single oversized cartoon eye and the same little curl of a mouth line, on every species including the rhino and tapir. Neck carriage is the give-away: there is effectively NO neck on any of them - the head is welded directly onto the front of the barrel at the shoulder, which is why the horse has no arched crest and the donkey has no short thick neck to contrast with it. The tail hangs from the same low point on the same curve in five of six (the horse gets a flat paddle-fan instead of hair). What the shared chassis actually READS as is a sheep or a fleecy lamb - a fluffy oval body, no neck, a soft blunt head with one big eye, thin straight legs and dainty dark cloven feet. Only the zebra escapes, and only because the stripe pattern is loud enough to override the body underneath it; strip the stripes and it is the same sheep.

The family has only one member, so there is no sibling to compare against — but the single asset is plainly drawn on the project's stock plump-perching-bird chassis rather than on any hummingbird anatomy. Every shared part is the generic bird: a deep, near-circular body whose topline arcs unbroken from the nape over the back to a stubby wedge tail; a small round ball skull set directly on the shoulder with no visible neck carriage; a broad, rounded, folded wing painted as an overlapping teardrop panel on the flank, leaving the silhouette low and mid-body; two tiny three-toed yellow feet planted flat on a cast ground shadow; and a horizontal, gravity-bound standing posture. The only hummingbird-specific element is the needle bill, which is bolted onto the front of that stock head. The chassis reads as a green kiwi or a fat green quail chick that someone gave a shorebird's bill — it does not read as a hummingbird at any size.

These two are the same drawing with a palette and texture swap — the silhouettes overlay almost line for line. Shared topline: dead level from withers to croup, with if anything a slight RISE toward the hindquarters, which is the exact opposite of the one must-read both rows name (high shoulders falling steeply to low hips). Shared body depth: a deep, evenly rounded barrel of constant depth front to back, a pony ribcage, not the deep-chested / tucked-loin hyena wedge. Shared limb form: four straight vertical columns of identical length (front and hind indistinguishable, so the Striped Hyena's longer-forelimb note is unmet), leaving the silhouette at the four extreme corners of the barrel with no visible shoulder blade, no elbow, no hock angulation and no upper-limb mass inside the body outline. Shared foot: a small blocky splayed pad-block reading as a hoof/cloven block, not a compact digitigrade four-toed paw. Shared skull: a domed round cranium with a downward-drooping blunt muzzle and a low-set mouth line, small rounded ears sitting on the very top of the dome, big soft forward eye — this reads as a pony/foal head, and it carries no hyena mandible mass, no crushing jaw depth, no cheek bulk. Shared neck carriage: a short thick neck held horizontal-to-slightly-raised, joining the barrel at the same angle in both, with none of the massive fused shoulder-neck bulk the spotted hyena needs. Shared tail: an identical drooping brush hanging from the same point at the same angle in both images, only recoloured. What the chassis actually READS as is a stocky Shetland-type pony or a shaggy goat: one animal in two coats, an Appaloosa in image 1 and a cream shaggy pony in image 2. Nothing in either picture is hyena.

This is not fourteen organisms, it is four stamped chassis in fourteen colours. CHASSIS A (hunched shrimp): Amphipod, Copepod and Crayfish are the SAME painting - identical front dome carapace carrying one oversized black bead eye at the same spot, an identical second hump pasted behind it, the same short curled abdomen with a fanned bristle tail thrown to the lower right, the same two whip antennae sweeping up-left and down-left, and the same four short straight leg-sticks under the mid-body leaving the silhouette at the same points. Copepod is literally Amphipod recoloured cream-to-orange; Crayfish is the same body with two flat paddle claws bolted on. CHASSIS B (barrel crab): Crab, Coconut Crab and Hermit Crab share one vertically-striped barrel-oval carapace, the same two lollipop claws on 45-degree up-and-out arms, exactly two stick legs per side leaving the shell at the same coordinates with the same single knee kink, and the same two pin-thin eyestalks with white dot heads at 11 and 1 o'clock; Coconut Crab is that drawing in purple, Hermit Crab is it in orange with a coiled disc pasted beside the body. CHASSIS C (two-ball arachnid): Camel Spider and Harvestman share one front sphere with an eight-dot eye cluster, one mottled rear sphere behind a pinched waist, and eight identical straight-segment elbowed legs radiating symmetrically - no mouthparts on either. CHASSIS D (bead chain): Centipede, Giant Centipede and Cave Cricket share one body built of overlapping identical spheres; the two centipedes also share the same yellow head hooks, the same twin whip antennae and the same leg fringe hung under the rear two thirds only, with Giant Centipede being the same chain in red. What the shared chassis READ as: a hunched brine shrimp, a barrel-bodied toy crab, a generic house spider, and a caterpillar. Only Barnacle, Fiddler Crab and Horseshoe Crab escape the four moulds, and two of those escape into the wrong object entirely.

This batch is not twelve organisms, it is TWO chassis in twelve colours. Chassis A (Krill, Lobster, Prawn, Shrimp, Water Flea) is a single hunched shrimp puppet: one egg-shaped carapace ball seen from the left, a second rounded lump butted against its rear with three or four faint segment ridges, a downward-curled flipper fan tucked under that lump, exactly four short straight peg legs dropping from the carapace's belly line, one tiny black bead eye at the front-upper-left, two straight rods over the head plus one long curved whip trailing to the lower-left, and the same flat black ellipse shadow. Nothing about the topline, body depth, limb form, limb attachment point or tail carriage changes between them - Lobster only adds a flat dark paddle in front and Krill only adds a white zigzag and a spare pair of eyes, and Water Flea (spec: taller than long, Daphnia) is the same wide shrimp turned pale. Chassis B (Mite, Pseudoscorpion, Spider, Tarantula, Scorpion) is a single two-ball spider: two equal touching spheres with a 2x2 block of four black dot eyes on the upper-left of the front sphere, blotchy mottling on the rear sphere, two tiny ear nubs on the topline, and identical thin straight tapering stick legs raking out in fans from BOTH spheres with no knee, no arch and no foot, the whole thing hovering clear of a flat black ellipse. Scorpion bolts on a bead-chain tail, Scorpion and Pseudoscorpion bolt on featureless oval mittens; the body underneath is byte-identical in read. Only Isopod and Millipede have their own form (a segment chain), and even those share the same featureless straight peg leg. What the two chassis actually READ as: a generic hunched sea-monkey, and a generic cartoon two-ball spider.

Hedgehog and Shrew are the SAME DRAWING with a hue swap: identical egg-shaped loaf body, identical smoothly-domed topline that peaks over the shoulder and drops to a rounded rump, the identical dark comma-curl scribble at the hip, the identical pair of tall pointed triangular cat ears set on top of the skull, the identical oversized round eye with a single white catchlight, the identical three-strand whisker fan, and the identical flat white rectangle stuck on the front of the face standing in for a muzzle. Limbs on both are the same two nub stubs that emerge from the belly line with no shoulder, no hip, no elbow and no foot — the leg simply ends. Neck carriage is the same on both: none, the skull is welded to the body block. Shrew differs from Hedgehog by exactly two additions — grey paint and a thin arc tail — and Hedgehog by exactly one — a firework tuft of cream needles pinned to the shoulder. Mole is drawn on a stretched variant of the same language (same neckless welded skull, same belly-line nub legs with a pale tip, same domed dorsal line) pulled long and given a flat bill instead of a face. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a generic cartoon mouse: round-backed, cat-eared, big-eyed, blunt-faced. Nothing in the family says insectivore — there is no long mobile proboscis anywhere, no spade hand anywhere, and no spine cape anywhere; the three animals are one mouse in three costumes.

Yes — thirteen of the fourteen are one mannequin. The shared chassis is a strict left-facing profile built from three tangent spheres traced along one horizontal topline: a small featureless head sphere carrying exactly one glossy dot eye, a large egg-shaped thorax sphere of identical proportion, and a hatched/striped abdomen ellipse — Ant, Termite, Bee, Wasp, Thrips, Fly, Moth, Butterfly and Mantis are all literally this same bead-string, and Caddisfly, Dobsonfly and Fly Larvae reuse the same sphere-stack for the abdomen. Body depth never changes: the thorax sphere is the same fat ball whether the reference asks for a thread-waisted wasp (aspect 3), a slender cigar thrips (aspect 3.5) or a stubby springtail. Limb form is one part: a straight untapered stick with no femur/tibia bend, no joint, no tarsus and no foot — every leg simply stops in mid-air short of the ground, and they leave the silhouette from wherever two spheres happen to touch, which means legs sprout from the HEAD sphere (Butterfly, Moth, Bee, Thrips, Wasp, Termite) and from the ABDOMEN (Ant, Fly) instead of all six from a thorax. The skull is the same eyeball-on-a-ball in every asset: no mandibles, no proboscis, no rostrum, no mouthparts of any kind exist in this family, which is precisely why Ant, Dobsonfly, Butterfly and Thrips lose their identity feature. Neck carriage is identical — head sphere tangent to thorax at the same slight upward tilt — so the Mantis, the one animal that must have a neck, has none. Wings are one pasted pair of a lancet plus a radiating fan at the same angle on Bee, Wasp, Thrips, Fly, Moth, Butterfly, Caddisfly and Dobsonfly. Every specimen floats detached well above the same hard black shadow ellipse. What the chassis READS as is a three-ball plastic toy bee: put it in brown and it is the Ant, cream and it is the Termite, pale yellow and it is the Thrips, grey and it is the Fly. Only the Beetle breaks out, and only because it is drawn from a different camera (dorsal), not because it was drawn from a different body.

This batch ships exactly one asset, so a shared-chassis verdict across siblings cannot be established here — but the chassis this single asset is built on is worth naming because it is the generic one. Water Beetle is a symmetrical vertical egg (a dome-shaded oval with one hairline centre seam) with a small dark lollipop-shaped lump stuck on the top edge for a head, two white pinprick eyes, and six identical grey hairline arcs radiating from behind the oval's silhouette with no visible joint, no attachment point, no segmentation and no thickness variation. That reads as the default ladybug/tick body — an insect-shaped blank, not a dytiscid. There is no leg differentiation front-to-back, so if the other 14 insects in this family are drawn on the same egg-plus-six-wires template with hue changes only, the family will collapse into one bug in fifteen colours; nothing in this asset distinguishes it from that template.

This batch holds a single asset, so there is no sibling to compare against and no shared-chassis defect can be proven within it — but the one body present is worth naming because it is plainly a generic bird chassis rather than a kingfisher one. The topline is a smooth unbroken egg from crown to rump; the body is deep and rounded like a duckling's, with the widest point below mid-height; the head is a small ball perched on the front-top of that egg with a soft dip behind it that reads as a NECK, exactly the feature the reference says must be invisible; the legs are two thin yellow twigs leaving the silhouette from the underside near the body's centre of mass with splayed three-toe yellow feet, a perching-passerine arrangement; the bill is a slender downward-angled cone about the same length as the skull; and the tail is a long dark pointed wedge that projects well past the rump. Assembled, that chassis reads as a plump crested songbird or a stylised duckling in kingfisher blue — the hue and the little crest tuft are doing all of the identification work, and the three silhouette facts that actually make a kingfisher (huge head, heavy dagger bill, near-absent tail) are all absent or reversed.

These are one drawing with the hue swapped. Both share the identical egg-shaped body: a high arched topline that peaks at mid-back and drops in the same curve to the rump, the same deep rounded belly, and the same haunch ellipse pasted at the same coordinates over the flank (on the Arctic Hare it is a lighter oval that reads as a detached blob rather than a muscle mass). Limb form is identical on both: two short featureless stubs, one dropping straight down from the rear haunch and one tucked under the chest, leaving the silhouette at exactly the same points, ending in a rounded pad-less nub with no ankle, no hock and no foot plane. The skull is the same small rounded wedge fused directly into the shoulder with zero neck carriage, carrying the same single round eye with the highlight in the same spot, the same three straight whisker lines from the same origin, and the same pair of white incisor squares. The ears are the same two leaf shapes at the same splay angle with the same pink inner panel. Tail is the same nub, shadow is the same ellipse. What the chassis actually READS as is a pet-shop cottontail bunny in a crouch — compact, short-legged, round-rumped — which is the opposite of a hare's long-limbed, high-hocked, lanky build, so neither species can express its own identity. Nothing in the two silhouettes differs except colour.

Yes — these are one drawing in five colourways, and the shared parts are traceable point for point. TOPLINE: a single smooth convex ellipse hump, crown at mid-back, identical arc in all five; nothing about it changes between the 3.2-aspect Komodo and the 4.5-aspect Iguana. BODY DEPTH: the same ovoid roughly 40% as deep as it is long, so the specified aspect ratios are simply not honoured — every animal is the same stubby egg. LIMB FORM: four identical featureless tapering pegs, no upper/lower segment, no joint, no thigh mass. WHERE THE LIMB LEAVES THE SILHOUETTE: straight DOWN out of the belly's lowest curve at the same two stations in every asset (one just behind the head, one just ahead of the tail root) — vertical and tucked under the body in all five, even though three of the five are specced 'sprawling', which is precisely the trait that separates a Komodo or a monitor from a mammal. FOOT: there is no foot in this family — every peg ends in a blunt rounded stump; no toes, no splayed digits, no hooked claws anywhere, so 'long curved claws' and 'large hooked claws' are unreachable. SKULL: the same rounded ellipse, tilted a few degrees nose-down, with one large almond eye and a vertical slit pupil, plus one straight horizontal line ruled across the full width of the head as a mouth — this same line does duty for the Komodo, the monitor and the tegu, and no tongue of any kind appears in the batch. NECK CARRIAGE: there is no neck. The head ellipse simply abuts the body ellipse, so the monitor's long snake-like neck and the Komodo's loose scaly neck skin have nowhere to exist. TAIL: the same thick banana/comma sweeping up and back with the same dark interior stripe in all five — never flattened, never banded, never tapered to a whip. The ONLY thing that varies across the family is the fill hue and the speckle pattern, plus a row of small triangles added to the two iguanas' backs. WHAT THE CHASSIS READS AS: not a lizard at all — a plush cartoon newt or salamander toy, the sort of soft rounded amphibian a stranger would name 'a smiley newt', in green, taupe, sooty grey, brown and slate.

The two outer growth forms genuinely differ — Cabbage is a compact ball rosette at aspect ~1.1, Watercress is a wide low fan at aspect ~1.8 — so this is not one silhouette in two colours. But they are unmistakably built from the same painting recipe, and that recipe is the problem. Both are constructed as a perfectly radial spray emanating from a single origin node (Cabbage's lobes and white arcs all fan from the dead centre of the head; Watercress's every stem fans from one point at the bottom-centre), both use the identical flat dark forest-green fill with a soft airbrushed inner gradient and no separate leaf-surface texture, both are bilaterally symmetric about the vertical axis, and both plant exactly one bright pale-white blob as the focal accent at the radial apex — a pearl at the core of the cabbage, a domed lamp-head at the top of the watercress stem. The shared chassis reads as 'a symmetrical decorative rosette/fan emblem with a glowing bead at its origin', which is a heraldic device, not a vegetable: it makes the cabbage look like an unopened green flower with a pistil and the watercress look like a peacock's tail under a streetlamp.

This family has only one member, so there is no sibling to compare against — but the single asset is still not drawn as a peanut, it is drawn on the generic flora chassis that recurs across the earth-flora set: one perfectly straight vertical central stem rising from a flat elliptical ground shadow, a strictly symmetric ladder of ~14 opposite leaflet pairs stepping up it at even intervals, each 'leaflet' rendered as a feathery multi-tooth comb rather than a discrete oval blade, taper to a point at the apex, and a single small tan blob stuck on the very tip. That chassis READS as a fern frond or a mimosa/acacia sapling — a tall narrow feather-duster — and nothing about it is legume-specific. Swapping hue and the tip blob would turn this same drawing into any other pinnate-leaved plant in the catalogue, which is exactly the reuse defect the family question is asking about; the peanut's actual identity (a low sprawling mat, four fat oval leaflets per leaf, yellow pea flowers, pods buried in soil) has no representation in the geometry at all.

All four are one drawing recoloured. The chassis is: a single fat egg-shaped body ellipse with a flat convex topline and no shoulder, hip, ribcage or vent break; a second smaller oval butted directly onto the front of it as a head with no neck at all (head and body ellipses simply overlap, so the animal has no neck carriage to speak of); a single straight horizontal line for the mouth and one vertical-slit eye placed identically in the same spot on every asset, plus the same pale rim-light stroke on the head's upper right; a short club tail that leaves the body at mid-height, curls up and back, and carries an identical dark interior stripe on all four; and 2-4 featureless dark peg limbs that emerge from the BOTTOM edge of the ellipse (never from the side), each a plain tapered stub with no elbow, no knee, no ankle and no foot or toe of any kind. Every one of them also gets the same soft black oval ground-shadow. What that chassis actually READS as is not a lizard at all — it reads as a cartoon platypus or a newt/manatee blob: rounded, limbless-looking, belly-down, with the limbs hanging beneath like table legs. The single most damaging consequence is that the whole family is drawn with the mammalian under-body limb attachment, which is the exact opposite of the sprawling elbows-out posture that three of the four rows list as a must-read. The only things that vary across the four are hue (cream, orange, tan, grey-brown), tail length (only Land Iguana's tail was stretched long), and one added feature (the iguana's row of black triangle spikes). Head shape, body depth, topline, limb form, limb insertion, foot, neck and eye are byte-identical in silhouette.

Nine of the fourteen (Blue Whale, Dolphin, Gray Whale, Porpoise, Right Whale, Beluga, Narwhal, Pilot Whale, Beaked Whale) are the SAME drawing at different lengths and hues. Shared topline: one smooth convex arc that crests at roughly 40% of body length and then falls in an unbroken straight taper to the tail, with no dorsal fin cut into it on any of them beyond a 6-8px grey smudge dropped at the same relative station. Shared body depth: an identical teardrop, deepest just behind the head, with the same belly curve. Shared limb: exactly one grey teardrop pectoral, same size, same rotation, leaving the silhouette at the same point on the lower-left just behind the eye on every card - Beluga, Narwhal, Porpoise, Right Whale and Gray Whale are pixel-siblings here. Shared skull: no skull at all - the head is simply the front of the teardrop, so 'bulging melon' (Beluga, Pilot Whale), 'broad flat U rostrum' (Blue Whale), 'arched jaw' (Right Whale) and 'blunt no-beak head' (Porpoise) all resolve to the identical rounded point. Shared face kit: one black dot eye, one white blowhole speck above it, one thin white hairline sweeping from blowhole to jaw - stamped on nine cards. Shared tail: the same small dark notched fluke at the same absolute size whether the body is 200px or 340px long, so it looks correct on the porpoise and vestigial on the blue whale. There is no neck carriage anywhere. What the chassis actually READS as is a generic aquarium fish - a smooth lozenge with one side fin and a notched tail - and the cetacean identity survives only where a prop was bolted on top of it (Narwhal's tusk, Humpback's pectoral, Beaked Whale's tusks). Dugong and Manatee share a SECOND chassis: an identical vertically-banded barrel with the same lobe flipper and the same whiskered downturned snout, differing only in tail (notched fluke vs fan) - and the banding makes both read as a segmented grub. Fur Seal is off both chassis, drawn on the terrestrial quadruped loaf.

The three pinnipeds (Sea Lion, Seal, Walrus) are one asset in three colours, not three animals. All three share: an identical flat, dead-level topline that rises only in a small shoulder bump behind the head; the same shallow sausage body depth of roughly one head-height throughout with no blubber taper and no belly sag; four short cylindrical legs that leave the silhouette at exactly the same four points (fore-leg dropping vertically from a tucked shoulder just behind the neck, hind leg from a rear haunch about 80% back), each ending in the same small rounded three-toe paw pad planted on the ground; the same angular wedge skull with a flat crown, a big white cartoon eye ring with a black pupil, and a fat round black nose on a squared muzzle; the same short forward-level neck carriage with the head held out horizontally at back-height; the same tiny nub tail; and even the same angular flap shape behind the cheek, so the one feature that must separate an eared seal from a true seal is drawn identically on both. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a dachshund or a stubby otter-dog standing on four stumpy legs — a land quadruped. Nothing in it is a flipper: no long paddle-like fore-flipper lifting the chest, no trailing hind flipper, no blubber mass. Colour and one added prop (the Walrus tusks) are the only differences between the three. The Sperm Whale is off this chassis — it is a separate cetacean body — but it is its own generic: a smooth rounded-nose torpedo with a small pectoral, a slight mid-back bump and a fluke, i.e. a default whale with none of the sperm whale's box head or underslung jaw.

Yes — this family is two chassis and seven recolours. Possum, Sugar Glider, Tasmanian Devil and Wombat are literally the same quadruped body: an identical flat-topped barrel torso with a slight rump rise, the same shallow body depth, four straight columnar limbs of equal length that leave the silhouette vertically at the four corners of the barrel with no shoulder, elbow, hock or crouch anywhere, each ending in the same small dark two-toned block that reads as a cloven hoof, the same small rounded skull with a tapering dog/lamb muzzle, the same tiny round ear pair set high on the crown, the same short horizontal neck that flows straight into the topline with no carriage change, and the same thin tail hooked up off the rump. That chassis does not read as a marsupial at all — it reads as a LAMB, and a stranger shown Possum, Sugar Glider and Wombat side by side would name three sheep in three colours. Kangaroo and Wallaby are the second chassis and are the same drawing twice: same upright S-topline, same haunch blob, same forearm-less chest slab, same tail sweep and the same flat dark plank standing in for the hind foot; only the hue changes, so the packet's own note that a wallaby is shorter-faced, more compact and more hunched is not expressed by a single pixel. Koala is the only asset in the batch that is off-chassis, because it is drawn in a climbing pose rather than the shared quadruped stance.

These two are the same drawing recoloured. Both use an identical bead-string chassis: a round ball head carrying two dark dot-eyes stacked at the same angle, a second slightly larger ball for the thorax, then an abdomen built of five shrinking circles strung out horizontally to the right, ending in a bare bead with no terminal structures at all. Both carry the same pair of narrow lanceolate wings with the same three parallel vein strokes, splayed open in the same shallow backward V from the same insertion point, overreaching the abdomen tip by the same amount. Both hang the same three tiny hook-shaped legs in a row under the front third of the body — the legs leave the silhouette at the same place and are the same short comma stroke repeated. Both are placed at the same spot in frame (body up and left of centre, small in a large empty field) above an identical detached elliptical ground shadow far below and to the right of the body. Neither has antennae, neither has cerci or tail filaments, neither has a distinguishable thorax segmentation or head shape. The only difference between the two files is hue: warm cream-tan versus cold blue-grey. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a generic hovering gnat or midge — a caddis-ish nondescript two-winged bug — not a mayfly and not a stonefly; the two orders are distinguished in life by exactly the features this chassis omits (long tail filaments and upright wings versus flat overlapping wings and long antennae), so a single chassis cannot possibly serve both, and here it serves neither.

The family holds a single member, so there is no sibling to compare against — but the one asset is plainly not drawn to a eucalyptus growth form, it is stamped from the generic stock-tree chassis this flora set reuses everywhere: a perfectly straight, untapered, unbranched brown stick with a flat chopped-off top, plunged into a soft opaque green cloud-blob canopy, with short lance-shaped leaf darts scattered radially around the blob's rim and a handful of white ray-petalled daisy heads with yellow disc centres pinned on as the harvest token. Every part of that chassis is generic: the topline is a symmetrical puff-ball dome, the 'trunk' has no bark, no colour break, no ribbon, no limb leaving the silhouette anywhere, and the crown is dense and shade-casting rather than the open, see-through, sparse crown that IS a eucalyptus. Nothing on this render distinguishes it from the same chassis recoloured for any other broadleaf tree in the catalogue; the eucalyptus reference row asks for three specific reads and the chassis supplies none of them, so what it actually READS as is a child's lollipop tree with daisies stuck to it.

All six are the same drawing with the hue swapped. Every one is a fat smooth egg-shaped ovoid body in pure profile, outlined with the same pale seam along the topline, carrying the same scatter of dark oval speckles across the back. The head is an identical rounded blob stuck straight onto the front of the egg with no neck at all, split ear-to-ear by one straight horizontal mouth slit, with one eye set high and forward. The tail is the same part in all six: it leaves the body at mid-flank height, tapers, sweeps back and then CURLS UPWARD at the tip, and carries the same dark internal stripe down its length like a tadpole's fin. Each animal has exactly two visible limbs and they are the same two limbs everywhere: blunt dark featureless cones with no elbow, no knee, no ankle, no foot and no toes, one leaving the bottom-front of the ovoid angled forward and one leaving the bottom-rear angled back, both drawn behind the body in shadow tone. Every one sits on the same flat elliptical drop shadow. Only three things change across the family: hue (blue, green, beige, brown, olive, dark tan), how far the whole silhouette is stretched horizontally, and one bolt-on trinket each (a spike crest on Agama, a red blob at the jaw on Anole). What the shared chassis actually READS as is not a lizard at all: the neckless blob head, the plump un-scaled egg body, the upcurled finned tail and the toeless stump limbs read as a cartoon newt or salamander, a plush axolotl. The single most damaging consequence is that the sprawled five-toed foot, which is the identity of every animal in this family and is a named must-read in four of the six rows, does not exist anywhere in the batch.

These two are drawn on one chassis with only hue and a couple of head props changed. Both are a single glossy sphere head carrying one oversized black bead eye and one antenna off the front, butted directly against ONE body mass (blackfly: a sphere; mosquito: the same sphere squashed to a horizontal ellipse) — and in both the body simply STOPS there: neither has an abdomen, the translucent wing fan is bolted straight onto the back of the second mass and stands in for the whole rear of the insect. The topline is identical and dead level in both: two humps of equal height, no thoracic hump, no dip at the neck, no tapering rear. Limbs are identical too — four to six perfectly straight untapered dark sticks with no femur/tibia knee and no coxa, all dropping vertically from the UNDERSIDE of the two body masses rather than from a thorax, ending in bare points with no tarsi. Both wings are the same asset: a white radial vein-fan flaring from a point at the wing base, differing only in whether the outer membrane is stubby (blackfly) or swept long (mosquito). Both share the same lambert grey-taupe plastic material and the same flat black ellipse ground shadow, and both are marked posture 'flying' yet both stand level and upright on stiff legs above that shadow. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a big-headed winged ant or a stubby bee — a two-bead body with a wing puff — not a nematoceran fly; the only thing separating the two assets is that the mosquito got a plumose antenna and a short forward rod glued to its face.

With a family size of one there is no sibling to compare against, so a shared-chassis verdict cannot be established here — but the single asset is visibly built from the project's generic blob template rather than from newt anatomy. The parts are: a smooth capsule trunk with a pinched seam where a separate egg-shaped head oval is butted on, a flat horizontal topline with no shoulder or pelvic girdle interrupting it, body depth roughly uniform from neck to hip, and limbs reduced to two or three tiny dark peg-stubs that leave the silhouette from the BELLY line rather than from the flank, which is where a sprawling amphibian's humerus and femur must exit. There is no foot at all — the pegs end in points, no splayed digits. Neck carriage is a straight horizontal stack, no lift and no throat curve. The tail is a fat blunt club that is WIDER than the trunk at its midpoint and sweeps up and to the left, with a translucent brown mass ghosted behind it. Read together, the chassis reads as a smiling cartoon grub or a tadpole mid-metamorphosis — a sausage with a face — not as a tetrapod amphibian.

All six are the same fish drawn six times. The silhouette is one symmetrical almond/lens: a topline and a bellyline that mirror each other and converge to a point at both ends, so no species has a distinct back profile, a distinct jawline, or a distinct belly. The same crosshatched diamond scale-patch is stamped across the mid-body of every one. The same oversized white ring-and-black-pupil eye sits at the extreme upper-front of the head in all six, at the same relative position. The tail is one asset in six copies: a dark flat triangular fan with a shallow notch, hung off a thin peduncle at the same angle every time -- the tuna and marlin, whose identity is a stiff high-aspect crescent lunate tail, get the same soft triangle as the barracuda. Every fin other than the tail is rendered as a blurry, low-contrast dark BLOB sitting behind the body rather than as a fin with an edge: the barracuda's two dorsals, the marlin's sickle, the sailfish's sail, the swordfish's crescent and the wahoo's dorsal are all the same smudge, resized. Pectorals are the same small dark sliver in the same place. The only real per-species edits are hue (silver / blue / navy / mauve) and, on the three billfish, a thin straight spike glued to the nose -- and that spike is the SAME thin spike on marlin, sailfish and swordfish, so the swordfish's flat broad blade is not differentiated at all. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a generic recolourable 'fish icon' -- a mackerel-shaped lozenge with a fan tail -- not six distinct pelagic predators.

All four are the same bird drawn four times with a hue swap and one interchangeable tail part. The topline is identical in every image: a low round crown rising off a headless join into a single fat egg of a body whose back arcs up and drops to the rump on the same curve, with the same body depth (belly hangs to roughly the same fraction of frame height in all four). There is no neck in any of them — the small round skull is welded directly onto the shoulder, so 'slim neck' (Hoatzin) and 'goose-like' (Screamer) are the same non-existent neck carriage. The folded wing is one reused sticker: a dark-outlined lens with a swirl of streaky barb texture, planted at the same spot on the flank at the same angle in all four, and it never resolves into primaries. The limb form is identical — two thin yellow drinking-straw legs with no visible thigh, leaving the silhouette from the middle of the belly (far too far forward for any bird's centre of mass) and ending in the same three-toe splayed yellow foot with a stubby hallux. The bill is the same yellow wedge in all four, merely scaled up for the Kookaburra. The eye is the same small black bead with the same upper-left highlight at the same position. Even the ground shadow is the same ellipse. The only genuine variation is the tail, which is a flat plank of 2-3 parallel slats: long and striped brown (Hoatzin), long and green (Quetzal), short dark wedge (Kookaburra, Screamer). What the chassis actually READS as is a plump garden quail or a generic cartoon partridge — a round brown ground bird — and colouring it green does not make it a quetzal.

Yes — this is one chassis in two poses, and both poses are the same drawing. The four bipeds (Bustard, Sandgrouse, Seriema, Tropicbird) are pixel-for-pixel the same standing bird: identical fat ovoid body with a level topline that domes over the shoulder and falls straight to the rump, the same dark C-shaped wing-scallop arc stamped across the flank at the same angle and the same height, the same stippled feather noise fill, the same flat tail wedge leaving the rear at mid-body height, the same two thin yellow scaly legs with three splayed toes dropping from the same point on the belly, the same round head with NO neck at all, the same tiny black eye with a single white catchlight, and the same thin yellow triangular dagger bill. The only per-species edits are hue (warm brown / cream / tan / white) and, on two of them, a three-prong tuft glued to the crown. The two swimmers (Grebe, Loon) are likewise a single drawing — same half-submerged egg, same S-curved stalk neck, same upward-angled yellow dagger, same three concentric water rings — differing only in colour and a crest. The chassis reads as a generic plump gamebird/quail chick: none of the long-legged, long-necked, long-bodied or long-tailed silhouettes this family is actually built on survive. Because the chassis carries no neck, no leg length and no tail length, exactly the three axes that separate a bustard from a sandgrouse from a seriema are the three the family cannot express.

Not fourteen designs — five chassis recoloured thirteen times. CHASSIS A, a five-arm star with a small central disc, blunt-rounded arm tips, thick tapering arms leaving the disc at identical 72-degree spacing and a pale speckled dorsal surface, is drawn three times: Starfish (orange), Brittle Star (pink) and Sand Dollar (cream) are pixel-for-pixel the same star, same arm length, same tip radius, same one-arm-up orientation. CHASSIS B, a round segmented tube in an identical S-curve with the tail sweeping right and the head lifted at the left carrying one black eye dot, is drawn three times: Earthworm (pink), Flatworm (grey), Leech (olive) — same ring count, same curve, same blunt snout, only the hue moves. CHASSIS C, a squat truncated-cone column with a rimmed mouth ring and a crown of finger-like tentacles splaying left and right, is drawn three times: Sea Anemone (red), Giant Tube Worm (white), Tube Worm (cream) — the two tube worms are the anemone with the saturation pulled out, so both read as anemones and neither reads as a tube. CHASSIS D, an opaque grey dome bell with fine trailing filaments, carries both Jellyfish and Comb Jelly, the latter differing only by rainbow stripes painted on the same bell. CHASSIS E, a flat hard-edged lens/oval loaf seen three-quarters from above with a bright rim highlight, carries Chiton and Sea Cucumber. Only Sea Urchin is built from its own geometry. What the family READS as is three recoloured props — a star, a worm, an anemone — plus two bells and two dishes: the chassis carries the silhouette and colour is doing all the identity work, which is exactly why the Sand Dollar reads as a starfish, the Flatworm and Leech read as earthworms, and both tube worms read as sea anemones.

Yes - this batch is three stamped chassis with recolours, not fourteen designs. CHASSIS A, the pony: Bongo, Cattle, Duiker, Gerenuk and Hyena all share one rounded barrel torso with the same visible shoulder panel/seam where the neck plate overlaps the ribs, the same shallow-arched topline, the same four straight columnar legs that leave the silhouette at the extreme corners of the barrel and end in identical small dark blunt hoof-nubs on one shared ground line, the same tail leaving high on the rump and curving back-and-down to a frayed tuft, and the same skull - a rounded cranium, one oval eye with a white catchlight, a straight tapered muzzle ending in a bulbous nose pad, and a pale horn pair sprouting from the same forehead point. Only neck length (Gerenuk long, Cattle short), horn shape and paint change; the Bongo, the Duiker and the Cattle are the same animal in three colours and it reads as a toy pony/goat. CHASSIS B, the dachshund: Giant Anteater, Giant Otter and Marsh Rodent share one straight-sided tube torso of constant depth, the same very short stumpy legs planted at the four corners under a low belly, the same tiny rounded head set forward and slightly above the topline with a round dark ear disc and a short blunt snout, and the same thin tapering rope tail curling up off the rump - all three read as a sausage dog, which is why the anteater's tube snout, the otter's rudder tail and the rodent's incisors and scaly tail all fail to appear. CHASSIS C, the lens fish: Archerfish, Catfish, Icefish, Knifefish and Flying Gurnard are one pointed-oval body outline with a light rim stroke, stretched to different aspect ratios, carrying the identical eye (white ring, black pupil, top-left catchlight) at the same relative spot, the same soft translucent dorsal hump, the same small forked caudal fin and the same drop shadow ellipse; the species-specific gear (barbels, ribbon fin, wedge bars) is either omitted or floated on top as a loose decal.

Yes — this batch is two chassis wearing fourteen names.
