The eight quadrupeds (Mountain Goat, Mountain Tapir, Nilgai, Pronghorn, Quoll, River Otter, Serow, Springbok) are one barrel: an identical flat-to-slightly-humped topline that drops in the same curve to a rounded rump, the same medium body depth with the same faceted shoulder wedge notched into the front of the barrel, the same straight column legs with no visible elbow, stifle or hock, leaving the silhouette vertically at the four corners of the barrel rather than from a shoulder or hip mass, and the same tiny dark cloven-hoof foot — worn even by the Quoll and the River Otter, which should have paws. The neck is the same short stub rising at the same angle to the same wedge skull with a downturned muzzle and one white-ringed eye, and the fur is the same short comma-stroke hatch in every case. What the chassis READS as is a shaggy domestic goat/sheep: Mountain Goat, Serow, Nilgai, Springbok and Pronghorn are the same goat in five hues with five horn pairs pasted onto the same spot on the same skull; Mountain Tapir is that goat with a bigger blockier head; Quoll and River Otter are that goat with the legs cut short and the barrel stretched. The four fish (Mudminnow, Ocean Sunfish, Remora, Snailfish) are the second chassis: one pointed ellipse filled with the same diagonal scale hatch, the same single white-ringed eye at the nose, the same dark triangular fin blob on the flank and the same dark fan/blob tail — only the aspect ratio and the hue change, so the Sunfish is that ellipse squashed to a circle and the Remora is it stretched. Only the Scorpionfly is off-chassis, and it is off-chassis as a wasp.

The three hoofed mammals here — Tahr, Wild Sheep and Wild Pig — are one body in three tints. All three carry the identical dead-flat horizontal topline, the same deep rectangular barrel of the same depth-to-length ratio, and four straight columnar legs of identical length that leave the silhouette at the extreme four corners of the barrel with no shoulder or haunch mass anywhere along the way, each ending in the same tiny dark cloven hoof stub. The neck carriage is identical on all three: a short stub carrying the skull forward and slightly down, and the skull itself is the same object — a rounded cranium with one large white cartoon eye, a dark triangular ear tab, and a heavy bulbous muzzle that droops at the tip. All three wear the same hand-drawn hair-streak texture painted over the barrel only, leaving the neck conspicuously bare, and all three sit on the same soft ellipse shadow. Tahr and Wild Sheep are effectively the SAME PICTURE — swap tan for cream and the identical thin pale crescent horn is drawn in the identical place beside the identical head; nothing about the skeleton, coat distribution, leg length or hoof distinguishes a Himalayan tahr from a bighorn ram. Wild Pig is that same chassis with the muzzle stretched into a snout, a pink disc pasted on the end and a curl of tail added at the back; the barrel, legs, feet and coat treatment are untouched. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a generic stubby-legged farm goat. Separately, the batch runs two incompatible rendering styles: those three are painterly hair-streaked ungulates, while Tardigrade, Tigerfish, Tree Shrew and Weaverbird are smooth vector-gradient blobs with glossy rim highlights, and those four do at least use genuinely different silhouettes from one another.

Yes — 14 assets are drawn from FOUR recycled templates, and three of them are literal hue-twins. (A) The CABBAGE: Alpine Sorrel, Arctic Sorrel and Arrowhead are the same picture — the same six huge overlapping stalkless round discs stacked left-of-centre and right-of-centre, the same mirror-symmetric double-lobed outer silhouette, the same central notch where the two piles meet, the same vein rake on the right-hand disc — with only the fill hue changed (pale mint / olive / green) and the tip ornament swapped (orange bead spike / orange bead spike / white star). Arctic Sorrel is Alpine Sorrel recoloured, nothing more. (B) The FERN LADDER: Alfalfa, Alpine Mint, Angelica and Anise share one dead-straight vertical green stem of identical thickness rising from the exact centre, leaflets pinned in evenly-spaced opposite pairs from bottom to top in a rectangular column, no branching, no taper, all four terminating in a tiny ornament at the same height (purple bead / white bead / white crescent / white crescent). Angelica and Anise are near-indistinguishable. (C) The VASE SHRUB: Angel's Trumpet, Arctic Blueberry and Arctic Willow share one bundle of 5-6 tan stems splaying from a single trumpet-shaped basal boss, the same lattice of crossing stems, the same small leaves clipped in pairs along each stem, and the same tip ornament on every stem — only the ornament (white speck / blue berry cluster / cream catkin) and the leaf hue change. (D) The FAN ROSETTE: African Ginger and Arnica share the same radial spray of stiff pointed sword-blades and the same single bare stalk shooting straight up from dead centre. Across ALL 14 the ground shadow is the identical black ellipse, and every non-tree asset hangs its identity off one thin central stalk with a bead on top. What the chassis actually READS as: a cabbage, a fern, a twig-bundle and an agave, in assorted colours. Growth-form differences that ARE the identity — prostrate mat, low cushion, multi-stemmed stilt palm, sprawling dwarf shrub, emergent aquatic — are all flattened into these four shapes.

Yes — fourteen species are drawn from four reusable templates with only hue swapped, and the four templates share the same parts kit. TEMPLATE A, the cane vase: a short fat brown trunk that splits at the ground into 5-6 straight brown canes fanning into a narrow upright vase, small paired leaf-glyphs stepping up each cane, and one round fruit/flower ball parked on each cane tip. Bay Laurel, Beach Plum, Bearberry and Bilberry are literally this one object in white/purple/red/blue — a laurel TREE, a wide low plum thicket, a flat trailing bearberry MAT (aspect 2.4) and a bilberry mound are all the same tall narrow shrub. TEMPLATE B, the floating S-vine: an identical S-curved green spine hovering diagonally with no ground contact, the same little ring-glyph tendril curl repeated at the same intervals, leaves in opposite pairs off the spine — Beach Morning Glory, Beach Pea and Black Grape differ only in leaf cutout and one colour blob. TEMPLATE C, the leaf ladder: one perfectly straight unbranched vertical stem with a symmetrical rung of opposite leaves and exactly one item at the apex — Belladonna and Bergamot, and Bamboo Shoots' inner culms use the same rung motif. TEMPLATE D, trunk-plus-crown: a plain brown featureless column under a radial mass, giving Banana a woody forked palm trunk (the reference forbids a trunk outright) and Birch Sap a round lollipop of big round leaves with no white bark. Underneath all four: the same ellipse-with-midrib-and-herringbone leaf glyph, the same flat mid-brown for every woody part, the same black ellipse ground shadow, the same navy vignette. What the chassis READS as is a generic clip-art shrub kit — a bundle of brown sticks with tick-leaves and a coloured dot on top — and it is doing duty for a cactus, a tree, a groundcover mat, a banana and a stemless alpine rosette.

Yes — this batch is four stamped chassis, each reused verbatim inside its form bucket, with only a leaf glyph and an ornament hue swapped. TREE (Breadfruit, Breadnut, Cacao, Camphor, Carob): one flat brown lollipop stick with a rounded foot, no visible branching, no bark, rising into a soft airbrushed green glow-blob crown; leaf glyphs are stamped radially around the blob's rim and the fruit is stamped as two or three spheres near the crown's underside. The trunk enters the crown at the same height and the same width every time — it reads as a child's lollipop tree, not as a species. SHRUB (Bog Myrtle, Bog Rosemary, Calotropis, Castor Bean): one conical brown trunk flaring at the ground, splitting into six to eight straight rigid wands that fan out in a narrow flame/vase silhouette, leaves in alternating rows up each wand, ornament pinned at the wand tips, same ground-shadow ellipse. Bog Myrtle and Bog Rosemary are the same drawing with yellow catkins swapped for pink dots. HERB (Brooklime, Canola): one ramrod-straight vertical stem carrying a perfectly symmetrical ladder of opposite leaflets, with a single small ornament at the apex — both read as the same fern/vetch frond, one topped with blue, one with yellow. SEAWEED (Bladderwrack, Bull Kelp): literally the same tapered striped sheaf with three round blobs down the centreline, olive in one and brown in the other; no forking, no bulb, no blades. Nothing about growth habit, branching order, crown density or stem character is varied — only palette and the glyph stamped on top of it.

Seven of the fourteen — Chokecherry, Cliff Rose, Coastal Sage, Coffee, Creosote Bush, Crowberry and Curry Leaf — are literally the same drawing with the palette swapped. Every one of them stands on the identical stubby brown flared plinth-trunk that sits dead centre on the same black ground ellipse, splits at the same height into the same six straight tapered brown canes, and fans those canes into the same symmetrical vase silhouette of the same width and the same height. The leaves are never attached individually: on all seven they are a single repeating comb stamped along each cane at a fixed angle and spacing, so only the tooth shape changes (needle for Crowberry, narrow lance for Chokecherry and Coastal Sage, small oval for Coffee, pinnate feather for Cliff Rose, Creosote and Curry Leaf). The harvest is never placed where the reference puts it: on all seven it is one blob capped on the tip of each cane — pink pompom, cream daisy, white bead-string, red cluster, yellow daisy, grey pompom, white pompom — never in a hanging raceme, never in a leaf axil, never nestled among foliage. What the chassis actually READS as is a nursery bundle of cut willow whips tied at the base, or a florist's broom-shrub, and it overrides every reference growth form it is asked to serve: Coastal Sage's dusty mounded cushion, Coffee's tiered horizontal branch layers, Crowberry's flat creeping carpet and Creosote's open airy widely-spaced branching all collapse into the same upright vase. Separately, Cave Fern and Date share a second reused part — the identical stiff hard-sawtooth frond radiating in a flat disc from a central crown — which is why the fern reads as a cycad and the palm reads as the same cycad on a stick. The genuinely distinct assets in the batch are only Chicory, Cloudberry, Coralline Algae, Cotton and Crabapple, and three of those are wrong in other ways.

Yes — this batch is three stamped chassis with hue swaps, and one of them carries five species. CHASSIS A, the leaf ladder: Desert Mint, Devil's Claw, Fireweed and Flax are the same picture. One poker-straight stem of the same thickness rising from the same point on the same soft elliptical ground shadow, the same eight-to-nine pairs of identical almond leaves attached opposite at the same spacing and the same 45-degree upward angle, the same taper, the same overall height and width, and the same single ornament stuck on the tip — a bead column (pale on Mint, magenta on Fireweed) or a small pointed star (blue on Flax) or nothing at all (Devil's Claw). Devil's Club is the same stem with the leaf pairs broken into alternates and the leaves enlarged; Fenugreek is the same ladder compressed until the leaflets overlap into a column. What chassis A actually READS as is a generic nursery seedling sprig or a single fern pinna — nothing in it says mint, willowherb, flax, unicorn-plant or a spined cane. CHASSIS B, the rod broom: Desert Sage and Ephedra are the same fan of straight rods splaying out of a short brown trunk-cone on the same shadow, decorated with the same small tip clusters (pale beads vs red berry knobs) and the same scattered short sticks along the rods; it reads as a bundle of cut twigs in a vase, not a rounded silver salvia bush and not a jointed green ephedra. CHASSIS C, everything else, is one-off but equally generic: Date Plum is the stock lollipop tree (round blur crown, smooth rounded brown post, no bark, no calyx). The family-wide tell is the tip ornament: identity is being delivered by a 20px coloured bead or star glued to the top of an identical stem, so the harvest — the one thing that names these plants — is the smallest and least differentiated element in every frame.

Yes — this batch is not fourteen plants, it is about five reused armatures with a leaf-token and a fruit-token swapped in and the hue changed. Pair 1, Gentian and Holy Basil, is the same drawing twice: one dead-straight vertical stem of identical thickness, the same eight evenly spaced opposite leaf pairs stepping up it at the same angle, the same tiny beaded flower spike poking out above the topmost pair, the same elliptical ground shadow — only the leaf outline (narrow lance vs. oval) and the hue (green vs. pink) differ, and Hemp is the same ladder again with a palmate fan token stuck on each rung. Pair 2, Huckleberry and Juniper Berries, is one shrub chassis: a single stubby brown trunk that splays into five or six perfectly straight canes fanning from one point, the same small side-leaflets stitched alternately along each cane, the same round berry clusters parked at the cane tips — swap oval leaflets for grey bristles and purple berries for blue and you have the other one. Pair 3, Giant Kelp and Glasswort, is one bundle-of-tapering-vertical-strands spike, wide at the top and pinched to a point at the ground, in amber and in green. Pair 4, Grape and Kiwi Fruit, is one sinuous S-curve cane leaning right with alternating leaves and a fruit token hung at mid-height. Pair 5, Indian Gooseberry and Joshua Tree, share the same flat rounded-rectangle brown trunk with no taper and no bark, differing only in what is glued on top. What the shared chassis READS as is a stem-and-token construction kit: a vertical or S-curved armature with symmetric side stubs, each stub terminated by a stamped leaf glyph, plus an optional berry blob — a plant diagram, not a plant. Only Floating Green Algae, Ice Algae and Hardy Fern escape the kit, and two of those three read as the wrong object entirely.

Yes — these fourteen are built from a kit of three fixed skeletons with a leaf glyph and a tip ornament swapped in, not from each species' own growth form. SHRUB CHASSIS (Labrador Tea, Lingonberry, Marsh Rosemary): the identical fan of about seven brown rods springing from one flared basal knuckle, same 60-degree splay, same rod taper, same small leaves stuck on alternately along each rod, same ornament docked at every rod tip, same soft ellipse shadow — three renders that differ only in leaf tint and whether the tip blob is a white half-disc, a red berry triplet or a pink bud. TREE CHASSIS (Mangosteen, Mangrove Leaves, Maple Sap, Marula): one straight untapered brown pole with no branching whatsoever, plugged into a soft round green fog-blob crown, leaves scattered only around the blob's rim, fruit floated on top of the blob, identical ellipse shadow; the trunk is the same object in all four, so a mangrove has no stilt roots, a maple has no tap, a marula has no flaking bark and a mangosteen has no conical crown — the chassis has no vocabulary for any of it. STEM-LADDER CHASSIS (Licorice, Licorice Root, Milkweed): one vertical stalk with leaves stepping up it in a rigid mechanical ladder and a single tiny ornament capping the top. What the whole kit READS as is a nursery-catalogue icon set: a twig-broom bush, a lollipop tree and a leaf-ladder weed, recoloured. Only Lichen, Licorice Fern, Lotus Root and Melon step outside the kit, and three of those four land on the wrong organism anyway.

This is not fourteen plants, it is three templates recoloured. CHASSIS A (six of fourteen) is a single vertical wand: one straight green stem dead-centre, a symmetric ladder of identical leaf blades stacked in tiers from ground to top, and a small bead or daisy stuck on the tip - Miner's Lettuce, Monkshood, Mountain Mint, Mugwort, Nettle and Orchid Pods are all this one drawing with the blade width, blade colour and tip-bead colour swapped; the tip decoration is literally the same string of beads on Mountain Mint (white), Mugwort (grey), Nettle (cream) and Mountain Sorrel (red). It reads as a wheat-ear or a bottlebrush, never as a herb with real architecture. CHASSIS B (three) is a fat brown basal stub that splays into five or six straight brown twigs, small leaves pinned along them, and berry pom-poms at the twig ends - Mountain Blueberry and Mountain Cranberry are the identical armature with the berries changed from blue to red, and Mormon Tea is the same armature again with the leaves thinned out. CHASSIS C (two, plus a variant) is the most blatant: Mountain Papaya and Nipa Palm Fruit share a pixel-identical thick brown trunk with the same amputated stub branch angling up-right, the same radiating pinnate frond crown, and the fruit tucked in the same crown notch - only the fruit colour differs; Neem reuses the same trunk straightened out under a green blob crown. The family shares topline (flat-topped for herbs, dome for shrubs), stem-exit geometry (everything leaves the axis at the same repeating angle), the single central axis, the ground shadow ellipse, and the same terminal-bead harvest primitive. Only Mountain Sorrel and Mountain Thyme escape, and they do so by being nearly empty.

Not one chassis for all fourteen, but a kit of four templates reused across unrelated species with only hue and leaf outline swapped, which is the same defect. Template A, the symmetric fan-rosette: leaves radiate from one point at ground level in a bilaterally mirrored fan, one bare vertical stalk rising dead-centre from the same point, no branching, no basal stem - it carries Pickerelweed, Plantain Herb, Prairie Turnip and Purple Saxifrage, four plants from four different habitats, and the only thing that changes is whether the leaf outline is round, lance, broad-oval or a straight ray. Template B, the lollipop conifer: one straight bare cylindrical brown trunk of even width, a soft green fuzz ball crown, straight needle sticks fired radially out of the ball, two or three small brown cones pinned on the fuzz - Pine Nuts and Pinyon Pine are the same drawing at two scales, so the stone pine's flat umbrella crown and the pinyon's low crooked bush both read as the identical green ball on a stick. Template C, the splayed rod shrub: a bundle of straight brown rods leaving a single conical base and fanning upward with small leaflets pinned along them - Pigeon Pea and Rabbitbrush are the same bundle, Rabbitbrush just gets daisies stuck on the rod tips. Template D, the fountain grass clump: long tapering blades arching out from a dense point with a shadow ellipse under it - Pampas Herb and Papyrus Shoots are the same clump, and Papyrus, an aquatic sedge whose whole identity is a bare triangular stem and a firework umbel, is drawn as that grass tussock with a few floating dashes. Cutting across all of it is one harvest stamp: a thin bare stalk topped by a short string of identical spheres, appearing in white on Pampas, blue on Pickerelweed, white on Plantain Herb, lavender on Prairie Turnip and white again on Rainforest Nettle - five species, five completely different inflorescences in nature, one bead chain recoloured. The chassis reads as a stock decorative houseplant: a tidy symmetric ground fan with a single ornamental flower spike, the thing you would draw for any generic potted plant, and it erases the habitat cues (water, rock cushion, prop roots) that are the actual identity of half this batch.

This is not fourteen plants, it is a kit of about five procedural shells recoloured. Shell A: a straight vertical stick with identical opposite oval leaves stacked rung-by-rung to the tip and a tiny terminal spike - Riverbank_Nettle (green), Salmonberry (gold) and Sea_Fennel (same ladder with the ovals shrunk to threads) are the SAME drawing, and Scurvy_Grass is that ladder squashed to a mound. Shell B: a fountain tuft of flat arching blades erupting from one point, identical arch count, identical arch curvature, identical tip taper - Rush_Shoots and Saltgrass differ ONLY in hue (green vs blue-grey); overlay them and they are one image. Shell C: a splayed bundle of brown canes from a single trunk with dashed micro-foliage and round harvest blobs perched at the cane tips - Rose_Hip and Sea_Buckthorn share the trunk, the cane fan, the dash-leaf scatter and the tip-blob placement; only blob colour and leaf shape were swapped. Shell D: a salmon-pink starburst rosette repeated up or around a stem - Red_Grape and Roselle are the same starburst, one strung along a serpentine vine, one bunched. Shell E: a closed vertical spindle of parallel ribs - Samphire and Sea_Grapes_Algae. The kit reads as generic decorative houseplant clip-art: nothing here carries a species-specific silhouette, and the three notes in the packet that explicitly warn against a generic reading (rushes must be round not bladed, sea fennel must be fleshy not feathery, sea grapes must have no blade at all) were each violated by the shell that got assigned. Leaf colour is also driven by an arbitrary palette rather than the reference - grape and roselle foliage came out salmon-orange, salmonberry came out gold.

Yes — fourteen species are drawn from four stamps, and one of them does more than half the work. Six of the fourteen (Sea Lavender, Sea Rocket, Sesame, Solomon's Seal, Steppe Tulip, Swamp Mint) are the SAME picture: one dead-straight vertical olive stem rising from a flat elliptical ground shadow, the same regular ladder of ~9 evenly spaced pointed lance leaflets stepping up it at the same 45-degree angle and the same shrinking taper toward the tip, the same bare terminal 15% of stem, and one small harvest token stuck on the very top — a mauve dome (Sea Lavender), a mauve daisy (Sea Rocket), nothing (Sesame), three white bells (Solomon's Seal), three red blobs (Steppe Tulip), a lilac spikelet (Swamp Mint). Nothing about the plant changes; only the finial and the hue change. Stamp two is the basal fan: Sea Kale and Sorrel are one radial spray of ~11 smooth pointed spear leaves fanning symmetrically from a single ground point at identical angles, with a thin wire stem punching up through the exact centre carrying a tiny cap — glaucous with a white dome, or green with a red spire. Sea Purslane is the same fan with the leaves fattened into paddles. Stamp three is the lollipop tree: Spruce Tips and Star Anise share one straight brown popsicle-stick trunk with a rounded tip, planted centre-bottom, topped by the same soft round green cloud crown with small tokens scattered over it — sticks and cones, or leaves and slivers. A spruce and a star anise are the same broadleaf lollipop. Stamp four is the blade: Sea Lettuce and Sugar Kelp are a vertical strap narrowing to a dot holdfast, one in green and one in gold. Only Serviceberry escapes with its own multi-stem branching structure. The chassis READS as a generic craft-store sprig: a fern frond or a plastic aquarium plant, not a marsh herb, not a bulb, not a conifer, not a seaweed. Growth form — the one thing that separates a sprawling succulent mat from a tulip from a spruce — is not being drawn at all; it has been replaced by a hue and a bauble.

This is not fourteen plants, it is four templates with the decoration swapped. TEMPLATE A - 'splayed vase of straight tapering stems rising from one narrow ground point, same ellipse shadow, short straight side-ticks pinned along each stem, one blob at each tip' - carries Tamarisk, Tea, Tea Tree AND Wakame; the stems, the splay angles, the base pinch and the tick spacing are the same drawing, only the stem hue (brown / brown / brown / olive) and the tip sprite (pink bead spike / white daisy / white daisy / nothing) change. TEMPLATE B - 'serpentine S-curve wire stem with narrow lance leaves alternating off it and the identical little dark tendril curl' - carries Vanilla Orchid and Water Spinach; the two stems trace the same S, the same curl sprite appears in the same places, only the flower sprite (cream 6-point star vs white teardrop) differs. TEMPLATE C - 'one straight vertical stem with leaves stepping up in regular ranks and a flower unit parked on top' - carries Tobacco, Water Mint and Water Hemlock, differing only in leaf size (huge ovate / lance / tiny sprig-ladder). TEMPLATE D - 'fountain of arching strap blades from a point' - carries Sweet Flag and Tussock Grass. The same 8-petal white/lilac disc-daisy sprite is reused as the flower of tea, tea tree AND water mint - three flowers that share nothing in life - and the same pink beaded catkin sprite is the tamarisk plume and the sweet flag spadix. What the chassis actually READS as is a florist's stem kit: bare vase of sticks, wire vine, stalk-with-leaves, grass tuft. Only Tree Fern Shoots, Tree Tomato and Watermelon sit outside the kit, and two of those three are generic (lollipop tree, sago-palm rosette).

Yes — fourteen species are drawn on four reused templates plus three one-offs, and within each template only hue and the fruit blob change. TEMPLATE A, the lollipop tree (Wild Cherry, Wild Fig, Wild Mango): the identical flat brown trunk-stick with rounded ends rises dead-centre from the same elliptical ground shadow to the same height, topped by the same soft airbrushed green blob crown with the same small lance-leaf sprigs poking out of its rim, and four to five identical spheres pressed into the crown face — red for cherry, purple for fig, orange for mango. Nothing about bark, branching, crown spread or fruit attachment differs; it reads as a child's generic orchard tree. TEMPLATE B, the broom shrub (Wild Blueberry, Wild Chili, Wild Guava): the same fused brown wedge base splays into the same five-to-seven straight tapering stems, the same tiny paired lance leaves are stuck along each stem at the same intervals, and one sphere sits at each stem tip — blue, red, pale yellow. Guava is specified as a TREE and is drawn on the berry-shrub chassis. TEMPLATE C, the grass fountain (Wild Chive, Wild Garlic, Wild Onion): the same fan of arching strap blades from a single point with one bare stalk carrying one flat blob on top; garlic and onion are the same picture twice, and garlic's blades are the narrow grassy ones its own note explicitly forbids. TEMPLATE D, the S-curve vine (White Grape, Wild Melon): pixel-for-pixel the same serpentine stem, the same star-lobed leaves at the same nodes, the same coiled tendril rings — only the object at the middle node changes from a white cluster to a striped globe. Only Wild Ginger, Wild Mint and Wild Mustard escape the four templates, and each is a single generic form of its own. The shared chassis reads as a clip-art plant kit: a stick-and-blob tree, a bundle-of-twigs bush, a grass tuft and an S-vine, recoloured.

This is not ten plants, it is three generic templates recoloured, plus three one-offs. TEMPLATE A - 'radial fan of pointed toothed lobes rising from a single point at the baseline, with one straight vertical wand up the centre ending in a single small blossom' - draws Wild Rhubarb and Wood Sorrel as the SAME picture: same lobe count, same serrated lobe edge, same V-notch where the two lower lobes meet, same dead-straight centre wand, same terminal ornament; only hue (dark green vs lime) and the ornament (pink bead spike vs cream star) differ. Wild Taro is the same radial fan with the teeth rounded off and the wand deleted, so it reads as a pile of overlapping pebbles. TEMPLATE B - 'one dead-straight vertical stem with a symmetrical ladder of small opposite leaflets, tip finial on top' - draws Wild Sesame and Wormwood identically; the only differences are leaflet colour (dull mauve vs silver-cream) and leaflet count. Both read as a fern frond, neither reads as its own plant. TEMPLATE C - 'a bundle of bare brown sticks splaying up out of a single trunk-stub, sparse small leaves clipped onto the sticks, an ornament at each stick tip' - draws Wild Thyme and Yerba Mate identically; only the tip ornament (pink daisy vs red berry cluster) and leaf tint change. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a florist's dried-stem bouquet: nothing in the family has a real growth habit - no creeping mat, no crown of stalks, no woody crown, no twining. Only Wild Rye (grass tuft), Wild Strawberry (crown plus runner) and Wild Yam (S-curve vine) escape the kit, and of those only the strawberry is actually built around its own biology.

This is one drawing recoloured nine times. Every asset is the identical closed doughnut coil: the same outer ring diameter, the same oval hole in the middle, the same inner loop crossing the outer loop at the same pixel on the left, the same neck leaving the ring at the lower right and rising to a head at the same angle, the same blunt wedge skull with a single white eye bearing a dark vertical slit at the same spot, the same bright-red forked tongue stamped at the same angle, and the same soft elliptical drop shadow at the same offset below. Body gauge never changes: the aspect-12 needle-thin Vine Snake is drawn at exactly the same tube thickness as the aspect-4 King Snake, and no tail taper or tail tip is visible anywhere because the tail is always buried inside the coil. The ventral scute ribbing is the same hatch pass on all nine, oriented the same way. The only per-species variables are hue (dark olive, leaf green, near-black, blue-grey, dark grey with a rust smear, bright green, yellow-green, brown, khaki) and a scatter of faint pale blotches; not one animal in the batch has a stripe, a band, a ring, a collar, or any patterning at all. What the chassis actually READS as is a fat coiled ribbon-worm or a rubber gasket toy — a segmented earthworm doughnut with a snake head glued on — not nine distinct colubrids. Posture is also ignored: six of the nine are specified crawling and all nine are the same coil.

This batch holds a single member, so there is no cross-member repetition to observe and I will not claim a shared chassis on n=1. What I can say is that the one owl is not drawn on an owl chassis at all — it is built on the project's generic rounded-bird blank: a horizontal egg body whose topline is a single unbroken arc from shoulder to tail, maximum body depth at the mid-belly, a small ball head grafted low and forward onto the front of the egg with no neck carriage and no facial disc, legs that leave the silhouette at the very bottom-centre of the belly (not from a feathered thigh at the rear third, as a perched owl's do), bare yellow scaled tridactyl feet, and a tail that exits as a sharp grey spike off the right flank. That chassis READS as a white duckling or a fluffy waterfowl chick. An owl's chassis is an upright column — vertical topline, head sitting directly on the shoulders, the whole face a flat forward-facing disc, legs hidden inside a feathered trouser — and none of that is present. Whatever else is in the owl family, this is the blank they will all inherit, and it needs replacing before more owls are hung on it.

All three are the same bird recolored. The topline is one identical convex arc that rises off a round skull, crests over the back and drops to the rump with no nape break; the body is the same deep, near-circular plump oval filling roughly half the frame in every render; the same crescent wing-scoop with a hooked leading-edge sweep line is stamped in the same place on all three; the tail leaves the silhouette at the same mid-body height as the same flat horizontal slat (Cockatoo's is a grey point, Macaw's and Parrot's are the identical striped bar, pixel-for-pixel the same shape in red and in green); the legs are the same pair of short pale-yellow sticks emerging from the underside of the belly at the same x, ending in the same three-forward-one-back anisodactyl perching foot with no zygodactyl split anywhere in the family; the skull is the same small round ball with no forehead rise and no cere; the neck has no carriage at all - the head is welded onto the shoulder in all three. What the chassis actually READS as is a plump ground pigeon or a partridge in a horizontal, tail-trailing pose - not a parrot. Cockatoo differs from the other two only by a tiny white crest spray and a cone beak; Macaw and Parrot differ from each other by hue alone.

All five are one bird in two colourways. The chassis is a fat horizontal egg with a quilted scallop-hatch feather texture, a topline that arcs from a low shoulder over a high mid-back and drops straight to the rump with no tail root, and a single grey crescent wing painted flat onto the flank that exits the silhouette at the same rear-right point on every asset and terminates in one pointed grey blade doing duty as both wingtip and tail. The head is a separate sphere stuck on the front-top of the egg with almost no neck (Cormorant is the only one given a neck, and it is a short grey tube, not a snaky one), carrying one large side-set round eye — never a forward binocular pair — and a short yellow-orange cone bill of identical length and identical downward tilt on all five. The legs are two thin orange-yellow sticks with three splayed toes that emerge from the belly midline, not from the rear of the body, and no asset has a webbed foot. Booby, Gannet and Pelican are the same white bird with only the faintest bill and head-shading differences; Frigatebird and Cormorant are that same egg in charcoal, one with the wing blade fanned into streaks and one with it folded. What the chassis actually reads as is a cartoon duckling or bath-toy duck — a plump round-bodied yellow-billed waterfowl — which is the wrong superorder for every species in this family: nothing here reads as a plunge-diver, a wing-drying cormorant, an aerial frigatebird or a pouched pelican.

All four are the same lens/almond blob with the hue swapped and the lens stretched or squashed. Topline: one smooth convex arc from a sharp snout point to a sharp caudal point, with no nape hump, no head-to-body break and no operculum step. Snout: every fish ends in a bare geometric POINT - there is no mouth, no jaw line, no lip on any of the four, so the bucket mouth (Bass), the tiny mouth (Sunfish) and the toothed jaw (Walleye) are all the same nothing. Dorsal: a single crown of four flat isosceles triangles pasted on the back at the same relative station on all four - never two fins, never a soft rear lobe, and the identical crown appears on the deep-bodied Sunfish and the pike-shaped Walleye alike. Fins: the same small triangle pectoral at the same mid-flank spot, the same small triangle anal under the belly, the same two-lobe fan caudal, and every fin is the exact body hue with zero contrast, so Perch's orange-red pelvics and Walleye's white tail tip cannot exist. Eye: one white-ringed black dot at identical relative size and position hard against the snout on all four - the Walleye, a fish literally named for its eye, has the same dot as the Bass. Surface: the same mesh-of-dots scale hatch, the same faint gill arc, the same ellipse drop shadow. Perch and Sunfish are the same round pancake body at two hues; Bass and Walleye are that same body stretched. What the chassis READS as is a generic clipart fish decal wearing a paper crown - four colourways of one fish, not four species.

These two are the SAME drawing with a hue swap and nothing else. Overlay them and every landmark coincides: the same flat horizontal topline over a fat lozenge torso of identical depth; the same thick uniform-width sausage tail leaving the body at the same height and sweeping up-left to the same blunt rounded tip; the same pair of dull grey-mauve discs parked behind that tail tip in the same offset position (in both images they read as a smudge artifact, not a caudal fin); the same four stubby dark-brown/olive peg limbs leaving the silhouette at the same four belly points with the same bent-knee angle and the same clubbed foot; the same egg-shaped bulbous skull with no neck at all, jammed straight onto the torso; the same single cartoon eye with the same white catchlight in the same spot; the same shallow upcurved smile arc; and the same two pink gill fans in the same two places (one sweeping up-and-back off the nape, one hanging DOWN off the throat where it collides with the foreleg and reads as a splayed pink hand). Nothing about proportion changed either: the packet asks for aspect 3.5 vs aspect 8 and headFrac 0.25 vs 0.12, and both were rendered at the axolotl's stocky ~3 with a quarter-length head. What the shared chassis actually READS as is one chubby cartoon axolotl mascot, drawn once, and recoloured cream for the second slot.

These two are the same drawing twice with a hue swap. Identical egg-shaped body with a high domed topline that peaks just behind the head and rolls unbroken into the rump; identical body depth (a near-circular belly that nearly touches the shadow ellipse); the same single large oval wing patch pasted on the flank with the same dark comma-shaped outline curling from the shoulder down and around; the same thin dark blade of a tail leaving the lower-right of the body at the same angle and the same length; the same small round skull tucked at the upper-left with no neck at all (the head is welded straight onto the breast, no columbid S-curve, no visible throat); the same short straight yellow bill at the same pitch; the same pair of yellow legs emerging from the bottom of the body with the same three splayed forward toes and no visible tarsus length; and the same soft drop shadow. The only differences are cream-vs-slate plumage and a green cap painted on the pigeon's crown. What the shared chassis actually READS as is not a pigeon at all: it reads as a plump, effectively tailless ground-bird chick — a quail, partridge or duckling — because the tail is a wisp rather than a fan, the breast is spherical rather than deep-and-keeled, and the head sits directly on the shoulders. Neither the dove's slim tapering tail nor the pigeon's broad fan tail exists on this body; the chassis has one tail and it serves neither.

These are one pig drawn four times in four colours. Every asset shares the same dead-level topline running flat from the shoulder patch to the rump with no shoulder rise and no croup drop; the same deep oval barrel with an identical belly curve; the same four short columnar legs of equal length and thickness, all leaving the silhouette at the same four x-positions with a darker shoulder/haunch patch lapped over the top of each; the same foot, a pair of dark toe-nubs stamped at the bottom of each column; the same wedge skull hung at the same downward angle with the same oversized round snout disc carrying two nostril dots, the same single white eye with a black pupil in the same relative spot, and the same small dark folded ear; no neck at all in any of them, the head fusing straight into the shoulder at the same height; and the same elliptical drop shadow. What varies is hue (grey, pink, taupe, brown), coat-stroke density, and two appliques stuck onto the shared face/rump: a white crescent near the muzzle on Warthog and Wild Boar, and a hanging tufted tail on Warthog. The chassis itself reads as a stocky domestic pig with capybara proportions, so the two species whose identity lives in the SILHOUETTE (Wild Boar's front-heavy hump, Warthog's leggy flat-fronted wedge and dorsal crest) cannot express it at all, and the two whose identity lives in a small part (Peccary's downward tusks, Pig's corkscrew tail) simply lost that part.

This batch has exactly one member, so cross-species chassis reuse cannot be demonstrated here — but the single asset is visibly drawn on the project's generic parametric FISH BLANK rather than on a pike. The blank is: a symmetric almond/lens body whose topline and bottomline are mirror curves with maximum depth at the exact mid-length; a hard white rim-light tracing that whole lens; a hex-cell scale net washed over the interior; one horizontal lateral line; a single dark triangular pectoral wedge leaving the silhouette just below mid-flank; a thin dark crescent gill arc behind the head; and a forked crescent caudal fin on a very short peduncle. Head and tail terminate in the SAME point — flip the image and you get the same fish — which is precisely the property a pike cannot have. Pike-specific identity is applied as a decal on top of that blank (a comb of white hooks hung on the ventral outline) instead of being built into the geometry, so what the chassis reads as is a generic green mid-water fish, closest to a mackerel or a small leaf-shaped cichlid, wearing borrowed fangs. There is also a registration fault: a soft green ghost silhouette sits offset from the crisp rim-lit body, bulging past it above the back and below the belly.

This batch contains a single asset, so there is no sibling to compare a chassis against — no shared-body defect can be proven or ruled out from one image. What can be said about the growth form on its own is that it is NOT the tooth-fungus growth form at all: it is a generic sphere-cluster generator (dozens of large, smooth, specular-highlighted balls packed into a rough blob) with a thin decorative fringe of short spikes pasted through the middle. That sphere-cluster reads as the same primitive a puffball, a coral fungus, a bunch of grapes or a soap-foam would get, which is exactly the shared-chassis smell — the identity is carried by the fringe overlay rather than by the growth form. When the rest of earth-fungi is judged, check specifically whether other cluster species reuse this same ball-packing mass, because it looks like a reusable body with a per-species decal on top.

Yes — these are one fish body with two parameter tweaks. Both are a single-piece lozenge that is MIRROR-SYMMETRIC about the lateral line: the topline and the ventral line are the same curve flipped, so neither fish has a back or a belly, only an outline. Both carry the identical kit of pasted decals in the identical places: one small dark triangular pectoral fan stuck flat on the flank at roughly 60-65% back from the nose; one thin crescent gill-arc scribed just behind the head; one white-ring-with-black-dot eye decal parked at the extreme top-front corner of the block; dorsal and anal fins rendered not as shaped fins but as a low-contrast dark smear tucked behind the body edge so it reads as shadow; a full-body machine-stamped texture grid that differs only in cell shape (scallop mesh on Arapaima, square knurl on Arowana); and the same soft ellipse drop shadow underneath. The only real variables between the two are hue (sage green vs khaki tan), how sharply the two ends taper (needle points vs blunt vertical faces), and caudal size (a big square paddle vs a tiny stub with hair rays). What the chassis actually READS as is a generic aquarium minnow or dace sticker — a symmetric leaf with a bubble eye and one triangle glued to its side. Nothing about either head, jaw architecture, or fin placement is species-specific, so neither the arapaima's bony blunt skull and far-back paddle-framing fins nor the arowana's near-vertical drawbridge jaw and chin barbels can exist on it; they are exactly the features the shared chassis has no slot for.

These are one image recoloured fourteen times. Every asset is the identical front-facing squat: an egg-shaped torso widest at the shoulder and tapering to a rounded rump, a pale rim-light outline tracing the same contour on all fourteen, a small round skull sitting directly on the torso with no neck at all, the same pale helmet-shaped arc painted across the crown, the same two tiny white circle eyes with a dark pupil dot set at the same spacing, and the same minimal dark snout smudge with no jaw projection on any of them. The arms are the same pair of uniform-width dark noodles leaving the silhouette high at the shoulder corner, bowing outward and reaching the floor beside the feet, ending in a blunt rounded paddle with no fingers, thumb or knuckle anywhere in the family. The legs are the same two dark thigh-blobs fused to the bottom of the torso with the same two stubby paddle feet, planted at the same stance width, over the same elliptical ground shadow. The tail is the same single smooth C-curve leaving the left hip and hooking up — pasted at the same angle and the same length on Baboon, Capuchin, Howler, Langur, Lemur, Macaque, Mandrill, Marmoset, Monkey and Proboscis — and simply deleted for Chimpanzee, Gibbon and Gorilla. The only real variables are hue, a blurry fluff ring stamped around the head on Lemur, Mandrill, Marmoset and Orangutan, and two small side ears added on Chimpanzee. What the chassis READS as is a plush toy gorilla in a squat: it is not a monkey posture, not a quadruped despite thirteen rows specifying quadruped, and not the upright long-armed brachiator the Gibbon row demands. Because the chassis has no muzzle, no fingers, no ear variation, no tail variation and no proportion variation, the family cannot express the very features that separate its members, so a stranger shown all fourteen would name a single animal fourteen times.

These two are the same drawing with a hue swap and one added accessory. Both share: an identical broad barrel torso with a pale-rimmed lighter ventral panel running crotch-to-chin; identical short thick arms that leave the silhouette low on the mid-flank and drape as paired tubes to blunt blob-mitts with no fingers; identical thigh lobes tucked under the belly ending in the same stubby splayed feet; the same small round skull set directly on the torso with no neck at all; the same flat brow-cap, the same tiny circular side-ears, the same white-sclera round eyes with dot pupils, two nostril dots and a smile line; the same thin C-hook tail sweeping up and left to a blunt point at roughly half body length; and the same drop-shadow ellipse. The chassis READS as a squat, front-facing crouching chimp/teddy-bear plush — an ape-shaped blob, not a monkey. Nothing about limb length, limb proportion, torso depth, tail length or hand structure differs between the two species; the only deltas are colour (dark brown vs orange) and the tamarin's radial mane fringe pasted around the same face.

Six of the seven (Bowfin, Coelacanth, Gar, Lungfish, Paddlefish, Sturgeon) are one fish drawn six times. The shared chassis is a pointed lens/almond body — a symmetric almond whose topline and ventral line mirror each other, deepest exactly at mid-length, with no belly, no gill cover, no pectoral or pelvic fin leaving the silhouette anywhere. Every one of them wears the same translucent grey membrane halo offset around the coloured core, the same single dark triangular dorsal bump sitting on the midline of the back, the same crosshatch scale stipple over the flank, the same white-ringed black eye stamped at the extreme front tip of the taper, and the same soft elliptical ground shadow at the same offset below. Only three things vary: hue (green, steel blue, olive, brown, grey, tan), how far the almond is stretched, and which of two tails is bolted onto the left end — a blunt trapezoid paddle (Bowfin, Coelacanth, Gar, Lungfish) or a small symmetric fork (Paddlefish, Sturgeon). Snouts are the only other bolt-on: a dark lozenge stuck on the nose, long on Paddlefish, stubby and visibly detached on Sturgeon. What the chassis actually READS as is a generic aquarium minnow or dace in flat side profile — no lobe fins, no scutes, no armour, no barbels, no beak, so the entire point of a 'primitive fish' family (the archaic hardware) is missing. Lamprey is the sole genuine outlier: a curved ribbon body with a radial sucker disc and gill pores, sharing none of the almond chassis.

These two are the same drawing at two widths and two hues. Both share: an unbroken soft-rounded ovoid outline with no hard edges or facets anywhere; the same low dorsal nub set just behind the body's midpoint; the same single small triangular pectoral flap low on the flank; the same broad rounded fan caudal attached on the LEFT via a short pinched peduncle, drawn at identical scale and angle in both; the same single small white ring-with-black-pupil eye placed high on the right shoulder of the oval; NO mouth at all on either; the same fine curved hatch/scale texture combed along the body; and the same soft grey ellipse shadow directly beneath. Change the fill from yellow to khaki and squeeze the horizontal axis by about 20 percent and one becomes the other. What the shared chassis actually READS as is a generic aquarium-shop reef fish silhouette - closest to a yellow tang or a discus - with none of the two things that separate this family from every other fish: the boxfish's rigid faceted carapace and the puffer's beak plus goggle eyes. The family question is answered plainly: one body, two colours.

These are one drawing in four colours. Every asset shares the identical hump-backed topline — a high rounded rump falling forward into a rounded shoulder with no dip and no withers — the same body depth (a fat egg/teardrop, deepest at the haunch, belly line sitting a fixed short distance off the ground), and the same rear marking: a dark comma-shaped swirl curled into the hindquarter in exactly the same place at exactly the same angle on all four. The limb model is identical and it is barely a limb: two thin dark rounded pegs, no joint, no hock, no thigh mass separate from the body, no toes and no foot of any kind — the peg simply ends where it meets the ground shadow. Critically the pegs leave the silhouette from the BELLY line, well inboard of the outline, rather than from a shoulder or a hip, so no animal here has a hindquarter that could push. The skull is one stamp reused: short domed cranium, blunt round muzzle, one round eye with the same white catchlight at the same fraction of the head, the same three-line whisker fan, and the same small white rectangle stuck on the nose that reads as a paper tag or a bandage rather than incisors. Neck carriage is identical — there is no neck; the head is fused into the shoulder at the same tilt on all four. What actually varies across the family is hue (warm gold, pale cream, mid tan, grey-brown), ear length, and overall scale. The chassis READS as a generic Easter-card cartoon bunny in a sitting crouch — so the hare is not leggy, the jackrabbit is not powerful, and the pika is not a pika.

All four are the same drawing with the fill colour swapped. Shared parts, item by item: a FLAT, level topline running dead straight from withers to croup with a slight rise at the shoulder and no hunch or rump-high arch anywhere; a deep, barrel-shaped ungulate chest whose belly line curves up sharply into a tucked flank (a hoofstock brisket, not a procyonid's low sagging tube); four straight column legs of equal length that leave the silhouette VERTICALLY at the four corners of the barrel, with a visible hock notch on the hind pair; feet that terminate in small dark WEDGE tips reading as cloven hooves, never as the long five-toed plantigrade hands every animal in this family walks on; an identical skull on every one — a short, blunt, DOWN-turned muzzle with a rounded ram-like forehead bump and a single hook-shaped ear that curls back on itself like a small horn; a short thick neck carrying the head HIGH and forward at grazing-alert height; and a tail that exits high off the croup and hangs limply down and slightly forward in the same lazy comma on all four. The chassis reads unmistakably as a lamb, ram or young sheep. Coati, Kinkajou, Raccoon and Red Panda are that lamb in tan, gold, grey and rust; three of them additionally get the same banded tail texture pasted onto the same drooping comma, which does not rescue any of them. Nothing in the silhouette is procyonid: no long low back, no plantigrade shuffle, no arched hunch, no hand-like forepaws, no flagpole or prehensile tail carriage.

All three are one drawing. The chassis is a horizontal egg-shaped body with a rounded rump, a topline that rises in a single unbroken arc from the tail base to a small round head parked at the upper LEFT of the mass with no neck junction of any kind — the skull is simply pasted onto the shoulder. Over the flank sits an identical folded-wing oval with the same stippled scallop-texture fill and the same lower-edge sweep, and out of its rear corner runs the same long lanceolate tail exiting bottom-right at the same downward angle on all three. The limb model is identical: two thin bare yellow sticks leaving the silhouette from the same point on the belly's underside midline, each ending in the same three splayed forward toes plus one short hallux, drawn at the same tiny scale relative to the body. Every one sits on the same soft grey ellipse shadow. What that chassis actually READS as is a plump perching passerine — a thrush or quail — not a raptor and not a perched owl: real owls are vertical columns with the feet under the chest and almost no tail, and real eagles have a deep keeled chest and massive scaled feet, and neither silhouette exists here. Desert Owl and Owl are the SAME asset in two hues, sandy-buff versus cocoa-brown, with identical ear-tuft triangles, identical eye placement and identical tail length; I can find no structural difference between them at all. Harpy Eagle is the same chassis recoloured mid-grey with the wings unpinned and stuck out sideways as two flat grey planks and the ear tufts shaved down to a single nub.

This batch holds a single asset, so there is no cross-member chassis to compare and no evidence of a reused body here. Judged on its own growth form, the one ray is built from a single hard-edged wedge: a shallow isoceles triangle with slightly convex leading edges from a blunt snout apex, two sharp lateral wingtips, and a perfectly straight trailing margin cut square across the rear with hard corners. Depth is about half the span, the surface is a flat vertical gradient with a soft blurred speckle pass over it, the tail is one tapering tube leaving the exact rear midline and sweeping down-left to a pale lance barb, and there are no pelvic fins, no fin thickness, no undulation in the wing margin. What that chassis reads as is a paper dart or a squid mantle with googly eyes stuck on rather than a living pectoral disc; the ray identity is carried almost entirely by the whip tail and barb, not by the disc. If a second ray species is added it must not reuse this wedge, because the difference between a stingray, a skate, a manta and an eagle ray lives entirely in the outline of the disc and the shape of the trailing margin.

All three are the same drawing with a hue swap and one added tail tip. The silhouette is identical in every asset: a smooth rounded-triangular mound whose apex sits right-of-centre, a long gentle convex topline sweeping down to a single sharp corner at the lower right, a soft rounded left shoulder, and a flat-ish underside hem — no lateral wingspan anywhere, because both 'wings' are folded down into the same drooping skirt. The head end is a blunt curve with no snout, no mouth, no cephalic lobes and no gill slits; two identical white cartoon eyes with black pupils sit at the same coordinates on all three, each with the same pair of grey oval nostril dots below and outboard. The same thin, evenly tapered whip tail leaves the underside at the same point (just left of centre, from beneath the body rather than from a tail base) and curves down-left to the same terminated length; the same scatter of soft pale blotches and the same detached hard-edged black shadow ellipse to the lower right appear on all three. Only the fill colour changes — slate grey (Eagle Ray), blue-black (Manta Ray), khaki-tan (Stingray) — plus a single pale spearhead added at the Stingray's tail tip. What the shared chassis actually READS as is not a ray at all: it reads as a small draped mound or a pup tent / closed umbrella / jellyfish bell with googly eyes and a string trailing off it. Because the defining wingspan is folded away, none of the three can express its own identity, and the Eagle Ray and Manta Ray are indistinguishable from each other except by colour.

Nine of the fourteen (Butterflyfish, Cardinalfish, Clownfish, Damselfish, Parrotfish, Rabbitfish, Surgeonfish, Tang, Triggerfish) are literally the same drawing with a hue swap. Identical topline: a symmetric egg/almond body whose highest point sits at ~40% of the length, identical body depth (the same fat oval at ~0.62 depth-to-length), identical cross-hatched scale texture stamped over the whole flank, the identical eye — a small black pupil inside a white ring at the same relative x/y in every one — the identical jaw wedge (a shaded triangle scribed under the eye that stands in for a mouth on all nine, so none of them actually has a mouth), the identical five-tooth sawtooth crest sitting on the same third of the back in place of a dorsal fin, the identical single lobe fin under the belly, and the identical soft ellipse cast shadow at the same offset. Only two variables move across the nine: hue, and which of exactly two tails gets attached — a swept crescent (Damselfish, Tang, Surgeonfish, Rabbitfish) or a rounded paddle lobe (Clownfish, Parrotfish, Butterflyfish, Triggerfish). The chassis READS as an aquarium-store 'generic tropical disc fish' — closest to a sunfish or a fat cichlid — and it reads as that nine times in nine colours; Surgeonfish and Tang in particular are the same file twice in two blues, and Clownfish and Parrotfish are the same file twice in orange and cyan. A second, smaller shared chassis carries Blenny, Goby and Wrasse: one elongate spindle that tapers to a point at BOTH ends, high eye at the snout tip, tiny fan tail, and the same hatch texture — it reads as a minnow, and nothing about it is blenny-, goby- or wrasse-specific. Only Angelfish and Lionfish sit off both chassis (different renderer entirely: smooth gradient, no hatch, no cast shadow), and Lionfish escaped the chassis by becoming a sea urchin. Not one fish in this family has a mouth, a gill cover, a pectoral fin distinct from the pelvic lobe, or a species-specific head.

Thirteen of the fourteen are the SAME drawing with the hue changed. The shared chassis is a single egg/ball body whose topline runs from a low shoulder up over a high domed rump and drops vertically at the back; the same crescent hip-swirl highlight is stamped on the flank of every one of them in the same place. There is no neck at all — a wedge head is welded to the front of the egg at the same angle every time, carrying the same round black eye with the catchlight at the same clock position, the same four straight radiating whisker lines, the same white two-tooth incisor block at the muzzle tip, and the same pair of erect pointed ears with a pink inner. The limbs are not limbs: two short dark pegs poke out of the BOTTOM of the belly outline (not from a shoulder or a hip), with no elbow, no stifle, no hock and no foot — every animal is standing on four blunt dowels of identical length. The only things that vary across the set are colour, ear length, and whether a tail tube is drawn and how thick it is. What the chassis actually READS as is a crouched cartoon RABBIT (or a chinchilla plush) — erect pink-lined ears, round tailless crouch, whiskered wedge face — so Capybara, Gopher, Mara, Guinea Pig, Hamster, Lemming, Marmot and Agouti are eight tints of one bunny. The single genuine exception is Beaver, which is drawn on a different, longer, lower body with four separately articulated legs, real pale feet and a crosshatched paddle tail; it proves the pipeline CAN draw a second body and simply is not doing so for the other thirteen. Flying Squirrel, Ground Squirrel, Chipmunk and Jerboa are the bunny chassis with a tail tube pasted on at three different thicknesses.

These are one chassis in seven colours, with a tail accessory swapped on the back end. Every asset shares the identical topline: a single smooth dome that rises over the shoulder, peaks just behind the head and drops almost vertically at the rump, giving the same fat egg/kidney body at the same depth (roughly 1.4 wide to tall) on ALL of them - the packet asks for aspect 0.9 (Squirrel), 2.2 (Voles), 2.8 (Mouse) and 4.4 (Rat) and every one of them renders as the same 1.4 oval. The limb model is identical and is barely a limb model: two short dark peg stubs that leave the silhouette from the BOTTOM edge of the oval near the belly midline, with no shoulder, no elbow, no hip, no hock and no visible upper leg, ending in a blunt toeless rounded foot; the same comma-shaped darker haunch swirl is stamped on the flank of every single animal in the same place at the same angle. The head is the same rounded wedge fused directly to the body with zero neck - no neck carriage exists in this family - carrying the same single round dot eye with the same white catchlight, the same pair of TALL UPRIGHT POINTED pink-lined ears standing well clear of the skull, the same three or four straight whisker lines, and the same white square incisor block at the muzzle tip. What that chassis actually reads as is a running rabbit, or a chinchilla: the bunny ears and the tailless fat egg dominate every read. Where a tail is drawn (Mouse, Rat, Squirrel) the viewer is pulled back toward rodent; where it is not (Prairie Dog, Vole, Water Vole) the animal is simply a bunny in a different brown. Nothing that distinguishes a squirrel from a vole from a prairie dog - eye size, ear size and set, muzzle length, back arch, sitting posture, tail form - varies at all.

These two are NOT drawn on one chassis — they diverge so hard they barely read as the same family. Carrot is built as root-plus-top: a hard-edged tapering cone occupying the lower two thirds with a foliage mass floating above it. Beet is built as foliage only: a low symmetric fan of pointed lanceolate blades radiating from a single hidden hub at the soil line, with no root organ drawn at all. The leaf primitives are different too — Beet uses a solid gradient-filled blade with a midrib and herringbone veins, Carrot uses an open wireframe lattice of little stroked crosses on a grid, which is not a leaf primitive at all. The one thing they do share is the drawing law that the harvest organ is optional: the family reference makes the swollen root the identity in both rows, and only one of the two puts a root on the canvas. The shared silhouette logic is 'symmetric radial fan of leaves rising from one point at the bottom centre', and in Beet that fan is the entire organism, which is why it reads as an agave rather than a beet.

All four are one drawing with a hue swap and nothing else. Shared topline: a short deep loaf-shaped trunk whose back arches in a single smooth dome from shoulder to hip, then drops into a pinched waist before the tail. Shared body depth: identical, roughly 2.2x the trunk length is NOT achieved - the trunk is stubby and deep, closer to a guinea pig than to a long low amphibian. Shared limb form: four identical thin dark twigs that leave the silhouette VERTICALLY from the underside midline and hang straight down with no elbow, no knee, no outward sprawl at all, ending in a tiny angled pad - despite every row specifying 'sprawling'. Shared foot: the same small dark wedge on all sixteen limbs. Shared skull: the same big rounded egg bulb, wider than the neck, carrying one enormous forward-facing cartoon eye with white sclera, a black pupil and a specular dot, plus a curved smiling mouth line and a pale rim-light hook over the crown - identical on the animal whose spec says 'eyes: hidden' and on the one whose spec says 'tiny lidless dot eyes'. Shared neck carriage: none - the head is glued directly onto the shoulder at the same slight downward tilt in all four. Shared tail: the same fat comma-shaped paddle that sweeps up and back OFF the ground, broader than the trunk at its base, with the same duplicated ghost-blob of tail sitting behind it as a stray second layer. Even the ochre spot scatter is reused verbatim - it appears on the 'jet-black' Alpine, on the 'chalk-white unpigmented' Blind, and on the Giant that should be wrinkled and plain. What the chassis actually READS as is a cartoon otter pup or a plush axolotl toy - big-eyed, smiling, deep-bodied, paddle-tailed - not a salamander; the four species are that toy in black, cream, mid-brown and dark brown.

All five are one drawing recoloured. The outline is a symmetric almond/lens that comes to an identical needle point at BOTH ends, so the topline and the belly line are mirror arcs of each other and the widest point sits dead centre on every fish; body depth is the same on all five despite aspects listed from 3.5 to 4.0. There is no skull: no jaw line, no mouth, no lip, no gape anywhere in the family — the head is only a single thin crescent gill arc at about x=0.2 plus a small white-ring-and-black-dot eye pasted at the same coordinate on all five, which is why the snout reads as a knife tip rather than a fish face. Every fin is the same primitive in the same place: a translucent dark rounded dorsal lobe with vertical ray hatching drawn BEHIND the body so it reads as a smoke shadow rather than a fin attached to the topline, a matching dark lobe under the belly, a small pale triangular pectoral fan tucked just behind the gill arc, and one identical caudal — a long swept upper lobe and shorter lower lobe with a deep notch — hinged at the same pinched peduncle. Not one of the five has an adipose fin, though four of the five reference rows demand it. The same diamond-mesh scale stipple and the same soft blotch-mottle generator run over all of them; Char, Salmon and Trout are the same blotch field in orange-red, pink-salmon and olive-gold, and Grayling and Whitefish are that same body with the blotches switched off. What the chassis actually READS as is a generic leaf-shaped fishing-lure pictogram or a sardine-tin silhouette — a shape that says 'fish' and nothing more specific, which is fatal in a family whose five members are separated only by snout shape, dorsal shape and spot polarity.

All four are the same drawing with two sliders moved: hue and body depth. The silhouette in every case is a single lens made of two mirrored arcs meeting at a knife point at the snout and a second knife point at the caudal peduncle; there is no distinct head, no jaw break, no operculum edge, no forehead slope. The dorsal is the same soft translucent blob smeared over the top arc (with the same stray hair-like spikes poking out of it) in all four; the pectoral is the same small grey triangle with radiating spokes planted at the same mid-flank height and the same fraction along the body; the anal fin is the same faint bulge under the belly; the caudal is the same swallow-tail V with the same fan-spoke fill and the same notch depth. Every one carries the identical white ring eye pushed to the extreme front tip, the identical single curved gill arc behind it, the identical repeating diamond/dot scale texture, and the identical soft ellipse drop shadow. Most damning: three of the four (Anchovy, Mackerel, Sardine) have NO MOUTH DRAWN AT ALL - the head simply tapers to a bare point - and Herring's mouth is a single generic curved line. Anchovy, Mackerel and Sardine are literally indistinguishable apart from colour (silver-blue, green, grey-blue) and a slight aspect change; Herring is the same parts with the depth parameter cranked until the lens becomes a disc. What the chassis reads as is a generic aquarium clip-art minnow - a 'fish icon', not any named species.

All ten are the same drawing. The topline is one fat egg-shaped body ball, widest at mid-belly, with no neck and no separate chest; a small round head-bump is stuck onto the upper-left shoulder of that ball at the same angle every time, carrying one identical black eye with a white catchlight. The bill is always the same flat yellow triangle leaving the head-bump horizontally — only its LENGTH changes (stub on Albatross/Gull/Puffin/Skua, long dagger on Guillemot/Petrel/Seabird/Snow Petrel/Tern); not one bill in the batch has a hook, a tube-nostril, a lateral plate or a colour other than yellow-orange. The wing is the same painted grey swoosh that starts as a crescent over the back and exits the right side of the ball as a single grey point past the rump — it is a decal on the sphere, never a folded feather tract with a leading edge. The limbs leave the silhouette from the exact centre of the ball's underside, two thin yellow sticks with three splayed toes, no webbing on any of them, planted on the same soft ellipse of ground shadow. Skull, neck carriage and tail are literally interchangeable. The chassis reads as a plump ground-standing chick or a kiwi — a fluffy round garden bird — and it defeats the family: five of these are specified as posture FLYING (Albatross, Petrel, Skua, Snow Petrel, Tern) and every one of them is standing on legs on a cast shadow. Albatross bolts two extra flat planks onto the ball and Tern cuts a notch into the grey tail-point; those are the only two shape edits in the batch. Everything else is a hue swap: white ball, black ball, brown ball, grey ball.

These two do NOT share one body, and the problem here is the opposite of the twelve-canids case: they do not even share one drawing language. The Pipefish is a horizontal, uniform-depth ribbon with blunt rounded ends, a soft grey rim-light halo, and a dense stippled/dashed paint texture; the Seahorse is a vertical S-curve of flat gouache-orange with hard hairline ring bands, no texture, no rim-light and no painterly shading at all. Topline: pipefish is a dead-straight lens with zero curvature; seahorse is a deep S with a pronounced nuchal hump behind the head. Body depth: pipefish is constant 1/14 of length end to end; seahorse tapers from a thick trunk to a thin tail. Head/skull: pipefish head is simply the last 8% of the same tube with an eye stuck on it and no jaw break; the seahorse has a genuinely separate skull mass with a coronet, a cheek and a distinct snout lobe set at right angles to the neck. Snout: pipefish gets a 1-2px hairline spike, seahorse gets a fat rounded duck-bill lozenge - two unrelated solutions to the same syngnathid tube. Tail: pipefish ends in a second identical hairline spike (so both ends of the animal look the same); seahorse ends in a proper forward-curling prehensile hook with cross-hatched terminal rings. The only genuinely shared habit is a lazy one - both animals get their single fin as a flat semi-transparent blob dropped over/next to the trunk (a grey triangular wedge on the pipefish belly, a detached olive ellipse floating clear of the seahorse's back). If anything this family needs MORE shared chassis, not less: the ringed bony armour that defines Syngnathidae is a crisp banded plate on the seahorse and an almost invisible stipple on the pipefish, so they do not read as relatives.

The two growth forms are genuinely different and are NOT one body: Coral is a wide multi-trunk fan built from thin uniform-width forking strokes, Sponge is a single solid lathe-turned frustum with a rim, so there is no shared topline, no shared base, no shared silhouette. What they DO share is one surface chassis: in both assets the only texture is the same soft-focus blob layer -- scattered circles of varying radius, heavily gaussian-blurred, stamped in a slightly darker/lighter tint of the base hue -- doing duty as coral polyps in one and as sponge pores in the other. In both it sits as an out-of-focus smear that never attaches to the geometry it is supposed to belong to: on Coral the pale pink blobs float BEHIND the branch fan in a cloud instead of cupping the branch surfaces, and on Sponge the brown blobs are painted flat onto the cone with no rim, no depth and no perforation. Both also share the same staging chassis -- a small centered object, well under half the canvas, sitting on an identical soft elliptical floor shadow against the dark blue vignette -- and both share the same stroke language of flat solid fills with a single vertical gradient and zero grain, which is why neither reads as calcified or as living tissue. The shared chassis reads as 'a smooth plastic model with dirt smudges airbrushed on it'. Worse, the Sponge carries four dark peg-shaped nubs poking out of its left and right edges in near-mirror pairs -- a limb/appendage routine leaking onto an organism whose reference explicitly forbids limbs and symmetry.

All nine are literally the same fish sprite with a hue swap and one or two bolt-on decals. The shared chassis is a symmetric lens/leaf-shaped body pointed at BOTH ends, with an identical shallow topline arc and an identical mirrored belly curve, so back and belly are the same shape flipped; the flank carries the same diamond scale-mesh texture on every one, which is a bony-fish cue no shark has. The tail is the same symmetric forked fan with visible fin RAYS on a thin peduncle in all nine - there is no heterocercal shark tail, no long upper lobe, no crescent, anywhere in the family. The dorsal fin is the same faint translucent grey triangle ghosted BEHIND the body rather than standing on the topline, paired with the same ghost blob under the belly and the same thin pectoral sliver leaving the silhouette low at the right; every fin is drawn at the same anchor, the same size, the same washed-out alpha. The head is the same short cone tipped by the same tiny ringed eye at the extreme front point, with the same little cluster of four to five diagonal tick marks on the shoulder standing in for gill slits, and the same drop-shadow ellipse beneath. What the chassis actually READS as is a mackerel or herring - a generic bony fish - and no colour change or decal rescues it: the family is one mackerel in nine paint jobs, with Basking given a flat disc glued to its face, Hammerhead given a detached floating bar, Great White/Mako/Tiger given a row of white spikes outside the jaw line, and Whale given grey blotches.

Yes — all five are one body with a hue and a fur-texture swap. The topline is dead level from withers to hip on every asset, then drops abruptly to a rump that carries NO TAIL on any of the five. Body depth is the same slab-sided barrel (roughly 45% of frame height) with a flat horizontal brisket line, so no animal here has a chest that is deeper than another's. The limbs are four straight untapered posts of near-identical length front and rear, with no stifle, no hock angle and no pastern anywhere in the family; they leave the silhouette well INBOARD of the barrel's ends, so every asset has the same slab of body overhanging fore and aft of its feet. The foot is the same small blunt dark stub with no cloven split. The skull is the same wedge on all five, ending in an oversized bulbous down-curved muzzle that overhangs the mouth line — a tapir's or a Shire horse's nose, not a caprine's — with one large ringed eye set high. There is effectively no neck: the head is docked straight onto the shoulder and carried horizontal on every one. Horns are the only differentiator attempted, and three of the five (Goat, Ibex, Sheep) wear the identical short pale ram-curl. What the chassis actually READS as is a carved wooden pull-toy lamb: a stumpy tailless woolly ram with a tapir snout, recoloured tan for the Chamois, white for the Goat, cream for the Ibex and Sheep, and golden-shaggy for the Takin. There is no bison in the Takin, no antelope in the Chamois and no goat in the Goat.

This is one bird recoloured seven times, not a family. Every asset shares the identical chassis: a fat egg-shaped body with its long axis horizontal, the same single swooping crescent wing-scallop stroked across the flank at the same angle, the same small ball head tucked at the front-top-left with no neck at all, the same short straight yellow-orange cone bill of about one head-length, the same single dark bead eye placed dead-centre on the cheek, the same short brown wedge tail spiking off to the right at the same downward angle, the same pair of thin yellow legs leaving the belly at the same two points with the same forward-toe-plus-back-toe foot and the same slightly straddled stance, and the same soft ellipse drop shadow. Only the hue of the body fill and the density of the mottling speckles change: white-grey (Avocet), buff (Curlew, Sandpiper), mid-brown (Godwit), near-black (Oystercatcher), grey-cream (Plover), dark umber (Snipe). What the chassis actually READS as is a downy game-bird chick or a stubby-billed quail poult - a plump, neckless, short-billed ground chick - and NOT a wader. The bill is the entire diagnostic axis of this family (upswept needle, long downcurve, long straight dagger, orange chisel, stubby pigeon nub) and the chassis renders exactly one bill for all seven, so the family's whole identity space collapses. Leg length, body depth and neck carriage - the other axes that separate a plover from a godwit - are likewise frozen. Plover is the only asset the chassis accidentally flatters, because a plover is genuinely round-bodied and short-billed.

All three are the identical drawing with only hue and markings swapped. Shared verbatim: a dead-straight horizontal topline running from croup to shoulder with no scapular rise and no lumbar arch; a deep slab-sided barrel whose belly line sweeps UP into a tucked flank between the fore and hind pairs, the classic hoofed-stock silhouette; four straight column limbs that leave the silhouette at the extreme four corners of the barrel rather than beneath it, each with a visible pastern band low on the cannon and terminating in a small blunt blocky foot that reads as a hoof, not a paw — no toes, no digitigrade wrist break, no pad. The skull is the same long tapering wedge muzzle on every one, carried level and jammed straight onto the shoulder with effectively ZERO neck, one oversized round amber eye set high and far back on the wedge, and two small triangular ears pinned at the very top-rear of the skull. Nothing about this chassis is feline: cats need a short rounded skull with a foreshortened muzzle, a flexible arched spine, a slung low chest, digitigrade paws, and a long counterweight tail. What this chassis actually READS as is a stocky shetland pony or donkey foal, and the three assets are that same pony in appaloosa spots, cream, and zebra stripes respectively.

All three are the SAME image with the hue swapped — not a family style, a single re-tinted sprite. Every asset is one flat closed torus of constant-diameter tube coiled clockwise into a ring with the identical inner hole, the identical outer diameter, the identical break where the body crosses over itself at the upper left, and the identical drop shadow ellipse at the identical offset. The head leaves the coil at exactly the same point (lower right of the ring), at the same angle, at the same tiny scale, as the same narrow rounded lozenge no wider than the neck, with the same single white bead eye in the same position and the same crimson Y-shaped forked tongue at the same 30-degree downward flick. Not one of the three shows a tail: the tube simply merges back into the ring, so there is no taper, no tail tip, and therefore no head-to-tail read at all. The body ribbing is the same on all three — regular ladder rungs wrapped the WHOLE circumference including the dorsal surface — so the chassis reads less like a scaled serpent than a ribbed rubber vacuum hose or a segmented annelid coiled on a table, with a small toy head glued to one end.
