The aspect field varies (8 / 1.3 / 8) but the drawing does not: the Mountain Viper at aspect 1.3 is the SAME slender 8:1 rope as the two colubrids, so the one asset in the batch that was supposed to be stocky is indistinguishable from the ones that were supposed to be slim. What the chassis actually reads as: a coiled hose in grey, a coiled hose in olive, and a coiled hose in tan.

All nine are one drawing. The chassis is a near-circular egg body with its widest point at mid-height, a topline that rises in one unbroken dome from bill to rump with NO neck break and no shoulder, a small ball head glued onto the front-upper-left of the dome so the skull sits INSIDE the body outline rather than on a neck, and a tiny wedge bill of the same length and angle on every bird (only its hue changes: yellow, orange, gold). Every bird carries the identical folded-wing mark — a single comma/hook stroke swept from the shoulder down and back across the flank, closing in a scroll — and the identical tail: one stubby dagger spike leaving the body at mid-height on the right, never forked, never square, never notched, at the same angle on all nine. The legs are the same two thin yellow sticks with three splayed forward toes, and on all nine they leave the silhouette from the BOTTOM CENTRE of the belly rather than from the rear third, which is a galliform leg placement, not a passerine one; all nine stand on the same elliptical drop shadow. What the chassis actually READS as is a plump ground-nesting galliform — a quail, partridge or day-old chicken chick — not a songbird. The only per-species edits are hue, a surface fleck pattern, and an optional 6-pixel spike tuft on the crown (Cardinal, Lark). Cardinal and Tanager are literally the same red bird distinguished only by that tuft; Sparrow and Lark are the same sandy bird distinguished only by that tuft. The three 'flying' entries are not a second chassis either — Swallow and Swift are the same egg squashed horizontally, still wearing planted legs and a ground shadow, so they read as a bird lying prone rather than in flight.

Four of the five (Alligator Lizard, Frilled Lizard, Gila Monster, Horned Lizard) are the same drawing recoloured. Shared parts, part by part: the topline is one smooth unbroken convex arc from the neck over the back to the hips with no shoulder, no hip, no vertebral break; the body depth is a single plump ovoid egg with the identical top-left radial highlight and the identical soft blotch field scattered across it; the limbs are dark-brown tapered pegs with NO feet and NO toes on any of the four, and they leave the silhouette at the same two anchor points on the belly line (one just behind the head, one just ahead of the hips) so the animal always stands on two visible legs plus a ghost pair; the skull is the same rounded wedge snout with one ivory almond eye carrying a vertical slit and one straight ruled mouth line (Frilled Lizard swaps the mouth for a pink gape but keeps the same skull); there is no neck at all, the head is butted straight onto the front of the egg; and the tail is the same crescent sweeping off the rear, thick on Gila and Horned Lizard (identically curled up and forward like a handle), thinned to a rod on Alligator Lizard and to a hairline wire on Frilled Lizard. Gila Monster and Horned Lizard in particular are the SAME image twice: same egg, same up-curled fat tail, same four brown pegs, same snout — only hue plus a pasted spike spray tells them apart. What the chassis reads as is not a lizard at all but a chubby spotted newt or salamander with peg legs, onto which each species' one identifying gadget (frill disc, horn spray, orange hue) has been stuck. The Chameleon is the one genuine exception and shows what the family should look like: a laterally compressed leaf body, a real dorsal crest, stilt legs with forked grasping feet, a spiral tail and a branch to stand on.

This batch holds a single member, so chassis REUSE across siblings cannot be demonstrated from within it — but the one asset is plainly built from the generic small-arthropod chassis this project keeps reaching for, and that is worth naming because it is what a stick insect must NOT be built from. The parts are: a smooth sphere for the head carrying one black dot eye, a SECOND sphere immediately behind it for the thorax (two beads in a row), then a segmented carrot — wide where it meets the thorax and tapering to a needle point — for the abdomen. The topline is therefore bumpy (ball, ball, then a long downward-tapering cone) rather than a constant-diameter twig. Limbs are five identical unjointed straight pins that leave the silhouette from a single row along the ventral midline, all raked backward and downward at nearly the same angle, with no femur/tibia bend, no left/right pairing, no tarsal feet, and several ending in mid-air above the cast shadow. Two long straight antennae sweep forward-up from the head and are the only correct element. Assembled, the chassis reads as a wingless mosquito or a damselfly that has lost its wings — a bead-head-plus-tapered-tail bug — and not as a twig. Any future leaf insect or phasmid added to this family must be re-derived from a uniform-diameter cylinder with jointed, elongated legs, not colour-swapped onto this one.

Yes — eight of the nine are the same lens-shaped fish stretched to different aspect ratios and recolored. Shared topline: one smooth convex arc from snout to peduncle with the same faint low dorsal hump (visible identically on Barreleye, Lanternfish, Fangtooth, Viperfish, Oarfish). Shared body depth logic: an almond/lens with its deepest point ~40% back from the snout, simply squashed (Anglerfish, Blobfish, Fangtooth are the fat setting; Barreleye and Lanternfish the medium; Dragonfish, Viperfish, Oarfish the stretched setting). Shared 'limb form': one small triangular pectoral wedge on the flank and one flat triangular tail flag on a short peduncle, the same wedge at the same angle on Anglerfish, Blobfish, Fangtooth, Barreleye, Lanternfish, Viperfish and Tripod Fish. Shared skull: there is no skull — the head is just the front end of the body oval, with no jaw line, no gill cover and no mouth; teeth are stamped on as loose white triangles floating over the face (Anglerfish, Fangtooth, Viperfish, Dragonfish all wear the same spike decal). Shared eye: one white disc with a black pupil and thin outer ring at the same relative spot, the same size whether the row asks for 'small' (Anglerfish) or 'prominent' (Lanternfish) — the eye spec is not being read. Shared decal kit: a crosshatch scale mesh over the flank (even on Blobfish, whose reference says no scales), a chain of equal cyan belly dots (Barreleye, Dragonfish, Lanternfish, Viperfish), and an identical drop-shadow ellipse under every asset at the same size and offset. What the chassis reads as is a generic pet-shop tetra/piranha silhouette that has been recolored and rubber-stamped with teeth, dots and scales; the abyssal specifics (illicium stalk, chin barbel, dorsal lure whip, ribbon body, pitted skull) are exactly what the chassis cannot produce. Tripod Fish is the only asset that escapes, and only because the three stilts change the outline — its body, tail wedge and eye are still the chassis.

This batch holds a single asset, so cross-asset chassis reuse cannot be measured inside it — but the one body present is itself a generic blank rather than a killifish-specific form, and that is worth flagging for the wider sweep. The chassis is a perfectly symmetric almond/lens: the topline and the ventral line are mirror images of each other, both tapering to a sharp point at the head end and to an equally sharp point at the tail end, with maximum depth at dead centre. There is no head demarcation of any kind — no operculum line, no jaw, no mouth, no cheek — so the 'head' is simply the front third of the lens narrowing to a spearpoint, and the only thing marking it as a head is a small white eye ring parked on the dorsal contour. Neck carriage and limb form do not apply, but the fin model is the same generic solution seen on other fish blanks in this project: dorsal and anal are soft dark smudges painted BEHIND the crisp body outline with no rays, no leading edge and no attachment, and the caudal is a separate darker near-rectangular slab hung off the rear point by a hairline join with no caudal peduncle. What the chassis actually READS as is a leaf — a pointed green almond with a paddle stuck on the back — not a fish with a skull, a gill cover and a mouth.

These are one tree drawn twice with a leaf-decal and fruit-decal swap. Shared verbatim: a single smooth, untextured, gently tapered brown pole trunk of the same width, standing dead-centre and occupying the lower ~45% of the frame with zero branching, zero fork, zero bark relief and zero root flare; the same soft-edged oval green crown blob seated at the same height with the same inner radial glow and the same dark green core-to-bright-rim gradient; the same starburst fringe of small leaf sprigs pinned around the crown perimeter and radiating outward/upward at even intervals; the same handful of harvest tokens scattered across the front face of the crown blob; and the same flat dark ground ellipse at the same scale. Nothing that distinguishes an oak from a willow in life — crown architecture, branch habit, twig direction, bark, silhouette proportion — varies at all; only leaf blade outline (spiky-serrated vs long lance) and harvest sprite (brown sphere vs pale beaded string) change. What the chassis actually READS as is the child's-drawing lollipop tree: a green ball on a brown stick. Because the trunk carries no branches, the crown floats as a decorated pom-pom, and both species inherit an upward-radiating leaf spray — which is fatal for willow, whose whole identity is downward-hanging whips, and useless for oak, whose identity is a wide low-spreading limb frame.

These two are the same drawing with a different bill decal. Both share an identical fat egg-shaped body with a high domed topline that peaks just behind the shoulder and rolls in one unbroken curve down to the rump; identical body depth (the belly sits low, almost touching the ground shadow, so there is no visible leg length above the tarsus); the same single crescent wing-oval scribed onto the flank with the same interior swirl strokes; the same short pointed tail-wedge exiting the right side of the silhouette at mid-body height rather than off the rump; the same tiny round pea-head with no neck at all, set directly against the shoulder at the same 10-o'clock position; the same beady white-ringed eye at the same offset inside that head; the same pair of stubby yellow three-toe feet planted dead centre under the belly at the same angle; and the same soft grey elliptical drop shadow. Every one of those parts is pixel-comparable between the two files. What the chassis actually READS as is a duckling or a coot chick — a squat, neckless, short-tailed swimming bird — and neither a hornbill nor a toucan is that animal (both are long-tailed, long-bodied, upright-perching arboreal birds). The only differences in the batch are body value (charcoal grey vs near-black) and the bill decal: a plain yellow wedge on the Hornbill, a slightly longer yellow wedge with one orange band on the Toucan. No casque, no bib, no bare facial skin, no long tail, no perching stance appears on either. This is one pony in two colours.

All three are the same lollipop tree with a different sticker set. The trunk is byte-for-byte the same object in every image: a straight, untapered brown bar of identical width, identical height and identical X position, with the same rounded cap at the ground end, no root flare, no taper, no fork, no branch of any kind — it simply enters the underside of the crown and stops. Under each one sits the same soft black elliptical drop shadow at the same offset. The crown is the same construction three times: a blurred airbrushed green cloud blob roughly as wide as it is tall, centred on the trunk axis, with one leaf stamp repeated ~20 times around the blob's PERIMETER, every copy rotated to point radially outward from the blob centre, so all three get the same pincushion/spoke rim and the same empty soft-focus middle. The harvest is handled identically too — 4 or 5 hard-edged decals pasted flat on the face of the crown at similar radius, sitting on top of the foliage rather than hanging from anything. What actually varies between the three is the leaf stamp (a pinnate comb for Acacia and Tamarind, a jagged palmate spike for Baobab), the crown hue (grey-green, saturated green, yellow-green), and which decal is pasted on. Because the trunk carries all the woody identity in a tree and it is the same stick every time, the chassis reads as a child's cotton-ball-on-a-stick tree — and it destroys the two species here whose identity lives in the trunk and branch architecture, since a baobab without its barrel and an acacia without its bare bole and flat layered canopy are just this lollipop in two colours.

All four are drawn on one identical three-bead insect chassis with only hue and bolt-on accessories changed. The shared parts are exact: a smooth sphere head bead carrying ONE large glossy black dome eye with a specular hotspot on the near side and two thin curved antenna filaments off the crown; a second smooth featureless ovoid thorax bead that is the high point of the topline; a third ovoid abdomen bead finished with the same parallel incised ribs in every asset; and the same topline in all four (head bead low and forward, thorax bead crested, abdomen sloping away rearward). The limb model is identical and identically wrong everywhere: straight tapered dark spikes with no femur/tibia break, no joint, no tarsus and no foot, leaving the silhouette straight down from the underside of the thorax and abdomen beads rather than from a thorax that owns all six legs. Every asset floats above the same detached soft ellipse ground shadow with no contact point. What the chassis READS as is a generic cartoon ANT — the aphid is that ant in green, the cicada is that ant in grey with a fan of straws stuck on the back, the water bug is that ant in gold scaled up with a triangular arm added, and the strider is that ant in brown with the spike legs stretched to the frame edges. The only real per-species work is the raptorial foreleg on the water bug; nothing about the head, thorax, abdomen, antennae, legs or eye distinguishes one true bug from another.

This family has exactly one member, so there is no shared-chassis comparison to make — nothing here is a recoloured sibling of anything else. Judged on its own growth form, the single turtle is nevertheless built from an assembled-parts chassis rather than one animal: a semi-transparent domed cap, a separate rectangular trunk slab beneath it, and two straight untapered leg columns dropped off the slab's underside. The topline is a smooth low dome, body depth is a flat box, the limbs leave the silhouette from the bottom face of that box (not from under a shell rim), the feet are square pads with scratched-in toe lines, the skull is a small wedge with a yellow beak and a single round eye, and the neck is a short horizontal stub with no visible attachment into the body. If more turtles are added later, the risk to watch is exactly this: the dome-on-a-box construction is generic enough that it would recolour into a tortoise, a terrapin and a sea turtle without any of them changing shape.

Five of the six (Box Turtle, Pond Turtle, Sea Turtle, Snapping Turtle, Tortoise) are one drawing with the hue swapped. Shared parts, item by item: the SAME high hemispherical carapace whose topline rises in a single smooth arc from a pale highlighted rim and is filled with the same concentric spiderweb fan of arcs radiating from the rear quarter; the SAME flat horizontal plastron slab cutting the belly at exactly the same height, leaving the same wide open gap between shell edge and legs; the SAME two rectangular column legs, front and rear identical, dropping vertically from under the shell rim with the same three tiny notches scratched into the flat bottom edge for toes (no scales, no claws, no ankle, no foot mass); the SAME rounded head blob with one white ring eye and a small downturned wedge beak, carried on the SAME short thick horizontal neck that exits the shell at mid-height and never varies in length, wrinkle or carriage; and the SAME small triangular wedge hanging under the throat on the HEAD end of every animal. What that chassis reads as is one specific organism: a generic cartoon tortoise. The Tortoise and Box Turtle assets are effectively the same picture in two browns; the Pond Turtle is that picture in green even though its own reference note says the shell must NOT be high-domed like a tortoise; the Sea Turtle is that tortoise with the leg columns swapped for two short lobes; the Snapping Turtle is that tortoise with the throat wedge stretched into a long spike. Only the Softshell Turtle changes the carapace (a genuinely flat mottled pancake, correct, and the one real variation in the batch) and even it reuses the identical legs, neck and head blob. Nothing in this family varies in limb form, limb attachment point, foot, skull, neck carriage or tail placement; only colour, one lobe shape and one spike length change.

Family-wide this is a grab-bag of unrelated taxa (a lemur, an insect, two corals, three fish, an octopus, a bat, a siphonophore) so there is no single chassis across all ten — but two exact-duplicate pairs sit inside it, which is the same defect at smaller scale. Cold-Water Fish and Deep-Sea Fish are ONE fish drawn twice: identical fusiform outline and body depth, the same low arched topline cresting at the same fraction of the body, the same small soft triangular dorsal at the same station, the same swept solid wedge caudal with the same shallow notch, the same dark chevron pectoral in the same spot, the same tiny white ring-eye at the same height, and the same diagonal diamond scale mesh. Only the hue changes (steel blue to plum) plus a bolted-on row of cyan photophore beads; nothing bathypelagic was modelled. Cold-Water Coral and Deep-Water Coral are likewise ONE colony drawn twice: the same fan of five or six rounded trunk columns, the same dichotomous branch tree with the same crown width and the same fine terminal twigs, the same scatter of soft round polyp beads low on the trunks (never at the tips), the same ground-shadow ellipse. Only the hue changes, white to crimson, which is exactly the colour the Deep-Water reference forbids. Mahi-Mahi is on a THIRD, unrelated fish chassis (a deep round disc), so the three fish do not even agree with each other about what a fish is. What the shared fish chassis actually reads as is a generic aquarium trout; what the shared coral chassis reads as is a leafless winter shrub.

The batch holds a single asset, so there is no sibling to compare it against and no shared-chassis verdict can be earned here — but the one plant present is visibly built from the generic stock herb chassis rather than from Rudbeckia: one perfectly straight unbranched vertical stem of constant width, eight strictly OPPOSITE pairs of the identical lanceolate blade (same outline, same single midrib highlight, same upswept angle, only scaled down toward the tip) forming a mechanical leaf-ladder that reads as a fern frond or a clip-art 'plant' glyph, and one small radial daisy token stuck on the apex. The reference calls for ALTERNATE leaves on a rough stem and the render gives opposite pairs; the reference calls for a basal-heavy bristly herb and the render gives a smooth green wire. Nothing in the silhouette below the flower head is species-specific — swap the head token and the same stalk would serve any of a hundred herbs, which is exactly the leaf-ladder-reuse defect the packet warns about, visible even in a family of one.

Not one chassis across all 14, but a small kit of reused chassis with the hue swapped, which is the same defect. The clearest case: Bracket Fungus and Chicken-of-the-Woods are the SAME picture - the same flat dark-brown rectangular post pinned left of centre, the same four lens/canoe blades leaving the post at the same four heights with the same thin dark seam line above each, the same tapered point at the outer end - and the only difference is that one set of blades is cream and the other is ice-blue. Nothing about growth-band ridging, thickness, or pore surface distinguishes them; the shared chassis reads as four white feathers or canoe hulls stuck to a fence post. The second case: Death Cap and Destroying Angel are one object - a hard-edged half-dome cap, a white radial fan flaring under the cap rim, a perfectly straight constant-width cylindrical shaft, a flat circular collar disc slid onto the shaft a third of the way down, and a rounded solid pedestal foot - and both read as a 1930s domed table lamp rather than a mushroom; only the cap hue (green vs white) changes. Chanterelle and Bioluminescent Mushroom share a third: a flattened disc cap with a dark centre plate sitting on a thin uniform post, repeated 3-4 times in a row on one shadow ellipse - a row of patio umbrellas. The whole batch also shares one render language: a hard vector silhouette with a single vertical gradient, no fleshy surface, no substrate (no wood, no litter, no soil) under anything, and a single soft grey shadow ellipse under every subject regardless of what the organism actually grows on.

This batch is not twelve organisms, it is THREE templates hue-swapped plus two one-offs. Template A (the 'shelf' chassis) is used verbatim by Oyster Mushroom, Shelf Fungus and Turkey Tail: the same dark rounded-corner vertical post pinned to the left third of the canvas at the same width and the same height, the same sharply-pointed lozenge blade with the same internal pale swoosh arc and the same thin dark spine skimming its top edge, the same alternating left-inset stagger, the same left-to-right size taper. Only the blade COUNT (4 / 5 / 6) and the fill hue (amber, crimson, tan) change — nothing about the outline, the margin, the underside or the attachment differs. That chassis does not read as a bracket fungus at all: the pointed lozenges read as flame licks, canoe hulls or corn kernels stuck into a fence post, and because the blades are pointed and unbanded, Turkey Tail's concentric rings and Shelf Fungus's flat-topped semicircular staircase are both simply absent. Template B (the 'blob' chassis) is used verbatim by Mildew, Mold and Yeast: the identical lumpy pentagon silhouette with the identical notch on the upper-left shoulder, the identical soft halo glow, the identical scatter of round speckles at the identical density and the identical dark vignette; only hue (brown / green / beige) and speckle colour change. It reads as a speckled rock or a potato, not as powder on a leaf, not as hyphae with spore heads, not as budding cells. Template C is the tiny cap-and-stem doll shared by Porcini and Shiitake — a smooth dome on a straight pale cylinder, both rendered at roughly a sixth of the frame so the diagnostic detail (bulbous barrel stem, pore sponge, cracked cap, veil fringe) has no room to exist. The two remaining pieces, Maitake and Reindeer Lichen, share a fourth composition: a broad flat-topped canopy floating above a narrow pale base, which is a tree crown, not a fungal fruiting body. Morel is the only asset in the batch that carries its own purpose-built geometry.

Yes — 11 of the 14 assets sit on just four reused bodies with nothing changed but hue. (1) THE ROD CHASSIS carries five species (Acidophile, Cryophile, Halophile, Methanogen, Nitrogen-Fixing): the same ~8-11 identical capsules with hemispherical caps, the same length/thickness distribution, the same shallow top-left lit gradient, the same faint mid-body division seam on two or three of them, and the same loose diagonal scatter across an empty frame — recoloured red, ice-blue, magenta, grey-lilac and salmon. Halophile and Nitrogen-Fixing differ only in saturation of the same pink. (2) THE FILAMENT CHASSIS carries Cyanobacteria and Iron-Oxidizing Bacteria: four gently-arcing near-horizontal strands stacked one above the other, each with a single sphere bead planted at its midpoint and the same ladder-hatch running the length, alternating a lit strand with a shadowed one — teal in one, orange in the other, and otherwise the same drawing. (3) THE CILIATE-ELLIPSE CHASSIS carries Euglena and Paramecium: the identical tilted ellipse at the identical angle, the identical all-round bristle fringe, and the identical interior furniture of two pale outlined circles flanking a dark oval with a short straight tick beside them — green in one, khaki in the other. (4) THE GOLD WIREFRAME carries Diatom and Dinoflagellate: thin yellow outline geometry on black with regular hatch (parallel in the ellipse, radial in the disc) and no painted body at all. What the family READS as is a set of colour swatches rather than organisms: 'medicine capsules floating in black', 'a stack of caterpillar noodles', 'a fuzzy olive lozenge', 'a gold dartboard'. Compounding it, every single asset floats on the same near-black navy void with a faint vignette — not one of the fourteen renders the habitat its must-read demands (acid water and iron floc, ice crystals and brine veins, salt crystals, anoxic sediment and methane bubbles, root-nodule tissue, ochre sludge), so the environment cue that is the ONLY thing separating five of these species from each other is missing across the board.

Not one chassis across all six, but three of them are literally one primitive at three aspect ratios. Radiation-Resistant Microbe, Sulfur-Oxidizing Bacteria and Thermophile are all drawn from the SAME glossy lozenge: a capsule with an identical upper-left specular hotspot, a mid-tone body and a dark lower-right rim. At aspect 1 it is the bead in the coccus chain; at aspect 2 it is the Thermophile rod; at aspect 8+ bent along a spline it is the sulfur filament, and the lone sphere sitting on each filament is that same bead dropped in at aspect 1. Change nothing but length and hue and you get all three assets. The other three break form (a flat 2-D wireframe disc, a ball tiled with overlapping lens-scales, a soft speckled ellipse) but share a second, worse chassis: the COMPOSITION. All six are one object centred in an empty near-black void with no medium, no substrate, no water, no snow, no sediment, no steam and no scale cue - so the four assets whose scale is declared 'field of many' are each rendered as a single isolated specimen. The environment is exactly what carries the identity of red tide, snow algae, sulfur mats and thermophile mats, and it is absent in every one of them. What the shared chassis reads as is a lab diagram of one generic bacterium, re-lit in a different colour.

Yes — this batch is two clone-stamps plus three one-offs. Eight of the fourteen (s2, s3, s10, s12, s13, s14, s18, s19) are the SAME quadruped chassis with only hue, spot/stripe decals, leg-pair count and bolt-on dorsal plates/horn/glow-orbs changed: identical topline (a low arch that rises into a short thick neck at the RIGHT of frame, every single one facing right), identical body depth (a deep uniform sausage barrel with no ribcage-to-flank taper and no shoulder or hip mass — the forelimb blob is a separate lozenge pasted over the barrel), identical limb form (short featureless cylindrical tubes of constant diameter, no elbow, stifle, hock or pastern), identical exit point (the tubes drop straight down out of the very bottom edge of the barrel rather than out of a shoulder or a hip, so every animal is a barrel on dowels), identical foot (a small lumpy dark pad with two or three nick-cut toes, no ankle), identical skull (one generic rounded snout-blob with a single large round eye set far forward, a dot nostril and a smiling mouth line — the same meerkat/weasel head on the leopard, the six-legged plated one, the unicorn one and the eight-legged one alike), identical neck carriage (head held horizontal and jutting forward-right at the same angle on all eight) and identical tail root (a bottlebrush/feather plume off the left rear at the same height). Adding a third or fourth leg pair does not change the chassis, it repeats the same dowel. Separately, s0, s1 and s17 are ONE tortoise rendered three times in rust, pale blue and gold — geometrically identical down to the concentric shell arcs, the beak, the flipper and the two visible rectangular legs, with nothing but a hue rotation between them. Only s11 (a jellyfish/mushroom on noodle stalks), s16 (a legless spiked grub) and s15 (a broken fish) sit off the two stamps. Read as a set, the dominant chassis reads as one plastic barrel-bodied pony toy with a meerkat head, reissued in twelve paint schemes.

Nine of the fourteen (h0-s4, s5, s6, s8, s9, h1-s1, s11, s13, s14) are one body in nine paint jobs. Identical topline: a dead-level barrel that steps up at the withers into a long neck arcing forward at the same ~40 degrees in every one. Identical body depth: a single fat sausage with a SEPARATE overlapping oval shoulder/haunch mass whose hard seam is visible in all nine at the same place behind the neck. Identical limb form: featureless tapered tubes with no elbow, stifle, hock or muscle, leaving the silhouette straight down from the extreme underside of the barrel with no shoulder or haunch to emerge from, ending in the same dark splayed three-toe boot pad. Identical skull: a small rounded wedge with a blunt down-turned muzzle carrying one oversized cartoon eye with a white catchlight, set at the same angle every time. Identical tail root, high off the rump, either a thin whip or the same brush tip. What varies is only hue, a decal-like surface pattern stamped on the mid-barrel, an optional horn/antler pair, and the leg COUNT (four or six). What the chassis READS as is a stubby toy llama-meerkat: a long-necked plush quadruped, and it is the same plush quadruped whether it is painted as a leopard (s8), a goat (s9), a striped hexapod (s5, s13, s14) or a bioluminescent moose (h1-s11). A SECOND shared chassis carries h0-s7 and h1-s12: a horizontal chain of overlapping spheres for a torso, the same crescent sail on the back, the same thin neck to a tiny head, the same spiked tail, differing only in whether the legs are ball feet or hairline sticks. Only three assets escape the two chassis entirely - the fish (h1-s0), the tortoise (h1-s10) and the snake (h1-s15) - and those three are the only ones a stranger would name correctly on sight.

At the top level this batch is genuinely varied — five distinct body plans appear across fourteen assets: a long-necked barrel quadruped (s16, s2, s4, s6, s18), a torpedo fish with a forked caudal fin (s3, s5, h2-s0, h2-s1), a radial dome-and-fringe bell (s17, s9, and the turtle shell in s7 uses the same ribbed dome primitive), a spined sphere (s8), and a segmented many-legged worm (s19). But INSIDE the largest group the one-pony defect is fully present. The five quadrupeds share every part: the same near-horizontal topline that runs flat from withers to croup and then drops in a single soft curve; the same shallow slab torso whose depth never changes with the animal; the same limb — a straight untapered post with no elbow, stifle or hock, all four the same length, all four leaving the silhouette from the extreme corners of the belly so the animal stands like a table; the same rounded pad foot with three faint toe grooves; the same S-neck of two tubes rising off the front corner at the same angle; and the same skull, a lozenge with a rounded muzzle, one oversized round eye placed dead centre, and a smile-line mouth. Put s16, s4, s6 and s18 side by side and the only real differences are hue, the surface markings, and one bolt-on accessory (dorsal plates, a sail, stripes, spots) — the underlying animal reads as the same plush toy pony every time, and s2 is that pony with a third pair of legs added. The two jellyfish, s17 and s9, are worse than that: they are the same bell, the same eight tentacles in the same positions, and the same three ocelli, differing only in the bell's panelling artifact. The fish group is more honest — h2-s0 is deep-bodied and h2-s1 is a slender almond — but s3 and s5 are the identical hull in two colours.

Nine of the fourteen (s2, s3, s5, s10, s12, s13, s16, s17, s18) are drawn on one identical chassis, and s11 and s15 are that same skeleton with extra sticks bolted on. The shared parts are specific and unmistakable: a long horizontal lozenge barrel with a flat, faintly sagging topline and no ribcage-to-flank transition; a short thick neck that rises at the RIGHT end only, always at the same angle, into a small rounded blob skull carrying one large round eye and a stubby forward muzzle bar; four cylindrical, taper-free legs that leave the silhouette straight DOWN from the underside of the barrel at its extreme front and rear corners, with no shoulder mass, no hip mass and no elbow or stifle, ending in the same little three-lobe pad; and a thin whip tail that exits the LEFT rear at a low angle and ends in a feather plume. Neck carriage is identical in every one of them. What changes between assets is only the dorsal decoration (radial fan sail on s5/s10/s18, rounded plates on s2, spikes on s11, branched antlers on s13, curled horns on s16/s17, nothing on s3/s12), the leg length, the hue and the pattern decal. What the chassis actually READS as is a stubby show pony or a dachshund: a barrel on four posts with an ornament glued to its spine. The three genuine exceptions are s4 (a fish), s14 (a jellyfish bell) and s19 (a fungal fan) — those escape the pony, but s14 and s19 share their own defect, a soft blurred no-edge render that looks like it came from a different engine.

The four fauna are genuinely different body plans (a domed bell-and-tentacle jelly, a lateral fusiform fish, a low limbless segmented sail-back, a radial spined urchin) and share no topline, limb form or skull — so the batch as a whole is not one chassis. The flora, however, are not fourteen designs but four templates with parameters swapped, and inside each template the reuse is blatant. Template A ('fan shrub'): flora-h0-s0, s14 and s16 share the identical tapered cone-stub trunk, the identical splayed fan of straight rod stems leaving that stub at the same angles, the same terminal berry clusters and the same 35%-of-frame footprint — only leaf primitive (lozenge vs starburst) and hue (red vs gold) change; s0 and s16 are the same plant twice. Template B ('skewer stack'): s13 and s17 are the same generator — one hairline vertical stick with N flat untextured primitives threaded on it, largest at the bottom, shrinking upward — with the primitive swapped from triangle to ellipse; neither has bark, taper, root flare or any foliage texture, and both read as clip-art rather than as painted organisms. Template C ('blob on a rod'): s10 and s11 share a perfectly straight, untapered, rounded-end capsule trunk with no branching whatsoever, capped by a soft amorphous cloud blob. Template D ('teal slab'): s1 and s12 are the same broken scene — an unexplained hard-edged opaque teal bar spanning the bottom, above which sit blurred white-headed pin stalks with no plant structure. What the flora chassis actually READS as, collectively, is 'a vertical stick with something stuck on top' — a stem-and-topper generator, not a set of plants.

At the top level this batch is NOT one chassis in fourteen colours — the archetypes genuinely differ (column, radial rosette, sinuous vine, weeping strands, stacked discs, twig shrub, canopy tree, blade bundle, single flower). But there IS a hard sub-chassis repeated four times and it is the worst thing in the batch: flora-h0-s3, flora-h0-s7, flora-h0-s9 and flora-h1-s1 are the SAME drawing with only the hue swapped (grey, ruddy orange, cream, purple). In all four the stem is an identical dead-straight, perfectly untapered dark stick of the same width, rising from the same black ellipse shadow at the same x, to the same height; the same tiny three-prong dark fork sits at the same point near the top; and the same flat horizontal pancake slab is pasted on top of the fork with a straight underside and a jagged straight top edge. What that chassis actually READS as is a mop or a cafe table — not a canopy — because the slab has no lobes, no branch structure entering it, no depth and no silhouette breakup. Two lesser repeats also exist: flora-h0-s6 and flora-h0-s8 share one fan-of-twigs shrub (same trunk, same radiating straight segments, same tiny scale in frame — only the tips differ, sticks vs. beads), and flora-h0-s19 and flora-h1-s0 share one point-origin radial splay (every blade emanating from a single mathematical point at the base with no caudex or root mass). Family-wide the shared tell is the untapered uniform-width stem primitive and the identical drop-shadow ellipse under every asset regardless of footprint.

This batch is NOT one chassis in the twelve-canids sense — the growth forms genuinely vary across about seven distinct archetypes: parasol/umbrella-on-a-rod (s12, s2), arching fountain-grass clump (s13, s14), pinnate frond fan (s17, s3), spiky agave rosette (s7), lollipop canopy tree (s15, s16), multi-stem berry shrub (s18, s19), and ribbed column/slab (s4, s6). BUT the same defect appears one level down: the archetypes come in exact-duplicate PAIRS that are the identical stamp with only a hue swap. s13 and s14 are the same fountain arch-for-arch — same nine blades, same V-crotch, same floating hatch-dashes up the inner stems, ice-blue vs orange. s3 and s17 are the same frond fan frond-for-frond, including the same small curled crozier at the lower-right of the crown, green vs violet. s18 and s19 are the same six-stem fascicle with the same brown zigzag stems and the same four red berry clusters at the same tip positions, differing only in leaf shape and leaf hue. Shared across nearly ALL of them is one structural habit: a single point of emergence at the ground with no root flare or basal spread, an untapered or wrongly-tapered axis (s15 is a flat popsicle stick, s16 is widest at the MIDDLE and narrowest at the soil, s12 is a uniform rod), and a hard elliptical drop-shadow puck stamped underneath every specimen at the same size. What the chassis reads as, when you see the batch together, is a set of icons planted in a pot rather than plants rooted in ground. Three assets (s2, s4, s5) fall out of the plant vocabulary entirely and read as furniture and instruments.

The batch as a whole is NOT one chassis — nine distinct growth forms appear (weeping strand-curtain, fuzzy pompom, skewered blob, vase-and-blooms, flat radial fan, branching cloud-canopy tree, grass tussock, horizontal slab canopy, stacked-triangle conifer, daisy flower, arching gold sedge). What IS shared, and shared to a fault, is the substructure: a single dead-straight untapered vertical pole planted at exact frame centre, the same flat brown-to-dark gradient on that pole, the same soft black ground ellipse under it, and the same rule that the canopy is one object dropped onto the pole's top with no branch-to-foliage transition — so ten of the fourteen silhouettes are literally 'stick with a thing on it'. Worse, inside the batch there are outright hue-clones: flora-h1-s8, flora-h2-s11 and flora-h2-s17 are the SAME weeping-strand asset in magenta, cyan and violet — identical strand count, identical hairpin loops at the crown, identical blunt uniform strand ends, identical trunk — and flora-h2-s14 and flora-h2-s18 are the SAME horizontal lumpy slab canopy in two barely-different purples. Only flora-h2-s13 grows an actual branch armature and only flora-h2-s12 and flora-h2-s19 abandon the pole entirely. A second split runs across the batch: half are painterly (soft volumetric canopies, gradient blades) and half are hard-edged flat vector primitives (flora-h2-s10's triangle fan, flora-h2-s15's five stacked triangles, flora-h2-s16's eight rounded petals), so the family does not even read as one rendering engine.

Not one body but worse in kind: fourteen assets drawn from a deck of roughly five reusable skeletons, each stamped twice or three times with nothing changed but hue. flora-h2-s2 and flora-h2-s5 are the SAME asset — the identical bundled sheaf of vertical ribs, identical splayed rounded rib-tips at the crown, identical needle-point base with no root flare, and three glowing bead-pods sitting at the identical three heights down the identical central channel; gold versus green is the entire difference. flora-h2-s4 and flora-h2-s8 are the same again — one dead-straight vertical pole with five flat zero-thickness ellipse tiers at the same five heights and the same five widths, the pole capped by a bare stub above the top tier; pale blue versus teal is the entire difference. flora-h2-s6, s7 and s9 share one serpentine stem: the same S-bend entering the ground at the same point, the same lean, the same little dark coil-rings alternating left and right at the same intervals — only the thing stamped onto the stem changes (blade needles, rosette clusters, ovoids), and the stamp repeats itself unrotated and unscaled four to eight times down each vine, so the appendages read as decals rather than as growth. fungi-h0-s0, s10 and s11 are one amorphous mound outline with one speckle field over it, recoloured grey, near-black and purple. What the chassis deck actually READS as is a shape library, not a biosphere: a paintbrush, a plastic tiered Christmas tree, a decorated wire, and a boulder — four manufactured objects, each available in assorted colours. Only flora-h2-s3 (forked woody branch, blossom masses), fungi-h0-s1 (sectioned spiny sphere) and fungi-h0-s12 (cap-and-stipe mushroom) carry a form that is not reused elsewhere in the batch.

This is not fourteen fungi, it is four generators recolored. CHASSIS A - the coral fan - is used three times (s2, s8, s19) and the three are visually indistinguishable: identical ground point, identical count and splay of six pale trunks, the same dichotomous branch topology with the same left-and-right outrigger arms drooping to the same height, the same finely-twigged fringe, and the same flat-bottomed dome canopy silhouette; only a barely perceptible warm-white vs cool-white tint separates them. A player who collected all three would be looking at one picture three times. CHASSIS B - the shaded ball - carries s4, s16, s15 and s17: the same lambert sphere with a rim light at upper-left and a hard elliptical drop shadow, varied only by hue, a freckle scatter, a low-frequency bump (s15), or six flat unshaded triangles stuck on in the picture plane (s17). CHASSIS C - the floating substrate bar - carries s3 and s5: the identical brown arc, identical length and sag, with a cluster of three overlapping glossy spheres hung beneath it, hue-swapped blue-grey vs yellow, and in both the spheres fail to boolean together so you can see the buried circle outlines through the surface. CHASSIS D - the fringed dome - carries s7 and s18: a smooth dome with a bright rim and a fringe of grey hair primitives under the edge. Only s14 (cap on stalk), s6 (pins on stalks) and s9 (blades) sit outside the four. What the dominant chassis actually READS as is not a fungus at all - it reads as a lit sphere, a ball with stuff added, which is why half this batch names a balloon, an orange, a grape bunch or a sea mine before it names a mushroom. The fungal kingdom's real vocabulary - a stipe with a base, a cap-to-stipe junction, a hymenium (gills, pores, teeth), a volva or mycelial mat gripping the substrate - appears on exactly one asset in fourteen.

This is not fourteen organisms, it is FIVE master shapes recoloured. The exact recolour groups: (a) fungi-h1-s0 and fungi-h1-s14 are the same bullet-cap-on-pale-stipe master — same silhouette, same flat dark diamond-lattice wallpaper on the cap, same cream trapezoid stipe, same elliptical ground shadow, only the stipe is a few pixels taller in s14; (b) fungi-h1-s1, fungi-h1-s11 and fungi-h1-s18 are ONE sphere with the identical eight in-plane triangular spikes and the identical single dark ostiole dot, in cream, green and red; (c) fungi-h1-s10 and fungi-h1-s16 are one big-bowl-plus-small-bowl pair with the identical rim polygon, identical interior gradient and identical black bristle fringe hung under the rim, in white and orange; (d) fungi-h1-s2 and fungi-h1-s3 are the same multi-stem dichotomous branch generator at two densities; (e) fungi-h1-s12, fungi-h1-s15 and fungi-h1-s19 are all the same lumpy-sphere/blob primitive with different surface speckle. The shared chassis parts are literal: one ground-shadow ellipse anchored at the same y, one radial vignette behind everything, one silhouette per master with zero variation in proportion, stance or attachment, and lighting baked from the same upper-left key on every asset. What the chassis pool actually READS as is generic prop geometry, not biology — a bullet-shaped bollard, a naval mine, a pair of ceramic bowls, a bare tree, and a rock. Colour is doing all the differentiation work; not one member of a recolour group has a different cap profile, stipe taper, spine distribution, rim shape or substrate. The one genuinely distinct asset in the batch is fungi-h1-s17 (toothed caps on a log), which is the only place a real fungal feature was modelled rather than tinted.

Fourteen slots resolve to only SEVEN drawn templates, and every template is reused verbatim with nothing changed but hue — the recolour defect in full. The three trees (h2-s0, h2-s10, h2-s13) are literally the same asset: same number of thin arching trunks fanning from one ground point, same flare width, same lobed cloud-crown outline, same tiny speck cluster in the trunk gap, only the mint/grey tint differs. The two blade clusters (h1-s8, h2-s14) share the identical fan of hard-edged pointed straps, same count, same lean, same flat foot line — purple vs amber. The two amorphous blobs (h2-s11, h2-s15) share the same lumpy silhouette with a notch on the upper right, same granular dot scatter, same soft outer bloom — blue vs violet. The two spiked spheres (h1-s5, h1-s6) share the same ball, the same eight straight lance spikes at the same angles, and the same single dark centre dot — teal vs cream. The two speckled spheres (h1-s4, h1-s9) share the same smooth matte ball with a rim highlight and a pepper of dark craters. What the shared chassis READS as, across the whole batch, is NOT fungus: it reads as a planetary body set — moons, a cratered asteroid pair, a naval mine — plus a banyan tree in three tints, a tuft of grass in two tints, and two nebula smudges. There is no shared fungal vocabulary at all: no stipe, no cap margin, no gills or pores, no annulus, no volva, no mycelial base mat, no substrate the body grows OUT of. Exactly one asset in the batch (h2-s1) is a mushroom. The family has no chassis in the sense of a fungus body plan — it has a bag of unrelated primitives that happen to be seeded, and the only thing genuinely varied is which primitive got drawn.

Yes — this batch is 14 assets drawn from only SIX growth-form templates, and inside every template the geometry is bit-for-bit the same with nothing changed but hue. Template A, the amorphous speckled lump: fungi-h2-s16 (brown), fungi-h2-s5 (green), microbe-h0-s0 (blue) and microbe-h0-s1 (near-black) all share the identical wide low-slung polygon with the same lumpy left shoulder, the same flat-ish bottom edge, the same soft radial glow behind it and the same scatter of dots — it reads as a boulder or a potato, not as an organism, and it is the SAME boulder four times. Template B, the shelf stack: fungi-h2-s4, s7 and s9 share one flat untextured brown rectangle trunk clipped off both the top and bottom of the frame, with the same five/four pointed lanceolate blades attached at the same heights, the same interior midrib arc and the same black hairline that overshoots past each tip into empty space — the shelf that IS the identity of a bracket fungus (semicircular fan, concentric zonation, pored underside) is nowhere; what is drawn is a leaf blade, so s9 in orange reads as salmon fillets nailed to a post. Template C, the hanging cluster: fungi-h2-s17 and s19 are the same brown drooping branch at the same height with the same six overlapping glossy spheres beneath it, specular highlight in the same place on each — grapes, twice, once green once teal. Template D, the branching thicket: fungi-h2-s18 and s8 share three identical tapered stipes rising from one shadow ellipse into hairline twigs that fork at woody elbows and droop at the tips — a leafless winter shrub, once purple once orange. Templates E (fungi-h2-s2, hairline stalks with ovoid heads on a soil ellipse) and F (fungi-h2-s6, a fan of pointed blades) appear once each and are the only silhouettes in the batch that are not repeated. Shared across ALL of them: the same ground shadow ellipse, the same vertical top-lit gradient, the same absence of any surface texture, and above all the same missing fungal grammar — no cap-and-stipe junction, no gills or pores, no annulus, no mycelial base. The chassis reads as generic dark-background stock shapes tinted per species.

This is not one chassis in fourteen colours — it is FIVE chassis each stamped out TWICE with nothing changed but hue, plus four one-offs, and the pairwise cloning is exactly the same defect at half scale. The pairs are: (a) s2 / s15 — an identical sphere tiled with overlapping oval scales, each scale carrying the same concentric ring dimple, the same knobby scale-lumps breaking the silhouette at the same clock positions, the same rim-light arc upper-left; only teal vs blue-white differs. (b) s11 / s13 — the same four-sphere spiral chain (one big sphere lower-right carrying the same dark elliptical crater, three shrinking spheres curling up-left), sitting on the same hard black starburst of straight radial lines whose convergence point is BEHIND and below the cluster rather than at any cell wall; only tan vs cream differs. (c) s3 / s18 — the same rectangular full-bleed soft-focus smear with the same scatter of short capsule-rods, the same handful of grey circles, and the same three or four curved hooks trailing off the RIGHT frame edge in both; only amber vs violet differs. (d) s4 / s5 — the same tardigrade: identical barrel topline, identical body depth, four straight vertical scratch-lines for segmentation that stop short of the body edge in both, the same eight stubby ventral legs leaving the silhouette at the same points with the same tiny claw prongs, the same blunt right-facing head with an eye dot up top and a flat dark mouth disc, the same cast shadow; only orange vs green differs. (e) s10 / s17 — the same lobed amoeboid blob with the same three overlapping circular vacuoles and one dark nucleus in the same arrangement; only value differs, and s10's value is so close to the background that the organism disappears. What the shared chassis READS as, taken together, is not an organism library but a shape-primitive sampler: scaly ball, ball-chain, blur-smear, water bear, blob. The four singletons (s12 jar, s14 comb, s16 sausage stack, s19 pill spill) do not rescue it — three of them read as manufactured objects rather than life, so the generator's variety budget is being spent on props instead of on bodies.

Not one animal body but the same defect one level up: fourteen assets are stamped from only six morphotype dies, re-rolled with the hue rotated. The dies are (a) a glassy shaded sphere with a dead-straight horizontal fill line across its lower third and a grey rim ring — h0-s6, h1-s12, h1-s15, identical down to the specular dot at 10 o'clock and the three white specks; (b) a curled cluster of pale spheres with one dark elliptical groove on the largest sphere and a perfectly radial starburst of dead-straight dark rays — h0-s8 and h1-s1 are geometrically IDENTICAL, sphere for sphere and ray for ray, tan versus mint; (c) a lozenge-capped segmented rod with a bead ganglion set off-centre and a dark unlit ghost copy behind it — h0-s9 (3 rods, teal) and h1-s0 (4 rods, orange); (d) a chain of equal cocci beaded along a curve — h0-s7 and h1-s14, same blue, only the walk of the chain differs; (e) a hollow unfilled ellipse outline with a comb of radial hairs and one horizontal axis line dotted at both ends and centre — h1-s11 and h1-s13, pixel-identical, orange versus white. Only h1-s10 (flagellates) and h1-s17 (colony cloud) are singletons. What the shared chassis READS as is a stock-icon sheet: sphere, chain-of-spheres, rod, wireframe oval — the same four primitives a placeholder generator emits, with no membrane texture, no organelle, no cytoplasm and no scale cue distinguishing any one species from its recolour twin.

This batch is not one chassis — it is roughly six generators shuffled by hue, and one of them is a four-way clone. Generator A is a bead-chain: identical unshaded spheres strung nose-to-tail with the same radius, the same top-left specular dot and the same overlap fraction (s18, s4, h2-s1, and s5 as a balled-up version of the same beads). Generator B is a sine-ribbon helix with hair-fine tapered tails at both ends, same amplitude, same wavelength, same taper (s19 magenta, s9 coral — literally the same coil painted twice). Generator C is the real defect: a rimmed circle with a hard 1px outline, one white specular blob at ten o'clock, three or four tiny white speck-bubbles, and a perfectly FLAT horizontal chord across the lower third filled darker green. It appears four times — s2 (slate), s7 (olive), s8 (green), h2-s0 (green, stretched to an oval). Nothing but hue and one aspect-ratio nudge separates them, and what the shared chassis READS as is not a cell at all: it is a glass marble or a snow globe half-filled with liquid. A flat liquid line inside a glossy sphere is a manufactured-object cue, not a biological one, and no membrane, nucleus, organelle, vacuole or flagellum is drawn anywhere on any of the four. Generator D is a capsule rod (s11 scattered, s6 stretched long and ticked with rungs). Generator E is a frame-filling fog blob (h2-s10). Only s3, the tardigrade, has anything a limbed audit could even ask about — a segmented barrel topline, eight stubby ventral legs leaving low on the flank, claw tips, and a blunt fused head — and it is the single asset in the batch that a stranger would name without help. So the family varies in growth form; what it fails at is that within each generator the variation collapses to a colour picker.

Not one chassis across all fourteen, but the same defect at smaller scale: the batch is eight drawings distributed over fourteen slots, and ten of the fourteen are hue-recolours of a sibling. Group A (s17, s5, s2) is one tardigrade drawn three times - identical topline (a high dome cresting just behind the head and falling in one unbroken arc to the rump), identical body depth (deep barrel, roughly 1.6:1), the same seven vertical segment ribs, the same four stubby conical legs leaving the silhouette straight down off the belly line at even spacing, the same three-clawed foot, the same blunt snout fused to the trunk with no neck at all, the same single dark eye dot with a second smudge behind it, and the same soft elliptical ground shadow; s17 and s5 are even the same green, so nothing whatever separates them, and s2 is that identical animal in white. Group B (s13, s19) is one vector wheel drawn twice - same circle radius, same sixteen radial spokes, same three concentric rings, same flat gradient fill - grey once, violet once. Group C (s12, s16) is one blurred colony smear drawn twice, down to the same lumpy cloud outline and the same six stray curved hairs hanging off the right edge - pale once, amber once. Group D (s15, s4, s7) is one teardrop-flagellate cell body reused with different counts and rotations - same pointed-oval outline, same off-centre nucleus dot, same single whip trailing from the blunt end. What the chassis reads as, in a sentence per group: a fat glossy jellybean on stumps (A), a bicycle wheel or radar dial (B), an out-of-focus photo of dust (C), and a sperm cell (D). The four true singletons - s14 cocci chain, s3 spined cluster, s18 ciliate, s6 plain sphere - carry all the actual variety this batch has.

These two are the same drawing twice with the hue swapped from magenta to mint. Every structural landmark is identical and in the same pixels: the same high-domed egg topline that peaks just behind mid-body and falls in one unbroken arc to the tail; the same body depth and the same left-facing three-quarter-profile pose at the same scale and the same canvas position; the same three faint vertical scratch lines standing in for cuticle segmentation, at the same spacing; the same small rounded head-bump fused to the front of the body with no neck and no mouth, carrying the same two dark dots stacked one high one low; the same five stubby conical leg nubs that leave the silhouette straight down from the belly line rather than from a shoulder or hip, each ending in the same three-tine claw tuft; and the same soft elliptical ground shadow with the same offset. The only genuine differences are colour, a slightly taller/rounder body outline on s9, and s9's legs being tonally darker so they separate from the belly while s8's legs are the same pink as the body and nearly vanish. What the shared chassis reads as is a tardigrade/water-bear plush toy: a smooth inflated balloon body on vestigial hairy stumps, more soft-toy than organism. Nothing about the pair says these are two different species — a stranger would call them the same animal in two colours.

This batch holds only one asset, so there is no sibling to compare it against — but the cross-family question still answers itself, because the Aardvark is plainly not riding an aardvark body: it is riding the project's stock woolly-ungulate chassis with a long face pasted on. Named part by part: the topline is dead level from withers to rump with a slight sag mid-back (an aardvark's defining line is a steep arch peaking over the hips); body depth is a uniform fleecy barrel with a flat belly line, no hindquarter mass at all; the four limbs are identical straight columns of the same length and the same thickness front and rear, each leaving the silhouette vertically at the four corners of the barrel with almost no shoulder or haunch modelling; the feet are small dark two-toed hooves, not the broad splayed digging claws that ARE the animal; the neck carriage is short and level, head held at back height rather than dropped low to snuffle; the tail is a thin smooth crescent set high on the dock, curving down and forward like a lamb's, with no thickness at the base and no taper. The skull is the only part attempting the species, and it is grafted rather than built. What the chassis actually READS as, unprompted, is a sheep or a lamb — the fleece stroke texture, the level back, the columnar legs and the cloven hooves all point the same direction, and a stranger would say 'sheep with a weird face' before they said any African mammal.

This is one asset in five colours. Every entry is the same flat spiral doughnut seen three-quarter from above: a tube of near-constant diameter laid in a horizontal plane with an open hole at the centre, the tail tucked away at the lower left, and a straight neck leaving the coil's right side at the same angle in every frame. The body surface is the same dense transverse annulation on all five -- rings, not scales -- so the topline reads as an earthworm or a vacuum hose rather than a snake; there is no dorsal keel, no ventral scute band, no taper worth the name. The head is the same small rounded bud on all five (Cobra excepted, which is the same bud with a fan bolted to it), no wider than the neck it sits on, with the identical white lozenge eye and vertical slit, and the identical red Y-shaped tongue at the same length and the same angle. Even the soft elliptical drop shadow is the same ellipse in the same place. The declared aspect ratios (1.1 for Cobra, 10 for Mamba) and postures (Mamba is specified crawling) change nothing on screen -- the whip-slender mamba and the short heavy adder are the same tube at the same thickness. What the chassis actually reads as is a coiled tan earthworm with a bead eye and a party-blower tongue; the pit-viper wedge head, the thin neck, the vertical rear, the dorsal chain pattern and the gape are all absent from the chassis, so no member of the family can express them.

Yes — one chassis, four hues, one length slider. Every asset is the identical fat egg-dome body: same topline (a single smooth convex arc from shoulder to stern with no rump break and no tail at all), same body depth, same flat waterline where the dome is cut off by the identical three concentric water rings and the identical dark blue reflection ellipse beneath. There are NO limbs anywhere in the family — no legs, no feet, no webbing, not even a foot suggestion under the surface — so 'webbed feet set far back' and 'heavy body on webbed feet' cannot be judged because the limb model does not exist. Every skull is the same sphere with one oversized white-catchlight eye, and every bill is the same tapered orange-yellow cone stuck on at the same downward angle — a snowman's-carrot, not a bill; nothing in the family is spatulate, flat, wedge-profiled or knobbed. Every flank carries the same dark grey scythe-shaped wing swoosh and the same quilted/scalloped crosshatch patch over the back. The ONLY thing that varies across the four is neck length (zero on Duck and Eider, a medium bent tube on Goose, a long thin tube on Swan) and fill colour (olive, white, tan-speckle, white). Duck and Eider are pixel-for-pixel the same drawing with the hue swapped. What the chassis actually READS as is a carved wooden hunting decoy or a bath toy — a legless floating egg with a cone nose — and the neck tube reads as a grebe's, which is why the Goose lands on the wrong bird entirely.

All nine are one drawing. Every asset has the identical dead-flat horizontal topline with no shoulder hump and no croup, the same deep loaf-shaped torso whose belly line runs parallel to the back, and the same four straight column legs that leave the silhouette at the extreme front and rear corners of the belly and drop vertically to identical pale hoof-like toe clusters. The head is the same unit every time: a small wedge on a short thick upward-angled neck at the right end, with a tapering dog muzzle, a pale nose tip, one visible round eye and two tiny nub ears — never the broad flat rounded ear of a weasel, never the blunt whiskered muzzle of an otter, never the wide flat skull of a badger. The tail is one of exactly two stamps: a short bushy plume sprouting off the top-rear (Fisher, Marten, Mink, Sea Otter, Wolverine) or a thin bare tapering curl (Otter, Stoat), and on Weasel it is simply missing. Ground clearance, leg length and the drop-shadow ellipse are pixel-similar across all nine, so nothing here is longer, lower, bulkier or more streamlined than anything else. What the chassis actually READS as is a dachshund — a sausage dog with hoof-tipped legs — and the family is that dachshund in seven colours plus two fur-texture passes. Nothing distinguishes a 2.2-aspect wolverine from a 4.0-aspect weasel, and the sea otter, whose posture field says swimming, is the same dachshund standing up on all fours.

This family has exactly one member, so there is no sibling to compare against and no shared-chassis defect can be established by cross-comparison. What can be said is what the single chassis reads as on its own: a plump, near-circular perching-bird body (a starling/blackbird blob) with a big folded teardrop wing, a ball head set straight on the shoulders with no neck at all, and a body axis that runs diagonally down-left rather than parallel to the trunk. It is a generic songbird chassis with a trunk painted behind it, not a woodpecker chassis: nothing in the topline, body depth, neck carriage or foot placement is specialised for vertical clinging. The one foot drawn is a yellow zigzag claw sitting entirely off the left edge of the trunk, gripping black background, and the bill is attached to the crown rather than the face. When siblings are added to this family, the elongated trunk-hugging torso, the short thick neck angled up along the bark, and the zygodactyl foot clamped ON the bark must be built into the chassis, not repainted onto this round perching body.

All five are literally one drawing recoloured. Every asset is the identical left-facing S-curve tube: the same shallow rise out of a bulbous left-hand head, the same crest at about 60 percent of the length, the same dip, the same short up-flick that ends in the same blunt taper at the right. The segmentation is the same stack of ~30 overlapping crescent rings at the same pitch and the same tilt, thickest at mid-body and pinching identically at the tail. Every one carries the same blunt bulbous cephalic knob with a single small black dot eye at the same position - including the two species whose reference says eyes are HIDDEN and one (Lancelet) that has no head or eyes at all as a matter of anatomy. Every one sits on the same soft elliptical ground shadow at the same offset, so even the 'swimming' Lancelet is lit and shadowed as if crawling on a floor. The only two variables in the entire family are hue (slate-grey, cream, salmon, orange, khaki) and a boolean 'bristles on/off' that stamps the same straight red-orange matchsticks at the same angles and same spacing along both flanks of three of the five. There is no paddle lobe, no scale plate, no chevron, no oral fringe, no palp or antenna anywhere in the batch - every diagnostic feature that separates a lancelet from a ragworm from a scale worm has been replaced by the same recoloured earthworm. What the chassis actually READS as is a plump garden earthworm, and with the spikes switched on it reads as a cartoon centipede, not as any polychaete.

rows.readsAs: an agave or yucca with a thin red flower stalk
rows.defect: The fan of stiff pale grey-green blades is flat and spiky rather than arching strap leaves, there is no vase-shaped cup or pool of water at the centre — the leaves radiate from a single point with no interior volume — and there is no grey scurfy banding or red central flush. The bract spike is a bare thread with a short column of small red beads rather than a brilliant coloured bract spike.
rows.fix: Curve the inner ring of leaves upward into a closed funnel with a visible dark water surface inside it, and thicken the spike into a broad red bract cone with purple-blue florets emerging.

rows.readsAs: a small conifer or bottlebrush shrub with a yellow star ornament on top
rows.defect: The plant is a tall dense column of ten stacked pairs of needle-clustered leaves — nothing about it is a buttercup. There are no deeply cut palmate basal leaves; the leaves are all up the stem and are needle rosettes. The flower is a single 6-point flat yellow star about 25px across at the apex, not a glossy five-petalled cup, and it has no lacquered highlight at all.
rows.fix: Delete the leaf column entirely: put a low tuft of three-to-five-lobed palmate basal leaves at the ground and carry two or three big five-petalled yellow cups with a specular varnish highlight on thin branching stalks above them.
rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, with corrections to the described geometry. Verified at 1x plus 4x/8x/20x nearest-neighbour crops of the flower head (src 200,75 45x45), the mid column, and the base.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. A single bare dark-green vertical stem rises from the ground shadow. The lower ~60px of that stem is COMPLETELY BARE — there are no basal leaves at all, so the judge is right that the palmate basal rosette is absent, and it is absent in the most literal way (nothing is drawn there). Above the bare stem the plant is a tall, parallel-sided, densely packed COLUMN of foliage roughly 150px wide by 250px tall on a 440x440 canvas, with a hard serrated sawtooth silhouette on both edges. The column is built from stacked whorl/fan units centred on the stem: each unit is a radiating fan of about 11-13 narrow, entire, sharply-pointed lanceolate lobes spraying outward and slightly downward from one point on the stem. I count 8-9 such tiers, overlapping so heavily that they read as one solid mass. CORRECTION to the claim: they are NOT 'needle-cluster leaf PAIRS' and there are not exactly ten of them — they are radiating multi-lobed fans (~11-13 lobes each), 8-9 tiers. That distinction matters for the fix, because each individual fan unit is arguably palmate-ish in construction; the failure is that the lobe count is 11-13 instead of 3-5, the lobes are smooth-edged spikes instead of deeply toothed segments, and the units are repeated all the way up a tall stem instead of sitting as a few large leaves at the base.

THE FLOWER. At 20x the head is unambiguous: a flat, face-on SIX-pointed star of narrow triangular petals (upper-left, upper-right, left horizontal, right horizontal, lower-left, lower-right) with a dark outline and a pale cream circular centre disc. Petals are flat-filled saturated yellow with essentially no internal modelling. Judge's '6-point yellow star' is correct. Corrections: (a) it is six petals, so the five-petal must-read fails on COUNT as well as shape; (b) petal tips are sharp points, the opposite of the required rounded petal; (c) the form is a flat star, not a cup — nothing curves toward the viewer; (d) the pale cream blob at the centre is a centre disc, not a lacquer highlight, so a reader could mistake it for the missing gloss — it is not, and there is no specular/varnished highlight anywhere on the petals. (e) Scale: the head is ~45px across against a ~150px-wide foliage column, so the defining organ is roughly a tenth of the silhouette and is read last.

BAND. All three must-reads fail: no lacquered/varnished petal gloss (flat fill), not five rounded petals (six pointed ones), and no 3-5 lobed deeply toothed palmate basal leaf (11-13 smooth spike lobes, stacked up the stem, none basal). The overall silhouette reads as a bottlebrush, horsetail or small dense conifer with a star ornament on top — the judge's organism call is right. Nothing was hiding at small scale that rescues it. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a fanned rosette of serrated leaves with a small pink daisy on a stalk
rows.defect: The trifoliate leaf IS clover and it is absent — instead there are roughly thirteen large pointed sawtooth-edged blades splayed in a radial fan, and no leaflet is grouped in a three. There is no pale V chevron watermark anywhere. The flower is a flat pink rayed disc with a yellow centre, i.e. a daisy, not a globe pompom.
rows.fix: Replace the fan with several long-stalked leaves each carrying exactly three rounded leaflets bearing a pale crescent band, and swap the apex flower for a spherical clustered pompom head.
rows.verifyWhy: UPHELD, with three corrections to the stated cause. WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON CANVAS (440x440, organism bbox x99-340 y85-351, w242 h267, aspect h/w 1.10 vs the reference's 1.4): a single vertical green stalk runs from the bottom of the frame straight up to a small flower head at the top; the entire lower two-thirds of the stalk is buried in one dense mass of long pointed blades. A radial peak-trace from the leaf origin (cx220, cy305) counts 18-20 blade tips, not ~13 as claimed, spread at roughly 10-12 degree intervals across ~210 degrees of arc, from horizontal-left through the apex to horizontal-right, plus two long blades pointing down-left and down-right below horizontal. CORRECTION 1 (structure): this is not a true radial rosette. It is TWO MIRRORED HALF-FANS meeting at a hard vertical seam on the stalk, with a distinct V-shaped notch at the bottom centre where the two halves part - it reads as one leafy stem, chrysanthemum/dahlia/aster-like, not as a clump. CORRECTION 2 (margins): the blades are lanceolate with SMOOTH, ENTIRE margins. The sawtooth silhouette the other judge saw is the stacked tips of the overlapping ranks behind, not toothed leaf edges. A fix that files teeth off the margins would be fixing something that is not there; the defect is blade COUNT, blade SHAPE (pointed lance instead of rounded obovate) and blade GROUPING. CORRECTION 3 (watermark): the claim 'no pale V watermark' is right in effect but wrong in detail. At 7x zoom each blade does carry a faint chevron/herringbone texture - but it is rendered as thin DARKER-than-lamina venation/tile outlines, so the polarity is inverted and the marks are per-tile texture rather than one bold crescent per leaflet. The fix is invert to pale and promote to one crescent band per leaflet, not 'draw chevrons from scratch'. MUST-READS: (1) 'three rounded leaflets' - ABSENT. There is no grouping in threes anywhere; nothing separates the mass into leaflets, no petiole carries three blades, and the blades are pointed, not rounded. (2) 'pale V mark on each leaflet' - ABSENT as specified (see correction 3). (3) 'globe pompom flower head' - ABSENT; the other judge is exactly right here. At 6x the head is a flat, face-on rayed daisy: ~12 narrow pale-pink rounded ray petals radiating from a solid dark olive/mustard central DISC, on a long bare green stalk. It is the Daisy head of this same family batch recoloured pink, and it carries the one feature a clover head must not have - a differentiated central disc instead of a globe of many tiny tubular florets. It is also tiny relative to the plant (head ~34px across against a 242px leaf span), so even the mass reads wrong. Also worth logging for the family pass: leafColour is a flat mid-green with no paler crescent banding at all. Net: all three must-reads fail; the asset reads as a pink-flowered chrysanthemum or aster, not as clover.

rows.readsAs: a daisy-flowered weed, or chamomile
rows.defect: The flower head itself is correct — white rays around a flat yellow-brown disc — but the two structural must-reads are both absent. There is no ground-hugging spoon-leaf rosette, and the stalk is not bare: it carries eight opposite pairs of lance leaves all the way up, which is the shared family chassis rather than anything daisy. No pink tipping on the rays.
rows.fix: Strip every leaf off the stem and put a flat basal rosette of small spoon-shaped leaves on the ground, leaving a single naked scape to the flower.

rows.readsAs: a yellow daisy on a spiky ground rosette — dandelion is a fair guess
rows.defect: The rosette and the single bare stalk carrying one yellow head are both present and legible, which is the best structure in the batch. But the leaves are smooth-edged pointed lances with no jagged backward-pointing teeth at all, so the diagnostic runcinate leaf edge is missing, and there is no seed clock. The head is a flat 8-ray star rather than a dense mass of fine ligules.
rows.fix: Cut deep backward-raked triangular teeth into each leaf margin and pack the head with many fine strap ligules instead of eight broad rays.

rows.readsAs: a generic pinnate weed with four pink specks at the tip
rows.defect: The one-sided spike of hanging bells IS foxglove and it is not drawn: there are four tiny flat pink dots clustered at the apex, radially placed, none of them bell-shaped, none hanging, none speckled inside. The stem is the shared leaf-ladder of eleven opposite pale lance pairs, not a basal rosette of large downy oval leaves. The flower zone occupies about 8 percent of the plant where it should be the top third.
rows.fix: Replace the apex dots with a tall column of a dozen tubular bells all hanging off the same side of the stem, throats forward and spotted, and move the leaves into a big soft basal rosette.
rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, but two parts of the stated cause are wrong and the fix should be made against this description instead.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN (440x440; plant occupies y~65-350, x~170-265, so aspect ~0.33 which correctly matches the packet's 0.3 - aspect is NOT the defect). A single straight olive stem rises from a flat ellipse ground shadow. Eleven opposite pairs of narrow lance/blade leaves ladder up it, each pale sage-green with a lighter airbrushed midrib streak - the generic leaf-ladder chassis shared with the rest of this family batch. At the very tip, four small pink shapes.

CORRECTION 1 - they are not 'dots' and they are not 'radial'. Zoomed 8x, each of the four is a flat-topped shield roughly 10x12px whose lower edge is scalloped into two rounded lobes: a crude bell/thimble silhouette with the mouth pointing DOWN. So a bell hint does exist in the outline; 'no bells' overstates it. Their placement is a left-right alternating pair-of-pairs flanking the stem tip (upper-left, upper-right, lower-left, lower-right), not a radial umbel on the apex.

CORRECTION 2 - the alternation is exactly why must-read 2 still fails. Bells appear on BOTH sides of the stem, so there is no one-sidedness at all; and each shape is butted flush against the stem with no pedicel, no nodding attachment and no overlap, so nothing reads as HANGING. They read as stickers, not as pendent flowers.

MUST-READS, all three missed:
1. 'a single tall unbranched flower spike' - the stem is unbranched, but there is no spike. The flower group is 37px tall and 19px wide on a 285px plant (13% of height), a four-blob tuft perched above a fully leafy stem. A foxglove reads as a tall dense raceme occupying roughly a third to a half of the plant.
2. 'bells hanging along one side only' - both sides, no hang (see correction 2).
3. 'dark spots inside each speckled throat' - genuinely absent. Every bell is one flat unmodulated pink fill: no darker throat interior, no mouth opening, no speckling, no shading whatsoever.

LEAF/BASE - the judge's 'no basal downy rosette' is correct and is worse than stated. The lowest ~70px of stem is completely bare above the shadow before the first leaf pair, so there is no basal mass of any kind. The leaves that exist also contradict the packet on two counts: they are narrow lance blades in opposite pairs, not 'large soft downy oval leaves' graded larger at the base and smaller up the stem, and their colour is pale sage-green rather than 'dull grey-green, felted'.

NET: this reads as an anonymous pink-flowered herb on the family's shared chassis - substitute yellow blobs and it would be the Goldenrod. None of the three identity must-reads is readable. FAIL stands.

FIX ORDER: (a) build a real one-sided raceme covering the top ~40% of the stem with 10-14 overlapping bells all on one flank; (b) give each bell a short pedicel and tilt it mouth-down-and-outward so it hangs; (c) paint a darker magenta throat interior with a few dark spots on at least the near-side bells; (d) replace the lowest 3-4 leaf pairs with a broad downy grey-green oval basal rosette sitting on the ground and taper the stem leaves smaller upward.

rows.readsAs: a fern-like weed with a few yellow grains stuck on the tip
rows.defect: The arching one-sided pyramid plume is the whole identity and it is absent — what is there is a straight vertical column of about nine small yellow beads sitting directly on the stem tip, perfectly upright, no branching, no arch, no pyramid taper, no sense of many small heads. The leaves are opposite pinnate pairs rather than alternate crowded narrow lances, which is the shared chassis showing through.
