rows.fix: Build a branched plume at the top: several side branches curving out and down to one side, each carrying dozens of tiny yellow heads, so the mass reads as a nodding golden pyramid.
rows.verifyWhy: Upheld, and I found a second defect the first judge did not mention. MEASURED, not eyeballed: the yellow flower mass is a bounding box of 11 px wide x 46 px tall (x210-220, y75-120) in a 440x440 frame, total 310 yellow pixels. The green foliage bbox is 78 px wide x 233 px tall (x179-256, y118-350). So the entire 'plume' is a hair-thin column one seventh the width of the foliage, sitting dead-centre on the stem axis (stem centre x~217, yellow centre x~215 - a 2 px offset, i.e. NOT one-sided in any readable way). At 6x zoom the head is a single-file vertical stack of ~10-11 overlapping round yellow beads, each about 10 px across, alternating left-right by 1-2 px in a faint zigzag. Parallel-sided: the topmost bead is marginally narrower but there is no pyramid outline, no taper, no lateral branches, no nodding tip, no arch. It reads as a tiny plantain/catkin spike, not a goldenrod panicle. CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM: (a) the bead count is ~10-11, not nine; (b) 'no mass of many small heads' is overstated - there ARE many small discrete heads, so must-read #3 ('many small heads, not one big flower') is weakly satisfied; what is absent is must-read #1, 'pyramid plume of tiny yellow flowers arching to one side', which fails on all three counts (not pyramidal, not plume-massed, not arching/one-sided). (c) The claim says the head sits 'on the stem tip' - correct, but it is worth noting the yellow column starts at y75 and the leaves start at y118, so there is a 43 px bare gap of stem between the last leaf and the first bead; real goldenrod carries the inflorescence directly out of the leafy stem with leafy bracts continuing into it. SECOND DEFECT THE JUDGE MISSED: the leaves are wrong too. The packet asks for 'narrow lance-shaped leaves, ALTERNATE and crowded all the way up the stem'. What is drawn is ~13 strictly OPPOSITE/sub-opposite pairs, every pair at the same node height, every leaflet identical in length and set at the same uniform ~35 deg, springing from a single unbranched rachis. That is the generic pinnate-frond chassis; combined with the thin terminal spike the whole silhouette reads as a fern frond or a vetch with a catkin, not a composite wildflower. Must-read #2 ('unbranched leafy stem below') is technically met - the stem is unbranched and leafy - but the arrangement is the wrong phyllotaxy. FIX DIRECTION: replace the bead-stack with a broad conical panicle - a central axis with 8-12 short side-branches whose length shortens toward the apex to make the pyramid, every branch loaded with 15-30 sub-2px golden florets, the whole mass swept and bowed to ONE side so the outline is convex on one flank and concave on the other, occupying roughly the top third of the plant height and at least as wide as the foliage span at its base. And restagger the leaves to true alternate spacing (half-node offset left/right) with the leaves shortening toward the top.

rows.readsAs: a red gerbera daisy stuck on top of a silver fern

CORRECTIONS to the original judge's wording, all of which stand as errors even though the verdict is right:
(a) They called the foliage BIPINNATE and "reads as yarrow". It is not bipinnate and it does not read as yarrow. Yarrow foliage is a finely dissected feathery lace with no resolvable individual leaflets; here each side-branch carries a row of clearly separated, entire, rounded-oval leaflets with visible gaps between them -- ONCE-pinnate, closest to a vetch, false indigo, mimosa or a fern frond. Verdict: the asset reads as the wrong organism at every level -- wrong flower architecture (composite head vs four-petalled corolla), wrong leaf architecture (compound vs lobed), and all three named must-reads absent. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a column of round leaves with a tiny yellow daisy badge on top

Their defect is shape and arrangement, not detail: spec says 'very large heart-shaped rough-hairy leaves, ALTERNATE up a thick bristly stem' and 'large coarse heart-shaped leaves' - the render gives strictly OPPOSITE decussate pairs in 13 tiers, no cordate notch at the leaf base, no coarse/sandpapery/bristly surface treatment, no toothed margin.

WHAT ACTUALLY FAILS. FIX DIRECTION: scale the head to roughly 140-180px (a third to 40% of canvas width) so it dominates; give the disc real seed structure (spiral/phyllotactic packing or at minimum dense stippled florets) once it is large enough to carry it; thicken the stalk to a visibly stout 12-18px bristly stem and let it read up the whole height; cut the leaf count from 13 tiers to 4-6 ALTERNATE large cordate leaves with a notched base and a coarse edge, spaced so the silhouette breaks and the stem shows between them.

rows.readsAs: a low clump of big round leaves with one small purple star flower above it
rows.defect: The flower colour and five-point form give a workable violet cue, but it is a flat radially symmetric star with no spurred lower petal, no nodding tilt, and it is held on a single straight stalk far above the foliage instead of just above the leaves on a curved stalk. rows.readsAs: a cannabis / hemp cutting, or a generic seven-finger palmate vine
rows.defect: The leaf is a deeply divided fan of seven narrow finger lobes cut almost to the petiole - the classic cannabis silhouette - not ivy's broad shallow-lobed 3-5 point triangular blade. Colour is a pale mint-teal, not very dark glossy green, and there is no pale grey-green vein NETWORK, only a single light streak down each lobe. Both remaining must-reads are entirely absent: the cane is a smooth bare stroke with no dense mats of short brown clinging rootlets anywhere along it, and there are no spherical umbels of black berries on any shoot. Worse, the stem carries coiled tendril spirals at every node - ivy has no tendrils at all, so the one conspicuous stem feature present is positively wrong for the species.
rows.fix: Replace the palmate fan with ivy's actual blade - a broad dark glossy triangular leaf with 3-5 shallow lobes and a pale grey-green vein net radiating from the base - delete every tendril coil and replace them with a fuzzy brown rootlet mat hugging the stem, and hang one globe-shaped umbel of black berries on the upper shoot.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, and the underlying cause is worse than stated. What is on the canvas: a single S-curved climbing stem running bottom-right to top-centre, bearing EIGHT leaf nodes. I zoomed each node to 8-10x. Every leaf is the same stamp: a palmate fan of ~7 narrow lanceolate leaflets divided nearly to the petiole insertion, each leaflet a pointed spearhead with a straight taper and no marginal teeth. That is a cannabis / Virginia-creeper silhouette. Ivy's shallow-lobed, broad, entire-margined triangular blade (juvenile) and the unlobed diamond adult leaf are BOTH absent — there is not one broad blade anywhere in the frame.

CORRECTION 1 (colour): 'mint-teal' overstates it. At true pixel values the blade is a muted dark sage-teal — dominant body #285848 and #284838, highlight band #386858, brightest pixel in the whole plant rgb(55,101,82), L=90/255. So the leaves ARE dark; the mintiness is a contrast illusion against the near-black backdrop. The real colour defect is different and should be fixed as such: the hue is blue-shifted to ~156 deg (green-cyan) instead of ivy's warm forest green, saturation is washed flat, and there is NO specular gloss pass at all — ivy's must-read is a GLOSSY dark leaf and this blade is matte.

CORRECTION 2 (veins): 'no pale vein network' is directionally right but the reason is misstated. Pale veining IS drawn — each of the 7 leaflets carries one lighter midrib streak radiating from the petiole. What is missing is the branching NETWORK across a broad lamina, because there is no lamina to carry it: the blade is shredded into separate fingers, so the veins can only ever be 7 parallel streaks. Fixing the vein pass alone will not help; the blade shape has to change first.

CONFIRMED 3 (rootlets): absent, exactly as claimed. The stem is a clean smooth olive-yellow taper (~#6f7a2b) with a soft gradient and zero surface texture — no brown, no bristle mats, no clinging side, no aerial-root fringe on the shaded flank. Identity must-read #2 is simply not drawn.

CONFIRMED 4 (berries): absent, exactly as claimed. I scanned the full 440x440 for any round dark cluster; there are none. No umbel, no peduncle, no fruit of any kind. Identity must-read #3 is not drawn.

CONFIRMED 5 (tendrils) with an added defect: 8-9 flat dark-green (#183818) spiral coils sit one per node along the stem. Ivy has no tendrils at all — it climbs by rootlets — so these actively read as the WRONG climbing mechanism. Additionally they are drawn DETACHED, floating beside the stem with a visible gap rather than emerging from a node, so even on the species that should own them they read as unattached debris.

DECISIVE NEW FINDING (chassis collision, family-level): Ivy is the SAME BODY as Passionflower in this batch. Side by side, the two share the identical S-curve stem path, identical node count and spacing, identical 7-finger palmate fan stamp, and identical detached coil spirals. Passionflower is that chassis plus purple flowers; Ivy is that chassis minus the flowers with a teal tint. In other words Ivy has been drawn as the family's PASSIONFLOWER, which is why the palmate fan and the tendril coils are present — those are Passionflower's must-reads, correctly placed on the wrong species. The fix is not a retint or a vein pass: Ivy needs its own chassis — a broad shallow-lobed entire-margined glossy dark blade, a rootlet-furred stem, and a globe umbel of black berries on the upper growth — and the tendril coils must be deleted from it entirely.

Minor: plant bounding box is 145 x 272 px, h/w = 1.88 against a spec aspect of 1.5 — too narrow, but immaterial next to the identity failure.

rows.readsAs: a purple star-flowered creeper - bindweed or a nightshade - on a hemp-leaved vine
rows.defect: The flower IS the identity of this plant and the rendered flower is a generic six-point mauve star about 20px across with a white centre dot. There is no corona: not one of the fringe of many fine radiating filaments that is the single feature every viewer recognises. There is no raised central column, no 5 stamens, no 3 hooked styles - the flower is flat, symmetrical and featureless. The leaf is the identical seven-finger cannabis fan reused verbatim from Ivy (same sprite, same nodes, same 139-300 bounding box) rather than a passionflower's 3-5 broad pointed palmate lobes. No egg-shaped fruit is present either. Only the wiry coiled tendrils survive as a correct must-read, and they are the shared family furniture, not something drawn for this species.

rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 PNG, then re-cropped and upscaled each of the three flowers 10x and the leaf whorls 6x, and ran a numeric radial scan on the mauve blobs. UPHELD, and the core of the claim is confirmed by measurement, but three parts of it need correcting so the fix is aimed right.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. An S-curved dark-olive stem climbing bottom-right to top-left, four to five whorls of bright mid-green (90,171,93) palmate leaves, small dark-green coiled tendril loops at the nodes, a soft ground-shadow ellipse, and three small mauve flowers spaced up the stem at roughly (159,132), (198,199) and (248,260) in canvas coords.

MUST-READ 1 (flat flower with a fringe of many fine radiating filaments over the petals) - ABSENT. Each flower is a flat six-point mauve star. I verified the petal count numerically rather than by eye: sampling a ring at 0.80 x max-radius on the two least-occluded flowers gives exactly 6 mauve runs on both, so the judge's "six-point" is correct, not an eyeball guess. Petals are a single flat fill 176,122,216 with no gradient, no vein, no tonal break. Flower diameter is only ~34px (max radius 17px) on a 440px canvas. There is no corona: not a ring of filaments, not even a suggestive darker annulus. Zero radiating marks anywhere between the disc and the petal bases.

MUST-READ 2 (raised central column with 5 stamens and 3 hooked styles) - ABSENT. I sampled the centre radially. On the largest flower the pixel is 243,230,168 (pale butter-cream, NOT white as claimed - minor correction) and holds that flat value out to r~3px, then jumps straight to petal mauve at r~4px. That is a hard-edged flat filled circle roughly 7px across with no shading, no rim, no highlight, and nothing standing proud of it. No androgynophore, no anthers, no styles, no hooks - not small, not faint, simply not drawn. This is the feature that IS the species and it is the one that is missing.

MUST-READ 3 (wiry coiled tendrils) - PRESENT. The judge did not mention this and it is the one thing the asset gets right: there are clear spiral/looped tendrils at the nodes, most legible just below the top flower and to the right of the middle flower. They are drawn dark and low-contrast against the background so they nearly vanish at thumbnail size, but they are genuinely coiled and they do read. Credit where due; it does not save the asset, because two of three must-reads are gone and the missing pair is the identity.

CORRECTION TO THE LEAF CLAIM. I rendered Ivy.png from the same batch and compared. The judge's conclusion is right but the wording "the Ivy cannabis-fan sprite reused verbatim" overstates it and would misdirect the fix. It is not a pixel copy - silhouette IoU between the two assets is 0.455, Ivy has more leaf whorls, and the hues differ (Ivy is a desaturated dark teal-green, Passionflower a brighter mid-green). What is actually shared is the whole CHASSIS, which is worse than sharing a leaf: identical S-curve stem path, identical whorl-of-narrow-fingers leaf motif, identical node tendril coils, identical ground-shadow ellipse. Passionflower is Ivy re-seeded and re-hued with three mauve stars dropped on. Additionally the leaf fails its OWN packet spec, independent of Ivy: the packet asks for "deeply palmate, 3-5 pointed lobes" and the drawn leaf is a 7-lobed narrow-finger cannabis/Virginia-creeper fan. So the leaf needs redrawing to 3-5 broad pointed lobes regardless of what Ivy does.

ALSO ABSENT (not a must-read, so not load-bearing for the band): the egg-shaped purple/yellow fruit from the harvest line does not appear anywhere.

STRANGER TEST. Agreed with the judge's outcome, phrased differently: a stranger sees a cannabis-leaved vine carrying small six-petal mauve stars with a cream centre - clematis, periwinkle or a generic star-flowered creeper. Nothing about it says Passiflora, because the only thing that ever says Passiflora is the corona-plus-column, and neither exists here. FAIL stands.

FIX ORDER: (1) rebuild the flower head - flat 10-tepal disc, dense ring of many fine radiating corona filaments banded light/dark over the tepal bases, and a central column carrying 5 splayed anthers with 3 hooked styles above them; it must be drawn far larger than 34px to hold that detail. (2) Replace the 7-finger Ivy fan with a 3-5 broad-lobed passionflower leaf. (3) Keep the tendrils but raise their contrast.

rows.readsAs: a broken render - a green fern-frond vine with a column of white confetti chips floating beside it

rows.defect: The rosette shape is there but nothing that makes it an agave is: no hard black terminal spine on any of the thirteen tips (they simply taper to a soft point), no hooked teeth anywhere on the leaf edges, and the blades are flat papery sheets carrying a full herringbone leaf VENATION pattern - the exact opposite of a thick unveined succulent. rows.readsAs: a young saguaro or organ-pipe cactus with a pink daisy stuck on top
rows.defect: This is the wrong organism. What is drawn is a single tall narrow vertically ribbed green column, widest at the base and tapering to a point, with one flat pink daisy-form flower sitting on the apex. Every must-read is absent: there is no swollen bulbous grey caudex (the trunk is the same width all the way down and is thin, not bottle-shaped), there are no thick stubby branches at all, there are no glossy spoon-shaped leaves anywhere in the image, and the flower is a flat radial daisy rather than a deep-pink trumpet with a pale throat. rows.fix: Redraw from the ground up as a squat grey bottle-shaped caudex occupying the lower two thirds of the frame, with two or three short thick tapering branches off its shoulder, each ending in a small tuft of dark glossy spoon leaves and a cluster of pink trumpet flowers.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD. I read the 440x440 PNG at native size, again at gamma-boosted brightness, and then at 3x/4x zoom on the base and the apex, and I also measured the subject's per-row silhouette width directly from the pixels. The asset contains exactly one object: a single unbranched green spire rising from the ground plane, with one pink flower stuck on its point. Measured silhouette: subject spans y=85 (top of flower) to y=339 (ground). The stem emerges below the flower at y=114 only 6px wide and widens MONOTONICALLY and smoothly all the way down, 6 -> 20 (y150) -> 34 (y180) -> 46 (y234) -> 52px maximum at y=303-318, then it actually NARROWS very slightly to 50px where it meets the soil at y=339. So the body is a straight-sided cone/candle roughly 52px wide by 255px tall (about 1:5) with a perfectly continuous taper and no waist, no neck, no shoulder, no inflection anywhere. Surface is a flat sage/grey-green fill with about six soft vertical flute seams and a lighter lit edge on the right - no areoles, no spines, no ribs with tubercles.

ALL THREE must-reads are absent, not merely small or misplaced - I specifically hunted for each:
1. 'hugely swollen bulbous grey caudex base' - ABSENT. The only thing in the neighbourhood is the cone's ordinary basal taper, and I want to be precise that this is NOT a shrunken caudex the judge overlooked: a caudex needs the widest point low and a distinct narrowing above it into stems. Here the widest point (52px) is at 80% of the way down and the profile is a single unbroken straight line from apex to soil. There is no separate base volume of any kind, and nothing grey - the base is the same sage-green as the rest of the column, ending flush on a flat dark elliptical ground shadow.
2. 'few thick stubby branches' - ABSENT. Zero branches, zero stubs, zero forks. The silhouette is convex on both sides for its entire height; row scans show a single contiguous run of subject pixels on every row from y=114 to y=339 (n equals width on every row), so nothing detaches from the trunk anywhere.
3. 'bare stems with leaves and flowers only at the ends' - ABSENT as to leaves. There is not one leaf in the image. No glossy spoon-shaped tufts, no dark glossy green, no tuft at any tip. Only the single terminal flower sits at the one 'end' that exists.

The harvest read also fails: at 4x the bloom is an unmistakably flat, face-on radial daisy - about eleven separate rounded pink petals evenly spaced around a solid olive/gold disc centre - not a trumpet, no pale throat, and it is ONE solitary bloom rather than the specified cluster at the branch tips.

CORRECTIONS to the original claim, which was substantially accurate: (a) calling the column 'narrow' and 'vertically ribbed' overstates the cactus read - the taper is broad and cone-like rather than parallel-sided, and the vertical lines are soft shading flutes, not the deep ridges of a saguaro, with no spines or areoles at all; (b) the green is a desaturated sage/grey-green, not a saguaro green. Those details make the read closer to a smooth green candle/spire than to an organ-pipe specifically, but they do not rescue it - by every identity criterion in the packet ('Adenium obesum; the fat bottle-shaped trunk is the whole point') this is the wrong organism. FAIL stands. The fix is a ground-up re-form: a squat bottle caudex whose maximum width sits at the very bottom and is roughly as wide as the plant is tall, in grey-tan not green, pinching into two or three short thick green stubs, each capped with a small rosette of glossy dark-green spoon leaves and a cluster of deep-pink pale-throated trumpets seen partly in three-quarter view.

rows.readsAs: a pale green succulent rosette or a closed lotus flower, with a sunflower floating in the sky above it
rows.defect: The render is broken - the small yellow flower is stranded in empty space roughly a third of the frame ABOVE the plant, touching nothing, at the height where the sibling rosettes put their stalk-tip beads, so it reads as a detached artefact. Beyond that the plant is not a prickly pear: the pads all radiate from one ground point in the family fan arrangement instead of being stacked end to end off each other, and it is completely smooth - no areoles, no glochid tufts, no long spines anywhere on any pad (only two or three stray hairline scratches), and no magenta tunas ringing the top pad rims. A stranger names this a fat-leaved succulent, not an Opuntia.
rows.fix: Reattach or delete the floating flower, restack the pads as two or three flat ovals joined edge-to-edge in a jointed chain, then cover every pad face with a regular grid of areoles carrying spine tufts and ring the upper pad rims with upright barrel-shaped magenta fruits.
rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, and the packet's three must-reads are 0-for-3. I read the 440x440 PNG at full size, then re-cropped and upscaled the plant 4x, the flower 8x, and the silhouette at 3.2x exposure boost, and ran a per-row pixel classifier.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. The body is 4-5 overlapping smooth ovals fanned out from a single point at the ground line, occupying only rows 176-320 of 440 (33% of frame height, sitting low). Each oval is a plain ellipse with a rounded tip. Their fill is NOT the specced blue-grey green: it is a warm yellow-green with a blown-out near-white central hot spot, which reads as a fleshy leaf blade lit from within. The blown-exposure silhouette pass is decisive - the outline is a perfectly smooth, unbroken scalloped curve, a cloud/lotus profile with ZERO protrusions, bumps, tufts or needles anywhere on the edge, top, sides or base. MUST-READ 2 (areoles with tufts of fine glochids and long spines) is absent in every sense.

CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM - the pads are NOT blank. Each oval carries a faint pale line glyph, and at 4x it is clearly a LEAF MIDRIB WITH BRANCHING LATERAL VEINS (a central rib running tip-to-base with 2-3 chevron veins forking off it, plus a small hooked mark near the base). That is pinnate venation. This is worse than blankness for the identity, because the one piece of surface detail present is actively arguing 'leaf' when the must-read needs areole dots. The fixer must delete the vein glyph and replace it with a scattered grid of areole dots + glochid tufts + paired long spines, not merely 'add spines on top'.

MUST-READ 1 (flat overlapping paddle pads joined end to end) fails on topology, not on shape. The ovals themselves are roughly paddle-proportioned and they do overlap, but every one of them radiates from the SAME single basal origin like petals of a closed lotus or leaves of an agave rosette. There is no joint, no narrowed neck, no pad growing off the upper rim of the pad below it - i.e. no jointed end-to-end chain, which is the whole grammar of an Opuntia. The judge described this correctly.

MUST-READ 3 (magenta tunas ringing the pad edge) is absent absolutely: a pixel scan across all 193,600 pixels returns ZERO magenta/pink pixels in the entire image. The only harvest mark is a single small 12-petal YELLOW daisy with a brown center disc.

CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM - the flower's float is real but the judge overstated the distance. Yellow pixels occupy rows 85-114; the topmost green pixel is row 176. So the gap is 61 rows of pure background, ~14% of frame height (roughly twice the flower's own 30px height), not 'a third of the frame'. The direction of the error does not matter to the verdict: the flower is fully detached, touches nothing, and has no stem, pedicel or receptacle of any kind. It is also the wrong glyph twice over - a flat composite/daisy rosette rather than the Opuntia's many-petalled shallow bowl, and yellow rather than the specced magenta barrel-shaped tuna, and there is only ONE of it rather than a ring of them along the top pad rim.

NET READ: a pale fat-leaved rosette succulent or half-open lotus with a daisy hovering above it. Nothing in the image identifies it as a cactus, let alone an Opuntia. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a yucca or agave rosette with a thin flower stem
rows.defect: The narrowest blades in the batch make this the closest read of the five, but it is still the shared fan chassis, and its own two distinguishing must-reads are missing or too weak. There are no curly white fibres peeling anywhere along the leaf edges - every margin is clean - and the promised tall panicle of waxy cream bells is only five tiny white ovals clustered in a two-centimetre knot at the very top of an otherwise bare hairline stalk, so it reads as a bud or a berry rather than a hanging flower panicle. The blades also carry the same herringbone venation as the Agave, which a stiff sword leaf should not show.
rows.fix: Hang loose curling white threads off both edges of most blades, and expand the top of the stalk into a broad branched panicle of dozens of nodding cream bell flowers so the harvest reads at thumbnail size.

rows.readsAs: a cluster of green-and-red ice-cream cones, or Sarracenia if you already know Sarracenia
rows.defect: The third must-read is simply absent: the pitcher throat has no red vein network. Zoomed in, the tube carries a few flat vertical dark-olive ribs that read as celery/bamboo ridging, the mouth is a single clean pink outline ring, and the interior is a uniform flat dark brown with no netting, no reticulation, no crimson at all. The pitchers also taper to a sharp POINT at the bottom and float on those points — nothing meets the ground, there is no basal rosette or soil, so the cones read as standing on their tips like traffic cones inverted. The hood is one flat solid leaf-blade with no underside, no vein and no attachment, so it reads as pasted on rather than as a continuation of the pitcher.
rows.fix: Draw the red vein reticulation — an anastomosing crimson net over the upper third of each tube and across the hood's inner face and the peristome — and flatten the pitcher bases into a ground-level cluster so the tubes rise out of a rosette instead of balancing on points.

rows.readsAs: an orange pinwheel or a spoke diagram with white beads on the rim; a sea anemone at thumbnail size
rows.defect: The tentacle-plus-droplet must-read is present but confined to the wrong place: the glandular hairs only fringe the OUTER rim of each paddle, and the entire paddle face is bare flat orange. Real Drosera is furred with tentacles across the whole blade, and that furred surface is what makes the plant legible. The colour is also wrong on the reference's own terms — leafColour calls for green flushed crimson, and there is not one green pixel anywhere; every leaf, every petiole and the hub are the same single orange-red. The scorpioid flower stalk is entirely missing. Composition is a perfectly symmetric radial spoke wheel converging on a single hard point, drawn dead top-down, which reads as a logo or a wiring diagram rather than a low rosette, and the droplets render as opaque white pearls with no transparency or highlight, so they read as popcorn rather than glue.
rows.fix: Cover the whole paddle surface with tentacles, not just the margin, and make the drops translucent with a specular dot; give the petioles green with a crimson flush and tilt the rosette off dead-top-down so it sits on ground rather than reading as a wheel.

rows.readsAs: red rambutan or spiky strawberries on green stalks — a bunch of bristly fruit, not a trap
rows.defect: The identity must-read is absent. At 4x there is no clamshell anywhere in the image: every trap is a single solid red BALL with a green collar, with no midrib, no hinge, no seam, no two lobes and no gape. The teeth do not interlock along a closing edge — they radiate outward from the whole circumference like a sunburst, which is a burr, not a fringe. Because the trap is a closed sphere and its exterior is red, the red glandular INTERIOR must-read cannot be present either; the red is on the outside, which inverts the plant. The third must-read fails too: there is no low ground rosette and no flat winged petioles, only narrow uniform green rods converging to a point, so the whole thing reads as a picked bouquet floating above its shadow. The two central traps also overlap into one undifferentiated red mass, losing even the count.
rows.fix: Rebuild the trap as two hinged lobes seen from the side, open at 45 degrees on a visible midrib hinge, green outside with the crimson glandular surface only on the inner faces, and put the marginal teeth as interlocking cilia along the two lip edges only; broaden the petioles into flat leaf-like wings lying in a ground rosette.
rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440px render, then decoded the PNG and re-read it at 4x (whole cluster), 8x (the two central traps), and 10x (leftmost and rightmost traps individually) plus a 7x crop of the base. Verdict FAIL stands, but two of the stated causes are wrong and the fix should not be made against them.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE: five straight green rods radiate from one point; each rod ends in a red spiky head. Each head is NOT 'a single solid red ball' as claimed — at 10x every head is clearly TWO overlapping circular lobes. On the leftmost trap a smaller lobe sits low-left over a larger lobe up-right, and the small lobe's green rim visibly crosses the large lobe's red field; the rightmost trap has the same pair rotated (upper-left lobe + lower-right lobe) with a soft arc where the second disc's gradient overlays the first; the two central traps each show a left disc and a right disc with a faint vertical boundary and a small notch in the top rim between them. So the two-lobe COUNT exists in geometry. What is genuinely absent is the HINGE: the lobes are offset like two overlapping coins rather than butted along a straight midrib, there is no midrib stroke, no seam line, no gape, and no dark hinge shadow. Nothing tells the eye these are halves of a clamshell.

CORRECTION 1 (their colour claim is backwards): they say 'the crimson glandular interior is inverted to the outside'. It is not inverted. Each lobe is a radial gradient with GREEN at the outer rim fading to deep crimson at the lobe centre — the correct polarity for a face-on open trap, green margin around a red glandular floor. The red therefore is not the defect; the defect is that with no gape or seam the red centre reads as fruit flesh instead of trap lining.

CORRECTION 2 (teeth coverage overstated but the substance holds): on the two CENTRAL traps the bristles only occupy the upper ~180 degrees of the rim, not the entire circumference; on the outer three they wrap ~270 degrees including under the lower-left/lower-right rim. In all cases they are single white/cream sticks of varied length pointing radially OUTWARD from the lobe centre, several crossing each other at random angles. There is no pair of opposing tooth combs, no meshing along a closing edge, no teeth on the inner side of a gape. So 'radiating like a burr rather than interlocking' is correct as an identity failure even though the coverage is not the full circle everywhere.

CORRECTION 3 (central merge): at 1x the two middle traps do read as one continuous red mass and the claim is fair, but at 8x there is a discernible boundary and a notch — it is a readability failure at gameplay size, not literally one undivided blob.

CONFIRMED AS STATED: the rosette must-read is entirely missing. The base crop shows five perfectly straight, CONSTANT-WIDTH green rods converging to a single vertex that sits above the ground-shadow ellipse — a hand-tied bouquet, not a plant. No flat winged petioles (no widening anywhere along a stalk), no low ground-level rosette, no basal spread. Also absent: the harvest stalk of small white flowers — no flower stalk of any kind is drawn.

NET: mustRead 1 (hinged clamshell with interlocking teeth) fails — lobes present, hinge/midrib/gape/interlock absent; mustRead 2 (red glandular interior) is half-present with correct polarity but unreadable without a gape; mustRead 3 (low rosette with winged petioles) is absent. The silhouette reads as five spiky red fruit on bare stems — rambutan or a lychee bouquet is a fair description. FAIL upheld.

FIX DIRECTION IMPLIED: keep the red-centre/green-rim gradient (it is right); replace the two offset coins with two mirrored lobes meeting along a straight midrib, open the pair to a shallow V gape with a dark hinge line down the join, move the teeth off the outer perimeter and onto the two facing gape edges as two interlocking combs, and rebuild the stems as short flat petioles that widen toward the trap and lie in a low ground rosette instead of converging to one point.

rows.readsAs: an ornamental fountain grass or a small pampas clump with a seed bristle
rows.defect: The identity of a cattail is the fat brown velvet SAUSAGE, and it is not here — the brown spike is a thread barely wider than a leaf blade, and it has no separate thin male spike above it. The leaves also splay outward almost to horizontal in a fountain instead of rising as straight vertical straps, and no bare round stem is visible because the stem is buried inside the leaf spray. This is the same fountain drawing as Papyrus and Wild Rice, recoloured.
rows.fix: Draw the spike as a genuinely thick brown cigar — roughly one-sixth as wide as it is tall, blunt at both ends — carried on a clean bare stem that stands clear ABOVE the leaves, with a thin pale bristle continuing above it; and straighten the strap leaves to rise near-vertically from the waterline.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, and the measurements make it worse than stated. I decoded the 440x440 PNG and scanned it pixel-by-pixel, plus rendered three zooms (6x on the head, 4x on the stem/base, 12x gamma-boosted on the spike tip).

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE: one green fountain of ~14 strap blades all radiating from a single point at the base, and one thin near-vertical central stem carrying a small brown column at the top.

THE SPIKE — measured, not eyeballed. Brown pixels occupy exactly 201 pixels of a 440x440 canvas (0.1% of the frame). The brown mass runs y=105 to y=141 (37 px tall) and its per-row width is 4-7 px, mean ~5.5 px. For comparison, measured on the same rows: the bare stem below it is 3-4 px wide (x 209-212 at y=145-170) and the neighbouring leaf blades are 7-8 px wide. So the spike is roughly 1.5x the stem and NARROWER THAN A LEAF BLADE. The judge said 'barely wider than a leaf blade' — that is if anything generous; it is measurably thinner than one. There is no cigar mass, no bulge, no velvet body. Its silhouette is a straight-sided column with lumpy stepped edges (a stack of beads), blunt-cut flat at the top and bottom rather than rounded. It reads as a plantain or dock flower spike stuck in an ornamental grass clump, not as the defining brown velvet sausage. Must-read 1 ('dense brown cigar-shaped spike') is not satisfied.

MALE BRISTLE — confirmed absent. At 12x with gamma boost the brown column terminates flat at y=105 with pure background above it. The pixel scan finds zero brown-hued pixels anywhere above y=105 in the entire image. Nothing rises from the spike tip. Must-read 2 ('thin spike of male flowers directly above the brown sausage') is absent.

WHERE THE JUDGE IS WRONG: they wrote 'no bare round stem visible'. A bare stem IS visible and is one of the better parts of the drawing — a continuous green line runs from the underside of the spike at y=142 straight down through open air to the base, unobstructed by leaves for roughly 15-20 px below the spike and traceable all the way to the crown. The defect with it is not absence but rendering: it is only 3-4 px wide, flat single-tone green with no round shading, so it reads as a wire rather than a round culm. Fix the description before fixing the art — the stem exists and should be thickened and shaded, not added.

LEAVES — judge is correct. The blades all spring from one point and splay across nearly the full 180 degrees: the outermost pair on left and right leave the crown at ~70-80 degrees from vertical and arch over and down so their tips point at the ground, giving a symmetric fountain / pampas-clump habit. Only the two or three innermost blades are near-vertical. The reference calls for 'flat sword-like strap blades rising STRAIGHT from the waterline' and must-read 3 is 'vertical strap leaves from the base'. As drawn this is a splayed grass fountain, not a stand of vertical straps. Related: no waterline or water plane is indicated at all — the base sits on a dark elliptical ground shadow, so it reads as a dry-soil clump rather than an emergent aquatic.

SECONDARY DEFECT NOT IN THE ORIGINAL CLAIM: the leaves carry pale horizontal tick marks as texture, and a number of these ticks land in empty background beyond the blade silhouette (clearly visible in the open dark space on the right of the plant around x~280,y~165 and scattered up the left flank). Detached floating dashes are a clipping bug in the leaf-texture pass, not a stylistic choice.

VERDICT: FAIL stands. Two of the three must-reads (cigar spike, male bristle) are absent or unreadable and the third (vertical straps) is contradicted by the splay. The single organ that IS a cattail is missing, so the asset does not identify as the organism. To fix: fatten the brown head to roughly 3-4x the stem diameter and clearly fatter than any leaf blade (~18-22 px wide at this canvas size), round both ends into a true cigar, give it a soft velvet nap rather than stepped beads, add a thin bristly male spike ~40% of the sausage length directly above it, thicken and round-shade the bare stem, and pull the outer blades up toward vertical so they rise as straps and only arch in the last third.

rows.readsAs: three olives or green pea-shaped sweets sitting on a dark serving plate
rows.defect: Duckweed is a carpet of dozens of millimetre-scale discs; this shows exactly THREE huge glossy yellow-green ovals, each large enough to be a lily pad, resting inside a rimmed dish that reads as crockery rather than water. No hair root hangs from any disc — instead a short straight line lies flat ACROSS each oval like a scratch. The scale cue that is the entire point of the species is inverted.
rows.fix: Replace the three big ovals with forty-plus tiny two-and-three-lobed fronds scattered irregularly across the whole width, each dropping one fine hair root downward into darker water, and delete the plate rim entirely.
rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, and the original description is essentially accurate — but it under-reports two things and I want the fix to be made against exact geometry, so here is what I actually saw at 1x, 4x and 10x (gamma-boosted crops).

WHAT IS IN THE FRAME. One object, centred, occupying roughly the middle third of the 440x440 canvas, with completely empty background above, below and to both sides. The object is a shallow open vessel drawn in three-quarter view: a thin near-white rim ellipse (~200px wide, ~30px tall), a darker blue-grey interior basin filling it, an outward-flaring lower body that converges to a narrow flat base, and a soft elliptical drop shadow floating in the void beneath it. It has an outside and an underside. That is a dish/saucer, not a body of water. There is no waterline running off the edges of the frame, no shore, no meniscus, nothing that continues past the object — so the water surface the must-read requires is not depicted at all; it has been substituted with a container.

THE FRONDS. Exactly three ellipses, each about 70-80px wide and 45px tall, heavily overlapping, sitting in the basin. They are not flat films: each carries a strong volumetric gradient — hot near-white specular highlight at the upper left falling through bright yellow-green to a shaded olive lower-right edge — so they read as solid three-dimensional beans/olives/lemons with real thickness. Duckweed fronds are paper-thin, matte, and essentially two-dimensional from above. The colour hue (bright yellow-green) is defensible against 'bright light green above'; the gloss and the implied volume are not.

MUST-READ 1 — 'carpet of tiny oval green discs floating on the surface': ABSENT. Three discs is not a carpet, and at 75px against a 200px dish each frond reads as roughly plum-sized. The scale inversion the other judge names is real, and I would state its mechanism precisely: the dish is the ONLY scale-reference object in the frame, and it reads as tableware, so it fixes the fronds at fruit size. The species is a millimetre-scale free-floating carpet.

MUST-READ 2 — 'one fine hair root hanging from each disc': ABSENT, and the other judge's description of the substitute is correct — I confirm it at 10x. Each of the three discs carries exactly one short, thin, slightly darker line. It begins near the disc's centre and runs rightward and very slightly downward, staying entirely on the disc's upper face; on the rightmost disc it terminates exactly at the disc's own rim and does not cross the silhouette edge; on the left and centre discs it stops short of the edge entirely. Nothing descends below any disc, and nothing descends below the dish. IMPORTANT FOR THE FIX: the root primitive clearly EXISTS in the draw code — three of them, one per frond, correct count, correct weight, correct near-hairline thickness. It is only mis-oriented: drawn in-plane across the top face instead of anchored at the frond's underside and hanging down into the water. This is a re-anchor and re-angle, not a missing feature.

MUST-READ 3 — 'no stem, no upright structure at all': satisfied for the plant itself; no stalk rises from any frond. (The dish's own body is upright structure, but it is scenery, not plant anatomy.)

DEFECT THE OTHER JUDGE DID NOT REPORT: z-order. The pale rim ellipse of the dish is painted OVER the fronds — the bright rim line runs straight across the front of all three discs at roughly their mid-height, visible as a continuous light band cutting each one in half. The near rim should occlude nothing at that height and the far rim should sit behind the fronds. This bug is a large part of why the group reads as 'contents inside a bowl' rather than 'things lying on a surface'.

NET: two of three identity must-reads are absent and the organism reads as three olives on a plate. FAIL stands. The fix is scale (many dozens of small fronds in budding pairs and threes, not three large ones), substrate (an open water plane that runs out of frame — delete the vessel, its foot and its drop shadow), root orientation (rotate the existing hair to hang from the underside), gloss (kill the specular volume; these are flat matte films), and the rim z-order.

rows.readsAs: a water lily — a stranger would name the wrong species outright
rows.defect: Every leaf lies FLAT on the surface at water level, which is the one thing the reference explicitly forbids; nothing is held up on a stalk. There is no shower-head seed pod anywhere. The bloom is a small flat six-point pink star lying on the surface, not a large cupped many-petalled bowl. Structurally this is pixel-for-pixel the Water Lily asset with the pads tinted paler and the star tinted pink.
rows.fix: Redraw from a side view: lift two or three big round peltate leaves high above the waterline on tall single stalks meeting each leaf at its CENTRE with the rims curled up like shallow bowls, add a flat-topped green shower-head seed pod on its own stalk, and make the bloom a deep pink multi-layered cup held above the leaves.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, and confirmed by pixel comparison against Water_Lily.png. What I actually saw at 440x440 and again at 4x/12x zoom: a flat dark navy water ellipse with a thin lighter rim highlight and a soft drop shadow beneath it; three plain green ovals lying ON that ellipse plane (one left, one centre-front overlapping the rim, one right); a single small pink star flower sitting flat on the pads. Nothing rises above the water plane anywhere in the image. The topmost inked row of the whole composition is y=181 of 440 — and the topmost inked row of Water_Lily.png is ALSO exactly y=181, i.e. the Lotus has no more vertical reach than the asset it is supposed to be distinguished from. Sampling every 2nd pixel, the two silhouettes share 2470 inked samples with only 30 unique to Lotus; the pad centres, the water ellipse, the shadow and the flower are at identical coordinates. It is the Water Lily chassis recoloured, exactly as claimed.

Against the reference row (aspect 0.9; mustRead = leaf held high above water on a central stalk, never floating flat; shower-head seed pod; large pink cupped bloom; note: 'Lotus leaves stand above the water; water lily leaves float on it. Do not conflate.') all three must-reads fail:
1. STALK/EMERGENT LEAF — absent. There is no vertical element of any kind: no stalk, no petiole, no peltate disc held clear of the surface. All three leaves are flat ellipses at waterline. Nor are the leaves peltate-round with up-turned rims — they are simple flat-shaded ovals, each scored by ONE straight dark line (not a lily V-notch either, so the pad reads as neither organism's leaf correctly). Wider than tall by roughly 3:1 overall, so the rendered aspect also contradicts the specified 0.9.
2. SEED POD — absent. I searched the whole frame at zoom; there is no flat-topped receptacle, no wells, no shower-head. The only yellow in the image is a small circular disc at the flower's centre, which is the same daisy-eye the Water Lily flower has, not a lotus receptacle.
3. CUPPED BLOOM — absent. Corrections to the claim's wording here: the bloom is a SEVEN-point star, not six, and it is not merely 'small flat pink' — it is seven narrow lance-shaped pale-pink petals radiating in one plane around a yellow disc, i.e. a daisy/anemone form. It is flat, single-whorled, lying on the pad surface, roughly 40px across against a ~250px composition. A lotus bloom must be a large many-petalled cup with overlapping layers standing above the leaves; none of that is present.

One part of the claim I want to soften rather than reject: the retint is not purely cosmetic-random — the pads ARE lifted to a paler grey-green versus the Water Lily's dark saturated green, which is a genuine (if solitary) nod to the row's 'blue-grey green with a waxy bloom', and the flower is pink where the lily's is white. Those two hue moves are the ONLY differentiation carried; the geometry is byte-for-byte the same family chassis. Fix direction: this needs new geometry, not a palette pass — raise at least one peltate disc on a visible vertical stalk clear of the waterline with an up-turned rim, add a flat-topped green shower-head pod on a second stalk, and replace the seven-petal daisy with a tall multi-whorl pink cup also held above the pads.

rows.readsAs: a clump of dead or drought-yellowed ornamental grass
rows.defect: The whole identity of papyrus is a tall bare triangular stem with a firework of fine threads bursting from the very TOP — here there is no stem at all and no terminal umbel; the arching parts are thick leaf-blades that leave the ground directly, exactly as in the Cattail and Wild Rice fountains, in khaki. The blades are also far too coarse to read as thread-like rays, and the hatch ticks on them are the same artifact carried over from the shared chassis.
rows.fix: Draw three or four tall naked stems rising two-thirds of the frame height with nothing on them, then explode fifty hair-fine drooping rays radially from each stem tip, with tiny brown spikelets at the ray ends.
rows.verifyWhy: Upheld, and confirmed at 5x magnification plus a pixel bbox measurement. WHAT IS ON CANVAS: a single low fountain. Every element in the image converges to ONE point on the ground at roughly x=232,y=320 (the 5x base crop shows ~18 blades funnelling into a hard V-apex sitting on the ellipse shadow). From that apex the blades fan outward and upward, the inner few running near-vertical to y~106 and the outer ones arching hard over and drooping with blunt rounded hooked tips at x~25 and x~415. Ink bbox is x:22-417, y:106-322, i.e. 396 wide x 217 tall = aspect 1.82 wide. THE TWO MUST-READS ARE BOTH ABSENT. (1) 'tall bare three-sided stem with no leaves along it': there is no stem at any point in the image. Nothing rises bare off the rhizome before branching; the rays ARE the plant and they start at soil level. The one candidate — a single near-vertical stalk in the centre reaching highest — is the same width and the same tapered strap form as its neighbours, is not solitary, is not bare (it carries three hatch ticks along its length), and terminates bluntly in empty space carrying nothing. (2) 'firework explosion of fine drooping threads at the very top': the burst exists but it is BASAL, not terminal, and it is coarse. Each ray is a thick tapered leaf blade 6-10px wide with a rounded blunt tip, not a hair-fine ray; there are ~18 of them, not the hundreds an umbel needs; and there are no brownish spikelets at any tip. CORRECTION TO THE STATED CAUSE — one nuance the other judge understated and one they got exactly right. Understated: they wrote 'no terminal firework of threads', which reads as though no radial burst exists at all. A radial burst DOES exist and is the dominant shape of the picture; the defect is that it is planted at the ground instead of held at the top of a stem, and that its elements are blades rather than threads. The fix is not 'add a burst', it is 'lift the existing burst onto a tall smooth bare stem and shatter each blade into many fine drooping rays'. Got it right: the shared-chassis charge is literally true and I verified it side by side. Cattail's ink bbox is 377x221 against Papyrus's 396x217 — the same wide fountain, the same single-point ground convergence, the same blade count and arch curvature, the same blunt hooked tips. Papyrus is Cattail with the brown cigar spike deleted and the palette shifted; Cattail's spec aspect is 0.35 and Papyrus's is 0.5, and both were drawn at ~1.8 wide, so the aspect field was ignored for both. Two further defects worth logging: the hatch-tick artifact is present and in places BROKEN — short bright horizontal bars are stamped across the blades at regular intervals, and at least three of them float completely detached in empty background (clearest at roughly x=145-175 y=157 and x=270-285 y=160, sitting on bare canvas with no blade under them). And the colour is off-spec independently of the chassis: the reference calls for bright green stem and rays, the asset is uniform khaki/olive-gold. Net: this reads as a coarse ornamental grass clump or a de-spiked cattail, not as Cyperus papyrus. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a leek, a scallion, or a young aloe — an upright kitchen vegetable, not a seabed meadow
rows.defect: The blades form one narrow closed bundle standing dead vertical and symmetrical: none of the three must-reads survive. There is no lean with the current, no horizontal creeping rhizome with shoots at intervals, and no meadow of parallel straps — it is a single tuft. Three bright green pill-shaped capsules are stuck onto the middle of the blades with no anatomical reading at all; they look like a render artifact pasted over the leaves.
rows.fix: Lay a horizontal rhizome across the bottom of the frame with shoot-fans sprouting at intervals along it, and rake every ribbon blade over to the same side at roughly forty degrees so the whole meadow reads as combed by one current; delete the pill capsules.
rows.verifyWhy: Upheld, with three corrections to the stated cause. WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN (verified at 3x and 6x magnification of the source PNG): a single isolated clump of roughly seven or eight blades that converge to ONE narrow pinch at ground level -- at 6x the neck is about 25px wide and every blade terminates flat on a generic elliptical drop shadow. From that pinch the blades splay upward and outward into an inverted-cone / wine-glass / celery-heart silhouette, widest at the very top (about 40 percent of frame width) with individually resolved rounded tips. It is not closed -- there is a real upward fan with blades crossing in front of each other and one darker blade set behind on the left, and the tips ARE rounded as the packet asks. That fan and those rounded tips are the only parts of the leaf spec that land, and a fix pass should not destroy them. CORRECTION 2: the blades are not constant-width straps -- each one tapers from wide at the tip to hairline at the base and carries a bright convex highlight down its centre, so they read as tubular succulent stalks, not flat ribbons. That taper plus the single-point base is exactly what produces the leek/scallion read, and it is the taper (not merely the verticality) that needs to change: seagrass blades are flat and near constant-width along their whole length. CORRECTION 3: the judge described the three pale shapes as 'pill capsules pasted onto the mid-blades'. Precisely, they sit on the vertical centre-line straddling one narrow central blade at roughly 35, 52 and 70 percent of height, in a pale mint far lighter than any blade; the lowest is not a capsule at all but a near-perfect white-mint circular disc. More importantly the judge missed that the packet says 'harvest: none visible (inconspicuous flowers hidden inside the leaf sheaths)' -- so these three marks are not merely badly drawn, they should not exist at all. NOW THE MUST-READS, all three genuinely absent: (1) 'flat ribbon blades all leaning one way with the current' -- zero lean. The form is bilaterally symmetric about the vertical axis; blades splay equally left and right and there is no unidirectional bend anywhere, so nothing communicates water movement. (2) 'horizontal creeping rhizome with shoots at intervals' -- no horizontal element exists in the image. I zoomed the base specifically to look for one; there is only the pinch and the shadow ellipse, no root, no runner, no lateral shoot. (3) 'meadow of parallel straps rooted in sand' -- one solitary clump, no repetition, no second shoot, no sand or substrate cue, and the blades radiate rather than run parallel. With all three identity must-reads missing and a spurious harvest element added against an explicit 'none visible', the asset does not read as seagrass; it reads as a leek or a celery heart. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a water lily — correct

rows.readsAs: a grass clump with a screw or a nail standing in it

rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 PNG, then re-cropped the seed head at 6x and 12x. The FAIL stands, and the core of the claim is correct, but two parts of its description need correcting so the fix is aimed right.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. A single vertical pale-green culm rises from the centre of a leaf fan and terminates around y=86-160 in ONE rigid, parallel-sided, unbranched column about 10px wide. At 12x that column is not a bristle or an awn cluster: it is two stacked COLUMNS OF SHORT HORIZONTAL TAN BARS (roughly 11 pairs) flanking a dark near-black central slot, with the bars stepping slightly so the edges look helical. It reads as machine thread, or a zipper, not as grain. Capping it at the very top is a solid, filled, hard-edged inverted trapezoid, wider than the shaft and about 22px across, tapering down to meet it. Trapezoid cap + threaded shaft + slot = a countersunk flathead wood screw driven point-down into the plant. That much of the judge's read is exactly right and if anything understated.

I checked the whole upper canvas at 6x: there is no second axis anywhere, no pedicel, no splay, no separated spikelet, no divergence of any kind. The outline of the head is a strict rectangle. The open airy panicle is the one feature that separates wild rice from every other grass, and nothing in the image gestures at it.

There is also no water cue at all - the blades arch down to a flat dark ground ellipse shadow, exactly the terrestrial-clump base used elsewhere in the set.

CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM'S SECOND SENTENCE. 'The leaf spray beneath is the Cattail fountain in brighter green' is not accurate. I opened Cattail.png to compare. Cattail has roughly 14 THICK dark-olive sword blades, each carrying small white tick dashes, splaying from a loose open base. Wild Rice has roughly 24 very THIN needle-fine blades, no tick marks, brighter yellow-green with a pale luminous core, and critically they are FUSED into a solid opaque pale-green wedge for the lower third before separating - closer to a pandanus/agave rosette than to the Cattail draw. So this is a different fountain, not a recolour of the Cattail one. Blaming Cattail reuse would send the fix to the wrong place; the leaf spray is a plausible if generic emergent-grass fan and is the least broken thing in the image. Its real faults are that the blades are needle-fine rather than the specified flat ribbon blades, and that the fan is far too wide for the 0.5 aspect.

FIX TARGET. Replace the head geometry entirely: kill the trapezoid cap and the threaded/slotted column, and build a genuinely open panicle - a central rachis with 6-10 whorled branches diverging 30-60 degrees, each carrying a few long narrow pendulous purple-brown grains, occupying a loose triangular-to-ovate airy envelope roughly a third of total plant height. Then narrow the whole silhouette and lengthen the culm so the plant stands tall and emergent at aspect ~0.5 rather than squatting at 1.6.

rows.readsAs: a pale-green sago palm or small cycad rosette, or a bristly agave

rows.verifyWhy:
I looked at the 440x440 PNG at 1x and then re-cropped the crown and the left frond mass at 4x, and decoded the pixels to check the colour claims. The FAIL stands, but two parts of the stated cause are wrong and must not be carried into the fix.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: a low, wide, radially-spread mound of ~16 once-divided fronds fanning out from a single squat basal crown that sits on a soft dark ellipse shadow. Each frond is built as a THICK TAPERING PALE-GREEN MIDRIB (a solid lance-shaped blade body ~6-10px wide at the base) with narrow pointed pinnae combed off both edges at a shallow forward angle -- at 4x these are elongated lanceolate teeth, not merely 'sawteeth', but they are unambiguously pointed spikes, never fans. Every stipe/rachis is the same pale apple-green as the blade, and it is a thick tapering midrib rather than a hair-fine wire; the darkest structural colour in the whole silhouette is the olive #435F3F crown/shadow. The row's own note ('drawn with green stalks it is unrecognisable') is exactly what shipped, so this alone is fatal.
CORRECTION to the claim 'there is no black anywhere in the image': the canvas background is near-black (#05060C), the deep gaps between the combed pinnae read as black slots, there is a dull dark-olive basal crown clump, and a dark ground-shadow ellipse under the plant. ~2,100 in-silhouette pixels fall below L=40. None of that is a stem. The precise defect is 'no black STEM strokes', not 'no black pixels'.

MUST-READ 2 -- fan-shaped scalloped leaflets: ABSENT, confirmed. Every leaflet is a narrow pointed spike with straight edges and an acute tip. Nothing anywhere in the image has a wedge/fan outline or a scalloped (crenate) outer margin.

MUST-READ 3 -- airy open lacy spray: ABSENT, confirmed. The fronds overlap heavily into an opaque dense mound; the interior is solid green with no see-through negative space, and the fronds are laid down in a broad flattened fan rather than an open lacy spray.

FEATURE THE FIRST JUDGE MISSED (does not rescue the asset): there IS a small tightly-coiled crozier/fiddlehead spiral drawn at roughly x=225,y=270, just right of the crown, and a fainter one lower left near x=232,y=272. That is a legitimate fern cue and the only thing in the image saying 'fern' beyond the pinnate combing. It is genus-neutral and does not supply any Adiantum identity.

CORRECTION to 'pixel-for-pixel the Sword Fern asset lightened': FALSE as stated. The two files differ (md5 9ac5b045... vs b49b7b77...) and the silhouettes have IoU 0.736, i.e. the frond count, curvature and individual frond placements genuinely differ. What is true, and is the real finding, is that the two ferns are ONE CHASSIS with different parameters: identical vertical envelope (both plants span y=107 to y=317 exactly), near-identical widths (381 vs 367), the same squat basal crown, the same drop-shadow ellipse, the same radial low fan layout, and the same thick-midrib-plus-combed-spikes frond construction. Ironically this asset reads closer to the Sword Fern row's own must-reads (once-divided fronds, leaflets running the frond's whole length in one plane) than to its own -- though even for Sword Fern the 'tight upright shuttlecock' is missed, since both are low spread fans.

FIX DIRECTION: this needs a different frond generator, not a recolour -- hair-fine near-black wire stipes and branching rachises drawn as 1-2px dark strokes, small fan/wedge leaflets with scalloped outer margins hung off the ends of those wires, and large gaps of background showing through, on a taller (aspect ~1.1) rather than a 1.8-wide footprint.

rows.readsAs: a dark-green cycad or sago palm mound; a stranger might guess fern but would not commit
rows.defect: The primary must-read, a tight upright shuttlecock crown of long stiff fronds, is not there: the crown is a low spreading mound distinctly wider than tall, with the outer fronds sweeping out horizontally and hooking downward past the base rather than standing up in a vase. The leaflets are not many narrow pointed leaflets running the frond length; they are small triangular sawteeth notched into the edge of a broad solid blade, and the blade centre reads as one continuous paddle rather than a single plane of separate pinnae, which pushes the read toward cycad. rows.readsAs: a white agave or century plant / a yucca rosette in soil
rows.defect: The leaves are dead-straight rigid spears radiating in a perfect symmetrical fan - no curl, no spidery droop, and no fine furred scale texture; they read as agave blades, not Tillandsia. The identity harvest is completely absent: there is no flattened pink or red bract paddle anywhere, only a bare olive stem carrying a thin lavender bead-spike. And the epiphyte read is inverted - the rosette base plants straight into a ground-shadow ellipse as if rooted in soil, with no bark, branch or wire to cling to.

rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 PNG at full size and then re-cropped it at 3x and 5x over the spike, both leaf wings, and the base. The FAIL stands, and the judge's central charge is correct, but two parts of their wording need correcting so the fix is aimed right.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: a radial rosette of ~17 flat, chalk-white lance blades converging to a single point on a ground line, with one thin olive stem rising from that same point through the centre of the rosette to a small knobbed violet spike near the top of the frame.

MUST-READ 1 - 'no soil and no real roots, clinging to bark or wire': FAILED, and this is the worst defect. At 5x the base crop shows every blade converging to a single vanishing point sitting exactly on a dark elliptical ground shadow that spreads left and right beneath the plant. There is no bark, no branch, no wire, no host of any kind, and no aerial-attachment cue whatsoever. Compounding it: the rosette is a strict upper hemisphere - the lowest blades run out horizontally and NOT ONE blade drops below the attachment point. A Tillandsia rosette is read as epiphytic largely because its lower leaves recurve DOWN past the point of attachment into empty air; here the horizon line cuts the fan off cleanly, which is the single strongest signal that this thing is planted in dirt.

MUST-READ 2 - 'silvery furred narrow curling leaves': FAILED on curl and on fur, partially met on narrowness. The blades are narrow and taper to needle points, so 'narrow tapering' is satisfied. But there is ZERO curl - each blade is a dead-straight flat wedge with a straight centreline from base to tip; not one has a recurve, an S-bend, a droop or even a slight arc. CORRECTION to the judge: they say 'no furred scale texture', which is true as a conclusion but overstates it as 'no texture'. At 3x each blade does carry a darker olive-grey midrib groove running its full length plus a faint low-poly facet/crease pattern across the blade face. That existing detail reads as a stiff structural rib - it actively reinforces the rigid-agave read - and is the opposite of the fine matte trichome fuzz the row asks for. So the fix is not 'add texture', it is 'replace rib+facet with soft furred scale stippling and a fuzzed silhouette edge'. Colour is also off: the dominant leaf clusters are 208-224 neutral grey and near-white (histogram peaks at 224,224,224 / 208,208,208 / 192,192,192) with only a slight green tint low near the stem - it reads chalk-white, not 'silvery grey-green, frosted'.

CORRECTION to the judge on 'perfect symmetrical fan': it is near-perfect and reads mechanical, but it is not literally perfect - blade lengths vary and the right wing is slightly longer and denser than the left. The criticism holds in substance (the spacing is even and the radiation is machine-regular), but do not chase 'break the mirror symmetry' as the fix; the problem is rigidity and the flat 180-degree spread, not mirroring.

MUST-READ 3 - 'flat pink bract with a purple tubular flower': the bract is ABSENT, and I verified this by measurement rather than by eye. I scanned all 193,600 pixels for anything reddish or pink (R > G+25 AND R > B+10): the count is exactly 0, bounding box empty. There is no pink or red anywhere in the asset. The judge is fully correct here. What IS present, per the 5x spike crop, is a single thin olive stem (~4px wide, roughly 96,112,64) carrying a ~55px column of stacked violet beads/knobs (roughly 176,112,208) - it reads as a lavender or grape-hyacinth raceme, not as tubular flowers, and it emerges from bare stem rather than from any paddle. So the identity harvest is missing its defining half and the surviving half is the wrong flower morphology.

NET READ: with 2.5 of 3 must-reads failing, this is unmistakably a white Yucca rostrata / silver agave with a lavender flower spike, planted in soil. It is not a Tillandsia. FAIL is the right band.

FIX PRIORITY: (1) put it on a host - a bark chunk or a stretched wire the rosette grips, kill the ground shadow, and let the lower third of the blades recurve DOWN past the attachment into open air; (2) curl every blade - narrow it, give it an outward S-arc and a soft drooping tip, and swap the midrib groove and facets for fine furred scale stippling with a fuzzed edge, warming the value from chalk-white toward silvery grey-green; (3) build the harvest properly - a flattened pink/red bract paddle with tubular violet flowers pushing out of its edge, replacing the bare-stem bead spike.

rows.readsAs: a huge red five-lobed spotted flower - most viewers would land on Rafflesia or at least 'giant corpse flower'

The spots render as glossy white bubbles clustered in random foam-like clumps rather than flat cream warts spread evenly over the lobes. rows.readsAs: a generic lollipop shade tree with a spiky halo and a few brown bugs on it
rows.defect: The broad FLAT-TOPPED crown with tiered horizontal branch plates - the single thing that makes a Cedrus a cedar - is absent; the crown is a plain round green cloud on a bare straight stick. Needles are straight single sticks radiating from the blob centre, never the tight rosette tufts on spur shoots called for. The barrel cones are small screw shapes floating inside and off the side of the foliage rather than standing upright on top of horizontal branch plates, so the 'eggs on a shelf' read is gone. rows.verifyWhy:
Verified by reading the 440x440 PNG whole, then decoding it and re-reading three zoomed crops (crown 3x, top edge 4x, right-hand cone pair 8x). The FAIL stands; every must-read on the reference row is missing or unreadable.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. A single straight brown dowel of near-uniform width runs from the ground shadow (y~390) up to y~215, with NO taper, NO flare at the base, and ZERO lateral branches anywhere along it. On top of it sits one soft airbrushed foliage mass, roughly x=95..355 by y=55..215 — so it is wider than tall (~260 x 160), but the top edge is a single smooth continuous DOME (confirmed at 4x: an unbroken convex arc from left shoulder to right shoulder), and the interior is 4-5 overlapping vertical-ish cloud lumps with no horizontal organisation of any kind. This is a lollipop shade-tree chassis; it would read as an oak or a generic 'tree' icon with spikes added.

MUST-READ 1, 'broad flat-topped crown with tiered horizontal branch plates' — ABSENT, and this alone is fatal. There is no flat top (the top is a dome), no tiers, no horizontal plates, and no branch geometry at all: not one twig leaves the trunk. The tabular, layered, wind-flattened Cedrus silhouette is the whole identity of this species and none of it is present.

MUST-READ 2, 'needles in tight rosette clusters, not single rows' — ABSENT. Roughly 30 individual straight pale-green line segments radiate outward from the canopy centre like porcupine quills / a sea-urchin fringe. Each is a lone stroke; none originate from a shared point, none are grouped into the whorled pompom that a spur-shoot rosette must show, and several extend well past the foliage edge onto bare background (the leftmost pair at x~75-115, y~135-160 are entirely outside the green). The needle strokes are also individually far too long relative to the crown.

MUST-READ 3, 'barrel cones standing upright on the branch tops' — MISPLACED, and I correct the other judge on the SHAPE. Four cones are present. Their axis IS vertical, so 'standing upright' is technically satisfied. But at 8x they are not barrels: each is an INVERTED truncated cone, widest at a flat top edge and tapering steadily to a narrow base, with stepped notches down both sides — a bollard / upturned megaphone / wasp-nest read. A Cedrus cone is widest at mid-height with a blunt flat crown sitting on a short stalk. So the other judge's phrase 'barrel cones' is generous; even if these were placed correctly they would not read as cedar cones. Placement is as reported and worse than reported: two cones (~x230,y120 and ~x175,y145) are buried INSIDE the foliage cloud with green painted over/around them, and two (~x320,y125 and ~x322,y168) sit on the right-hand edge floating almost entirely on bare navy background with no foliage or branch beneath them. Nothing supports any of the four. The 'eggs on a shelf' read is dead because there are no shelves anywhere in the image.

ADDITIONAL DEFECT THE OTHER JUDGE DID NOT NAME: colour. The row specifies 'dark blue-green to silvery grey-green'. The canopy is a warm mid grass-green with yellow-green highlights and no silver, grey or blue anywhere. The cones are a saturated orange-brown that reads as terracotta rather than resinous tan.

FIX DIRECTION: rebuild as a layered crown — 4-6 flattened horizontal foliage plates of decreasing width stacked with visible gaps, the topmost plate wide and cut flat rather than domed; give the trunk real lateral limbs that run out horizontally under each plate; replace the radiating single strokes with short tight rosette pompoms clustered on those limbs; reshape the cones to barrels widest at mid-height and seat them standing on the UPPER SURFACE of the plates, silhouetted against sky above the foliage line; shift the foliage toward blue-green with silvery grey highlights.

rows.readsAs: the exact same lollipop conifer-ish tree as Cedar and Redwood
rows.defect: Wrong organism outright. The reference is poison hemlock, a hollow-stemmed umbellifer HERB (form: herb, aspect 0.6), and the render is a tall woody tree - the identical brown trunk, green blob crown and radiating needle sticks used for Cedar and Redwood, decorated with the same brown screw cones. Not one must-read exists: no smooth hollow stem, no purple-red blotching, no finely cut fern-like foliage, no flat white umbrella flower head. A stranger names a pine, not a poisonous weed.

rows.verifyWhy: UPHELD after direct inspection at full size plus 4x nearest-neighbour crops of the crown and the stem. The packet row is unambiguous: form: herb, aspect 0.6, leaf 'large triangular leaves cut three or four times into fine fern-like segments, on hollow stems', harvest 'flat-topped umbrella-shaped clusters of tiny white flowers, then ridged green seeds', mustRead 'smooth hollow stem blotched with purple-red spots / very finely cut fern-like leaves / flat white umbrella flower heads', note 'Read as poison hemlock (Conium maculatum), not the hemlock conifer'. What is actually rendered is a woody lollipop tree. ZERO of the three must-reads are present, not even faintly, not even small: (1) STEM — the 4x stem crop shows a single flat mid-brown (~#8B5A38) bark-coloured trunk, uniform in hue from the ground to the crown junction, ~28px wide, dead vertical with a slight taper, capped at the bottom by a rounded stick end that floats on an elliptical drop shadow. There is no purple, no red, no magenta pixel anywhere on it; no spotting, no blotching, no mottling of any kind; no green in the stem; no hollow-tube cue (no rim highlight, no interior shading, no ribbing/striation); no basal rosette, no sheathing leaf bases, no branching umbel stalks. It is opaque woody bark, and it is the single most load-bearing mark on this species per the packet note. (2) LEAVES — the crown is a soft airbrushed green cloud blob with ~45 straight single-stroke green line segments radiating outward from it like a pin cushion. Those strokes are NEEDLES, one undivided stroke each. There is no rachis, no leaflets, no pinnae, no second or third order of division, nothing thrice-cut or ferny anywhere; the crown is a conifer's spray, not a Conium frond. (3) FLOWERS — there is no white in the image at all. No umbel, no flat top, no radiating ray-stalks, no dot clusters. Instead there are four brown/rust cone objects (~#A8663C) with horizontal ridge bands, tapering downward like drill bits, three in the upper crown and one hanging below it near the trunk junction. These are woody cones, and I confirm they are not a mis-coloured attempt at 'ridged green seeds' — they are brown, they are conical rather than the paired ovoid mericarps of an umbellifer, and they are the exact same cone asset. CHASSIS CONFIRMED: I opened Cedar.png and Redwood.png side by side. All three are one drawing — same brown tapered lollipop trunk on the same rounded stick foot, same soft green cloud crown, same radiating straight-needle spikes, same brown ridged screw-cones scattered in the crown. Hemlock is nearest to Redwood (same trunk height and thickness, same crown offset up and slightly left); Cedar differs only by a thicker trunk and a broader crown. Only the count and placement of needles and cones vary. Two CORRECTIONS/ADDITIONS to the original claim, both of which strengthen it rather than weaken it: (a) the cones are not 'sitting on top' shelf-style as Cedar's row would require — they are scattered inside and hanging below the crown, so the same generic cone asset is also wrong for Cedar; (b) the claim did not mention that the aspect ratio is not being honoured either — Hemlock (aspect 0.6), Cedar (aspect 1) and Redwood (aspect 0.3) all occupy nearly identical proportions in the frame, so the one parameter that could have differentiated them is inert. FIX DIRECTION: this asset needs to be rebuilt from scratch as a herb, not repainted. Required: a slender smooth green hollow stem carrying distinct purple-red blotches (the packet's key mark), an aspect that reads herb-height not tree-height, alternate large triangular leaves resolved into at least three visible orders of fine division, and a flat-topped compound umbel of tiny white florets on radiating ray-stalks replacing every brown cone. No part of the current tree is salvageable.

rows.readsAs: a bare leafless twig shrub carrying a few bunches of pale berries - an elder or viburnum in winter

rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, but two parts of the stated cause are wrong and would send the fix in the wrong direction. WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON CANVAS (read at native 440px and again at 4x/6x crops of crown, mid-cane and base): a single flat mid-brown tapered trunk about 25px wide rising from the ground shadow, splaying at ~1/3 height into SIX bare canes (not eight) that fan outward like a besom broom. Each cane is a flat solid brown stroke with zero bark rendering — no shredding stringy fibrous bark, which is one of juniper's own reads and is simply not attempted. MUST-READ 1, 'dense prickly bushy or columnar form': ABSENT, and this is the killing defect. The interior of the silhouette is majority background — at 6x on the mid-cane region the dark navy field shows through between every element; there is no mass, no depth, no occlusion, nothing prickly. MUST-READ 2, 'needles in threes flashing a white stripe': ABSENT — but NOT as the judge described. They are NOT 'tiny green tick marks'. They are LONG single straight tapered blades, some ~40px at native res, i.e. longer than the gap between two canes, and many of them sail clear across two or three canes into open air with nothing at either end. They are one flat desaturated sage-green with no silvery band, no lighter upper surface, no highlight of any kind. They attach SINGLY (occasionally two making a shallow V), never in whorls of three, at wide irregular intervals of 15-25px along each cane, at scattered angles. So the fault is not needle size — it is count, attachment and placement: isolated line segments floating in open air instead of dense whorled sprays clothing the twig. MUST-READ 3, 'blue-black bloomed berries mixed with green unripe ones': PARTIAL and the only half-credible element. Five tight spherical clusters of six or seven globes each, pale silver-blue with warm cream specular dots, sit as knobs exactly on the tip of five canes. The waxy bloom colour is roughly right in character but far too pale — these are silver-white, not blue-black. There are NO green unripe berries anywhere. And the placement is wrong: juniper cones sit in the leaf axils scattered ALONG the twigs, not as terminal pom-poms crowning bare wands. On the identity call: 'leafless elder or viburnum in winter' is the right instinct but the wrong species — elder and viburnum carry flat-topped compound umbels, whereas these are tight round balls on stick ends, so the render actually reads as a dried besom/florist bundle or a snowberry stem posy. Net: nothing in this image says conifer, evergreen, or shrub. Two of three must-reads are wholly absent and the third is misplaced and miscoloured. FAIL stands.

FIX DIRECTION: rebuild the foliage as dense overlapping whorled sprays that CLOTH each cane and fill the silhouette to near-opacity (juniper should be a solid prickly mass, not a wireframe); give each needle a paler silvery inner face so the white stripe flashes; move the berries off the cane tips into axils scattered along the twigs, darken them to blue-black under the bloom, and mix in a few green unripe ones; add shredding fibrous vertical bark to the trunk.
