rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, with three corrections to the stated causes. What I actually saw, at 1x, at 2x brightened, and at 5x-8x crops of the base, crown and cones, plus a pixel measurement pass.

SILHOUETTE / ASPECT — the FAIL is right but the diagnosis needs restating. Measured non-background bounding box is 277 x 390 px, aspect 0.71. The reference row asks for 0.3. The judge called it 'a wide round crown ball on a short stick'; the stick is NOT short — the trunk runs y=234..413, about 180 px, i.e. 46% of the total height, and the crown y=24..233 is 210 px. The trunk length is roughly correct. The defect is entirely CROWN WIDTH: the crown peaks at 246 px wide (y=164) on a 390 px tall tree, so the foliage mass alone is 89% of the total figure width. Fix the crown diameter (it needs to collapse to roughly 100-120 px, a narrow plume), not the trunk length. A redwood must read as a spire whose foliage barely exceeds the trunk; this reads as a lollipop / palm.

BASE — must-read 'buttressed flaring base' is ABSENT, and the judge's description of what is there is WRONG. There is no 'flat brown taper'. The trunk is DEAD PARALLEL: exactly 29 px wide at every sampled row from y=244 through y=404, narrowing to 27 px only in the last 8 px where it is capped by a semicircular rounded end. It is a capsule / popsicle stick that stops short and floats on a flat elliptical drop shadow — it does not meet a ground plane and does not widen into root buttresses at all. The fix is to add a flare, not to correct a taper.

BARK — must-read 'thick fibrous cinnamon-red bark in deep vertical ridges' is ABSENT, confirmed by sampling. The trunk interior is a single flat fill of RGB(107,74,46) at y=240, 280, 320, 360, 395 and 405 — literally the same three bytes at every height. The only variation anywhere is a 1 px darker edge stroke (RGB ~82,58,39). Zero vertical fissures, zero fibrous texture, zero hue break-up. The hue is a neutral mid-brown at roughly 30 degrees, not cinnamon-red; it needs to move toward a rust/red-brown AND carry deep vertical ridging.

FOLIAGE — must-read 'flat two-ranked needle sprays' is ABSENT; the judge is correct here and an 8x crop confirms it precisely. The crown is a soft airbrushed green blob with two bright highlight lobes near its centre, over which single flat tapered straight strokes fan outward radially in all directions from the crown centre, urchin/dandelion fashion. No twig axis exists anywhere, so there is nothing for needles to be two-ranked ON, and there is no flat spray plane. Stroke colour is uniform dark green (sampled 21,37,24 up to 38,68,39) with no pale banding on any underside, so 'dark green above with two pale bands beneath' also does not read.

CONES — the judge is right that they are too large, and I can quantify it, but they also missed a second, equally wrong thing about them. There are exactly four, each measured at 15 x 26 px (blob bounds 179,97-193,122 / 169,144-183,169 / 164,175-179,200 / 231,158-245,183). Each cone is 26 px tall against a 29 px wide trunk and is 6.7% of the whole tree's height — for a species whose row says the cones are 'about the size of an olive' and whose note explicitly warns 'drawing large cones reads wrong', that is a direct violation. MISSED BY THE JUDGE: the cone SHAPE is also wrong. They are not egg-shaped. Each is a stepped inverted cone — four stacked horizontal ridge lobes, WIDEST AT THE TOP, tapering downward to a blunt point, reading as a drill bit, a screw, or an upside-down waffle cone. They also float free in the foliage fog with no attachment to any twig or branch. Both the scale and the shape need redrawing.

FAMILY CHASSIS (the question the packet asks and the per-asset claim does not): I opened Cedar and Yew alongside. All three are ONE CHASSIS — the identical parallel-sided flat-brown rounded-end capsule trunk, the identical soft green airbrush blob crown, the identical radiating straight-stick needles, the identical flat ellipse ground shadow. Only the harvest decal changes (screw-cones on Redwood and Cedar, red berry clusters on Yew). Critically, Redwood's aspect spec of 0.3 versus Cedar's and Yew's 1.0 has produced no visible difference in silhouette whatsoever — the one property that should have separated Redwood from the rest of this family is unexpressed. Cedar additionally fails its own 'broad flat-topped crown with tiered horizontal branch plates' on the same chassis.

VERDICT: all three of Redwood's must-reads are absent, the note's explicit anti-pattern is committed, and the asset reads as a generic lollipop/palm shared with two siblings rather than as a redwood. FAIL stands.

rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld. All three mustReads are absent, and I verified the fruit and trunk at 5-6x magnification rather than trusting the thumbnail.

WHAT I SAW. (1) TRUNK — mustRead 'massive fluted trunk of fused stems with red-brown flaking bark'. At 5x the trunk is a flat, perfectly uniform-width capsule of a single mid-brown fill (~#7a5231), roughly 22px wide over 160px of height with ZERO taper, ZERO flare, ZERO buttress. It has no bark texture of any kind — no ridges, no plates, no flaking, not a single value break across its whole width apart from one soft airbrush shadow along the right edge. It is not fluted and shows no hint of fused multiple stems. It is also not red-brown; it is a neutral warm mud-brown, the same brown as Redwood's trunk (which the same batch requires to be 'cinnamon-red in deep vertical ridges'). TWO EXTRA DEFECTS THE ORIGINAL JUDGE DID NOT MENTION: the trunk terminates in a ROUNDED PILL END at the bottom that stops short of the ground and floats above the drop shadow — nothing anchors it, so it reads as a stuck-on lollipop stick; and its top end is likewise a rounded cap that simply disappears into the crown blob with no branching whatsoever.

(2) CROWN — mustRead 'dense very dark heavy crown', leafColour 'very dark blackish green'. The crown is a soft radial-gradient sphere, brightest at a mid-green (~#4f7a3a) core with a lighter yellow-green mottle left of centre, fading to translucent at the rim where the dark background shows straight through. It is airy and light, not dense, and it is nowhere near blackish. It is topped with ~40 straight single-pixel-width needle strokes radiating outward from the centre like a sea urchin / thistle, which is the family's generic spike-ball treatment and reads as a radiating spruce, not as the flat two-ranked sprays yew requires.

(3) FRUIT — mustRead 'scarlet open-ended berry-like arils', note 'the fruit is an open-topped red cup, not a closed berry'. Four clusters sit on the crown. At 6x each cluster is a tight rosette of 4-5 fully CLOSED spheres, bright scarlet with a hard white specular dot at the upper-left of each. There is no open top, no cup rim, no dark seed showing — the white dot is a plain shine highlight, not a seed. This is exactly the error the note names in advance. A SECOND ERROR THE ORIGINAL JUDGE MISSED: real yew arils are borne SINGLY along the twig, so even the rosette-of-five arrangement is wrong on top of the closed-berry rendering.

(4) CHASSIS CLAIM VERIFIED. I opened the sibling Redwood.png to test 'same chassis, fruit token swapped'. It is confirmed and is exact: identical mid-brown uniform pill trunk with the same floating rounded foot, identical radial spike-ball crown, identical proportions. The ONLY difference between Yew and Redwood is the fruit token pasted on the crown (red berry rosettes vs brown ribbed cones), even though the packet asks Redwood for aspect 0.3 (an extremely tall narrow column) and Yew for aspect 1 — neither honours its aspect.

CORRECTION TO THE ORIGINAL CLAIM: everything material in it is right, but 'so it reads as a rowan or holly' is imprecise. Rowan has pinnate leaves and flat corymbs and holly has spined evergreen leaves; this crown has neither — it is a needle spike-ball. The asset does not read as any identifiable species. It reads as the generic family lollipop tree with red berries applied, which is worse than being mistaken for a rowan, because it carries no organism identity at all.

FIX TARGETS, in priority order: (a) rebuild the trunk as a wide, short, deeply fluted column of visibly fused/merged vertical stems that flares into the ground and carries red-brown flaking bark plates; (b) drop the crown to a near-black green and make it opaque and heavy, with drooping two-ranked flat needle sprays replacing the radial spikes; (c) redraw the fruit as SINGLE open-topped scarlet cups scattered along the foliage, each showing a dark olive-black seed in the open mouth — not clustered, not spherical, no specular white dot.

(2) The trunk is a flat, smooth, untextured brown taper from base to fork — there is not one leaf-base diamond, scar, notch or shag on it, so must-read #1 is entirely absent. rows.verifyWhy: FAIL upheld, but three parts of the original claim need correcting. WHAT I SAW (440x440, subject bbox x94-346 / y25-411, aspect 0.654 vs spec 0.6 -- aspect is FINE, not a defect). (1) BRANCHING TRUNK -- confirmed and WORSE than reported: it is not a two-way Y, it is a THREE-PRONGED TRIDENT. A row scan at y=170 returns three separate brown limbs (x187-200, x207-230, x242-258) that converge into one column at y~205. The rightmost prong is the most damaging: it leans ~25deg out of vertical and its tip stands completely clear of the foliage against black sky, reading unmistakably as a bare hardwood branch. No palm branches; this silhouette reads as a young deciduous sapling or a candelabra cactus wearing a fern hat. This alone disqualifies the organism. (2) TRUNK SURFACE -- 'flat smooth untextured' is exactly right and I can put a number on it: a 160px vertical scan down the trunk centre (x=220, y=250-410) returns ONE distinct colour, rgb(107,74,46), for every single pixel. Zero texture, zero leaf-base diamonds, zero shag, zero rings, no interior shading -- only a 1-2px darker pixel column on the right edge. But 'taper' is wrong: the trunk is a CONSTANT 22px-wide column from y=250 to y=400 (runs 209-231 / 210-232, unchanging), which then FLARES outward as it climbs into the fork. It reads as a broom handle or wooden dowel, and it ends in a rounded cap at y=411 that does not meet ground. Must-read 1 (shaggy trunk patterned with old leaf-base diamonds) is ABSENT, categorically. (3) DATES -- absent as an identity read, and the numbers are brutal. The entire fruit mass is a single lumpy clump with bbox x190-229 / y156-177: 40x22px, 191 warm non-trunk pixels, 0.10% of the frame. It is ~10 cream/tan pips (rgb ~ 160,120,90 highlights) on a trunk-brown lump -- NOT amber. Orange-stalk-candidate pixels in the WHOLE image: 12. So there are no orange stalks at all, and there is only ONE clump where the reference calls for HEAVY BUNCHES (plural). Critically, its bbox top y=156 and bottom y=177 both sit ABOVE the frond bbox bottom (green ends y=182): the clump is nestled INSIDE the crown rosette, sitting on top of the middle trunk prong, not hanging below the fronds. At 100% it reads as a pinecone or a knot of nuts, not fruit. Must-read 3 (heavy date bunches hanging under the fronds) is ABSENT. (4) CROWN -- here the original claim is unfair and should not be used to drive the fix. The fronds themselves are the one GOOD thing in this asset and must be preserved: ~14 genuinely PINNATE fronds, each with a readable central rachis and stiff comb-like leaflets, in the correct blue-grey green, with real per-frond curvature and depth shading. Must-read 2 (stiff feather fronds) IS delivered. What is wrong is only the ARRANGEMENT: every frond sits at or above horizontal, producing a near-perfect 180deg semicircular fan with a flat bottom edge and no downsweep, so the crown reads as a cycad/sago-palm or tree-fern rosette rather than a date palm's open arching shuttlecock. Also missing: the spines at the frond bases the reference row asks for. (5) 'bottom 55% is bare trunk' -- directionally right, slightly overstated: fork junction y~205, base y=411, so bare single trunk is 206/440 = 47% of the frame (53% of the 387px subject). VERDICT: two of three must-reads (shaggy diamond trunk; hanging date bunches) are flatly absent, and the trunk branches into three limbs, which no palm does. FAIL stands. FIX ORDER: kill the fork to one unbroken column; put leaf-base diamond scaling + shag on it; hang 3-4 large amber bunches on orange stalks BELOW the frond line (target 6-8% of frame area, not 0.1%); drop the lowest fronds below horizontal. Do not redraw the frond leaflets -- they are correct.

rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, with corrections to the stated cause. I read the 440x440 PNG, then cropped the canopy at 4x and a single fruit at 12x with System.Drawing to be sure.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: a straight brown rounded-rectangle trunk (no branching, no taper, no fork) rising from a flat elliptical ground shadow to a small fuzzy round green canopy blob that occupies roughly the top 40% of the frame. Around the blob's rim sit ~26 copies of one small pointed-elliptic leaf sprite in bright mid-green, radiating outward and upward. Four fruit hang in the canopy: one upper-centre, two lower-left, one lower-right.

THE FRUIT, MEASURED: at 12x the fruit is a geometrically PERFECT CIRCLE - roughly 28x28 px on a 440 px canvas, width equal to height, zero pear taper, zero neck, no bulged base. It is filled with a dull grey-olive radial gradient carrying a large blown-out near-white specular highlight in the upper left, which makes it read as polished/waxy, the opposite of avocado's matt pebbled skin. So the identity must-read 'heavy pear-shaped fruit ... pebbled' is genuinely ABSENT, and the FAIL stands.

CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM (three):
(1) 'no stout stalk' is only half right - there IS a stalk on every fruit: a thin dark reddish-brown line about 10 px long, angled off the top of the sphere. It is thin and long, i.e. a cherry/plum peduncle, not the short stout avocado stalk the row asks for. Do not fix this as 'add a stalk'; the stalk exists and must be re-drawn short, thick, woody and sitting on the fruit's narrow shoulder.
(2) 'the same size as the apples on the Apple card' understates it. I opened Apple.png alongside: it is not merely the same size, it is the SAME SPRITE - identical sphere + upper-left specular blob + thin stalk, identical trunk primitive, identical canopy blob, identical leaf sprite. Avocado is Apple recoloured (red->grey-olive) with a slightly rounder/narrower canopy. This is a shared-chassis defect at the family level, not a per-fruit shape miss.
(3) 'reads as an olive tree' is loose. A real olive is ellipsoid, not spherical, and olive foliage is narrow and silver-grey; neither is here. What is on screen reads as a generic dark plum/berry lollipop tree. The judge's direction (small dark round fruit) is right; the species they named is not what the picture says.

TWO FURTHER MUST-READ FAILURES THE CLAIM DID NOT MENTION, both needed for the fix: (a) 'tall spreading crown of dark drooping leaves' - the leaves are the shared small BRIGHT mid-green pointed sprite, tips flicked outward and upward, none drooping, none large, none leathery, and none darker than the Apple card's leaves; the row asks for large elliptic leathery dark-green leaves hanging downward. (b) the crown is not tall or spreading - it is a small round puff on a bare stick, a lollipop silhouette, with no lateral branch structure at all, so aspect 0.9 is being met by canvas proportion rather than by canopy form.

Nothing in the asset is unique to Avocado except the fruit's grey-olive hue. FAIL is correct.

rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, but two of the three stated causes need correcting before anyone works the fix.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON CANVAS (440x440, measured by row-extent scan). The tree occupies y=22 (crown apex) to y=413 (trunk base), total height 391px. Foliage runs y=22 to y=248 (226px, 58% of the tree). Bare trunk runs y=250 to y=413 (163px, 42%). Crown max width 205px, reached at y=142 - i.e. the crown is widest at its MIDDLE. Trunk is a dead-uniform 22-23px wide from y=262 all the way to y=406.

MUST-READ 1, 'immensely tall straight bare trunk' - THE JUDGE IS WRONG THAT IT IS ABSENT, but right that it fails. A clean, straight, perfectly bare, unbranched bole IS drawn and it is substantial: 163px of clear stem, 42% of total height, with no lower branches and no foliage skirt. Do not tell the fixer 'there is no bole' - there is one, and it is longer than any sibling I sampled. The failure is proportion and form: an emergent needs the bole to DOMINATE (~70%+ of height with the crown a shallow cap on top), and here the crown is actually taller than the bole (226 vs 163). Worse, the bole is a featureless dowel - zero taper across 145 rows, no buttress flare, and the base literally rounds off into a lozenge cap (width collapses 23 -> 7 over the last 8 rows) floating on an ellipse shadow. A Brazil nut bole is a buttressed column; this is a lollipop stick.

MUST-READ 2, 'flat crown of branches only at the very top' - GENUINELY ABSENT, and this is the load-bearing failure. The crown is a round lollipop dome: 226px tall by 205px wide, so it is TALLER than it is wide, and it is widest at mid-height rather than near the top. A flat emergent crown must be broad-and-shallow (width several times its height) and confined to the topmost band. Additionally there is not a single branch drawn anywhere in the asset - the crown is a soft radial green blur with individual leaf blades stuck onto it, so 'crown of BRANCHES' cannot read at all even in principle. Nothing about the top of this tree says 'flat'.

MUST-READ 3, 'round woody cannonball pods' - half present, and the judge's description is wrong on scale. Five brown spheres sit in the canopy; I measured them at 26-28px diameter against leaves ~50px long, so they are roughly half a leaf length - plum/chestnut scale, NOT 'berry-sized'. Relative size is actually close to defensible. The real defect is treatment: each pod is a smooth glossy sphere with a hard white specular hotspot and a soft radial gradient - no woody rough rind, no ribbing, no seam, and crucially no small hole at one end, which the harvest line explicitly calls for. Round: yes. Woody cannonball capsule: no. They read as fruit, not as capsules.

CHASSIS EVIDENCE THAT SUPPORTS THE JUDGE'S FRAMING. I opened Avocado.png and Cashew.png from the same batch. Avocado is the SAME ASSET as Brazil Nut - identical round lollipop dome, identical uniform bare stick trunk at the same width, identical rounded base cap, identical shadow ellipse, identical scattered specular spheres - differing only in leaf outline and fruit hue. Cashew is the same chassis with a shorter trunk. So the judge's 'drawn at the same scale and proportion as a garden apple tree' is substantively correct: the aspect-0.7 emergent-giant identity is encoded nowhere in the geometry, and nothing in the silhouette separates Brazil Nut from the generic fruit-tree token.

FIX TARGETS, in priority order: (1) collapse the crown to a shallow wide cap occupying only the top ~20-25% of height and push the bole to ~70%+; (2) draw actual branch structure - a few heavy horizontal limbs fanning out at the very top - since 'crown of branches' is currently unreadable; (3) give the bole a buttressed flared foot instead of a rounded lozenge cap, and a slight taper; (4) re-skin the pods as matte rough-rinded woody spheres with a visible hole at one end, killing the specular hotspot that currently makes them read as fruit.

The lower-centre fruit has TWO such stalks emerging from it, which looks like a duplicated-stem artifact. The fix is not 'anchor the floating fruit', it is 'delete the upward twig stems and re-site the fruit on the trunk/limbs'.

(b) 'apple-sized' is WRONG by measurement. The jackfruit balls are ~40px across against a ~33px trunk width and a ~230px crown width; the Apple card's fruit are ~18-20px. Telling an artist to 'make them bigger' would miss the real defect, which is SHAPE (round instead of long barrel), SKIN (smooth ribs instead of knobbles) and ATTACHMENT (twig instead of trunk). Scale is at most a secondary polish item.

(c) 'reuses Durian's smooth striped oval' is CORRECT and if anything understated. Side by side, Jackfruit, Durian and Breadfruit all use the same striped-ball fruit primitive - same olive/tan body, same vertical rib set, same white highlight. Durian's should be spiky and Breadfruit's pebbled, and neither is; the three are mutually indistinguishable by fruit alone. Durian is in fact slightly better placed, because one of its fruit sits at the crown base right against the trunk top.

Cauliflory cannot be fixed by moving the fruit down alone - the tree needs a thicker trunk plus two or three heavy low limbs, with long oblong knobbly fruit clustered directly against them at multiple heights including well below the canopy, and the crown re-leafed with large dark glossy ovals.

PRICKLES - the first judge's account is INCOMPLETE here and should be corrected. (b) Placement bug: several of them are detached and FLOATING IN EMPTY SPACE - in the base crop there are three clear white bars sitting in the dark background to the left and right of the trunk, touching no stem at all. Each 'leaf' is a linear pinnate frond: one straight green rachis with about 15-20 tiny tooth-sized green segments running down each side, uniform in size, fading to a point. FRUIT - claim CONFIRMED. Six terminal heads. Read at full size that is a flower - a pom-pom umbel or a thistle head - not fruit. 1. 'a wiry creeping mat over bog moss' -- ABSENT. No mat, no moss, no bog. Rows 309-317 (the bottom 9 px of the plant) contain only 10-14 plant pixels total, i.e. the trunk and nothing else. Nothing spreads horizontally at ground level anywhere in the image.

What is missing is a moss/bog SUBSTRATE and any horizontal mat sitting on it -- not the shadow. A fix that merely adds a ground ellipse will not move this asset.

It is not a barked trunk; it is the six canes fused into one flat untextured brown wedge for the lowest ~50 px, widest at the top of the wedge and narrowest where it meets the ground -- it reads like a stump-in-a-pot silhouette. Worth naming precisely because the fix is to delete the fused base outright, not to re-texture it.
- 'berries sit as clusters on cane tips instead of single fruit on thin stalks' is correct and confirmed at 4x: five rosettes of 6-7 fused berries, all terminal on canes. The packet harvest row wants red berries singly on thin upright pedicels lifted above the mat.

The asset currently reads as a generic upright berry shrub -- a blueberry or a cotoneaster -- and would not be identified as a cranberry by anyone. FAIL upheld on three grounds: growth form inverted (0.75 vs 2.5), the flower must-read entirely missing, and the leaf/stem must-read contradicted.

Every cane carries the same feathery frond primitive: a green rachis bearing roughly 15-20 pairs of short narrow needle-like leaflets, opposite along the axis, giving a mimosa/fern/bracken texture. CHASSIS. Elderberry and Blackberry are the same drawing. Same cone (same width, same 4 split lines), same six-cane fan at the same angles, same frond primitive, same crescent-of-spheres cluster in the same pale grey-lilac. The ONLY differences I can find: Blackberry has ~14 pale cream straight tick marks scattered along its canes (its prickles) and 5 clusters; Elderberry has no ticks and 4 clusters, with slightly denser lower foliage. So the generator CAN swap leaf form and fruit colour per species; Elderberry simply received Blackberry's leaf primitive AND Blackberry's fruit colour, which is why it is a literal near-duplicate.

MUST-READ 1, 'big flat plate-like heads of creamy white flowers' - ABSENT. Confirmed. There is no flat plate and no umbel geometry anywhere; the heads are small upward crescents no wider than the frond behind them. One nuance the original claim understates: the spheres are NOT saturated purple, they are pale grey-lilac with white highlights, so at thumbnail size they could be misread as a whitish flower head - but they are the identical fruit primitive Blackberry wears, they are ball-shaped rather than the tiny five-petal florets of an elder umbel, and there is no flat corymb plate. So the must-read still fails, just not for the reason 'purple ball clusters' alone implies.

MUST-READ 2, 'opposite pinnate leaves' - the one place the FAIL's phrasing is wrong. The foliage IS pinnate and the leaflets ARE in opposite pairs along a rachis; calling it merely 'fern fronds' concedes too little. But it is still wrong for elder: ~15-20 leaflet pairs of narrow needle-like segments instead of 5-7 broad toothed pointed leaflets, and it is non-diagnostic because Blackberry (spec: palmate, 3-5 leaflets) is drawn with the exact same frond. This needs (a) a distinct broad-leaflet pinnate primitive, 5-7 wide toothed pointed leaflets in opposite pairs, replacing the shared needle frond; (b) a genuinely NEW terminal primitive - a wide flat horizontal corymb plate of many tiny cream-white florets, spanning wider than the foliage, and a second nodding state where that plate inverts into a heavy downward-hanging head of small dark purple-black berries; (c) crimson stalks on the flower/berry head and a crimson tint into the upper cane, which is what separates it from Blackberry at a glance.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. Silhouette: a fan of 6-7 straight brown canes rising from one fat conical basal trunk, each cane carrying tufts of deeply dissected 7-9-fingered green fronds. Five berry clusters, one capping each of the five tallest cane tips.

WHAT I SAW (440x440, read at full size, then 3x/4x/8x crops of crown, trunk and both dark shapes, plus a gamma-0.42 boost of the whole canvas to hunt for structure hidden in the dark).

TRUNK / ARCHITECTURE -- the claim is CORRECT and the defect is worse than stated. The trunk is a single perfectly straight vertical capsule running from a rounded stub at the bottom up into the fog, roughly x=196..246, i.e. UNIFORM WIDTH with zero taper and zero crook. Under gamma boost there is not one branch, fork or limb anywhere in the image -- no low branching, no secondary stems, nothing inside the crown. Both ends are rounded pill caps; the bottom cap hovers ABOVE the soft ellipse shadow rather than meeting ground, so the tree reads as a lollipop stick dropped on the plate. The colour is mid-terracotta brown, noticeably lighter than the 'dark trunk' the row calls for. mustRead 3 ('crooked low-branching dark trunk with a wide flat crown') fails on all four of its terms.

CROWN SHAPE -- an additional failure the original judge did not name. The crown is a rounded cumulus/cauliflower blob about as tall as it is wide (approx 100..355 x, 60..250 y), lobed at the top. A mesquite's defining wide, flat, umbrella-like canopy is not there.

FOLIAGE -- the claim 'soft amorphous green fog blob' is HALF WRONG and this matters, because the foliage primitive is already built and only needs redeploying. There are roughly 25 distinct drawn leaf sprigs radiating around the crown RIM. At 3x each one is clearly a rachis bearing many tiny paired leaflets in two ranks, and they do read as fine feathery pinnate foliage -- mustRead 1 is essentially satisfied where the sprigs actually appear. The real defect is placement, not absence: every sprig sits on the outer rim pointing outward, and the entire crown INTERIOR is undifferentiated gaussian green fog with no leaf structure at all, so the mass reads as vapour with a fringe. THORNS -- the claim is CORRECT. No thorns anywhere on the silhouette edge; nothing protrudes from the trunk or any sprig. NET: 1 of 3 must-reads readable (feathery pinnate foliage, rim only), 1 absent (thorns), 1 absent on every term (crooked low-branching dark trunk + wide flat crown). rows.readsAs: the Blackberry image with pink pom-poms instead of purple ones

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. Six straight brown canes fan upward out of a single fused tapering trunk, ink bbox 152x237 px (w/h 0.64 against the spec aspect 0.7 -- proportion is fine). Every cane carries fern-like fronds: a rachis with roughly 18-22 tiny linear pinnules per frond, each pinnule a pale sage dab over a dark green shadow. Five terminal fruit heads, each a flat face-on WREATH of 8-9 crimson drupelets with grey-lilac specular blobs. Scattered cream-white bars cross the canes at ~40 degrees.

CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM.
(1) 'Tip clusters recoloured pink' is inaccurate twice over. The clusters are deep crimson/carmine (peak 176,32,64-ish with grey-lilac 152,152,168 speculars), not pink; and the recolour is not confined to the tips -- the foliage palette WAS changed too. Raspberry's dominant greens quantise to 128,160,104 / 136,168,112 / 120,144,96 (pale grey-sage); Blackberry's to 16,40,16 / 56,112,40 / 64,120,40 (saturated dark green). So it is not a pure tip-only recolour of the same sheet.
(2) 'No hollow core' is wrong as stated. Three of the five clusters -- clearest on the top-right one -- show a distinct dark void at the centre of the drupelet ring, and that void is precisely what distinguishes them from Blackberry, whose identical clusters have a solid tan/orange RECEPTACLE PLUG filling the same spot (botanically the correct differentiator, receptacle pulls free on raspberry and stays in on blackberry). The artist did attempt the hollow core and it half-lands. The genuine fruit defect is the one the judge got right in the other half of the sentence: there is no thimble. No individual berry exists at all -- the drupelets are laid out as a flat annular wreath of 8 spheres facing the viewer, so the head reads as a pincushion flower / allium umbel, not as a domed conical aggregate fruit. The centre-top head is a solid striated dome with no ring and no hole, so it does not carry the read either.
(3) 'Same chassis and same fern fronds as Blackberry' is CORRECT and is the most damaging finding. Side by side the two are one generator: same fused-trunk cane bundle, same frond form and pinnule count, same cream cross-bars, same 8-drupelet ring cluster, near-identical bboxes (152x237 vs 139x221, aspect 0.64 vs 0.63). The packet note demanding raspberry's canes read 'upright and bristly, unlike blackberry's long arching hook-thorned stems' is therefore unrealised -- but note the direction: the shared upright cane bundle is RIGHT for raspberry and WRONG for blackberry (blackberry is drawn upright at aspect 0.63 against its spec 1.6). Fixing the contrast means re-drawing Blackberry to arch, not straightening Raspberry.

DEFECTS THE JUDGE MISSED.
(a) LEAF FORM IS THE WRONG ORGAN, and this is the primary failure. The spec is 'pinnate leaves of 3-5 toothed leaflets'. At 16x each frond is unmistakably a fern/bipinnate lace of ~20 tiny undifferentiated linear pinnules. There is not one broad ovate toothed leaflet anywhere in the image. Combined with the wreath heads the whole plant reads as a mimosa/acacia or a red-flowered yarrow, not a bramble.
(b) White-felted undersides: the judge is right that they never flash, and I confirm it at 16x -- the pale sage is a uniform top-light highlight applied to every pinnule identically, with no flipped leaflet showing a silver/white reverse. The palette carries no silver-white green at all; the only near-white ink (216,208,176, 183 px) is the prickle bars. Calling the foliage 'one flat green' understates it slightly (there IS a two-tone dark-under/pale-over dab), but the identity cue -- a distinct silver reverse on turned leaflets -- is genuinely absent.
(c) The prickles fail as drawn. They are fat cream-white BARS about 14 px long and 3 px thick lying across the canes; at 16x one reads as a splint, bandage or nursery label tie, not as fine bristles. Worse, at 4x on the whole plant at least five of them float in empty space with no cane under them (lower right quadrant and near the base) -- detached floating ticks.
(d) The base is a solid tapering TRUNK, not a ground-level crown of separate canes, which contradicts 'upright biennial canes'.

SCORE AGAINST THE THREE MUST-READS. Upright canes: present (the one clean win). Fine bristly prickles: present in intent, misreading as splint bars, several detached. White undersides flashing: absent. Hollow-cored red berries: red yes, hollow gap partially yes, thimble profile absent and the head reads as a flower. Plus the leaf, the single strongest bramble cue, is drawn as the wrong organ. Two of three must-reads unreadable, wrong leaf, and chassis-identical to its sibling in the same batch. FAIL.

rows.readsAs: A generic strap-leaved ornamental clump - liriope, spider plant or a plantain - topped by a single dense foxtail/Timothy-style bead spike; nobody names Poa meadow-grass.

The reference calls for an airy OPEN PYRAMIDAL PANICLE on fine whorled branches; what is drawn is a narrow, dense, unbranched cylindrical column of pale beads on a bare stick - a contracted spike, which belongs to a different grass tribe entirely and is the visual opposite of a panicle. There is not one branch anywhere on the inflorescence, so the 'fine whorled panicle branches' must-read is also entirely missing. Secondary problems: the blades are broad, stiff strap-shaped ribbons rather than soft narrow flat blades, no boat-shaped (cucullate) tips are visible on any of them, and the tuft base is a single solid opaque green wedge rather than individual culms rising from a loose crown, which pushes it toward the thatch-mound look the reference explicitly forbids.
rows.fix: Replace the bead column with an actual panicle: a central rachis bearing 4-6 whorls of 3-5 fine hair-thin branchlets each, longest at the bottom and shortest at the top so the outline is a wide-based open triangle, with small two-to-four-floret spikelets only at the branch TIPS and clear dark background visible through the interior of the head.
rows.verifyWhy:
Verified at full size and at 3x-6x crops of the head, the blade tips and the base.

HEAD (the decisive defect — claim CONFIRMED). There is exactly ONE seed head on the whole plant, on a single bare culm that barely clears the foliage. At 6x it is a short, dense, PERFECTLY UNBRANCHED cylinder of ~7-8 pale cream lobes stacked in one narrow column, roughly constant width from base to tip with a squared-off top — no taper, no pyramid, no rachis branches, no pedicels, no whorls, nothing lateral at all. The culm below it is a clean bare green stick for its entire visible length. So mustRead #1 'airy open pyramid of a seed head' and mustRead #2 'fine whorled panicle branches' are BOTH flatly absent, not merely small or hidden — I looked for faint branch strokes at 6x and there are none, and I scanned the whole upper canvas at 3x for a second, better head and there is none. What is drawn is a contracted spike (Phleum/Setaria/Plantago silhouette), which is the identity token of a different tribe entirely. Two of the three must-reads gone, and specifically the one a viewer reads first on a grass.

BLADES (claim WRONG — do not fix this). The other judge said 'broad stiff straps with no boat-shaped tips'. The 'broad stiff strap' half is incorrect and must not be actioned. At 5x the blades are narrow, soft and clearly tapering: each one narrows continuously along its length and ends in a hair-fine point, and the outer blades arch over in long graceful curves that fall well below horizontal. This is competent, soft grass foliage — the leaf/leafColour rows ('soft narrow flat blades', 'fresh green to slightly blue-green') are essentially satisfied on softness, taper and hue. The only true part of that sentence is the missing boat/hooded (cucullate) tips — tips are simple sharp points. That is a real Poa diagnostic but it is a POLISH-grade miss at this render size, not what sinks the asset.

BASE (claim PARTLY WRONG). The other judge called it 'a solid opaque wedge that edges toward the forbidden thatch mound'. At 4x the blades ARE individually readable all the way down — there are distinct darker seams between adjacent blades, so it is a fan of separate blades, not a poured slab. It is only in the bottom ~10-15% that they converge into an opaque narrow V. Critically that shape is the OPPOSITE of a thatch mound: a thatch mound is a wide domed pile; this is a tight vase/fountain converging to a single point, i.e. an over-narrow crown. The real base defect against mustRead #3 is that the tuft is too DENSE and too tightly gathered to read as 'soft loose tuft' — the blades share one origin point with no gaps or offset clumps — not that it is a mound.

BAND. The head alone decides it: the read-at-a-glance identity of Poa is an airy open panicle, and the asset draws an unbranched spike instead, so it reads as timothy/foxtail (or plantain) rather than a meadow-grass. 'Reads as liriope' is an overstatement — the foliage is genuinely grass-like, not liriope's broad straps — but the organism read is still wrong. FAIL upheld. The fix is entirely in the inflorescence: replace the single beaded cylinder with 2-4 culms carrying open pyramidal panicles, whorled fine branches spreading widest at the base of the head and carrying small spikelets at the branch tips, plus a slight loosening of the crown; the blade work can be left alone apart from adding hooded tips.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON THE CANVAS (440x440; I decoded the pixels and re-rendered 3x/4x crops of the crown and the base to check the small features). Plant bbox is x167-267, y89-337 -> 101 x 249 px, aspect 0.41 against a target of 0.50, so it is slightly narrower than spec as well. It is a column of about eight stacked round beads, 9px wide at its widest and 36px tall (y89-y124), sitting bolt upright on a bare 25px length of rachis above the topmost leaf pair. Colour #8b2645-#9b2a4b, a decent crimson. So it is genuinely present and it is genuinely crimson -- but it is a rigidly ERECT bead skewer, not a plume, and it carries zero droop, zero mass and zero fringe. At 36px it is 14.5% of plant height; the amaranth tassel should be the visual centre of gravity, a heavy drooping fleshy mass that outweighs the foliage. MUST-READ 1 ('thick fleshy plume or drooping tassel of seed') is therefore FAILED, but for the right reason: not 'too small to see' -- it is visible -- it is the wrong SHAPE and the wrong WEIGHT. The fix is a broad, multi-branched, arching/nodding panicle several times this width, not merely a taller version of the same bead thread.

CORRECTION 2 -- 'barely taller than one leaflet' is misleading. The spike (36px) is TWICE the depth of a leaflet (18px) but well short of a leaflet's 48px length. Sizing the fix against 'one leaflet' will underbuild it; size it against the 98px width and 178px height of the leaf mass.

CORRECTION 3 -- the claim never names the worst colour defect. MUST-READ 2 is 'strong crimson stem and veins'. The stem is #463219, a flat dark olive-brown for its entire length including the exposed 34px of bare stalk below the foliage -- no crimson anywhere on it. Meanwhile the LEAVES are a uniform dusty rose-pink (#b15460 core, #73353f shading) with no green at all, when the packet's leafColour is 'mid green, frequently flushed crimson'. The palette is inverted: the crimson that belongs on the stem and veins was poured over the whole blade, and the green that belongs on the blade is gone. That inversion is what makes the frond read as decorative-pink rather than as a crop. Veining does exist -- there are fine darker midrib and lateral lines inside each blade -- but they are the same pink family as the blade, so they do not deliver 'crimson veins'.

MUST-READ 3 ('big soft broad leaves') FAILED, and worse than stated: the packet also specifies ALTERNATE arrangement on a THICK GROOVED stem, and what is drawn is strictly OPPOSITE on a smooth uniform-width twig. So the leaf spec is wrong on shape (lance, not broad oval-diamond), on phyllotaxy (opposite, not alternate), and on stem character (smooth thin rachis, not thick grooved stalk). The identical 16px pitch across all eleven pairs is itself a defect -- real amaranth foliage is irregular and the lower leaves are much larger.

BAND: FAIL stands. Zero of the three must-reads survive, and the composite silhouette names a different organism (fern/compound frond). This is not a polish-level miss.

rows.readsAs: a generic green leafy rosette or a houseplant

rows.readsAs: an ornamental gold grass with a brass screw pushed into it
rows.defect: The single feature that makes barley unmistakable — awns longer than the head itself, fanning up in a long bristling sweep — is reduced to a small flared cap sitting on top of a short ribbed cylinder, so the awns are shorter than the ear rather than several times longer. rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld after looking at the 440x440 PNG at 1x and at 6x/10x crops of the ear (source box approx x180-240, y85-175). The FAIL claim is accurate on every point; two details need correcting because they understate the defect, and four further defects the judge did not name should go into the fix.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. A wide fountain-shaped fan of about 16 narrow, smoothly tapering, arching blades rising from a single point on the ground shadow, plus ONE dead-vertical thread-thin culm through the centre carrying a single ear at roughly y=85-175. Everything - blades, culm, ear - is the same straw-gold. The read is ornamental fountain grass / pampas / a gold dracaena fan, with a brass countersunk screw standing in the middle of it.

CORRECTION 1 - the awns are not 'a small flared cap', they are not awns at all. At 10x the structure above the ear is a SOLID FILLED trapezoid/funnel: one continuous gold shape, hard straight edges, flat top, no internal strands, no gaps, no taper to points. There is not a single individual awn filament anywhere in the image. The judge described it as a flared cap that is too short, which reads as 'the awns exist but need lengthening'; in fact the awn geometry has to be built from scratch as a fan of discrete near-parallel bristles. Measured: cap approx 15 px tall over an ear approx 42 px tall, so approx 0.35x, against a mustRead of longer than the head itself (barley runs 1.0-1.5x). It is a 3-4x miss, not a trim.

CORRECTION 2 - the 'screw' read has a second cause the judge did not name: the ear OUTLINE. The ear is a straight-sided rectangle of constant width with a hard flat cut-off base and a hard flat top, and inside it run exactly two perfectly regular parallel columns of identical small chevron/scale marks with a dark seam down the middle. Constant width + machine-regular chevrons = thread. A barley ear is a tapered spike whose outline is BUMPY because each plump spikelet bulges past the axis; nothing here bulges. mustRead 3 ('grains in tight rows') is therefore only half-credited: rows are present, grain is not - the marks read as milled thread, not as plump kernels.

CONFIRMED - 'ramrod upright instead of nodding' is exactly right. The culm and ear are plumb vertical with zero curvature over their whole length; the tip of the ear sits directly above the base of the culm. mustRead 2 (head nods over when ripe) is absent outright.

FURTHER DEFECTS NOT IN THE ORIGINAL CLAIM. (a) The leaf spec is 'broad flat blades clasping a jointed hollow culm' - the blades drawn are narrow whip/needle blades at maybe a quarter of the width they need, and none of them clasp or even touch the culm; the culm is a bare separate thread passing through the fan. (c) leafColour is 'mid green, ripening straw gold' and the asset is 100% gold with no green at any point, which is a large part of why it reads ornamental rather than as a food crop. (d) Proportion: the leaf fan is roughly 3x the height and 8x the visual mass of the ear, and there is only one culm - barley should show several culms whose ears carry the silhouette above a modest basal tuft. Here the ear is a small ornament on a big grass clump.

Every leaf is a broad obovate/rounded blade: widest at mid-length, blunt ROUNDED apex, tapering smoothly into the stem with NO basal lobes, NO sagittate/hastate flare, no pointed tip. Each has a simple pinnate herringbone midrib+side-vein pattern. Nothing anywhere on the asset carries an arrowhead or heart silhouette. This is the first-read identity feature and it is missing.

CORRECTIONS / ADDITIONS THE JUDGE MISSED (these matter for the fix):
(a) The judge said the harvest is simply absent. Half of it is actually attempted: the white crescent at the crown is the flower cluster. But it renders as a single flat white mushroom-cap / lollipop arc perched on a bare stalk - it does not read as 'loose clusters of small white-pink flowers'. It needs to become several airy sprays of tiny white-pink florets on branching pedicels, and it needs to be pink-tinged, not chalk white. Do not delete it; rebuild it.
(b) The leaves are OPPOSITE (perfectly mirrored pairs at each node). The packet specifies ALTERNATE. This is a second, unmentioned spec violation and it is exactly what creates the caterpillar/frond read - the mirrored pairs plus the dense node spacing produce the segmented ladder silhouette. Fixing leaf shape alone will not fix the read; the phyllotaxy must go alternate and the internodes must open up so individual leaves separate against the background.
(c) Silhouette proportion is wrong. Packet aspect is 0.80; the leaf mass measures roughly 115px wide by 210px tall, about 0.50-0.55. It is far too narrow and columnar for a bushy broadleaf herb.
(d) Leaf count/density: ~20 leaves crammed into ~200px of stem with near-zero visible gap. A buckwheat herb should read as a sparse open plant, few large leaves on long petioles, with background visible between them. There are no petioles at all here - blades attach directly to the stem.

VERDICT: three of three must-reads fail, and the organism reads as the wrong kingdom-level thing (an insect larva or a fern frond, not a flowering broadleaf crop). FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a young hemp or cannabis bush

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. Constant width plus protruding node collars is exactly the bamboo read the first judge described, and it is correct: a corn culm should be thicker, should taper toward the top, and its nodes should be hidden under wrapping leaf sheaths rather than drawn as free-floating dashes. No leaf sheath clasps the stem anywhere on this asset.

They strictly alternate side to side, so mustRead #3's 'alternating ranks' is genuinely SATISFIED and should not be listed as a defect.

CORRECTION 2 - the leaves are NOT midrib-less. Each blade carries a pale sage highlight stripe running its full length. At the base of the cob sits a rounded, spade-shaped pale-green bract overlapping the cob's lower-left quadrant and butting against the stem at a node. WHAT GENUINELY FAILS. (a) The crown is a radially symmetric fan of about twelve smooth, equal-length, salmon-pink tapered rays springing from a solid pink triangular cup, spread over roughly 160 degrees. NET. The topology of all three must-reads is present - crown flower at the apex, fruiting body at mid-height on the side of the stem at a leaf joint, alternating strap leaves - and cob-on-the-side-at-a-node is a genuinely corn-specific placement that partly rescues the asset. Two of three must-reads fail in character. FAIL is upheld.

PRIORITISED FIXES: 1) replace the pink radial fan with a straw/pale-tan branched drooping panicle - several unequal side branches, each hung with fine spikelets, asymmetric. 2) Wrap the cob in overlapping green husk leaves that taper past its tip, leaving only a small window of pale-gold kernel rows, and replace the gold spoke fan with a soft drooping tuft of unequal fine silk threads emerging from the husk tip. 3) Thicken and taper the culm, suppress the protruding node dashes, and let each leaf base wrap the stem as a sheath. 4) Centre and whiten the existing leaf midribs, widen the blades, and shift the leaf green brighter.

The plant is a symmetrical tussock fountain: ~24 narrow ribbon blades all radiating from ONE point at soil level, arching out and down to left and right, widest at about 60% height. Behind them a single hairline culm runs dead-straight from that same ground point to the top. BLADES / MIDRIB. Blades are 4-6px narrow ribbons in khaki-to-tan gold, shaded with a soft one-sided gradient (slightly lighter core, darker lower edge). It is a ~55px vertical element at the top of the culm made of two parts: (a) a threaded shank - a narrow parallel-sided rust-orange cylinder crossed by ~10 dark horizontal rungs, reading exactly like screw thread or a ladder, and (b) crowning it an inverted trapezoid that FLARES OUTWARD AS IT RISES to a flat top, i.e. a countersunk screw head / funnel. So the defect is not size but geometry: a grain head must be widest low-to-middle and taper to a point, and it must be dense; this one is a bare skinny spike that gets WIDER at the very top and is flat-cut across. It reads as hardware, not as 'a dense upright head of red-brown grain'. Must-read 3 (heavy compact seed head crowning the stem) is present in position and colour only; it fails on mass and shape.

MILLET COMPARISON. The judge's 'only a rust tint separates it from Millet' is close but not complete. Side by side, Sorghum and Millet share the identical chassis, identical blade count and fountain geometry, and the identical two-part screw head. The differences are: Sorghum is rendered ~1.6x larger with flatter, more widely arching blades, its foliage is rust-khaki where Millet is yellow-green, and its head is orange-rust where Millet's is pale gold. Scale and arch angle, not tint alone.
