rows.readsAs: a tan egg with five holes in a row - the Abalone stamp again
rows.defect: Wrong organism, and every must-read is missing. There is no simple uncoiled cone shell, no radiating ribbed ridges, no off-centre apex, and it is not clamped flush against anything - it floats above a drop shadow with clear daylight underneath, which is the opposite of the sessile clamped read the packet asks for. What is drawn is the Abalone/Cowrie ellipse with the abalone hole row, recoloured tan.
rows.fix: Replace it entirely with a low ribbed cone seen from a shallow side angle, apex slightly off-centre, ribs radiating from apex to a scalloped rim, and seat the rim flat on a rock line with no gap or floating shadow.
rows.verifyWhy:
FAIL upheld, and the shared-chassis part of the claim is stronger than stated. What is actually on canvas: a single tilted ellipse (long axis running roughly upper-right to lower-left, about -20 degrees, aspect near 1.4 not the specified 1.8), filled with a soft airbrushed khaki/tan gradient that is lightest along the upper-right rim and falls off to shadow at the lower-left. Over that fill sit blurry pastel cloud blotches -- pink at mid-right, pale green upper-right and lower-right, cream lower-left -- with no edges and no structural meaning. A thin pale crescent highlight runs along the upper-right rim, cut off by one faint arc line that reads as a shell lip. Dead centre-left of the mass is a horizontal row of FIVE small dark circular holes, evenly spaced, slightly rising to the right, drawn as flat dark dots with no bore depth. Below the body, separated by a clear band of empty dark background roughly a third of the body height, floats a detached soft-edged elliptical drop shadow. There is no rock, no substrate, no ground plane at all.

Must-read 1, 'simple uncoiled cone shell like a hat': ABSENT. There is no conical profile, no hat silhouette, no peak breaking the outline. The silhouette is a pure ellipse; read as a dome-from-above it still fails because nothing in the shading builds a cone -- the gradient is a flat directional wash across the whole oval, not a radial falloff from a summit.

Must-read 2, 'ribbed radiating ridges': ABSENT. I looked specifically for faint ribs and there are none -- zero radial lines, zero scalloped rim, zero alternating light/dark wedges. The only linework anywhere is the single arc near the right rim. Surface texture is entirely blurred blob mottling.

Must-read 3, 'slightly off-centre apex': ABSENT. No apex, and no highlight convergence point standing in for one. The specular is a rim crescent along an edge, not a point.

Must-read 4, 'clamped flush against rock' (posture: sessile): ABSENT and actively contradicted. The body floats with daylight fully under it and casts a levitation shadow -- the judge described this correctly. Every gastropod I sampled in this batch uses the same floating-shadow treatment, so this is a family-wide staging bug, not a Limpet-only slip.

On 'it is the Abalone/Cowrie holed ellipse in tan' -- I verified this directly and it is literally true, not an analogy. I opened Abalone.png and Cowrie.png alongside. All three are the SAME drawing: same ellipse, same tilt angle, same rim crescent and same cut-off arc line, same row of exactly five dark dots in the same relative position, same detached shadow at the same offset. The only differences are hue and blotch placement -- Abalone is mint green, Cowrie orange-tan, Limpet khaki-tan with pink and pale-green blotches. Three species, one chassis, recoloured.

The holes are worse than merely wrong: a row of open respiratory pores along one edge is Abalone's OWN defining must-read. Limpets have no such row (even keyhole limpets have a single apical hole, not five along a flank), so the borrowed feature does not just fail to say 'limpet', it positively spells 'abalone'. headFrac 0 and eyes hidden are satisfied only by accident, since nothing anatomical is drawn at all.

Fix direction: this needs a new primitive, not a repaint. Draw a side-three-quarter cone -- low conical dome with the apex set forward of centre, an elliptical base ring, 12-16 radiating ribs running apex-to-rim that widen and catch light on the lit side and read as scalloped notches where they meet the rim, growth rings as faint concentric arcs crossing them. Delete the five-hole row entirely. Seat the base on a visible rock band with the contact line hidden by a tight dark occlusion contact shadow at the rim, and remove the floating cast shadow so there is no gap of background beneath the body.

rows.readsAs: a magenta sea slug, or a small punk hairbrush
rows.defect: The best asset in the batch - the comb of cerata on the back reads clearly and the brilliant shell-less body is right. But the cerata are drawn as flat straight quills with no branching or tips, so they read as bristles rather than gills, and the rhinophores are the same generic 5-pixel jagged crest reused from Banana Slug, not a pair of club-shaped horns. The body underneath is the identical flat-bottomed loaf used for the Banana Slug.
rows.fix: Replace the head crest with two distinct club-tipped rhinophore horns standing clear of the body, and taper and tip the cerata so they read as fleshy gill fingers.

rows.readsAs: a walnut-brown ammonite on a foot - the same drawing as Snail and Water Snail
rows.defect: Reads roughly as a snail, but the shell is not tightly coiled with a visible aperture - it is the flat ridged disc stamp, and no aperture opening is drawn anywhere. The siphon tube, which is what separates a sea snail from the land snails beside it, is completely absent, and the head tentacles are the shared 3-prong fork.
rows.fix: Open a dark aperture at the shell's lower right and run a distinct tubular siphon forward from it past the head tentacles.

rows.readsAs: a snail (the most generic reading in the batch) - or an ammonite shell resting on a slipper
rows.defect: Silhouette reads snail, but the two long eye tentacles plus two short feelers are collapsed into one small 3-prong fork with no eye bulbs on anything, and there is no head between shell and foot. The shell is a flat planispiral disc rather than a spire carried up on the back, and the foot is a hard-edged flat lens with no sole texture.
rows.fix: Separate the head token into two long eye-tipped tentacles and two short feelers on a visible head lobe, and raise the shell's coil into a spire so it is carried on the back rather than lying flat.

rows.readsAs: a brass-coloured snail, identical in every line to Snail and Land Snail
rows.defect: Nothing distinguishes it from four other assets in this batch except hue - same disc shell, same lens foot, same fork. The flat-coiled shell technically satisfies its must-read, but the pair of slender head tentacles is the shared 3-prong stub with no separation between the two tentacles and no head, and no aquatic cue (siphon, water context) marks it as a water snail at all.
rows.fix: Draw two clearly separate slender tentacles from a modelled head and add an aquatic tell such as a raised breathing siphon, so it cannot be confused with the land snails next to it.

rows.readsAs: a hollow gelatinous tube or tube sponge standing in the water - close to a pyrosome but a stranger may say sponge
rows.defect: The bioluminescence must-read is the wrong colour entirely - the tunic and its ambient halo are magenta/violet, with no cold blue anywhere in frame. The cone also tapers the wrong way: it is narrowest at the open rim and widest at the sealed lower end, where a pyrosome is widest at the open mouth and tapers to a closed point, and the bottom corners are squared off so it reads as a flat-bottomed bag rather than a sealed cone tip. The zooids render as roughly a hundred flat pale confetti discs floating over the surface, not as thousands of raised pimples - there is no relief, no rim shadow and no density gradient, so the surface reads printed rather than encrusted.
rows.fix: Recolour tunic and halo to a cold cyan-blue bioluminescent glow and flip the taper so the open rim is the widest point, narrowing to a rounded sealed tip at the bottom.

rows.readsAs: a diagonal chain of banded pods - salp chain is reachable, but the first read is closer to beads or small grenades
rows.defect: Transparency, which is the whole identity of a salp, is absent: the barrels are painted opaque dark navy on a near-black field, so nothing shows through them and the chain nearly disappears into the background. The small coloured gut nucleus is missing from all four zooids - there is no internal organ mark anywhere. The muscle hoops are the one strong read and they land well, but 'open at both ends' only registers at one end of each barrel; the far end is closed off by shading, so each unit reads as a sealed pod rather than an open tube.
rows.fix: Drop the tunic to a high-value glassy translucent so the background reads through the body, and drop one small warm orange gut nucleus into each zooid.

rows.readsAs: two industrial chimneys or cement kilns standing on a hill; a tunicate only on a second look, once the paired nozzles register
rows.defect: The surface treatment fights the organism. The tunic is opaque achromatic silver-white with a hard specular sheen, and the internal basket is drawn as a rectangular grid ON the outside of the wall, which reads unmistakably as brick coursing - the combination turns two soft sacs into masonry smokestacks. Neither 'leathery' nor 'translucent' is present: there is no colour at all and nothing shows through the wall. The two raised nozzle siphons are correct and clearly legible, and the sacs do sit convincingly cemented onto the dark rock mound, so the identity survives, but the material read is wrong enough to send a stranger to the wrong noun.
rows.fix: Give the tunic a translucent warm ochre-pink cast and push the basket mesh behind the wall as a soft, blurred internal structure instead of a hard exterior grid.

rows.readsAs: a giraffe — named instantly and correctly
rows.defect: Long neck and knobbed ossicones both read clearly, but the third must-read is weak and the rear third is unfinished. The topline is a low rounded arch that crests mid-back, not a steep ramp from high shoulders to the hips — there is no withers, and the drop from shoulder to croup is shallow. Worse, the reticulated patch field stops in a hard vertical edge at the flank, so the whole near haunch, thigh and croup are a blank cream slab with no patches and no shading; the shoulder is likewise unpatterned. The tail is a fat cream tube as thick as a leg that emerges from the middle of that blank slab well below the topline, with a scribbly speckled artifact where it joins the body. The leg markings are angular splinters that read as cracked paint rather than patches, and the hind legs are straight posts with no hock.
rows.fix: Carry the reticulation continuously over the croup, haunch and shoulder (no hard cut at the flank), then raise and sharpen the withers so the topline ramps steeply down to a lower hip, and rebuild the tail as a thin cord docked at the TOP of the rump.

rows.readsAs: a brown llama or a striped-necked antelope wearing a white girth band — not an okapi
rows.defect: The striping — which IS the okapi's identity — is in the wrong places and the wrong colours. The hindquarters and croup, where the horizontal white bars belong, are plain unmarked chocolate with nothing on them at all. Instead a broad band of VERTICAL cream strands is wrapped around the middle of the barrel like a saddle girth or a shaved patch, sitting forward of the hip and reading as a blanket, not as rump stripes. And the neck carries four heavy DARK horizontal bars from the jaw down to the shoulder — an okapi has no neck stripes; that inversion (dark bars on the neck, nothing on the rump) is exactly backwards and drags the read toward kudu or bongo. The leg markings are irregular white blotches, not clean horizontal bands. The face is uniform brown with no pale muzzle or cheek mask. The eye is broken: it renders as a white crescent ring with the dark pupil occluded by the ossicone base, so it reads as a hole in the head rather than an eye. There is also a hard straight seam with a bluish-grey tint running along the top of the back where the dorsal plate meets the barrel.
rows.fix: Delete the dark neck bars and the vertical cream girth band entirely, and paint crisp horizontal white bars across the croup, rump and upper hind leg only — rear half striped, front half plain chocolate — then move the eye clear of the ossicone so the pupil is visible.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, with corrections to the stated causes. I read the 440x440 PNG at 1x and then cropped/upscaled five regions (head 4x, eye 14x, neck 8x, rear 6x, legs 5x, dorsal line 6x) and confirmed the pattern really is inverted.

WHAT I SAW ON THE REAR (packet must-read #1, 'horizontal white stripes on the hindquarters and upper legs' - FAILS). The white marking is a single solid cream MASS, not stripes. It sits over the loin/flank/mid-barrel, roughly x=115-215 of the ~x=75-375 body, and its internal texture is fine VERTICAL combed strands running top-to-bottom, so it reads as a wrapped girth/belt or a saddle blanket. Its forward edge is a hard vertical cut against the brown barrel. The croup and the rounded rear contour behind it - the exact place an okapi's horizontal bars belong - is plain unbroken mid-brown, with only one small white wedge poking in near the tail base. So the judge is right that the croup is bare and the white is misplaced forward; the one correction is that the white mass is NOT entirely off the hindquarter - it does overlap the front of the rump and the top of the hind thigh. It still contains zero horizontal bars anywhere.

WHAT I SAW ON THE NECK (an actively wrong feature). Confirmed, but recount: there are FIVE heavy near-black bars, not four, and they are DIAGONAL (running down-and-forward at roughly 30 degrees), evenly spaced, banding the entire neck from just behind the jaw down onto the shoulder and wrapping around onto the throat. This is the single most damaging defect - it is a zebra/kudu neck. The packet note explicitly says 'not a zebra; only the rear half is striped', and the asset does the exact opposite: dark bars on the FRONT half, a white belt at the middle, bare brown at the REAR.

WHAT SURVIVES (correcting the judge's 'brown llama' read). Must-read #3 IS satisfied: the crown carries two clearly modelled short skin-covered ossicones - rounded knobs on stubby stalks, correct okapi placement between and behind the eyes - plus a large dark ear behind them. The muzzle is long with a dark nostril, the feet end in dark cloven hooves, and all four legs do carry white markings (irregular white blobs on the cannons plus solid white lower legs / socks), so 'white on the upper legs' is partially present even though the leg bands are blobby rather than clean rings. The ossicones alone rule out 'llama'; what it actually reads as is a striped-necked antelope or a zebra-necked donkey.

MUST-READ #2 ('deep chocolate body with a sloping back') ALSO FAILS, which the original judge did not raise. The coat is a mid warm reddish-brown, several stops lighter than okapi chocolate, and the topline is essentially FLAT from shoulder to hip rather than sloping down from high withers.

MINOR DEFECTS - both real, both correctly spotted, both cosmetic next to the pattern inversion. (a) The eye at ~(310,102) is a small white blob with a dark bar cutting its lower-right; at 14x it is not a clean 'crescent ring', it is a white sclera with the dark pupil shoved off to the right and clipped by the shadow of the near ossicone stalk - so the intent was right but the pupil does not sit inside the white. (b) There IS a hard 1-2px light bluish-grey seam running the full dorsal line from behind the shoulder to the croup - a compositing edge, clearly visible against the dark background. Also the tail is over-long, hanging to the hock with a big black tassel; an okapi's is short.

BAND: FAIL. Two of three must-reads are absent, and the identity feature is not merely weak but inverted and relocated onto a body part where it constitutes a false species signal. Fix order: (1) delete all neck barring; (2) replace the vertical-strand cream mass with 5-7 discrete HORIZONTAL cream bars laid across the croup, rump and upper hind leg, running from the tail base forward and stopping at the flank; (3) darken the coat to true chocolate and drop the hip below the withers; (4) reseat the pupil and kill the dorsal seam.

rows.readsAs: a dark brown housefly or midge
rows.defect: Two of three must-reads are visibly absent. The antennae are short thin stubs reaching only about a third of the body length, when the reference demands antennae LONGER THAN THE WHOLE BODY — the single most diagnostic cricket cue. The hind leg is a hairline stick with a shallow bend and no swollen femur at all, so nothing reads as a jumping leg. The body is two overlapping brown ovals with a rear wing-fan, giving a fly silhouette; nothing about it says cricket.
rows.fix: Draw the antennae at 1.3x total body length sweeping back over the body, and rebuild the hind leg with a fat teardrop femur angled up above the topline over a thin tibia kinked sharply down.
rows.verifyWhy: Verdict upheld, but two of the three stated causes are measurably wrong and the fix list is different from what was written. Measured from the decoded PNG (440x440): dense body mass runs x=168..321 (154 px, head front to wing tip), body depth 56 px. ANTENNAE: they are NOT 'short stubs about a third of body length'. They are two slender tapered forward-swept threads emerging right at the eye (base ~x=167,y=190) and running to tips at (96,154) and (96,172) — length ~80 and ~73 px, i.e. ~0.50x body length, and they are the single most legible feature on the head. The mustRead 'antennae longer than the whole body' still fails, but it is a 2x shortfall, not a 3x one: the fix is to roughly triple them (to >=1.2x body, ~185 px) and give them the cricket's fine backward sweep/curve, NOT to 'add antennae'. HIND LEG: the judge is right that it is a hairline with no swollen femur — the stroke is a uniform ~2.2 px wide over both segments against a 56 px body depth (~4%; a cricket femur should be 25-30% of body depth). But the judge is wrong that 'no jumping leg reads' because of geometry: the crank IS drawn. There is a clean knee apex at ~(345,207) with a short back-swept femur (~22 px) and a long forward-raking tibia (~90 px) down to a foot at ~(310,285). The failure is MASS, not topology. And the decisive point the judge missed: the identical crank is drawn on the FRONT leg pair, with its knee apex sitting above the head at ~(170,185), so the hind leg is in no way differentiated from the others — that generic cranked-stick leg model applied to all pairs is why the jumping leg does not read. SILHOUETTE: not a housefly. Long spindly cranked legs on every pair, a small ball head, and large lobed wings read as a mosquito or a crane fly. Diptera either way, so the conclusion stands, but the target to move away from is a culicid/tipulid, not Musca. DEFECTS THE JUDGE DID NOT NAME: (1) the middle leg pair is two short strokes from the underside at ~(238,205)->(233,220) and ~(268,208)->(262,228) that terminate in mid-air, far above the ground shadow ellipse — no tarsi, no ground contact. (2) The 'wings' are three bulging overlapping leaf lobes splayed down over the flanks rather than flat tegmina laid over the back, so mustRead 2 only half-reads; worse, the pale venation strokes overshoot the wing outline and leave roughly six detached pale-blue slivers floating free in the background off the rear edge (visible around x=310..322, y=190..225) — an unclipped stroke, not intentional bristles. (3) The eye is a glossy vertebrate ball with a single white catchlight, not a compound eye. (4) There is no abdomen and no cerci behind the wings at all — the wing lobes run straight to the rear terminus, so the cricket's paired cerci, the feature that would sell it alongside the antennae, are entirely absent. Net: 2 of 3 must-reads absent (antennae length, jumping hind leg), the third only partial, and the assembled silhouette reads as a dipteran. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a pale green mayfly or lacewing
rows.defect: The identity must-read — huge angled jumping hind legs rising above the back — is entirely absent. Every leg is the same hairline stick of constant width, none rises above the topline, none has a femur. The abdomen is a blunt rounded blob, not a long tapered one, and the face is a small round ball with thread antennae rather than a slanted face with short stout ones. Recolored Cricket with a slightly larger wing fan.
rows.fix: Add a genuine saltatorial hind leg: a broad wedge-shaped femur whose apex sits clearly above the wing line, hinged to a long thin downward tibia with visible spines and a small foot.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, and it fails harder than stated: all THREE must-reads are absent, not two. I read the PNG at 1:1 and then re-cropped and upscaled the body (5x), head (12x) and rear (10x) to check for small features. What is actually on the canvas: a round ball head at far left with a large circular BLACK pupil carrying a single white specular highlight (a cartoon vertebrate eyeball, not a tall oval compound eye); two thin curved thread antennae rising from above the eye, about 0.35 of body length; two overlapping fat olive ellipses (thorax, then abdomen) with lightly scribed segment lines; four long translucent veined wing blades spread outward and projecting roughly 40% of body length PAST the abdomen tip; six hairline legs; a soft cast-shadow ellipse.

MUST-READ 1, 'huge angled jumping hind legs rising above the back' — ABSENT. Confirmed at 10x on the rear crop. CORRECTION to the claim: the hind LEGS are not absent, only their morphology is. Two thin sticks do descend from the rear of the body, angled down-and-back. There is no femur swelling, no cranked knee, and nothing whatsoever rises above the topline — the topline from head to wingtip is uninterrupted. The fix is therefore to RESHAPE an existing limb (add a deep leaf-shaped femur, a sharp knee apex above the wing line, and a thin backswept tibia), not to add a missing one.

MUST-READ 2, 'long tapered abdomen' — ABSENT, claim correct. The abdomen is a blunt-ended ellipse of roughly 2:1, wider than the thorax at its midpoint and rounded off at the rear. No taper, no terminal point, no ventral segment steps.

MUST-READ 3, 'short stout antennae and slanted face' — ABSENT. The judge described the face and antennae correctly but did not score this as a third failure. The head is a near-perfect circle in profile: no slanted/oblique face, no vertical fastigium, no mandible or clypeus mass. The antennae are thread-thin hairlines, i.e. the katydid/cricket cue the family packet explicitly warns off, not the short stout pair a grasshopper needs.

PARTIAL CORRECTIONS to the stated cause. (a) 'all legs are the same constant-width hairline sticks' — they are not strictly constant-width; each leg tapers from a slightly wider coxa to a bare point, and the front pair has a short angular elbow segment at the top. The substance stands (no femur, no crank, no tarsi/feet at all — every leg ends in a bare point), but a fix written against 'constant width' would miss that a taper is already there and the missing thing is the femur mass. (b) 'reads as a green mayfly' — closer to a green lacewing/mayfly, and the driver is the WINGS, which the claim never mentions: four translucent spread blades overshooting the abdomen, plus grey bristle-like strokes that escape past the wing membrane edge as loose stray lines. Grasshopper tegmina must be opaque leathery covers folded FLAT and tented along the back, ending at or just past the abdomen tip. Those wings are the single loudest wrong-organism signal in the image.

ADDITIONAL DEFECTS the claim missed, all fix-relevant. (1) Leg mounting is anatomically wrong: the mid and hind pairs attach under the ABDOMEN — the hind pair at the posterior tip of the rear ellipse — instead of all six mounting on the thorax in the front third. (2) No pronotum: the thorax has no saddle/shield, which is a primary grasshopper read. (3) Proportion: the green-pixel bounding box measures 188 x 102 px, aspect 1.84, against the packet's target of 2.6 — the silhouette is far too short and stubby for the spec.

Band FAIL is correct. This is not a polish-level asset; head, abdomen, wings and hind limb all need rebuilding.

rows.readsAs: a golden mayfly or long-winged crane fly
rows.defect: The hugely enlarged folded hind jumping leg is missing — the rear limb is a plain straight hairline stick angled down and back, identical in thickness to the front legs. The head is a small round ball, not the tall flat-sided head called for. The long wings do lie along the back and are the one thing working, but they spread and droop below the body line rather than folding flat, so the overall silhouette is a delicate flier, not a locust.
rows.fix: Replace the rear stick with a massive folded hind leg — deep ribbed femur packed against the abdomen with the apex above the back and the tibia folded up alongside it — and square off the head into a tall flat-sided helmet.
rows.verifyWhy:
Verified at 4x-9x magnification on crops of the 440x440 PNG (whole body, head, hind quarter). The FAIL stands, and the core cause is stated correctly, but two of the three sub-claims need correcting.

CONFIRMED — the defining must-read is absent. 'Hugely enlarged folded hind jumping legs' do not exist anywhere in the drawing. Six limbs are present, all identical: uniform thin tapered sticks about 3px wide at the top narrowing to a point, each a SINGLE straight segment with no femur swelling, no knee, no tibia crank, no Z-fold, and no spines. The rearmost pair drops from beneath the rear third of the abdomen straight down and slightly back to the ground; it is the same thickness as the forelegs and is if anything the LONGEST but not the thickest. Nothing rises above the topline at all — the back silhouette from pronotum to abdomen tip is an unbroken smooth curve, which is exactly the read a locust must not have. The judge's description of this is accurate.

PARTLY WRONG — 'small round ball' head. The head is not a ball and is not small. It is a horizontally elongated egg/bean roughly 40px long by 33px tall (about 0.25 of the head-to-abdomen-tip body length, so headFrac 0.22 is met), with a smooth continuous rounded outline, a rounded blunt snout tip, and a rounded occiput that plugs straight into the thorax. The defect is one of SHAPE ORIENTATION, not scale: it is a long-axis-horizontal ovoid where the reference wants a tall, vertically-deep, flat-sided (laterally compressed) head with a slanted face. There is no vertical face plane, no flat cheek, no mandible block. One large circular black eye with a white specular dot sits high and forward. Any fix note written against 'small round ball' will produce the wrong correction — the head needs to be rotated to a tall vertical oval and given flat sides, not enlarged.

PARTLY WRONG — 'the long wings work'. They half work. The wings ARE long and narrow (each roughly as long as the entire body), so that half of the must-read reads. But they are NOT 'folded flat along the back'. Two translucent gold blades splay apart in a wide V — the upper one angles up and back past the abdomen tip, the lower one angles down and back — with the abdomen visible between them, plus a set of long straight white/grey filament lines that run through the wings and project well past both wingtips as free bristles. Combined with the six identical stick legs, that is the crane-fly / mayfly silhouette the judge names, and the splayed spread wings are part of what causes it, not an innocent element.

What DOES pass: antennae are short (two fine arcs about 1.5 head-lengths, curving up and forward), correctly avoiding the katydid/cricket thread antennae the packet's note warns against. Posture is crawling. Aspect is near 2. Palette and painterly shading are clean, with segment hatching on thorax and abdomen.

FAMILY CONTEXT (the packet's chassis question): Grasshopper.png in the same batch is the identical drawing in green — same egg head, same splayed wing V, same six uniform stick legs, no jumping leg either. Locust and Grasshopper are one chassis in two tints, and that chassis reads as a crane fly. The hind-leg fix is therefore a family-level fix, not a per-asset one.

Band: FAIL. Two of three must-reads fail (jumping legs wholly absent, head shape wrong) and the third only half-reads, and the resulting silhouette reads as the wrong order of insect.

rows.readsAs: a small spotted brown bream or freshwater sunfish
rows.defect: Both identity must-reads are absent. There is no mouth on this fish at all -- zoomed 4x the head is a symmetric needle point with only a faint hairline stroke and a gill arc, no jaw break in the silhouette, no jutting lower jaw, no gape. And the body is the opposite of 'thick heavy blunt-headed': it is a pointed lens whose snout tapers to a sharp point, so the heavy square-headed ambush-predator mass is nowhere in the drawing. Only the rounded paddle tail lands. The sawtooth dorsal slab also floats clear of the topline with background showing under its base.
rows.fix: Rebuild the head: blunt the snout into a wide square muzzle at least as deep as the body midline, and cut an actual mouth aperture that opens roughly a third of the head length with the lower jaw jutting past the upper -- the gape must break the silhouette, not be a line drawn on it.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, with two corrections to the stated cause and one defect the first judge missed. What I actually saw, at 6x/13x crops and on a luminance-only pass of the whole animal (440x440 canvas; body silhouette measured at x=139..339, y=167..242, so ~200px long x 75px deep, aspect 2.67):

MUST-READ 1 — 'huge cavernous mouth with a jutting lower jaw': ABSENT, but the claim 'there is no mouth on the fish at all' is overstated and would send a fixer looking for the wrong thing. There IS a mouth stroke, and I located it: a thin dark hairline running from about x=296 to x=318 at y=217..221, i.e. ~22px long (11% of body length), hugging 2-4px INSIDE the ventral contour of the head and running parallel to it. Measured luminance ~62-80 against surrounding body flesh at ~100-115 — a delta of only ~30-45, and I verified it is a real local mark rather than rim shading by sampling the same inset band further aft (x=250..285 reads 95-120 just inside the ventral edge, so the darkening is specific to the head). But it is functionally a non-feature: it terminates ~21px SHORT of the snout point (tip at x=339), it never rises to meet an upper jaw, there is no gape wedge, no maxilla, no second stroke, and it does not break the silhouette anywhere. Because it lies flat along the belly line it reads as an edge shadow, not a jaw. Net effect matches the judge: no jutting lower jaw, no gape, no jaw break in the outline. The fix is not 'add a mouth line' — a line is there — it is to build an actual jaw: pull the stroke forward to the snout, split it into an upper and lower jaw with an open gape, and push the lower jaw PAST the upper so it breaks the silhouette.

MUST-READ 2 — 'thick heavy blunt-headed body': ABSENT, and the judge's 'pointed lens' is exactly right; I can now put numbers on it. Column-by-column depth: 6px at x=139 (peduncle), rising to a maximum of 75px at x=219-235, then falling to 2px at x=339 (snout). The profile is near-perfectly symmetric fore-and-aft — depth 60 at x=183 and depth 60 at x=275, equidistant either side of the maximum. In the desaturated whole-body view the head end and the tail end of the lens are indistinguishable in shape; only the eye and the gill arc tell you which end is the front. The head tapers 61px -> 2px over its last 66px as a straight wedge with zero mass. A grouper's deepest point belongs at the nape immediately behind a big blunt truncate skull, not at mid-flank.

MUST-READ 3 — 'rounded paddle tail': PRESENT. A dark rounded fan at x~95..138, correctly non-forked. The judge is right that this is the only must-read that lands. Note it attaches through a very pinched peduncle (only 9 warm pixels tall at x=141) and, being much darker than the body, reads slightly detached.

CORRECT IN THE ORIGINAL CLAIM: the gill arc is real and well drawn (a strong curved operculum sweeping from the topline down toward the belly across x~270..300); the snout really is a symmetric needle point; the overall read really is 'spotted brown panfish', not an ambush predator.

DEFECT THE FIRST JUDGE MISSED — the eye is not seated in the head. The white eye ring protrudes ABOVE the dorsal silhouette into empty background: at x=310 and x=315 I measured ring pixels at luminance 229-240 sitting above the body's dorsal edge (y=185-186), with pure background (lum 11-15) immediately beyond them. At 13x the ring visibly straddles the topline with roughly its upper third outside the fish. Whoever fixes the head must also drop the eye down into the skull.

MINOR: the pectoral fin is an unfilled radiating wireframe of thin strokes rather than a fin body; the sawtooth dorsal is a flat dark band whose base is buried under the topline. Neither is the reason for the band.

Band FAIL stands: two of three must-reads are missing, and the two missing ones are the ones that carry the identity.

rows.readsAs: a generic silver panfish -- bream, or a small silver perch
rows.defect: There is only ONE dorsal element, the shared floating sawtooth slab, so the required spiny-first-dorsal-ahead-of-a-soft-second reads as a single comb with no soft posterior fin behind it. The large mouth is entirely missing -- at 4x the snout is a closed symmetric point with a faint stroke and no jaw. The tail is a deep swallowtail fork more like a jack or tuna than the squared-to-slightly-forked bass tail called for. The body is the family lens, not a robust perch with a shoulder. The eye circle straddles the upper contour, half of it sitting over the background.
rows.fix: Split the dorsal into two attached fins -- a short spiny triangle over the shoulder joined to the topline, then a distinct lower soft-rayed lobe behind it -- and square off the caudal fin to a shallow notch.

rows.readsAs: a red bream or porgy -- the colour and depth get it close, the head does not
rows.defect: No sloping forehead: the topline is the shared unbroken arc that curves straight into a symmetric point, so the steep brow that makes a snapper's profile is absent. The pair of canine teeth -- the feature the animal is NAMED for -- is not drawn at all; at 4x there is no mouth opening, only a short stroke that stops short of the snout. The 'continuous' spiny dorsal is the shared detached slab hovering above the back over the rear half only, with visible background between its base and the topline, so it neither runs continuously along the back nor connects to it.
rows.fix: Give the head a straight steep brow dropping from the dorsal origin to a pointed snout, and open the jaw enough to show two forward-pointing canines at the front of the upper jaw; anchor the dorsal fin base directly onto the topline running from the shoulder to the tail root.

rows.readsAs: a brown quail or a small partridge
rows.defect: The reed-mimic freeze pose is completely absent — the body is horizontal and dumpy and the bill points DOWN and to the left, the opposite of the vertical sky-pointing dagger that is the whole reason this bird is recognisable. There is no thick hunched neck at all; the head ball sits directly on the shoulder of the egg. Only the brown-and-buff mottling survives, and mottled brown on a round gamebird body just reads as quail.
rows.fix: Rebuild it in the freeze pose: rotate the whole body to vertical, extend a thick heavily-streaked neck straight up from the shoulders, and align the dagger bill with the neck axis so bill, neck and body form one continuous vertical reed.
rows.verifyWhy: Looked at the full-size render and then re-cropped the head/neck at 4x to hunt for a small or hidden upward bill. There is none. WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: a fat, near-horizontal buff oval body carrying a second concentric oval (the wing/covert mass) with a dark rim, a pointed dark-tan tail wedge projecting to the lower right past the body edge, two thin tan legs with three-toed feet planted under the body's mid-line, and a small perfectly round ball head on a long, thin, smoothly tapering neck that rises from the FRONT of the body in a shallow S and carries the head clear of the shoulders. Silhouette aspect reads roughly square-to-wide, not the packet's 1.3 upright; the head is about 12 percent of figure height, not the specified headFrac 0.25. MUST-READ 1 (dagger bill pointed straight up in the reed-mimic freeze pose) - ABSENT, and this is the decisive failure. At 4x the bill is a slim saturated-yellow spike whose centerline runs from the head at roughly (392,250) to the tip at roughly (140,255) in crop coordinates, i.e. essentially HORIZONTAL to the left with only a hair of downward tilt. CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM: 'points down-and-left' overstates the droop - it is a level, forward-pointing bill, not a downward-angled one. Either way it is 90 degrees off the required skyward point, and nothing about the pose (level head, relaxed S-neck, weight settled on both legs) suggests a freeze. MUST-READ 3 (thick hunched retractable neck) - ABSENT, and the render is not merely missing it, it draws the opposite: a stork/flamingo-style thin tube of uniform diameter, roughly one-third the width of the head ball, fully extended and standing well proud of the body. The judge's 'no thick hunched neck at all' is correct. MUST-READ 2 (brown-and-buff streaked camouflage) - only PARTIALLY present, and the judge was too generous here. The streaking exists but is confined to the body and wing mass, where it renders as a woven-basket / fish-scale stipple following the oval's curvature rather than as bold vertical dark-brown streaks. Critically, the NECK AND HEAD ARE BLANK unstreaked flat buff with no crown cap, no dark moustachial/malar stripe, and no throat striping - which guts the identity twice over, because the bittern's vertical neck streaks ARE the reed mimicry and are the feature that would sell the pose even at thumbnail size. FINAL READ: with a long thin neck, long exposed legs and a level spear bill this does NOT read as a quail - correcting the judge there, since a quail has a short neck and no visible legs. It reads as a generic small stork/ibis/wader chick, or an unlabeled shorebird. Two of three must-reads absent, the third half-delivered on the wrong body part. FAIL stands. FIX DIRECTION: rotate the bill and head to vertical (bill in line with the neck axis, tip at the top of the frame), collapse the neck into a short thick column continuous with the breast so head-neck-body form one tapering vertical spindle, stand the body upright (aspect 1.3, weight on vertical legs, tail tucked down not projecting sideways), and run bold dark-brown vertical streaks down the front of the neck and breast, not just scale-stipple on the wing.

rows.readsAs: a white bantam hen or a dove
rows.defect: Pure white plumage is the only must-read present. There is no S-curved neck — there is no neck of any length, the round white head is stuck onto the front of the body. The legs are short yellow stubs about a quarter of body height when they must be long and dark, and the bill is a stubby cone rather than a thin spear. Stripped of neck and legs it is a white chicken.
rows.fix: Give it a long thin neck at least the body's length again, folded into a shallow S, and stretch the legs to roughly body-height and recolour them near-black.
rows.verifyWhy: I measured the pixels as well as looking. Bird occupies y101-327, x101-344 on the 440px canvas (total height 227px). THE FAIL'S TWO LOAD-BEARING CLAIMS ARE BOTH FACTUALLY WRONG. (1) 'The bill is a stubby cone not a thin spear' — false, and it is in fact the best-executed must-read on the asset. The bill runs x101-157: 56px long, 10px thick at the base, tapering to a needle point, against a head only 33px across (row 110 white span 156-188). That is a 1.7x-head-length thin yellow dagger held level and forward, exactly the spear silhouette the packet asks for. (2) 'There is no S-curved neck because there is no neck' — false. There is a clearly separated white neck column: at rows 140 and 150 the only white in the frame is an 11px-wide stalk (x165-176, x167-178), fully detached from both the 33px head above and the body shoulder that starts at row 160. It reads at a glance as a neck. What is TRUE about the neck is different from what they said: it is TOO SHORT and the wrong shape — head underside ~y132 to body top ~y158 is about 26px, only 0.8x head diameter, and its profile is a single shallow forward-bowed C (bulging forward at the throat, sweeping back into the shoulder), not the retracted S/kink of a heron. So the token 'S-curved neck' fails on curve and length, not on absence. (3) 'Legs are short yellow stubs' — half right and described wrong. They are not stubs: the legs run y265-327 (62px, x202-253) and are fully articulated waders' legs — visible backward-bending hock on both, a straight tarsus below it, and splayed feet with three forward toes plus a rear hallux, drawn cleanly at 5x zoom. The real defect is proportion and hue: 62px of leg on a 227px bird is 27% of standing height where an egret wants ~40-45%, and they are saturated yellow-ochre where the packet says 'long dark legs'. (4) A defect the FAIL did not mention at all: 'pure white plumage' is itself compromised. 3,390 mid-grey pixels sit against 10,383 white ones — a heavy grey scapular arc sweeps across the back, a second grey arc rings the folded wing, and a solid dark-grey wedge tail/wingtip juts out to x344 with dark filament streaks trailing under it. On a bird whose first must-read is pure white, a quarter of the body mass being grey is a real miss. VERDICT: it does NOT read as a white bantam hen — a hen has a short conical bill and no isolated neck stalk, and this has a 56px dagger and an isolated 11px neck stalk. It reads as a squat wading bird: correct organism class, wrong elegance. Two of four must-read tokens land outright (white base plumage, thin spear bill), two land partially (neck present but short and C- not S-curved; legs anatomically correct waders' legs but too short and yellow instead of dark). Nothing needs re-deriving; the fixes are parametric — lengthen the neck ~2.5x and put a real S-kink in it, lengthen the legs to ~40% of height and recolor them dark slate (keep the yellow feet if a snowy egret read is wanted), and drop the grey scapular/wing arcs and tail wedge to near-white with only faint shading. That is a POLISH list, not a FAIL.

rows.readsAs: a pink quail or a pink cartoon chick
rows.defect: All three must-reads are missing. The neck is not kinked into a long S — there is no neck. The bill is a short straight pink-and-yellow cone with no downward break at the middle, so the single most diagnostic feature of a flamingo is simply not drawn. The legs are short yellow stubs with a forward bend, nowhere near extremely long and with no backward-bending ankle. Pink is doing 100% of the identification work.
rows.fix: Draw the flamingo silhouette from scratch — leg length roughly two body-depths with a pronounced rearward ankle break, and a neck the same length again ending in a bill that snaps sharply downward at its midpoint.
rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 PNG whole, then cropped and upscaled the head (5x) and the legs (4x) with a pure-node PNG decoder, and measured the silhouette by scanning rows for pink/yellow pixels. Verdict upheld, but one third of the stated cause is wrong and the fix brief needs correcting.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE: a plump ovoid pink body (a folded-wing oval outlined in dark mauve, iridescent scale-hatch fill) with a pointed mauve tail sweeping back and slightly up, a small round head, a short straight yellow beak, and two thin yellow legs with three-toed feet. Measured bbox of the pink/yellow mass is x 97-279, y 104-326 (the mauve tail is outside that threshold and reaches roughly x 335). Standing height, head crown y=104 to ground y=326, is 223px.

MUST-READ 1 - 'neck kinked into a long S': ABSENT, and the judge understated it. There is not a short neck; there is NO neck. Row scan shows the head sphere spanning y 104-128 (diameter ~54px) and the body edge jumping from R=162 to R=229 at y=128 - the head is fused directly onto the shoulder with zero visible column between them. Head is ~24% of standing height against the packet's headFrac 0.16. Confirmed FAIL.

MUST-READ 2 - 'thick bill bent sharply downward at the middle': ABSENT, and the judge's description is correct. The 5x head crop shows a two-wedge yellow triangle (upper and lower mandible) running from x~97 to x~135, about 38px long, straight, tapering to a point, aimed forward and only very slightly down. There is no break, no kink, no downward hook, and no thickness at the base - it is a generic passerine/songbird cone. Confirmed FAIL.

MUST-READ 3 - 'extremely long pink legs with a backward-bending ankle': HALF PRESENT. The judge is WRONG that there is no backward-bending ankle. The 4x leg crop clearly shows a two-segment leg on each side with a distinct joint at about y=282: the upper segment runs down and REARWARD (to the right; the bird faces left), the lower segment runs down and FORWARD to the foot, so the joint apex protrudes backward. That is the correct avian ankle geometry and it is drawn, not missing. What genuinely fails is the LENGTH: legs run y~258 to y~322, i.e. 64px of a 223px standing height, or 29%. A flamingo needs legs at or above half the standing height. The judge's 'quarter-height stubs' is numerically close (29%) but must not be actioned as 'add a joint' - the joint exists; the segments need to be roughly doubled and the body raised, not re-articulated. The legs are yellow-ochre, not pink, which the packet also calls for.

ALSO: packet aspect is 0.55 (tall and narrow). The rendered creature measures 183 wide (excluding tail) or ~238 (including tail) against 223 tall, i.e. aspect 0.82-1.07 - the chassis is squat and wide, the opposite of the target proportion. This is the same generic plump-bird body used across the passerines, recolored pink.

BOTTOM LINE: with no neck, a straight cone bill, and legs under a third of body height, the silhouette reads as a pink songbird or a pink chicken plush. Strip the pink and nothing identifies it as a flamingo. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a grey-blue quail or a fat pigeon
rows.defect: Nothing that makes a great blue heron is present. There is no long neck, therefore no S-kink. The bill is a short yellow cone, not a heavy dagger. The legs are stubby yellow sticks planted under the belly with small flat feet — no stilt length, no long trailing toes. The blue-grey wash and a stray dark crest smear are the only nods to the reference, on a body that is proportioned like a gamebird.
rows.fix: Replace the chassis: deepen the body vertically rather than horizontally, fold a long neck back on itself into a tight S sitting above the shoulders, and lengthen the legs to at least body height with three long forward toes.
rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 PNG at 1x, then at 2x, and at 4-11x crops of head, neck, tail and both feet, plus a pixel scan of the yellow (bill+leg) mask. Bird bbox x77-361, y105-323 (285w x 219h).

MUST-READ 1, long neck kinked into an S - ABSENT, and this is the fatal one. The head ball (approx 49px diameter, x140-189, y105-153) sits directly on the shoulders. Between the base of the skull and the breast there is only a stubby grey column roughly 30px wide and 25px tall that immediately merges into a smooth convex shoulder. There is no S, no fold, not even a straight stork neck - there is effectively no neck segment at all. The dark grey band that curves down behind the head is shoulder/wing shading, not a neck edge. The packet note ('neck folds back in an S at rest; it is not held straight like a stork's') is not addressed in any form. Judge is correct here.

MUST-READ 2, heavy dagger bill - PRESENT BUT WRONG SHAPE, and the judge described it INCORRECTLY. It is NOT a 'short yellow cone'. The yellow bill occupies y127-138 and reaches from x84 to x146: about 62px of visible length against a 49px head, i.e. roughly 1.25x head length - a respectably LONG bill, and it is a straight-edged triangular wedge tapering to a fine needle point, not a cone. The real defect is DEPTH and MASS, not length: the bill is only 12px deep at its base (about 24% of head depth) and it is a thin isoceles sliver whose base does not fill the face. It reads as a tern/sandpiper spear, closer to the Egret row's 'thin spear bill' than to a heron's dagger. Fix is to thicken the base to roughly a third to a half of head depth, give it a slightly convex culmen and a defined gape line, and darken the upper mandible - not to lengthen it.

MUST-READ 3, stilt legs with long trailing toes - FAILS, but again not exactly as described. The legs are NOT unarticulated stubs: each leg has a correctly directed backward-bending ankle - upper segment runs down-and-BACK from the belly to a clear hock kink at about y280, lower segment runs down-and-FORWARD to the foot. That articulation is right and should be kept. The failure is pure length: yellow leg pixels run only y255 to y318, about 63px, which is 29% of the 219px standing height and only about 0.6x the body depth (belly y255 to back y150 is about 105px). A heron's exposed leg should be roughly 1.5-2x body depth; these need to be about triple their current length, which also means lifting the body off the ground plane. The feet are also mischaracterised as 'small': at 11x each foot is a single tapered horizontal slab about 30px long - a long forward bar (about 22px) plus a short rearward nub (about 6px) - so a hallux direction exists, but there are NO separate digits and nothing that trails. They read as a T-crossbar, not as three long forward toes plus a long hind toe.

SILHOUETTE VERDICT. Body is a fat rounded egg with a duck-like breast, a large nested oval wing on the flank, and a dark grey pointed tail wedge sweeping back and down past the rump with fine rectrix lines under it. Plumage is pale blue-grey with white scale/speckle stipple - the only heron-adjacent cue present. With no neck and 1/3-length legs the whole thing reads as a plump small wader or a grey-blue gamebird, not a great blue heron; the judge's 'quail' shorthand is fair in outcome. Two of three must-reads are absent and the third is present only in a wrong-family form, so FAIL stands. Priority of fix: neck first (a thick S-folded column, head pulled back over the shoulders), then leg length, then bill depth, then split the foot slab into toes.

rows.readsAs: a red robin or a scarlet toy bird
rows.defect: The bill is dead straight — a short yellow cone identical to the Egret's and the Heron's — when the smooth long downcurve IS the ibis. There is no bare facial skin; the red feathering runs uninterrupted to the bill base. The neck is absent rather than held out, and the legs are short stubs rather than long. Scarlet colour is the only signal left.
rows.fix: Give it a long bill that curves smoothly downward through about a quarter-circle, at least head-diameter-and-a-half in length, and clear the feathering off the face to a bare dark patch around the eye.
rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at Ibis.png at full size and again at 4x on the head and the legs, plus side-by-side with Egret.png and Spoonbill.png from the same batch. FAIL upheld: all three must-reads are absent.

(1) BILL — confirmed dead straight. At 4x the bill is a solid yellow-ochre triangular wedge with two perfectly straight edges converging to a sharp point, tilted very slightly UP-forward from the base. There is no curvature anywhere along either edge, not even a token droop at the tip. The ibis identity is a single long smooth downcurve (a shallow sickle, roughly 30-40 degrees of arc over the bill's length, tip clearly below the gape line); nothing here approaches it. Correcting the other judge on one detail: it is not literally identical to the Egret's — the Egret's spear is noticeably thinner/finer and springs from a small white head on a visible neck column, while the Ibis bill is a fatter, deeper-based wedge. But the SHAPE CLASS is the same straight spear, so the substance of the claim stands. Important counter-evidence for the fixer: the Spoonbill in this same batch DOES get a correctly modelled spatulate bill (a distinct swelling into a rounded paddle at the tip), which proves the renderer can carry a non-default bill profile. The Ibis has simply been left on the default straight-spear primitive; this is a missing bill-curve parameter, not an engine limitation.

(2) BARE FACIAL SKIN — confirmed absent. At 4x the entire head is one uniform red feathered dome with the same speckle texture as the body. There is no differentiated patch, no unfeathered lore, no colour or value break anywhere between the bill base and the eye. The eye is a small black bead with a white specular dot and a faint dark rim; that rim is a generic eye ring, not a bare-skin mask. Nothing in the head is even a candidate for the must-read.

(3) NECK — confirmed absent, and worse than 'not extended'. The head is fused directly onto the shoulder mass; there is no neck segment at all. Compare Egret.png in the same batch, which does render a short white neck column separating skull from torso. The Ibis reads as a headed ball, not a bird holding its neck out straight in flight-or-stride posture.

(4) LEGS — confirmed short. They are present and better drawn than the judge implies: at 4x there are two yellow legs with a clear rearward ankle bend and small forward toes plus a short hind toe. But length is wrong. The torso underside sits around y=248 and the feet at about y=310 in a 440px canvas, so total leg length is roughly 60px against a torso depth of about 100px — legs are only ~0.6 of body depth, and the feet stay inside the drop shadow. A long-legged wader needs leg length at or above torso depth. So 'short legs' is right, but the cause is proportion, not missing limb structure.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY READS AS: I would not say red robin — the long straight yellow spear is far too big for a robin. It reads as a plump red kiwi-or-generic-shorebird: a round speckled body, scroll-shaped folded wing, short pointed tail, no neck, stubby legs. Either way it does not read as an ibis.

SHARED-CHASSIS NOTE (relevant to the family question): Ibis and Spoonbill are the SAME body drawn twice — identical round torso outline, identical wing-scroll marking, identical pointed rear tail wedge, identical leg attachment point and identical head-on-shoulders skull placement. Only the hue (red vs pink) and the bill tip differ. Any fix for the Ibis should also lengthen the neck and legs on that shared chassis rather than patch the bill alone.

rows.readsAs: a spoonbill — but a fat pink quail-shaped one
rows.defect: The identity feature is genuinely here and legible: a long flat bill flaring into a rounded spatula at the tip, on correctly roseate pink plumage. Everything else is the family chassis. The long neck is missing entirely, the legs are short stubs rather than long wading legs, and there is no bare facial skin. The spoon is bolted to the same round-bodied gamebird as the other six.
rows.fix: Keep the bill and add the wader body under it — a long neck carried out and forward, and legs roughly body-height.

rows.readsAs: a white hen with a yellow beak
rows.defect: The bill is a short light cone, not a long heavy straight dagger — it is barely longer than the head is wide. There is no neck to hold straight, which makes the one feature meant to separate stork from heron unjudgeable. The legs are short and yellow rather than very long and red. It is the Egret asset with a slightly greyer wing.
rows.fix: Extend the bill to roughly two head-diameters and thicken it, run a straight neck of similar length forward from the shoulders, and lengthen the legs to at least body height in strong red.
rows.verifyWhy:
Verified by eye at full size, by 4x/5x crops of the head and feet, and by pixel measurement of the PNG (440x440, subject bbox x83-355 y111-317).

WHAT IS THERE: a plump egg-shaped white body with a dimpled/quilted feather texture, a grey wing swoosh sweeping to a grey point at x=355, a small white head sphere at top-left with a correct dark round eye + catchlight (eyes: normal, satisfied), a golden-yellow bill, two golden-yellow legs with a forward-bending joint and three forward toes plus a hind toe, and a cast shadow ellipse.

MUST-READ 1 - 'long heavy straight bill': PRESENT BUT UNDERSIZED, and the judge slightly understated the length while correctly naming the defect. Measured, the exposed bill is x89-150, y132-142: 62 px long by 11 px tall. The head is ~45 px wide (white span 144-188 at y=128). So the bill is ~1.4x head width, not 'barely longer than the head is wide' - but a stork's bill is roughly 2.5-3x head width and thick and near-parallel-sided along its whole run. What is drawn is a flat gold wedge 11 px at the base tapering to a needle point: it IS straight (that half of the must-read is met), but it carries no mass, so it does not read as a dagger. Critically it is the SAME bill primitive as its neighbours: Egret 58x11, Heron 63x12, Stork 62x11 - the three are interchangeable.

MUST-READ 2 - 'neck held straight rather than kinked': ABSENT, and the claim is right and if anything understated. There is no neck at all. The white width profile goes head 36 px (y=120), 45 px (y=128), then 87 px (y=132) and 114 px (y=140) - the head sphere fuses into the shoulder mass across four pixels. Since the extended straight neck is the ONE feature that separates stork from heron, and the packet note calls that out explicitly, its absence alone is disqualifying.

MUST-READ 3 - 'very long red legs': ABSENT on both counts. A colour sweep of the whole asset returns ZERO red pixels (red bbox null). The legs are golden yellow, bbox x190-248 y254-316: 63 px tall against a ~145 px body (head top y=111 to belly y=256), i.e. about 30% of standing height where a stork's legs are roughly as long as the body is deep. Confirmed.

CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM - 'It is the Egret asset with a greyer wing' is wrong in the most load-bearing way, and the fix must not be aimed at the wing tint. I opened Egret.png at the same path: the Egret HAS a distinct slender straight white neck column (~34 px wide running y=136 to ~y=190, plainly visible in a 4x crop) that the Stork does not have. Both also already carry a grey wing swoosh. So the truth is: Stork, Egret and Heron are ONE CHASSIS (identical 58-63x11 px gold cone bill, identical ~63 px gold legs, identical grey wing), and the Stork is the DEGRADED member of that set - it lost the neck the Egret already draws. The stork is not differentiated from the egret by a wing colour; it is currently a NECKLESS egret, which reads as a generic white gull/shorebird blob rather than any wetland bird.

FIX DIRECTION: (a) add a straight extended neck - a column roughly one head-height or more, held straight and slightly forward, explicitly NOT the heron S; (b) rebuild the bill as a heavy straight dagger ~2.5x head width, thick at the base with near-parallel edges to a blunt point, and give it its own value so it is not the shared egret cone; (c) lengthen the legs to about the depth of the body and recolour them red (currently the only red-legged bird in the family would be this one, so this is also the family's disambiguator); (d) the subject box is 273w x 207h (~0.76) against the required aspect 0.9 - the neck and leg work should bring that up rather than being applied on top of it.

rows.readsAs: a pink-grey pig, or a dachshund-shaped farm animal
rows.defect: Two of the three must-reads are absent. There is no enormous barrel body — the torso is a long shallow tube of constant depth with a straight belly line and a flat topline, so the animal reads long-and-low instead of massive-and-deep, and the legs are short tapering nubs with small dark trotter-like feet rather than pillar columns rising into visible shoulder and haunch mass. Worse, the ears/eyes/nostrils triad that IS the hippo is missing: the eye is a single large cartoon orb with a white sclera and dark pupil set on the SIDE of the head at mid-height (the packet calls for small eyes), there is no paired nostril bulge on top of the muzzle, and the only ear is an ambiguous notch at the back of the crown — nothing forms the signature horizontal line of ears, eyes and nostrils across the top of the skull. The muzzle block is squared and is the one credible hippo cue, but it is no wider than the skull behind it and the mouth is a thin closed line rather than a jaw that runs far back toward the ear. The head is also stacked above the topline on a visible neck step, where a hippo has effectively no neck. No tail.
rows.fix: Rebuild the torso as a deep barrel — roughly as deep as it is tall-plus-half, widest at the belly, with the topline dropping into a low sway behind a heavy shoulder — set the head DIRECTLY on the shoulders with no neck gap, and replace the side-mounted cartoon eye with the hippo triad: tiny bead eyes on raised bosses, small round ears just behind them, and two nostril bumps at the muzzle tip, all sitting on one horizontal line along the top of the skull.
rows.verifyWhy:
I read the PNG at 1x, then re-rendered it at 2x whole-frame plus 4x crops of the head, the underline/feet, and the rump. The FAIL stands: this reads as a hairless pig or a lop-eared hound, not a hippopotamus. Two of the three mustReads are absent and the third is only vestigial. CORRECTIONS to the original claim, several of which are wrong in detail:

(1) EYE — the judge said 'one large cartoon eye with white sclera'. There is no white sclera. The eye is a single large disc with a gold/amber iris ring, a black pupil, one small white specular dot, and a pale grey lid rim. The judge is right that it is far too large for the row's 'eyes: small', and right that it sits on the SIDE of the skull, but it is placed HIGH (upper third of the head, just under the crown plane), not 'at mid-height'. Regardless, it does not sit ON TOP of the head, so the triad fails here.

(2) NOSTRILS — the judge said there is 'no nostril bulge on the muzzle top'. The conclusion is right but the description is wrong: nostril geometry EXISTS and is misplaced. Two dark ovals sit paired at equal height on the CHEEK, behind and below the eye (roughly under the ear, over the jaw hinge) where they read as skin blemishes; and a separate small dark upward-curving arc sits on the upper-front of the muzzle where it reads as a single nose crease. Neither is a raised paired bulge on the muzzle top. The fix is to delete the cheek pair and replace the muzzle crease with two raised nostril domes on the dorsal muzzle plane.

(3) EARS — the judge said 'no ears form a line across the crown'. HORNS - CLAIM IS WRONG, MUST-READ IS PRESENT. The head faces right. The eye sits at source x~327. DEFECTS THE FAIL JUDGE MISSED. (a) The TAIL is inherited straight from the equid chassis in this packet: it is thick, roughly 40% of body length, arcs out and down well clear of the rump, and ends in a splayed six-strand fan tuft - a donkey/wild-ass tail. A rhino tail is short, thin, held close to the rump with a small flat tuft. This is the strongest single 'wrong family' signal in the asset. (b) The EYE contradicts the row spec 'eyes: small ... far back on the sides of the head': it is a large cartoon eye with golden iris, black pupil and white highlight, set well forward on the face right under the horns. The topline runs essentially level from withers to croup with the high point at the front of the back, and the rump rounds off at the same height or slightly lower before dropping near-vertically.
