rows.readsAs: a grey chinchilla or rabbit with a club stuck to its rump
rows.defect: All three must-reads fail. The tail is a thick smooth grey sausage with a lighter stripe down it, angled up and away to the left - it is not bushy, has no plume edge or hair separation, and does not arch over the back at all. The animal is not sitting on its haunches and holds nothing in its forepaws; it is the same running quadruped egg on two peg stubs as every other asset here. The eye is the same small white-dotted dot, not the large dark eye, and the ears are the family's tall pointed rabbit ears rather than rounded. Rendered at the family aspect, so the tail never makes it read taller than long as specified.
rows.fix: Sit it up on its haunches with forepaws at the chest holding a nut, and redraw the tail as a wide ragged-edged plume curving up and forward over the spine to head height.
rows.verifyWhy:
FAIL upheld. I rendered Squirrel.png at 4x and also strip-compared it against Mouse, Vole and Prairie_Dog from the same batch, plus a 6x side-by-side of the Squirrel and Mouse heads. All three must-reads from the reference row (aspect 0.9, eyes prominent, 'bushy plumed tail arched up over the back / sitting on the haunches holding food in the forepaws / large dark eye and rounded ears') miss.

CHASSIS — the root cause the judge named correctly. Squirrel, Mouse, Vole and Prairie Dog are ONE body with a swapped tail and a hue change. Shared verbatim: the same egg-shaped torso with the same pale rim-light arc over the shoulder, the same swirl/spiral crease on the hip, the same dome skull set low and forward on a non-existent neck, the same dark two-lobe hind foot thrown back, the same dark forelimb stub under the chest, the same 4-hair whisker fan, the same white two-tooth incisor block hanging below the muzzle, the same flat oval drop shadow with the body floating above it. Squirrel differs from Mouse ONLY by (a) grey instead of tan and (b) a thick tail instead of a thin one. The chassis reads as a leaping/running gerbil-rabbit. For most of this batch that chassis is merely generic; for the Squirrel it is fatal, because the squirrel's identity IS a different posture and a different silhouette.

TAIL — judge substantially right, with two corrections. It is a smooth-outlined tapering tube about 0.6x the head width and roughly a quarter of the body depth, with a pale rounded-lozenge specular highlight running down its length (that is the 'light stripe'). There is zero plume: no scalloped edge, no fur fringe, no hair strokes, no soft feathered outline — the contour is a clean vector curve, identical in treatment to a limb. CORRECTION 1: it is NOT 'angled up and away' as a straight sausage — it is genuinely curved, a candy-cane/question-mark hook that rises from the rump, sweeps up and rearward (leftward), and rounds over at the top with the tip curling back down toward the rump. CORRECTION 2: so an arch does exist, but it arches BEHIND the rump, entirely clear of the spine, with the tip pointing back down instead of forward over the shoulders. Nothing of the tail overlaps or crowns the back. Read as-is it is a chinchilla or jerboa tail, not a tree squirrel's. A fix needs the tail rooted higher on the rump, swept forward over the back so its mass sits above the shoulders, at least as wide as the torso is deep, with a plumed/scalloped silhouette edge and internal hair banding.

POSTURE — judge fully correct, no correction needed. The animal is horizontal, airborne over its drop shadow, one hind foot extended back in a run cycle, forelimb tucked as a dark stub. It is not sitting on its haunches, the spine is not vertical, the forepaws are not raised, and nothing is held. It is the identical gait pose as Mouse, Vole and Prairie Dog.

EYE AND EARS — judge right on the verdict, slightly off on the description. CORRECTION: the eye is not a bare dot; it is a small ringed eye — white sclera annulus, black pupil, single white specular highlight. But it is pixel-for-pixel the same eye primitive and the same diameter as the Mouse's, which the packet specs as merely 'normal', so the 'prominent' spec is simply not delivered: it measures roughly 13-15% of head width where a tree squirrel needs a large glossy dark orb nearer 25-30%, and the white ring reads as bird-like rather than dark and liquid. The ears are correctly called out: two upright narrow triangles with pink inner lining and pointed tips, essentially the Mouse's ears at slightly reduced height — a rabbit/mouse ear, not the low rounded disc of a tree squirrel.

ASPECT — additionally wrong and not mentioned by the judge. The reference wants 0.9 with the note 'the arched tail makes it read taller than long'. The rendered silhouette including the tail is roughly 1.5-1.6 wide-to-tall; it reads clearly longer than tall.

Nothing in the asset identifies a squirrel except a thickened tail on a shared rodent chassis. Three of three must-reads absent.

rows.readsAs: a taupe rabbit
rows.defect: The must-read that separates a vole from everything else - ears half-buried in fur - is absent and inverted: the asset carries the family's tall upright pointed pink-lined ears standing clear above the skull. No tail is visible at all, so the stubby short tail is not readable as a stubby tail so much as a missing one. The blunt rounded muzzle is the only must-read present, and it is the same blunt wedge every animal in the batch has. Strip the colour and this is the Mouse asset with the tail deleted.
rows.fix: Sink the ears to two small rounded nubs barely breaking the fur line of the skull, and add a short visible stub tail so the rump does not read as tailless.
rows.verifyWhy:
I rendered the PNG, then re-cropped and upscaled it 4x-10x (whole body, rump silhouette, head) and rendered Mouse.png and Water_Vole.png at matching crops for comparison. The FAIL stands, and the judge's most specific claim -- 'this is the Mouse asset with the tail deleted' -- is literally true, not rhetoric.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON THE CANVAS: a plump taupe ovoid body in left-facing quadruped pose. Head is a rounded dome joined to the body with almost no neck. Two TALL NARROW LEAF-SHAPED EARS rise fully clear of the skull dome, each roughly 40% of head height, dark outer rim with a pink/mauve inner surface visible along their entire length. Eye is a bold disc: white ring, dark pupil, white catchlight -- prominent, not small. Muzzle tapers forward from the dome to a small pointed snout carrying a projecting two-square cream incisor block and a fan of four long straight whiskers. Rear leg is a large circular haunch outlined by a white rim arc, with a dark elongated plantigrade hind foot flat on the ground; a small dark forefoot under the chest. Cast ellipse shadow beneath.

MUST-READ 1, 'stubby short tail' -- ABSENT, CONFIRMED. I scanned the rear silhouette at 10x. The rump is one clean unbroken ovoid arc from topline to belly with zero protrusion, not even a nub, not even a fur bump. The dark mass visible at the lower rump that could be mistaken for a tail is the hind leg crossing under the haunch (verified at 10x -- it terminates in the flat foot on the ground). The rump therefore reads TAILLESS, not stubby-tailed, exactly as claimed.

MUST-READ 2, 'ears half-buried in fur' -- ABSENT AND INVERTED, CONFIRMED. The ears do not merely fail to be buried; they are the tallest, highest-contrast feature on the head, standing entirely above the skull with the inner ear coloured in for their full length. This is the single loudest signal in the asset and it points away from vole.

MUST-READ 3, 'blunt rounded muzzle' -- NOT MET, and the judge did not mention this. The skull is round but the muzzle wedges forward to a point with an oversized protruding incisor block. It is pixel-for-pixel the same snout the packet assigns to Mouse as 'pointed twitching snout'. So the one must-read the judge implicitly conceded also fails.

SPEC DEVIATIONS THE JUDGE DID NOT NAME: (a) eyes are spec'd 'small'; the drawn eye is the identical prominent white-ringed disc used on Mouse, whose spec is 'normal'. (b) aspect is spec'd 2.2; the drawn body measures roughly 158x105 px, about 1.5 -- rounder and shorter than called for. Neither of these is the reason it fails, but both should be fixed in the same pass.

CHASSIS PROOF: side by side with Mouse.png the two share -- identical ovoid body outline, identical thigh circle with the same white rim arc in the same place, identical dark hind foot and forefoot shapes, identical head dome and neckless join, identical eye disc, identical two-square incisor block, identical four-whisker fan. The ONLY shape differences are that Mouse carries a long curved tail and Mouse's ears are marginally wider/rounder. Everything else is the same body at a slightly different hue. Water_Vole.png is the same chassis again in a browner hue, also completely tailless, with only marginally smaller ears -- so Vole and Water Vole are currently near-indistinguishable from each other as well.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM'S WORDING: 'reads as a taupe rabbit' is only half right. The rabbit read comes from the upright pointed ears plus the long plantigrade hind foot; but the protruding incisor block, the four-whisker fan and the haunch/foot construction are the shared rodent chassis, so it reads as a generic plump mouse-rabbit hybrid rather than a clean rabbit. That does not soften the verdict -- the organism drawn is not a vole.

FIX DIRECTION: shrink the ears to low rounded lobes sunk into the head fur so only the top arc clears the pelage; blunt the muzzle to a rounded rodent nose and shrink or delete the incisor block; shrink the eye to a small dark bead with no white ring; add a short furred tail nub of roughly one quarter body length off the rump; and lengthen the body toward the 2.2 aspect. Do this in a way that also separates Vole from Water Vole by more than hue.

rows.readsAs: a brown rabbit - indistinguishable from the Vole asset except for hue
rows.defect: Two of three must-reads are absent. The small ears almost buried in fur are instead the family's tall upright pointed ears clear of the skull, and the short furred tail about half the body length is nowhere on the image - the rump ends bare. The chubby blunt face is present only as the same generic blunt wedge shared by all seven. Side by side with the Vole asset the only difference is the brown, so the batch spends two slots on one drawing.
rows.fix: Add a distinctly furred tapering tail about half the body length trailing from the rump and shrink the ears to fur-buried nubs.
rows.verifyWhy:
FAIL upheld, and the two named defects are both real — I verified them at 8x magnification and with a pixel scan of the silhouette, not by glance. But the claim understates the damage: THREE of the three must-reads fail, not two.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON THE CANVAS (440x440; the animal's body bbox is x137-317, y153-252, so ~181x100px, aspect 1.81). A plump egg-shaped body carried low, a very large rounded haunch occupying the rear half with a crescent hock/thigh line rim-lit in white, two short dark stub feet under the belly, a fat rounded skull merging into the body with almost no neck, a long whisker fan of 4 straight dark lines, and a hard-edged white rectangular incisor block sitting OUTSIDE the muzzle contour. Warm mid-brown fur with a white rim light along the topline. The overall gestalt is a crouching rabbit.

1) EARS — claim CONFIRMED, and stronger than stated. At 8x there are two ears, both fully upright, both clearly proud of the skull, leaf/lance shaped with a pointed tip and a pink-mauve inner surface against a dark brown outer. Near ear stands ~26px tall on a ~45px-tall skull. There is nothing 'half-buried in fur' about them: they clear the head silhouette entirely and are the single loudest feature after the haunch. These are lagomorph ears. Must-read 'small ears almost buried in fur' is definitively absent.

2) TAIL — claim CONFIRMED, and I ruled out the usual escape hatches. There is NO tail: not short, not stubby, not tucked, not drawn dark-on-dark, not hidden behind the far haunch. I scanned the leftmost lit pixel of every row from y153 to y252; the rear edge runs 241 -> 189 -> 166 -> 149 -> 143 -> 139 -> 137 (minimum at y209-213) -> 142 -> 153 -> 168, a perfectly smooth convex arc with zero protrusion at any row. The white rim-light traces that arc unbroken. An 8x crop of x100-190,y180-270 shows clean background right up to the rump curve. The only dark shape near the rear is the hind foot/leg, which sits UNDER the belly at x~155-200, well inside the body outline, and is a foot not a tail. Must-read 'short furred tail about half the body length' is entirely missing — for a ~180px body that would be a ~90px appendage, i.e. the largest single missing feature on the asset.

3) MUZZLE — the judge did NOT mention this and should have. Must-read is 'blunt rounded muzzle with a chubby face'. The face does read chubby, but the muzzle tapers to a fairly narrow rounded point and the incisors are rendered as a detached white rectangle with two vertical dividers pasted on the OUTSIDE of the face contour, floating below the whisker root rather than emerging from under a lip. It reads as a cartoon buck-tooth decal, not a rodent's chisel incisors. Marginal at best; combined with the ears it pushes the head firmly toward rabbit.

Also note the packet asks for eyes: small. The eye is drawn large, with a bold white sclera ring around a black pupil and a highlight — it reads prominent, not small, which further removes the small-eyed vole cue.

4) 'INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM THE VOLE ASSET EXCEPT FOR HUE' — substantially correct, with one factual correction. I rendered Vole.png at the same crop. It is the identical chassis: same egg body, same oversized haunch with the same crescent hock line, same two upright pink-lined pointed ears, same detached white incisor block, same 4-line whisker fan, same two stub feet, same missing tail. The ONLY differences are hue (Vole is cool grey-taupe, Water Vole is warm brown) and a small proportion delta — Vole's body bbox is 184x114 (aspect 1.61) versus Water Vole's 181x100 (aspect 1.81), so Water Vole is very slightly shallower. That delta is invisible at a glance and is the wrong delta anyway: a water vole should read as the BIGGER, rattier, heavier-bodied animal of the pair. So the judge's 'except for hue' is off by a hair but right in substance.

FIX DIRECTION: this is not a polish-level correction. The head needs new ears — small, low, rounded, set well back and mostly sunk into the neck fur so only the top arc of each shows. The rump needs a tail added: a thick, furred, tapering tail ~half the body length (~90px at this scale), same fur colour as the body rather than a naked pink rat tail, trailing back and slightly down from the base of the haunch. The muzzle should be blunted and widened and the incisor block brought inside the face contour. The eye should shrink and lose the heavy white ring. And Water Vole must be given a distinct chassis from Vole — heavier, longer, less lagomorph — or the pair remains one drawing in two colours.

rows.readsAs: a small olive-green agave or aloe rosette — a spiky succulent, not a vegetable
rows.defect: Every must-read is absent. There is NO root: nothing red, nothing round, nothing half out of the soil — the image is a leaf fan and a faint ground shadow, full stop. There are no crimson stalks and no crimson veins; the veins are drawn in a darker olive of the same hue as the blade, and no stalk is visible anywhere because the blades spring straight from a hidden hub. The blades are narrow pointed lanceolate spears with straight edges, the opposite of broad glossy heart-shaped wavy-puckered beet leaves, and the whole rosette is flat and outspread rather than upright on long petioles. Colour is a uniform pale yellow-olive with no maroon flush at all.
rows.fix: Draw the organism the reference describes: seat a round-to-top-shaped deep purple-red root half out of the soil with a slender tail below it, and rebuild the foliage as broad heart-shaped puckered blades on long visible crimson petioles with crimson veins running into a dark green maroon-flushed blade.
rows.verifyWhy: FAIL upheld, and confirmed by pixel measurement as well as by eye. WHAT IS ON THE CANVAS: a single wide low fan/rosette of roughly 13-15 blades radiating from one convergence point at about (220,290) in the 440x440 frame. Organism bounding box is x 94-344, y 146-292 — i.e. 250px wide by 146px tall, a landscape fan of aspect ~1.7 where the reference row asks for 0.9. Below y=292 the canvas is pure background except one very faint darker ellipse at y~293-300 (RGB 5,8,11 against a 8,13,19 field) which is a soft cast ground-shadow, not a body. There is no root, no tuber, no shoulder, no tail, nothing sitting in or half out of soil anywhere in the frame. COLOUR, MEASURED: I decoded the PNG and counted pixels with r>g+18 — the count is ZERO across all 193,600 pixels. There is not one reddish, maroon, crimson or purple pixel in the image. Every organism pixel is yellow-olive: base of the rosette ~ (46,57,32) to (69,83,45), mid-blade ~ (100,117,67) to (110,127,75), i.e. green channel always leads red by ~15-17 and blue trails by ~35-50. So the judge's core claim is exactly right: all three mustReads are absent. CORRECTIONS AND REFINEMENTS TO THEIR WORDING: (1) 'same-hue veins' is slightly off — each blade does carry a visible midrib plus a herringbone of 5-8 lateral veins, drawn as thin lines a shade DARKER than the blade, so venation exists and is legible; it is the crimson colour and the puckered/quilted relief between veins that are missing, not the veins themselves. (2) 'flat pale olive' undersells a real vertical gradient: the blades are notably darker and browner where they converge at the base and lighten toward mid-blade before dimming again near the tips, so there is form-shading — but it is matte and diffuse, with no specular highlight, so 'glossy' still fails. (3) 'narrow pointed lanceolate spears' is right about the tips but not uniformly about the width — the lower outer blades are fairly broad, closer to a lotus/water-lily pad petal, while the upper central ones are the narrow spears; what unifies them and kills the read is that EVERY blade terminates in a sharp acute point and has straight-to-slightly-convex margins, where a beet leaf is a broad blunt-tipped, wavy-margined heart/oval. (4) One thing the judge did not mention that reinforces the verdict: there are no petioles at all, crimson or otherwise — the blades are sessile, attached directly at the single convergence point with no visible stalk length, so the 'upright rosette on long stalks' structure is absent as well as its colour. IDENTITY READ: the silhouette reads as an agave/aloe/yucca succulent rosette, or at a glance a lotus fan; nothing in it says root vegetable, let alone beet. Family note: this shares the earth-flora radial-rosette chassis with Carrot's brief, so the fix must differentiate more than colour. TO FIX: draw the tuber — a round-to-top-shaped deep purple-red root ~ (110,25,45) sitting half above a soil line with a slender tapering tail below it, occupying the lower third the fan currently leaves empty; replace the pointed blades with broad blunt heart/oval blades with wavy undulating margins and quilted puckering between veins; recolour blades to very dark green flushed maroon; and add long vivid crimson petioles from the crown to each blade with crimson midribs continuing into the lamina. Also correct the aspect from the current ~1.7 wide to the specified 0.9 upright.

rows.readsAs: a carrot — the tapering root plus green top gets there, though the root looks like a wafer ice-cream cone
rows.defect: The taproot is pale tan-gold, not orange — it is desaturated to about the colour of raw pastry, and its sides are dead-straight with a hard flat cut across the top, so it reads as a cone rather than a shouldered root. There is no green shoulder where root meets leaves; the junction is a hard horizontal edge with a visible gap of dark background above it. The fine side hairs are three rigid straight sticks, all on the left side only, projecting downward like snapped twigs rather than fine rootlets around the whole root. The carrot-top is not feathery: it is an open wireframe lattice of small stroked crosses arranged on a regular diagonal grid, reading as chain-link fencing or a snowflake mesh instead of finely divided thread-like segments, and no grooved stalks connect it to the root.
rows.fix: Warm the root to true carrot orange, taper it with a slightly convex shoulder that greens where the petioles emerge, and replace the cross-hatch lattice top with soft filled feathery frond silhouettes on visible stalks.

rows.readsAs: a dark cartoon otter pup or spotted newt toy, nearly invisible against the background
rows.defect: The identity IS uniform glossy jet-black skin, and the body is painted with a scatter of ochre-yellow spots - the exact marking of a fire salamander, so it reads as the wrong species. Nothing is glossy: the skin is flat matte with no wet highlight, and the near-black value on a near-black field makes the tail and hind legs merge completely into the backdrop. The tail is a flat dark wedge lifted off the ground, not a rounded tail. The head is the family's big-eyed smiling bulb, not a blunt amphibian skull, and it is the same drawing as the generic Salamander asset in this same batch with the paint darkened.
rows.fix: Delete every spot and repaint the body a single unbroken jet-black raised off the background value, then add a hard specular sheen strip along the spine and skull to sell the glossy wet skin.
rows.verifyWhy:
FAIL UPHELD, and the core charge is confirmed by direct pixel measurement plus a side-by-side with the family's generic entry. I decoded the PNG and re-rendered it at gamma 2.6 and at 3.2x gain so the near-black shapes could actually be inspected.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. Right-facing sprawl-posture amphibian: one ovoid torso, a separate ovoid head butted onto the front with a visible overlap seam, a thick up-sweeping tail roughly torso-length with a blunt rounded tip, and four limbs. Scattered across the dorsum, both flanks, the cheek and the throat are roughly a dozen warm ochre-yellow blobs measuring (36,34,26)-(39,36,28). A flat mid-grey capsule (49,49,53) sits along the topline. A 2-3px hard rim stroke peaking at (100,106,116) traces the topline and the head. The eye is a small white annulus with a dark hole; its ring at (356,194) is (243,240,232), the single brightest pixel in the asset.

1. WRONG-SPECIES MARKING - CONFIRMED, and it is the defect that sinks the asset. Salamandra atra's whole identity is uniform, unmarked, glossy jet black. The packet mustRead says 'glossy jet-black moist skin'. What is painted is a broad ochre-yellow spot scatter, i.e. Salamandra salamandra. This is not a subtle miss: the spots are the ONLY high-contrast feature on the body, so the asset reads first and loudest as a fire salamander. It also collides inside its own family - packet entry 4 ('Salamander') carries the note 'generic representative: a fire/spotted salamander', so the Alpine is wearing the generic's diagnostic marking and the two are not tellable apart by pattern.

2. 'IT IS THE GENERIC SALAMANDER WITH THE PAINT DARKENED' - CONFIRMED, and stronger than the judge stated. I rendered Salamander.png beside it. The two share: the same ovoid torso, the same thick up-sweeping tail at the same curve, the same flat grey dorsal capsule in the same position, the same white rim stroke, the same white-ring eye, the same spot scatter, and the same limbs. The only difference is the base hue - warm brown vs near-black. Packet aspect targets differ (3.5 generic vs 4.5 Alpine) and the silhouettes do not visibly honour that difference. One chassis, two paint jobs.

3. 'FLAT MATTE WITH NO WET SHEEN' - RIGHT VERDICT, WRONG DESCRIPTION. Correct this before fixing. There ARE two highlight elements, so 'no sheen' is inaccurate: the rim stroke and the dorsal capsule. The real defect is that both are FLAT hard-edged shapes and the skin itself has zero modulation. Scanning down x=240 the dorsal capsule holds (49,49,53) constant for seven straight rows then hard-cuts to (9,10,14) - no gradient, no falloff, no soft terminator anywhere. The torso fill is (9,10,13) essentially everywhere. So the gloss is faked with a grey bar and an outline rather than painted; nothing on the surface reads as moist. Two further edge defects the judge missed: the rim stroke crosses itself at the neck where the head oval meets the torso oval and leaves a short orphan segment floating clear of the silhouette, and the head/torso seam is visible rather than blended.

4. 'TAIL AND HIND LEGS VANISH INTO THE BACKDROP' - RIGHT PHENOMENON, WRONG SCOPE AND WRONG PARTS. The whole animal vanishes, not the tail and hind legs specifically. Body, head and tail all sit at (9,10,13) against a backdrop of (7,11,17) to (8,12,18) - a WCAG contrast ratio of about 1.02:1, i.e. below any visibility threshold. A horizontal scan at y=200 from x=70 to x=180 returns an unbroken (8,9,12) with the backdrop reading (8,12,18): the tail is separated from the field ONLY by a ~6-unit blue-channel hue shift, no luminance step at all. The legs are (3,3,4)/(4,4,4), which is DARKER than the background, so they in fact separate marginally better (about 1.05:1) than the torso does - the judge had that backwards. In the unmodified PNG the only things that read are the ochre spots (~1.20:1), the eye ring and the rim stroke, which is why the asset presents as a scatter of dim yellow dots floating in the dark.

5. NEW DEFECT THE JUDGE DID NOT NAME - THE LIMBS ARE NOT AMPHIBIAN. At 6x each limb is a two-segment tapered rod with a distinct knee joint (marked by a small teal joint pip) terminating in a blunt wedge/hoof. There are NO TOES on any of the four feet, and the limbs are held vertically UNDER the body (parasagittal), lifting the belly well clear of the ground. The packet demands 'short sprawling legs' and posture: sprawling; an amphibian limb is held out sideways with elbow/knee out and four to five soft splayed digits. What is drawn is the ungulate/pony limb - precisely the shared-chassis defect the family card header warns about, and the generic Salamander carries the identical limb.

6. MUST-READS SCORED. 'Glossy jet-black moist skin' - FAILED twice over (spotted, and flat-shaded). 'Blunt rounded head with bulging eyes' - HALF PRESENT: the head genuinely is a large blunt rounded ovoid and that half should be credited, but the eye is a small flat annulus lying on the skull surface, not breaking the silhouette, so it does not read as bulging despite the packet's eyes: prominent. 'Short sprawling legs and a rounded tail' - the tail is rounded and roughly body-length and is fine (if over-thick at the base and swept up like an otter's); the legs fail as described in 5.

FIX ORDER: delete the spot scatter entirely and give it an unbroken black; replace the flat grey capsule with a graded specular that runs along the spine and wraps the head, and add a second wet highlight over the flank so the black reads as lacquered; lift the base value so the silhouette clears the backdrop by a real luminance step rather than a hue shift; rebuild the limbs as short sprawling toed limbs with the elbows out; close the neck seam and the orphaned rim stroke.

rows.readsAs: a cream-coloured cartoon otter or ghost newt plushie with a big open eye
rows.defect: Both defining must-reads fail. There are NO blood-red feathery external gills anywhere on the neck - the single feature that makes this animal recognisable is simply absent. And a large open eye with white sclera, black pupil and a specular highlight is drawn on the head, which the reference explicitly forbids ('eyes are absent or buried under skin - never draw open eyes'). The head is a rounded egg bulb rather than broad and flat. The legs are dark olive-brown pigmented stubs, not spindly unpigmented toothpicks, and the supposedly unpigmented chalk-white body carries the same ochre spot scatter as the other three assets. A grey duplicate blob of the tail is stranded behind the real tail as a stray layer.
rows.fix: Remove the eye entirely (leave a faint skin-covered depression) and attach three branching blood-red feathery gill plumes behind the jaw on each side.
rows.verifyWhy:
Verified at 5x-10x crops of the head, neck, limbs and tail, plus a whole-image pixel scan. FAIL is upheld, but three of the four stated causes are described wrongly and would send a fixer at the wrong things.

GILLS - CLAIM CONFIRMED, AND HARDER THAN CLAIMED. The first and most identifying mustRead ('blood-red feathery external gills') is not merely hard to see, it does not exist anywhere on the canvas. A scan of all 440x440 px for any pixel with r>90 and r-g>35 and r-b>35 returns ZERO hits. There is no red, crimson, pink-red or maroon anywhere in the file. The head-to-trunk junction (crop x290-380, y165-245 at 10x) is a plain smooth taper of pale skin with nothing attached above, behind or below it - no plumes, no stalks, no nubs, not even a colourless suggestion of them. This alone is fatal: without gills the animal is a generic pale amphibian, and the olm/Texas-blind-salamander identity is carried almost entirely by that scarlet triple plume behind the jaw.

EYE - REAL DEFECT, WRONGLY DESCRIBED. There IS an open eye and the note forbids it ('Eyes are absent or buried under skin - never draw open eyes'; eyes: hidden). But it is NOT 'a large open eye with white sclera, pupil and specular highlight'. At 10x it is a SMALL solid black bead roughly 5-6 px across on a 440 px canvas, with a single 1-px white catchlight at its upper-left. No sclera is drawn at all - the white surrounding it is simply the head's own unpigmented skin. The fix is deleting one small dot and its catchlight (or replacing it with a faint sub-dermal shadow), not removing a big cartoon eyeball. The judge also missed a second face defect on the same head: a drawn smiling mouth line, a long grey upcurved arc across the lower face, which pushes the read further toward cartoon character than cave animal.

LEGS - HALF WRONG. They are not 'stubs'. Each limb is a comparatively long, thin, tapered rod sprawling well clear of the body; front and hind limbs on each side read as a scissored pair of straight sticks. In proportion they are arguably already 'spindly toothpick legs'. The actual defect is colour and finish: every limb is filled opaque dark olive/khaki-brown, in violent contrast against the chalk-white trunk, which is exactly backwards for an unpigmented cave animal whose limbs should be the same translucent white/pink as the body. Secondary: no toes are drawn - each limb tapers to a blunt point with no foot, no digits.

YELLOW SPOTS - CONFIRMED. Pale ochre-yellow blobby spots run the whole length of the trunk and onto the flank, the same shared spot motif carried by the rest of the set. Directly contradicts 'chalk-white unpigmented skin'; on this species the skin should be flat translucent white with at most a faint pink blush of subdermal blood, no markings whatsoever.

GREY SHAPE BEHIND THE TAIL - REAL, BUT NOT A TAIL DUPLICATE. There is a flat mid-grey mass sitting across the tail, occupying roughly x73-220 / y172-241, formed of two overlapping lobes - a large ellipse projecting ABOVE the tail line and a rounded lobe projecting BELOW it. It is not a copy of the tail's shape or contour; it crosses the tail rather than trailing it, and unlike the body it carries no gradient, no rim light and no painterly shading at all, just a hard uniform grey fill with an aliased edge. It reads as either a stray silhouette/shadow layer left in world space instead of ground space, or a botched attempt at a tail fin. Whatever its origin it breaks the silhouette and must go (or be redrawn as a proper shaded tail fin, which this species actually should have).

UNMENTIONED ADDITIONAL DEFECTS: the tail terminates in an abrupt flat rounded cap with no taper and no fin, so the animal reads as truncated; and the head is a fat bulbous egg (widest through the middle, ballooning above the neck line) rather than the broad FLAT spatulate skull the note asks for - it is not pointed, so that half of the note is satisfied, but 'flat' is not.

NET: one of three mustReads (spindly limb proportion) is arguably met; the defining one (red feathery gills) is provably absent; the second (chalk-white unpigmented skin) is broken by both the ochre spots and the dark limbs; and an explicit never-do (open eye) is violated. Composite read is a pale cartoon newt with a smiley face, not a blind cave salamander. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a brown cartoon otter cub or river-mammal mascot

The flanks are smooth and spotted with no wrinkled fleshy skin folds at all, which is the texture the whole animal is known for. rows.verifyWhy: Looked at the 440px master and at 6x-7x crops of the head, flank and feet, and side-by-side against Salamander.png and Alpine_Salamander.png. The FAIL stands: none of the three must-reads is present. (1) SHOVEL HEAD - absent. The head is a blunt domed egg, ~71px long x ~60px deep (1.2:1), with an ARCHED crown that sits noticeably taller than the neck junction and a snout that rounds off short. A hellbender/giant-salamander skull in profile is a shallow flattened wedge (~3:1 length to depth) with a straight low top line, a squared-off overhanging upper jaw wider than the neck, and a gape that runs nearly the full length of the head. Here the mouth is a short shallow arc confined to the lower FRONT third of the head, curling up at the posterior end into a plain smile. Correction to the other judge: the skull is not 'narrow' - it is a fairly wide, blunt, unpointed egg. The failure is that it is DOMED and SHORT-GAPED, not that it is narrow; a fix that only widens it will still miss. (2) WRINKLED FLESHY FLANK FOLDS - absent, exactly as claimed. At 7x the flank is a single smooth ovoid: one continuous unbroken silhouette arc carrying a thin white rim light along the topline, filled with soft airbrushed ochre-yellow spot blobs and one pale dorsal highlight band running nose-to-hip. There is zero fold geometry - no lateral skin frill, no crenellated or scalloped ventro-lateral edge, no cross-hatched wrinkle lines, no shadow breaks that could be read as folds even generously. This is the single most damaging miss: the lateral skin frill IS the giant salamander's silhouette. (3) TINY LIDLESS DOT EYES - inverted. The eye is a white annulus roughly 14px across on a 71px head (~20% of head length) containing a dark pupil and a white specular highlight - i.e. a visible white sclera ring, a cartoon eye. Correction: 'enormous' overstates it; it is medium-prominent, not oversized, and it is pixel-for-pixel the SAME eye token the other three family members wear at their own scales. But it is categorically the wrong eye - a giant salamander eye is a lidless black pinprick with no sclera at all, and the packet spec for this row literally says eyes: small. (4) 'Generic Salamander asset in a lighter brown' - substantively right, and I confirmed the shared chassis directly. Giant, generic Salamander and Alpine Salamander are one body: same domed head ovoid, same white-ring eye and smile arc, same scatter of ochre spots (Alpine carries them too, though Alpine is spec'd jet-black unspotted), same pale dorsal band, same up-swept blunt-tipped tail, same two visible dark-olive tapering leg stubs with no toes drawn, same ground-shadow ellipse. Precise correction for whoever fixes this: it is NOT a flat recolor - Giant is drawn at a larger frame scale with a fatter barrel and a longer, higher-sweeping tail than the generic, so the chassis does take size/aspect parameters. What it does not take is any per-species HEAD, SKIN or EYE geometry, which is why all three of this row's must-reads land on nothing. Also noted: the limbs read as two mammal-angled stubs rather than four sprawling elbows-out limbs, and the toes are cut off into a dark blob, so the 'sprawling' posture token is only weakly served.

rows.readsAs: a spotted amphibian-ish cartoon critter, though a stranger might first say otter or axolotl toy

rows.readsAs: a generic orange-red fish; indistinguishable from this batch's Salmon and Trout except for hue
rows.defect: The single defining field mark is INVERTED. The reference says pale spots on a dark ground, explicitly '(not dark on pale)'; the render is dark grey-brown blotches scattered over a LIGHTER salmon-orange flank — exactly the polarity the row warns against. The white leading edges on the lower fins are also absent: the pelvic/anal lobe and the caudal are flat translucent maroon with no light edge anywhere. And the body is not slender — it is the family's deep symmetric lens, as deep as the Whitefish.
rows.fix: Darken the ground to a deep olive-slate and repaint the blotches as discrete pale cream/pink dots with a thin red halo, then run a 2px pure-white stripe along the leading ray of the pelvic, anal and lower caudal lobe.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD after reading the PNG at 1x, then cropping and nearest-neighbour upscaling the body (4x), the ventral fin (14x), the head (11x) and the tail (12x), plus a pixel-luminance sample of the flank of all five batch members. All three mustReads fail, and the first one fails in exactly the way the row warns against.

(1) PALE SPOTS ON A DARK GROUND — INVERTED, the judge is correct. The flank is a mid-light salmon-orange (median rgb(159,78,60), L=100 on the 5th-95th percentile band L67-L127). The markings are the DARK tail of that distribution: soft grey-brown smudges around rgb(100,56,41) sitting on the lighter ground — roughly eight diffuse blotches, largest along the belly and behind the pectoral, plus one on the cheek. There is no pale spot anywhere on the body. A real char (Salvelinus) is the inverse: cream/pink/white spots scattered on a dark olive-green flank, which is why the row spells out 'not dark on pale'. What is drawn is the anti-mark.

(2) WHITE LEADING EDGES ON LOWER FINS — ABSENT, the judge is correct, but the reason needs stating precisely so the fix is not mis-aimed. There IS a pale line near the lower fins and it is easy to mistake for the field mark: a 1-2px light grey-pink rim runs the entire silhouette — along the belly, up over the snout, along the dorsal, all the way to the tail joint. It is a whole-body rim light, not a fin marking; it passes over the fin roots without changing, and it is present in identical form on the Salmon and Trout renders which have no such mark in their rows. The lower fins themselves — a single low dark-maroon crescent under the belly (pelvic/anal read as one lobe) and a radiating pectoral fan behind the gill arc — are solid dark maroon edge to edge with zero white on any anterior margin.

(3) SLENDER STREAMLINED BODY — not met, but the judge's wording is wrong here and should be corrected. The body is the family's symmetric double-pointed lens/almond, deepest at midspan and tapering to needle points at both ends, so 'lens' is right. But 'the family's DEEP lens' is factually backwards: measured silhouette bboxes give Char 232x80 = 2.90, the SLENDEREST of the five (Trout 2.82, Salmon 2.64, Whitefish 2.57, Grayling 2.32). Char is not deeper than its siblings; it is simply short of its own spec aspect of 3.8, and the lens profile reads as a leaf rather than a streamlined fish regardless of ratio.

SHARED-CHASSIS FINDING (the batch question, and the real root cause): Char, Salmon and Trout are one drawing recoloured. Identical in all three: the pointed-both-ends lens body; a knife-point snout with NO mouth or jaw line drawn at all; a white ring eye placed so high it overhangs the dorsal outline; the same single arc gill line; the same low dorsal hump behind the topline; the same radiating pectoral fan at the same station; the same lateral-line stripe; the same thread-thin caudal joint into a bowtie tail with a concave trailing edge; the same all-round rim light. Correct the judge on one detail: 'just redder' describes Char against the olive Trout, but Char and SALMON are the near-duplicate pair — both are orange, Char merely darker and more saturated (159,78,60 vs 184,110,87). The blotch field is the same generator on all three.

No mitigating feature found on a close look: no pale spot rendered small or dim, no white fin margin drawn anywhere the first judge did not look, no mouth, no adipose fin. FAIL stands.

FIX ORDER: invert the spot pass (pale cream/pink spots, ground darkened to olive-green) before anything else — that alone is the species; then paint a white anterior stripe on the pelvic and anal fin margins that is distinguishable from the global rim light; then break the lens chassis so the head end is blunter than the tail end and add an actual mouth.

rows.readsAs: a generic silver-blue fish; a Whitefish in a cooler tint
rows.defect: The tall spotted sail dorsal that IS the grayling is not there. What is drawn is the same translucent dark rounded lobe every other fish in this batch carries — measured against the Whitefish beside it, it is a few pixels taller and otherwise the identical shape — with no spot rows, no banner-like square trailing edge, and no visible attachment to the topline, so it reads as a shadow behind the back rather than a fin. The 'small mouth' must-read cannot be judged because there is no mouth at all, only the family's needle point. No adipose fin between the dorsal and the peduncle.
rows.fix: Replace the shared dorsal lobe with a purpose-drawn sail: base running from 35% to 60% of body length, height at least 1.2x body depth, square-cut trailing edge, and 3-4 rows of dark red-violet spots between the rays — drawn ON the topline, not behind the body.
rows.verifyWhy:
FAIL upheld, but two of the three stated causes are factually wrong and must not be fixed as described.

WHAT I MEASURED (440x440 render, fish faces RIGHT, head at high x). Body silhouette spans x=138..336 (198px long), depth ~52-57px at midbody. A dorsal fin IS drawn and it is NOT the batch's generic lobe. Column-scanning luminance above the body topline: the fin apex sits at y=157 against a topline of y=180 -> 23px of fin above the back at x=244, and it holds >=18px from x=230 to x=284. Its base runs x=200..305, i.e. ~105px = ~53% of body length. Compare the same measurement on the batch mates: Whitefish 13px tall / 56px base (32% of body), Salmon 14px / 86px. So the Grayling's dorsal is 77% TALLER and 2.2x LONGER-BASED than the Whitefish's. The claim 'measurably the same shape as the Whitefish's, only a few pixels taller' is WRONG -- side-by-side crops of the identical region (x120-350,y140-260) show the Grayling lobe reaching visibly further forward and higher. Do not 'add a dorsal'; one exists and is already the largest in the family.

Also WRONG: 'no attachment to the topline, so it reads as a shadow behind the back.' A vertical colour scan at the apex (x=257) runs fin RGB 55,59,77 at y=176-178 -> rim 71,76,94 at y=180 -> body 122,129,151 at y=182. There is NO background gap anywhere along the base; the fin meets the topline contiguously for its whole 105px run, and it carries ~7 evenly spaced darker ray striations (luminance dipping 60 -> 50-56 every ~14px at y=170). It reads dark, not detached.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG, and why it still fails:
1. The dorsal is a smooth symmetric DOME that tapers to zero at both ends -- not the grayling's square-cut banner with a straight, near-vertical trailing edge and a top margin that stays high to the rear. Height profile from x=200: 4,8,11,14,16,18,21,22,22,23,23,21,21,19,17,13,9,6,1,1,1 -- a perfect arch. That part of the judge's claim (no square banner trailing edge) is correct.
2. NO SPOTS ON THE FIN. Horizontal scans across the fin interior at y=162/166/170/174 return a flat wash: luminance 60 everywhere with only the ray dips. Zero bright dots, zero spot rows, no colour banding. The must-read word is 'spotted' and the spotting is entirely absent -- the body carries the pale scale-dot mesh instead, and the fin got none of it.
3. Height is only ~42% of body depth (23/55). A grayling sail is ~0.8-1.1x body depth. It is a big dorsal, not a sail.
4. The fin's LEADING edge runs forward to x=305, which is on top of the gill arc (x~300) and only 13px behind the eye (x=318). Anatomically the dorsal is sitting on the nape/skull, not on the mid-back.
5. NO MOUTH -- confirmed, the judge is right. At 18x the snout is a needle-sharp spearhead wedge that tapers to a single point with no jaw split, no lip line, no maxilla, no aperture of any kind. There is no small mouth because there is no mouth. The head is also not trout-shaped: it is the same pointed lens-tip the whole batch shares.
6. NO ADIPOSE FIN -- confirmed. I profiled the topline across the whole dorsal-to-tail gap (x=140..198, step 2): the >30-luminance edge and the >110-luminance body edge differ by 1-2px everywhere (pure antialias). The curve is a clean unbroken arc. Nothing sits on it.
7. Forked tail IS present and good: deeply forked, two pointed lobes, clear notch -- the one must-read fully satisfied.

FAMILY CHASSIS: matched crops of Grayling vs Whitefish are the same drawing. Identical body outline, identical diamond scale-mesh, identical triangular pectoral fan in the same place, identical gill arc, identical belly shadow blob, identical eye-ring placement and identical pointed snout. Body toplines across the batch peak within 8px of one another (Grayling 178, Whitefish 174, Trout 173, Salmon 171). Only hue and dorsal scale change. The faint vertical dark streaks in the black above the fish appear in BOTH images -- they are a background vignette pattern, not fin rays; do not mistake them for dorsal structure.

VERDICT: FAIL stands. The organism reads as a generic silvery lens-shaped fish with an enlarged grey dorsal dome. Fix list: give the dorsal a square banner trailing edge and raise it to ~0.9x body depth, move its leading edge back off the gill to start at ~x=270, paint 3-4 rows of pale/dark spots across the membrane, cut an adipose fin into the topline at ~x=175, and give the chassis an actual mouth (a short terminal slit under the snout tip).

rows.readsAs: a pink-orange trout-ish fish — the salmonid family is legible, the species is not

rows.readsAs: a brown trout-ish fish — the olive-gold ground and dark speckling carry it further than the rest of the batch

rows.readsAs: a pale silvery lake fish — believable as a generic silverside or shad, not specifically a whitefish

rows.readsAs: a juvenile barracuda or a needlefish - a slim silver predator with a spear snout
rows.defect: The identity feature is completely absent: there is no mouth on this animal at all. The snout is a needle-fine knife point that tapers to nothing, instead of the blunt pig-snout overhanging a cavernous gape whose corner runs back past the eye. The eye is a tiny white ring at the very tip, not the huge forward-set eye called for, and there is no bright silver lateral stripe anywhere - the flank is uniform pale scale texture with only a soft shading gradient down the midline. What is left is the generic lens body plus a spear nose, which reads as a barracuda.
rows.fix: Rebuild the head: give it a short blunt translucent snout that overhangs a wide open gape whose corner terminates BEHIND the eye, triple the eye diameter to roughly a third of head depth, and lay a hard-edged bright silver band the full length of the mid-flank.
rows.verifyWhy:
Verified by decoding the PNG and re-rendering the head at 12x and 20x, plus per-column luminance probes. Subject bbox is x109-331, y178-222 (length 222px, max depth ~34px, aspect ~5.0 vs spec 5.5 - proportion is fine). A gill/operculum arc is drawn at x~281, so headFrac ~0.22 against the spec's 0.25 - also acceptable. The failure is entirely in the identity features.

MUST-READ 1, 'pointed snout overhanging a huge underslung mouth reaching past the eye': ABSENT, and the judge is correct. Forward of the operculum arc the head is a single smooth featureless wedge. There is no mouth line, no jaw split, no maxilla, no gape, not even a faint slit - I probed every column from x=296 to x=331 at 1px vertical resolution and the only sub-body-luminance features are the continuation of the dorsal shading and the midline dark line (dip to ~171-188 against ~200-215 either side), both of which run the full body length and are shading, not a jaw. The snout tapers to a needle: body depth is 11px at x=315, 8px at x=320, 4px at x=325 and 3px at x=330, terminating in a spear point. That is exactly wrong for an anchovy, whose profile is a blunt overhanging pig-snout with the jaw hinge BEHIND the eye and a gape that swings down like a scoop.

MUST-READ 2, 'bright silver lateral stripe': the judge's verdict is right but the description is imprecise, and the imprecision matters for the fix. The body is not unsilvered - it is pale silver-white overall with a specular sheen and a visible diamond scale mesh. What is wrong is that the identity mark is INVERTED: the only longitudinal linear mark on the flank is a DARK line running the midline (measured at x=200: y=200 luminance 208, y=202-204 drops to 163-169, y=206-210 back to 211-222), with a second dark ridge along the dorsal edge. So where the anchovy's defining bright silver band should be there is a dark lateral line instead, and the brightest zone is the belly, i.e. ordinary countershading. Do not tell the fixer 'no silver' - tell them 'the flank band is drawn dark; it must be a brighter-than-flank silver band, and it must sit above the midline against a darker blue-green back'.

MUST-READ 3, 'large eye set far forward': the judge is PARTLY WRONG here. The eye IS set far forward - it sits about 10px from the snout tip, right at the front of the head, which satisfies 'forward'. Its outer diameter is ~11px, roughly a third of maximum body depth, so it is not literally 'tiny' in absolute terms. The real defects are (a) it is rendered as a thin bright metallic annulus with a small dark pupil - it reads as a machined eyelet or bolt, not as an eye - and (b) it is drawn HALF OUTSIDE the silhouette: at x=320 the head mass occupies y199-206 while the eye ring occupies roughly y188-199, so the top two-thirds of the ring protrudes above the dorsal contour of the head into empty background. That silhouette break is the more damaging error and no one has flagged it yet.

OVERALL READ: long low needle-snouted body, single mid-dorsal fin, an oversized triangular ventral fin, deeply forked tail, no mouth, dark midline. It reads as a needlefish / saury / juvenile barracuda, exactly as claimed. Two of three must-reads are absent or inverted and the third is malformed and breaks the silhouette. FAIL upheld.

rows.readsAs: a sea bream, pomfret or silver moonyfish - a deep round reef disc, or a piranha
rows.defect: The body is a near-circular disc: measured off the render the length-to-depth ratio is roughly 1.7:1 against the 4.2 the reference specifies. The must-read is a STREAMLINED silver body with a keeled belly and this is the opposite of streamlined - the belly is a fat convex curve with no keel, the topline is a high domed hump, and the caudal peduncle is a stubby pinch. The dorsal is a dark translucent smear draped over the back rather than a single small fin at mid-back, the jaw is a plain downcurved line with no upturn, and the tail fork is shallow. Nothing about this silhouette says clupeid.
rows.fix: Cut the body depth by more than half so the fish is a long low torpedo at the specified 4.2:1, flatten the belly into a visible saw-edged keel, and replace the dorsal smear with one small crisp triangular fin at mid-back.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, with corrections. Measured from the pixels (440x440 canvas, background #04050b): the whole animal occupies bbox x120-319, y152-270 = 200 x 119 px, aspect 1.68:1 INCLUDING the caudal fin. The body alone (snout tip x319 back to the caudal-fin insertion at x~156) is 163 long x 104 deep = 1.57:1. The reference row calls for aspect 4.2. So the judge's '~1.7:1' is accurate and if anything generous; the fleshy body is a near-circular disc. The column profile confirms it: max depth 104 at x=220, i.e. the deepest point sits at 60% of body length, and depth stays >100 across x=212-240 — a flat-topped dome, not a fusiform taper.

WHAT THE JUDGE GOT RIGHT: (1) The ventral line is a single smooth convex arc from the throat to the anal region (colBot 254->259->256 across x=200-224) with no angular break, no serration, no scute line — there is NO KEEL of any kind. Zoomed on the belly, the only ventral structure is a soft dark-grey pelvic/anal lobe hanging under the rear belly. The must-read 'keeled belly' is absent. (2) The topline is a high smooth dome peaking at x~232 (top y=152) and falling steeply to both the nape and the peduncle — a bream/pomfret topline. (3) The caudal peduncle is pinched to almost nothing: depth drops from 104 at mid-body to 19 px at x=152, over a very short run, so the tail appears bolted straight onto the disc with no caudal stalk. (4) The overall read is a deep-bodied disc fish — sea bream / pomfret / moonfish is a fair identification. It does not read as a clupeid.

WHERE THE JUDGE IS WRONG OR IMPRECISE, and this matters for the fix:
- The DEEPLY FORKED TAIL IS PRESENT AND IS GOOD. Zoomed 5x on x110-190: the caudal fin is a clean V-notched fork with two long pointed lobes spanning y154-270, with visible ray striations and a translucent membrane. The judge's sentence folds the tail into the failure ('stubby pinched peduncle'), which conflates the STALK (bad) with the FIN (correct). Do not redraw the caudal fin — only lengthen and narrow the peduncle in front of it.
- The DORSAL IS NOT A FORMLESS SMEAR. Zoomed 6x on x185-300, y138-198: it is a real fin with distinct vertical ray lines in a mid-grey translucent membrane. The defect is its GEOMETRY, not its rendering: it runs roughly x195-x270, i.e. ~46% of body length, and rises only ~8-12 px above the topline — a long low ridge, where the reference demands a SINGLE SMALL fin at mid-back. Fix = shorten its base to ~15% of body length and raise it into a discrete triangle; do not just repaint it.
- The judge MISSED an inverted must-read: the JAW IS DOWNTURNED, not upturned. Zoomed 7x on the head (x255-325): the mouth is a single arc that leaves the snout and curves DOWNWARD and rearward, giving a terminal-to-slightly-inferior bream mouth. The reference asks for an upturned jaw (protruding lower jaw, oblique gape) and the drawing does the opposite.

WHAT DOES READ CORRECTLY and should be preserved: the large prominent eye with a dark pupil and a pale cream iris ring, set forward and high (matches 'prominent'); head length snout-to-opercle ~45 px of 163 = headFrac 0.28 vs spec 0.24, close enough; the silver colour with dense iridescent scale speckle and a fine lateral line arc; the triangular translucent pectoral fin on the mid-flank.

NET: three of the identity clauses fail — streamlined proportion, keeled belly, small mid-back dorsal — plus the jaw is inverted. Two sub-clauses pass (forked tail, large eye). The organism is the wrong shape at the chassis level, so FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a generic green pelagic fish - a mullet or a small pike

rows.readsAs: a fat pigeon with two flat grey planks glued on horizontally

Verified at 6-14x magnification on the head, feet, tail and both wing tips. FAIL stands, but two parts of the stated cause are wrong and one is confirmed exactly.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. Body: one large smooth egg/oval (approx x95-250, y165-280 on the 440 canvas) covered in a dappled overlapping-scale pattern that reads as golf-ball dimpling or fish scales rather than feather tracts. CORRECTION 1 - THE WINGS ARE THE ONE THING DONE RIGHT, NOT A DEFECT. Calling them 'two flat grey planks' is wrong as a criticism. Total span is roughly x=10 to x=425 (about 415px) against a 155px body, i.e. 2.7x body length, matching the 2.6 aspect. Both wings are narrow, stiff, plank-straight and taper to sharp points - which is precisely what the reference note demands ('narrow and plank-straight, not broad and fingered like a raptor's'). The near (right) wing is NOT flat and undetailed: it carries five drawn primary-separation lines at the outer third and a pale elliptical underwing panel at the root. mustRead #1, 'immensely long narrow stiff-held wings', is PRESENT and readable. The real wing defect is geometric, not shape: both wings exit the body at the SAME mid-flank height and read as a single rod skewered fore-and-aft through the belly, with no shoulder/scapular join, no carpal bend, and the far (left) wing is a plain untextured dark silhouette with no feather structure at all.

CORRECTION 2 - THE BILL, described slightly wrong but the substance holds. It is not a triangle; at 14x it is a downward-angled parallelogram wedge with a dark brown outline and a faint darker line hinting at a lower mandible, blunt/rounded at the tip, only about 0.6x the head diameter long. There is NO hook, NO terminal nail, NO gape line, and critically NO tube nostril anywhere on the side or top of it. mustRead #2, 'heavy hooked bill with tube nostrils on the sides' - the single feature that IS the albatross and the only thing separating it from the nine other birds in this family batch - is entirely ABSENT.

CONFIRMED - POSTURE. The claim that it stands rather than flies is exactly right. Reference posture is 'flying'; the asset has two weight-bearing legs with toes splayed on a cast ground ellipse. Feet are not tucked, there is no body pitch, no motion, and the ground shadow nails the bird to a surface. So it is a standing bird with two glider wings taped through its waist.

VERDICT. 2 of 4 identity criteria fail, including the defining tubenose bill and the required posture. The organism as drawn reads as a plump generic perching bird - the judge's 'fat pigeon' is fair, allowing that the surface texture is scale-like rather than pigeon plumage. FAIL upheld.

FIX LIST: (1) build a real heavy tubenose bill - long, deep at the base, distinct upper/lower mandible plates with a visible gape line, a strongly hooked terminal nail, and a raised tube nostril cylinder on the side of the upper mandible; pink-horn rather than saturated yellow. (2) Put it in the air: tuck/remove the legs, delete the ground shadow ellipse, pitch the body. (3) Keep the long narrow planks but re-root them - a shoulder mass and a carpal bend so they leave the back, not the belly, and give the far wing the same primary separations as the near one. (4) Give the head a neck join into the shoulders and drop the golf-ball dimple texture for directional feathering.

Upheld, with corrections to the stated causes. I zoomed the 440px master at 6-14x and sampled pixels.

BILL (must-read 1: 'heavy hooked-tipped bill') - ABSENT, and the judge described it correctly. At 14x the bill is a symmetric isoceles triangle in flat ochre-yellow (approx #E0A62B) with a straight upper edge, a straight lower edge, a single dark gape line down the middle, and a sharp apex. There is no hooked tip, no drooping nail, no gonydeal bulge, no red gonys spot. It is also not heavy: it spans roughly x=117..145 (about 28px) against a head ball roughly 55px across, so it is a small slim wedge, not the deep blade a herring gull needs. Minor correction to the judge's wording: at low zoom the apex can look like it droops, and the shape is a pointed triangle rather than a duck's spatulate bill, so 'duckling' misnames the bill even though the overall chick read is right.

WINGTIPS / MANTLE (must-read 2: 'clean white body with a grey mantle and black wingtips') - the judge is exactly right and I can put numbers on it. The arc swoosh over the back samples RGB(101,102,104) at (228,190) and (236,190). The single grey point projecting past the rear samples RGB(101,102,104) at (268,235) through (298,235) - byte-identical to the swoosh. There is one grey in this asset and it is mid-grey, not black; true black wingtips would be near #1A1A1A. The only darker pixels are the 3-4px anti-aliased tip at x=304 (34,37,41) fading into the near-black background (8,13,19), which is edge falloff, not a black primary panel. Also, the grey is not a mantle: the crown, nape and upper back are all white; the grey is a crescent painted across the middle of the flank plus a second pale-grey teardrop 'folded wing' inside it, so the back-versus-underside two-tone that defines a gull is missing entirely. Body white itself is clean (250-255) - that part is fine.

WINGS BEYOND TAIL (must-read 3) - only nominally. A single undifferentiated grey dart does extend past the body to x=321, but wing and tail are the same shape and same colour, so there is no readable 'long wings crossing beyond the tail'. There is a set of very faint thin dark hatch strokes below and behind the dart (visible only when brightened) that appear to be intended as tail feathers; against the dark background they are effectively invisible and cannot be counted as a feature.

SILHOUETTE - the real killer, and something the judge did not mention. Ink bbox is 204x147 including the tail dart; the body alone is roughly 150 wide x 147 tall, i.e. aspect 1.0, a near-perfect circle, with a small round head sitting on top and no neck. The packet asks for aspect 2. Legs are thin ochre sticks with one forward and one rear toe each, unwebbed. The composite read is a round white chick/ball-bird, not a herring gull.

Fixes: give the bill real depth plus a downcurved nail and a gonys angle (and a red spot); repaint the grey as a true dorsal mantle over crown-to-back, not a mid-flank crescent; add a genuinely black (near #1A1A1A) primary block with white mirrors at the projecting tip so it separates from the grey mantle; and stretch the chassis from a 1.0 ball to the 2.0 horizontal body the packet specifies.

rows.readsAs: a kiwi
rows.defect: A brown sphere on two legs with a long straight yellow probe bill and a ground shadow — the flying posture is simply not rendered. The tubular nostrils riding on top of the bill, the named identity feature, are absent: the bill is smooth with no ridge. The narrow angled swept-back wings are the family's painted crescent ending in one grey point; there is no angle, no sweep and no wing edge. The compact gull-like body is a chick's ball.

rows.verifyWhy:
Verified at full size, then re-read at 5x-14x crops of the head, bill, tail and feet, plus a brightness-boosted (3.2x) pass to rule out features hidden in the dark. Packet row asks aspect 2.4, headFrac 0.22, posture FLYING, mustRead: (a) tubular nostrils riding on top of the bill, (b) narrow angled swept-back wings, (c) compact gull-like body. All three fail, so the FAIL stands - but two parts of the original claim need correcting before anyone works a fix from it.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON CANVAS: a near-spherical body with a short thick neck into a spherical head; a tiny round eye with a white catchlight; a long bright yellow/amber bill; two thin yellow scaly toed feet planted flat on the ground on a soft elliptical cast shadow. Body is roughly at rest, side-on, facing left.

CONFIRMED #1 - tubular nostrils absent. At 14x the bill is a single flat yellow wedge with a perfectly straight dorsal edge running unbroken from the feather line to a needle point. No naricorn, no tube, no ridge, no bump at the base - and additionally NO hooked nail at the tip, which a petrel also requires. The judge's 'long straight probe bill' is exactly right.

CONFIRMED #2 - flying posture absent. Two feet are planted on the ground and there is a distinct cast shadow ellipse under them, so this is a standing biped, not the flying posture the row specifies. Extra defect the judge did NOT mention: at 9x the feet are anisodactyl perching feet (three forward toes plus a hallux, thin scaly tarsi, no webbing at all). A petrel has fully webbed paddles. Whoever fixes this must fix the foot too.

CONFIRMED #3 - body is not gull-like. Measured silhouette bbox is 222 x 126 px = aspect 1.76, and about 30 percent of that length is bill; body-only aspect is roughly 1.3. Target is 2.4. It is a ball, with no gull chest line, no shoulder, no taper to the tail.

CORRECTION A - 'there are no swept-back angled wings' is over-broad and would send the fix in the wrong direction. There IS wing geometry present, just in repose: a large folded wing panel is drawn lying against the flank as an ellipse with a heavy dark outline arcing across the body; behind it ONE narrow dark pointed projection sweeps back and slightly down, extending clear past the rear of the body (visible at 8x as a tapered wedge); and below that a comb of about six thin dark filament strokes fans down-and-back as crude primary tips. So the wing exists - it is folded at rest on a standing bird instead of extended and angled. The fix is repose-to-flight (open the wings, lift the bird off the shadow, drop the feet), NOT 'add wings'. A second real problem here is legibility: that wingtip and the primary filaments render around RGB 40-60 against a RGB 4-11 background, so they disappear entirely at thumbnail scale even though they are in the file.

CORRECTION B - 'a brown sphere' understates the paint. The body carries fine feather-scale texture across the flank and a lighter mantle/coverts panel with its own shading, so this is not an untextured primitive. The defect is the SHAPE (spherical, aspect 1.3 where 2.4 is asked) and the value contrast of the wing, not a lack of surface detail.

The kiwi read is fair as a gestalt call - long straight probe bill, ball body, no neck, ground stance, cast shadow - though the bright yellow bill also pushes it toward a generic wader/shorebird. Either way it does not read as a tubenose. Three of three must-reads absent; FAIL upheld.

rows.readsAs: a black chicken
rows.defect: Every one of the three must-reads is missing. The bill is the family's small plain orange-yellow triangle, not a huge deep laterally flattened plate, and it carries no orange/blue-grey banding. There is no white face patch at all — the head is uniformly dark charcoal, so the black cap has nothing to contrast against. The feet are the same thin yellow sticks with separated toes as every other bird here, neither bright orange nor webbed. Without the bill and the face, this is indistinguishable from the Auk with a shorter beak.
rows.fix: Replace the bill with a bill roughly the depth of the whole head — a tall triangular plate banded blue-grey then yellow then orange with grooves — and drop in a large pale grey face disc under a black cap.
rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld after zooming the head (crop 80,110 110x90 at 6x), the feet (140,250 120x70 at 6x) and the whole body at 3x. All three packet must-reads are genuinely absent, and I could not find any of them drawn small or off-centre.

(1) BILL — must be a huge triangular LATERALLY FLATTENED plate striped orange and blue-grey. What is drawn is a small amber/mustard cone: a simple two-triangle wedge (upper + lower mandible split by one thin dark gape line), tapering to a sharp point, roughly 0.55x the head-disc diameter in length and only ~0.35x in depth. It is depth-thin, not a deep vertical plate; there are no vertical stripes, no blue-grey basal band, no pale rosette/cere at the gape, and no keel line. Judge's description of this defect is correct.

(2) FACE — must be a big white face patch on a black cap. The entire head is one flat charcoal disc (~#2f3236) with a thin cool rim-light along the crown only. There is no white, cream or pale grey patch anywhere on the face, no cap/face boundary, and no dark eye-triangle behind the eye. Worse, the eye is a plain dark bead on the dark head with only a tiny specular dot, so the head has effectively zero internal contrast. Judge correct.

(3) FEET — must be bright ORANGE WEBBED feet. Drawn as two thin mustard-amber stick legs with three splayed straight toes each; at 6x the gaps between the toes are clean background pixels, so there is definitively no web membrane. Colour is a desaturated yellow-ochre, not puffin orange-red. Judge correct.

Two things the judge understated or got slightly wrong, which matter for the fix: (a) "black chicken" — the bird is not black, it is a uniform mid-charcoal grey over the WHOLE body including the underside. A puffin's stark white breast/belly against black upperparts is also missing, which is arguably the loudest read of all and is not even in the mustRead list. Fixing only the three listed features on this grey body would still not read as Puffin. (b) The silhouette is wrong beyond the three features: the body is a plump rounded ovoid with a LONG dark pointed tail projecting well past the rump to the rear (roughly 25% of body length), plus a stray fan of thin dark filament strokes below it. Puffins have a very short stubby tail; this tail plus the round body is what pushes the read toward a gamebird/blackbird. The wing is also a large flat disc overlay crossed by a dark scythe arc rather than a folded wing.

Net: nothing of the puffin identity survives. FAIL stands. Fix order: white face patch + white underside first (largest area, restores contrast), then the deep striped laterally-flattened bill, then orange webbed paddles, then shorten the tail.

rows.readsAs: a small white plump chick with a long beak
rows.defect: It generically reads as a bird, but not as the representative gull the note calls for. The body is a sphere, the opposite of the streamlined form specified.
