rows.verifyWhy: FAIL UPHELD, but two parts of the stated cause are wrong and would send a fixer to the wrong code. WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE (440x440, read at 1x then re-cropped at 3-5x and pixel-sampled): five orange ellipses stacked on a dark-brown vertical bar over a near-black green-tinted vignette, plus a soft black cast-shadow ellipse on the ground (y~375-410). Disc bands at x=218 sit at y~48-72, 104-128, 154-182, 208-232, 264-288. CONFIRMED: each disc is a SINGLE FLAT FILL with literally zero internal variation - scanline y=272 from x=110 to x=335 reads c67b37 edge to edge, no gradient, no texture, no dappling, no lit/shadow side. Rims are mathematically perfect elliptical arcs with not one needle, notch, scallop or lobe. No branch armature anywhere connecting trunk to tiers. No bark: the trunk is flat 31241a with only a faint top-to-bottom darkening (2f2319 at y=324 to 251d16 at y=380) and zero striation. No root, no base flare - the trunk holds a constant ~10px width (x~215-224) from crown to bottom. CORRECTION 1 - THE Z-ORDER CLAIM IS FALSE. The skewer does NOT pass through or in front of the discs; the trunk is drawn BEHIND them. Sampled fine across the trunk column inside disc 2 (y=110) and disc 5 (y=272), x=205..235: values run c67b37 -> c77c38 -> c87c37 -> ca7d38 -> cb7d38 across x=213..224 and back. The trunk brown 31241a never appears inside any disc. What crosses the disc is a barely-perceptible 2%-LIGHTER orange band (cb7d38 vs c67b37, a 5/255 delta). The 'skewer' reading is a gestalt effect, not overdraw: the trunk is fully unoccluded in all four gaps between discs, the gaps and the discs are the same width in the trunk column, and the discs carry no shading to interrupt the line, so the eye completes a continuous rod. Reordering draw calls will change NOTHING. CORRECTION 2 - 'DECREASING WIDTH' IS BACKWARDS. Widths INCREASE downward (top disc ~100px, bottom ~225px), monotonic. That conifer/pagoda taper is the one thing the asset gets right - the silhouette is legibly tree-shaped, so this is not the wrong organism, it is a diagram of the right organism. CORRECTION 3 - 'hard-edged' is only approximate: rims carry a 2-3px antialias ramp and a faint warm outer bloom. TWO DEFECTS THE JUDGE MISSED: (a) a bare trunk stub protrudes ~12px ABOVE the topmost disc (brown 31241a at y=36-48 at x=218) - a naked spike sticking out of the crown; (b) the trunk NEVER REACHES THE GROUND - it terminates in a rounded cap at y~384 and floats over the shadow ellipse, so the plant has no ground contact at all. BATCH CALIBRATION (packet reference row is NONE, so judged for coherence and against batch-005): sibling flora-h0-s15 is a fern with pinnate fronds, serrated leaflet rims, overlap and depth shading; flora-h0-s16 has branched culms with individually drawn leaf blades and lit/shadow faces on the stems. s17 is far below both - it has no foliage rendering whatsoever, only primitive fills, which also violates the painterly-canvas HD engine law (no flat primitives). This is not a POLISH-sized gap: reaching the batch standard means building tier foliage geometry (needle/frond rims), per-tier undershadow, a branch armature from trunk to each tier, bark striation, and a root flare / ground contact. rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, and pixel-measured. The packet gives this species NO reference row (procedural: judge coherence), so the only must-read is 'reads as a plant'. It does not.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON CANVAS (440x440, measured by column/row scan, not eyeballed):

1. THE COLUMN IS A PERFECT RECTANGLE. Teal body occupies x=210..260 at y=60, y=200, y=245 AND y=300 — 51px wide, IDENTICAL at every height over ~350px of run. Zero taper, zero sway, zero thickness modulation, no node swelling. Fill is flat RGB(43,151,137) with only a faint vertical gradient. Nothing in the stem carries a growth axis.

2. THE TICKS ARE A GRADUATION SCALE, CONFIRMED EXACTLY. Seven of them, at y = 70, 110, 151, 191, 232, 272, 313 — spacing 40.5px +/- 0.5, i.e. mechanically even. Each one is a pair of hard rectangles: LEFT x=195..208, RIGHT x=262..274, for ALL SEVEN, identical to the pixel. They terminate exactly at the stalk's silhouette edges (208 vs stalk-start 210; 260 stalk-end vs 262), so they read as one continuous bar occluded by the column — the judge's 'pass behind it and protrude equally on both sides' is literally, measurably true. CORRECTION to their colour word: the ticks are not 'grey', they are a dark desaturated grey-GREEN, RGB(50,58,49), only ~20 values above the background vignette. That matters for the fix: they are near-invisible in value AND alien in hue to the teal body, so they read as engraved marks on a background instrument rather than as any part of the organism. They have no taper, no attachment point, no curvature, no colour relationship to the plant. No branch, thorn, spine, leaf scar or node ever reads like that.

3. THE APEX IS A THERMOMETER/RULER CAP, which the judge did not mention and which is half the misread. The top (y=28..55) is a plain symmetric rounded dome the exact full width of the shaft. No terminal bud, no apical meristem, no crown, no flower, no foliage mass, no fraying. It is a capped tube end.

4. THE BASE IS A HARD FLAT CUT. The column runs to y=390 at the same 51px width and stops dead on a straight horizontal edge inside the drop-shadow ellipse. No root flare, no basal rosette, no soil contact, no widening. Combined with (3), the silhouette is a capsule with a scale down it — an instrument, not a stem.

5. CORRECTING THEIR ONE BOTANICAL CUE. The judge calls it 'one tiny hooked leaf'. It is neither tiny nor correctly described, and the real defect is more actionable than 'it's small'. Traced: the blade spans y=92 to y=166 (74px, ~17% of frame height) and x=164..207, so it is a substantial appendage, not a speck. The problem is that it is ATTACHED BACKWARDS. Its top edge at y=92 is a DEAD-FLAT HORIZONTAL CUT from x=164 to x=189 — a squared-off chopped end — and that end floats free in space with a 20px air gap to the stalk (at y=128 the blade ends at x=189, the stalk starts at x=210). The blade then sweeps down and right, narrowing, and its POINTED TIP is what finally touches the stem, at x~207, y~164. A leaf attaches at its broad base and its tip is free; this one has its tip welded to the stem and its blunt cut end waving in the air. That inversion is why it reads as a sickle, hook, or bracket handle rather than foliage — and it reinforces the instrument reading (it looks like a clip hanging off a gauge).

SUMMARY OF THE FIX SURFACE: there is no plant here to polish. Needed are taper along the stem, at least one growth node where an appendage leaves the stalk, an apical structure other than a dome cap, a root/base flare, foliage in the plant's OWN hue rather than dead grey, and the leaf re-anchored base-to-stem with the tip free. The seven symmetric equal-length occluded ticks must go entirely; they are the single strongest signal in the image and they signal 'measuring device'. FAIL stands.

rows.verifyWhy:
Packet reference row is **NONE** (procedural, batch-006 entry #6), so this is judged on coherence and against the HD engine law. I read the 440x440 PNG at native size, at 6-8x crops on the bottom disc and the top two discs, and at gamma 2.4 to pull anything hiding in the dark. I also decoded the PNG and measured it numerically. The FAIL STANDS, but two parts of the stated cause need correcting and the real geometric defect is sharper than described.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. Five pink ellipses threaded on a brown vertical rod, over a green radial vignette, with a soft ground-contact shadow ellipse at the base (the shadow and vignette are only visible under gamma boost -- the judge did not mention them, but they exist). Measured discs, top to bottom: major axis 70 / 108 / 144 / 180 / 218 px. Because the widths widen monotonically downward and the stem meets a ground shadow, the SILHOUETTE does legibly read as a conifer / pagoda-plant. This is not the wrong organism. It fails on execution, not identity.

CONFIRMED PARTS OF THE CLAIM.
- 'Five perfectly flat ellipses': confirmed, exactly 5 connected pink regions.
- 'Pure uniform fill': confirmed in effect. The entire disc body measures RGB 189,82,164 (outer four) with no gradient of any kind -- a vertical scan through the bottom disc at x=160 reads 189,82,164 flat from y=268 to y=282, and the only non-uniform pixels in the whole asset are 1-2px of rim antialiasing (the 621 'distinct colors' are all edge interpolation). Correction of detail: the fill is not literally single-valued -- there is a ~10px band of 194,84,165 directly over the stem column. That is a 5/255 delta, imperceptible, and it is LIGHTER not darker, so it is not shading.
- 'Unbroken smooth rims, no leaf tips': confirmed and verified numerically, not just by eye. I traced the bottom disc's top and bottom boundary at 4px intervals across its full 212px width. Top edge runs 272-271-270-269-268...263...268-269-270-271-273 and the bottom edge mirrors it -- both are perfectly monotone arcs. Zero notches, zero lobes, zero serrations, no leaf tips, no radial veins, no midrib.
- 'No self-shadowing where they meet the stem': confirmed, and it is worse than stated. The stem is drawn BEHIND the discs and the pixels where they cross are 194,84,165, i.e. slightly LIGHTER than the surrounding 189,82,164 -- the exact inverse of a contact shadow. There is also no inter-disc occlusion: the pink on disc 5 that sits directly under disc 4's footprint is the identical 189,82,164 as disc 5's outer rim.

WHERE THE CLAIM IS WRONG -- 'no perspective'. Perspective is not absent; it is present and geometrically IMPOSSIBLE, which is the actionable defect. Every one of the five discs has an identical minor axis of 24px (measured heights 24/25/24/24/24) while the major axes run 70/108/144/180/218. So the axis ratio climbs 2.92 -> 4.32 -> 6.00 -> 7.50 -> 9.08. A stack of horizontal circles seen from one camera must share a CONSTANT major:minor ratio; here each tier implies a different viewing tilt. The top disc reads as a near-3:1 saucer seen from well above, the bottom as a 9:1 razor slice seen edge-on. The generator is clearly stamping a fixed 24px height and only varying width. That single constant is what makes the stack read as plates rather than foliage, and it is the thing to fix. (6) 'pins stuck in a shelf' - it is worse than that. Nothing is stuck in anything. Every stem terminates and fades to transparency at y~345-349, while the top of the dish is at y=362. WHAT ACTUALLY FAILS (fix against this list):
A. SEVERED CONTACT - the single worst defect. All six stems end ~14px short of the dish and fade out rather than meeting or entering it. No root flare, no contact shadow, no occlusion. Fix: extend stems to y>=364 and overlap the dish top, or lower the dish to y=348.
B. NO FOLIAGE - not one leaf, blade, frond, sheath or bract on any of the six stems except the two vague lobes on the right stalk. For a flora asset this is the identity must-read and it is absent.
C. STRUCTURELESS HEADS - the four left heads are featureless white discs (RGB>235) with zero interior modelling: no petals, no cap gills, no filament texture, no rim darkening, no hue variation. The right head is a lumpy fused two-lobe blob. They read as cotton buds / map pins, not as blooms or capsules.
D. FOCUS MISMATCH - the entire organism is heavily gaussian-blurred (head edges ramp over 8-10px) while the dish is razor-sharp with a 1px edge. Two render passes disagreeing in the same frame. Sibling flora-h1-s4 in this same batch is knife-sharp throughout, so the blur is this asset's fault, not the batch's.
E. COMPOSITION - the organism occupies only y=223..348, the bottom 28% of the canvas; everything above y=223 (the top half, not the top two-thirds as claimed) is empty background. s4 by contrast runs y=35..395. This asset is undersized and bottom-loaded.
F. TWO SPECIMENS, NOT ONE - a ~118px void separates the left clump (ends x~212) from the lone right stalk (starts x~330). It reads as two unrelated plants sharing a tray rather than one specimen.
G. GROUND-PLANE CONVENTION BREAK - siblings sit on a soft dark elliptical shadow; this one gets an opaque saturated violet slab that is the highest-chroma object in the frame and pulls the eye away from the organism.

The asset does not read as the WRONG organism - 'white-headed cotton-grass stalks' is a legible alien-flora idea. Each blob is painted as an independently shaded translucent disc carrying its own rim darkening, so where they overlap you get BOTH the near disc's rim AND the far disc's full circumference drawn across the front surface. Row scans through the mass show the interior dips: row 240 falls 111 -> 56 at x=174 and 101 -> 55 at x=264 mid-body; row 265 shows a spurious rise 51 -> 61 at x=270. Visually these are long thin dark crescents cutting straight across the lower-left sphere, the lower-centre sphere and the upper-right sphere. The mass has no single silhouette.

CONFIRMED 2 -- 'hovers in mid-air with no ground contact' is correct AND it is the batch-coherence break. Both siblings plant their subject on an explicit dark cast-shadow ellipse on an implied ground plane (fungi-h0-s2 and fungi-h0-s4 each have one). fungi-h0-s3 has none: max luminance below the cluster is 37 at y=305 (still cluster falloff), 18 at y=320, 15 at y=340, 12 at y=360 -- i.e. pure vignette. The bar and everything on it float in void.

DEFECT THE OTHER JUDGE MISSED, and it is the single biggest reason this reads as fruit rather than fungus: every blob carries the same oversized, blown-to-white, two-lobed specular roughly 25-30% of its diameter, and they are placed inconsistently relative to their own blob centres -- upper-left on the crown sphere, upper-centre on the right sphere, dead-centre-to-low on the large lower sphere. There is therefore no coherent light direction, and the uniform wet gloss on a cold desaturated blue-grey body (approx 74,78,101) is what produces the grape/berry read. Combined with the total absence of any fungal surface cue (sibling s4 at least stipples its cap with spots), nothing in the asset says fungus except the composition's intent.

BAND: FAIL stands. The composition -- a cluster fungus fruiting from the underside of a branch -- is a legitimate fungal habit and the sphere is this generator's established cap primitive (s4 is a single sphere), so I do not fault it as 'wrong organism by design'. But it fails on execution: the blob field must be unioned into one silhouette (currently seven-plus buried circle outlines cut through the front surfaces), the assembly must be grounded to match its own batch, the speculars must be reduced to one small consistently-lit highlight per lobe, the value range must be lifted toward the batch's 200+ peak, and at least one fungal surface cue (pore/wart/spore texture) must be added. Those are structural, not polish.

rows.readsAs: an orange, or a small desert planet
rows.defect: A single smooth orange sphere with a scatter of dark freckles, floating above an elliptical shadow. There is not one fungal feature in the frame - no stipe, no cap, no pore, no substrate, no mycelium, no second body, no texture. The freckle scatter plus the warm gradient plus the crescent rim light on the right edge is literally planet shading, and at this hue a stranger says 'orange' before anything else. This is the base sphere primitive shipped as a species.

rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD after gamma-lifting the frame (gamma 0.35) to expose anything hidden in the near-black background, and after 6x nearest-neighbour crops of the base contact zone and the right limb. Nothing is hidden: the entire asset is one circle plus one ellipse.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. A single circle, ~135px diameter, centred slightly above frame middle. It is a mathematically perfect circle — the 6x base crop shows an unbroken clean arc across the whole bottom with zero basal flattening, zero sterile base, zero flare, zero contact shading. Fill is a warm radial gradient, saturated orange (~#E8A45E) at the limb lifting to pale cream (~#F5D9A8) at a highlight sited upper-left of centre. Beneath it a flat, hard-edged dark ellipse ~230x45px, pure drop-shadow with no ground plane, no texture, no cast-direction agreement with the highlight. Along the right limb runs a thin cool bluish-white crescent stroke, ~3px, offset OUTSIDE the body's own edge, running from about the 1-o'clock position to about 5-o'clock and then stopping short with a visible gap before the bottom of the arc.

THE FUNGAL MUST-READS. All absent, confirmed at 6x: no stipe (the bottom arc is uninterrupted — nothing descends from it), no cap (no separate upper form, no margin, no overhang, no cap/stem junction), no pore field or gill radiation (the underside is simply the continuation of the same sphere gradient), no substrate (no log, no soil, no litter — the only non-body mark in the frame is the shadow ellipse), no mycelium or rhizomorphs (the gamma lift specifically ruled this out; the background is a clean vignette with faint tiling grain and nothing else), no veil, ring, volva, or scaly/reticulate skin.

CORRECTIONS TO THE ORIGINAL CLAIM — three parts are imprecise and should not be carried into the fix:
1. "no ... texture" is WRONG as stated. There IS surface texture: roughly 20 soft-edged darker dots, 3-10px, scattered over the lower-left two-thirds of the disc, plus a faint mottled noise over the whole body. The defect is not absence of texture, it is that the texture carries no fungal information — the dots are FLAT (each is a single darker blob with no paired highlight/shadow, so they do not read as raised warts), they are randomly scattered rather than organised into a pore field, gill fan, or peridium wart lattice, and at this scale on an orange sphere they read as cratering. A fix must replace the freckle pass with a structured surface, not merely add texture.
2. "floating over an ellipse shadow" is WRONG. The sphere's bottom arc overlaps and occludes the upper portion of the ellipse — it reads as set ON a plane, not levitating. The real problem is subtler and needs stating correctly: the contact is a bare circle-on-ellipse intersection with no basal flattening, no occlusion darkening, and no emergence from anything, so it reads as an object PLACED on a surface rather than a fruiting body GROWN out of a substrate.
3. "crescent rim light that is literally planet shading" is CORRECT and if anything understated — the stroke is cool bluish-white against a warm body, offset outside the silhouette, and terminates before completing the limb. That is the standard planet-terminator treatment, and it is also independently sloppy (a rim light should follow the whole lit edge or fade, not stop with a gap).

BATCH-COHERENCE EVIDENCE, which strengthens rather than rescues the FAIL. Sibling fungi-h0-s3 in the same packet draws a horizontal brown substrate branch across the upper third with a multi-lobed cluster of four overlapping bulbous bodies hanging beneath it, each with a wet specular sheen. That proves the generator already owns a fungal vocabulary — substrate, clustering, lobed fruiting bodies, sheen — and that fungi-h0-s4 exercises none of it. This is not a case of a small feature drawn somewhere the first judge did not look; the feature set was simply never invoked for this seed.

I considered and rejected the strongest refutation available: that a giant puffball (Calvatia/Lycoperdon) genuinely is a near-featureless sphere, which would make this a legitimate fungus. It does not hold. A puffball reads as fungal through cream-to-buff colour, a flattened partially-buried base, a visible sterile base or cord, and raised warts with their own micro-shadows. This asset has none of those four: it is saturated orange, perfectly circular at the base, unattached, and its markings are flat. Strip the shadow ellipse and this image is indistinguishable from the desert-planet sphere primitive.

Band FAIL. Fix direction: this seed needs the whole fungal skeleton added — substrate, stipe, a cap distinct from the stipe, and an underside treatment — not a texture tweak. Also remove the cool crescent rim, which is planet-vocabulary and will keep the planet read alive even after geometry is added.

rows.defect: Two smooth red domes with a dense curtain of long thin filaments hanging from their rims - that is medusa anatomy, bell plus tentacles, and it is what a stranger names instantly. It is made worse by the geometry: the filaments pass straight THROUGH the brown substrate bar and continue well below it, dangling into empty space, so the spines are not resting on or growing over the substrate at all, they are drifting past it. The domes themselves are featureless gradient hemispheres with a thin dark line at the rim and no cap texture, no stipe, and no attachment to the bar they are supposedly fruiting from.

rows.verifyWhy: UPHELD, but two of the stated causes are wrong and the real one is missing. What is actually on the 440px canvas: this is the hydnoid/TOOTH family (packet has no reference row; the generator is fungiTooth() in port/v2/packages/art/src/proceduralfamilies.ts:68, whose docstring says 'a cap whose underside hangs in soft downward spines'). heads=2, so a larger salmon dome at x~0.35S and a smaller one at x~0.65S, cap tops at y~100 and ~125px, cap bottom edges (flat, straight, no margin roll) at y~160 and ~183px. Below each, a curtain of ~46 thin threads falling to y~280-300px. A rounded arcing bough crosses behind them, and a soft ground ellipse sits at the bottom. CORRECT in the claim: it reads as two jellyfish, not fungus. CORRECT: neither dome has any stipe, boss, or contact with the bough -- the caps hover roughly a full cap-height clear of the wood with nothing but the threads spanning the gap, so nothing anchors the fruit body. WRONG #1: 'the teeth drift past the substrate rather than growing from it' inverts the anatomy. The teeth are the one part correctly attached -- they are drawn from y = cy + h*0.2, i.e. BEHIND and ABOVE the cap's own bottom edge at cy + h*0.28, and in the render they visibly emerge from under the flat cap rim. They were never supposed to grow from the substrate. WRONG #2: 'brown substrate bar ... filaments dangle well below it into empty space' overstates and mislabels. It is not a bar: it is a rounded quadratic bough with a darker bark under-shadow stroke and 12 pale horizontal bark hatch strokes, and it reads acceptably as a bough. Pixel scan: brown bough pixels run y=186 to y=280 and stop; red thread pixels persist to y=301 but only 1-17 px per row, i.e. roughly three to five tip-ends clearing the bough silhouette by ~20px (4.8% of frame). That overhang is real and should be fixed, but it is a minor blemish, not the reason this fails. THE ACTUAL CAUSE OF THE JELLYFISH READ, which the claim does not name: the teeth are wrong in every dimension. (a) LENGTH -- drop = h*(1.5 + cos(u*1.5)*1.15)*(0.7 + r()*0.55) with h = S*0.10 yields up to 0.33S, measured ~140px of thread under a ~60px-tall cap, i.e. 2.3x the cap height. Hydnoid spines are a short dense pelt, never longer than the cap is tall. (b) PROFILE -- each spine is a constant-width stroke (tw fixed per spine) with lineCap 'round', so it never tapers; it ends in a blunt rounded tip. A tooth is a cone. (c) VALUE -- the per-spine gradient runs p.dark at the top to p.lit at the bottom, so the tips are the BRIGHTEST pixels in the whole asset. A pelt of teeth is shadowed at its tips; lit glowing tips are precisely the cnidarian tentacle cue. (d) JITTER -- +/-25% random length per spine plus +/-4.5px lateral jitter at both the mid control point and the tip makes them cross and splay into separated tendrils instead of a solid combed underside; the 3.4px pitch is dense at the rim but opens into see-through gaps lower down. Also correcting 'featureless dome': each cap does carry one arc, the c.strokeStyle 'rgba(232,240,255,0.30)' specular at line 108, but at 30% alpha over the salmon lump gradient it renders as a DARK blue-grey hairline following just inside the rim, not a highlight -- so the one mark on the bell reads as a jellyfish bell margin and makes the misread worse rather than better. FIXES, in order of payoff: shorten the teeth to <= 0.6x cap height, taper them to points (per-spine tapering polygon, not a round-capped stroke), invert the gradient so tips are dark, cut the length and lateral jitter to a fraction of current, seat each cap ON the bough with a visible sessile attachment or short lateral stipe, repair the specular so it reads white, and clip the teeth so no tip crosses the bough's lower silhouette. Family note: the batch is not one chassis -- fungi-h0-s2 (a coral/branching white form) and fungi-h0-s6 (stalked knobs) are structurally distinct, so this is a per-family defect, not a shared-body defect.

Club and coral fungi are round in section, blunt or lobed at the tip and fleshy at the base; none of that is present. A stranger names this a plant every time.

rows.verifyWhy:
Verified at 1x and again at 3x/6x crops of the tip band and the base band. The asset is nine upright purple spikes on a dark ground with a soft elliptical drop shadow; no cap, no stipe/pileus distinction, no gills/pores, no substrate, no mycelial pad, no branching. Packet row is NONE (procedural), so the bar is coherence + reads-as-its-kingdom, and it does not read as fungus at any zoom. My first read was 'purple grass / sansevieria clump' and it held at 6x.

WHAT THE FAILING JUDGE GOT RIGHT (confirmed on the pixels):
- Points: ALL nine apices are acute triangular spikes with straight-sided taper. At thumbnail size three of them (fingers 3, 5 and 6 from the left) LOOK domed, and I initially wrote them down as rounded club tips; at 6x every one of them resolves to a needle point. No blunt or lobed apex exists anywhere in the asset.
- Curling tip: correct, the far-right finger is a sickle that arcs right and hooks over — reads as a wilting leaf blade, the single most grass-like element in the frame.
- Midrib: correct as described. Each finger carries one thin, hard-edged, near-constant-width pale line running most of its length, roughly central (drifting slightly left near the tips, slightly right near the base). It does not behave like a specular band on a cylinder — it does not widen, fade at the ends, or shift with the finger's lean; it is a drawn line, and it reads as a leaf midrib/keel.
- Flat section: broadly correct. The lower half of every finger is near-uniform mid-purple wall to wall with hard edges and no terminator darkening on the shade side, so the cross-section reads as a ribbon, not a rod. There IS a faint lateral gradient in the upper thirds of the two leftmost fingers, so 'flattened blades' is slightly overstated for those two, but not for the other seven.

WHERE THE CLAIM IS WRONG OR INCOMPLETE — fix against this, not against the original wording:
1. 'Club/coral fungi ... have a fused fleshy base' is not a safe rule and should not drive the fix. Clavaria / Clavulinopsis / Alloclavaria purpurea are caespitose: many separate unbranched purple spindles from separate bases in a dense tuft, and Clavaria acuta is literally named for its pointed apex. A tuft of separate pointed purple spindles is therefore a legitimate fungal form, so 'separate bases + points' alone does not condemn this asset. It fails for other reasons.
2. The real base defect is worse and different from 'no fused base'. At 6x, every finger terminates in a HARD, FLAT, HORIZONTAL CROP — a straight chopped rectangle end with a crisp edge — and those crops sit ABOVE the shadow ellipse with a gap. The stalks are clipped, floating rods that touch nothing. There is no foot, no ground contact, no taper-out, no attachment geometry of any kind. This is a rendering/composition defect independent of taxon and it must be fixed regardless of what organism this becomes.
3. Profile is wrong for a club in a way the claim never names: each finger is a long parallel-sided shaft that tapers monotonically to a point from roughly its lower third upward. Club and fairy-club fungi SWELL toward the apex and pinch to a hair-thin, often downy base. This one is thick at the bottom and thin at the top — the exact opposite distribution, and exactly a grass blade's profile.
4. Surface quality is not mentioned and is a major part of the wrong read: the fill is glossy, plastic-smooth and perfectly even, with zero waxy/matte fungal flesh, no longitudinal grooving or contortion, no translucency at the tips, no colour break between apex and base. Every finger is the same clean geometric extrusion, which is what makes the clump read procedurally generated rather than grown.

FIX DIRECTION: kill the hard central line and replace it with a soft off-axis cylinder gradient plus a terminator; round every apex to a blunt or slightly flattened lobe; delete the sickle-curl finger or reduce it to a gentle lean; invert the taper so each spindle is fattest in its upper third and pinches to a thin whitish base; fuse or at least seat the bases into a shared fleshy pad on the ground plane so nothing floats; break the geometric uniformity with slight contortion and grooving. As drawn it is a clump of purple grass, and it should not ship in a fungi family.

rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, with two corrections to the stated cause. WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON CANVAS (440x440, viewed at 1x, then at 3x and 8x with gamma boost so nothing hides in the near-black background): a single geometrically perfect circle, ~150px across, centred, filled with a soft radial gradient in desaturated periwinkle grey-blue (highlight centred around the 10 o'clock upper-left quadrant, falling off to a cool shade at the lower-right limb). Scattered across the surface, clustered heavily in the lower-centre and lower-left third and thinning to nothing above the equator, are roughly 35 small flat discs a few shades darker than the body, radii ~1.5-5px. Under the substrate is one hard-edged black ellipse ~185x40px. That is the entire drawing. There is no second form of any kind.

CORRECTION 1 to the claim — the drop shadow is NOT detached. At 8x on the base, the sphere's lower arc is drawn ON TOP of the shadow ellipse and descends to roughly the ellipse's vertical mid-line, so the contact point itself reads fine. The real substrate defect is different and worth stating precisely for the fix: there is no substrate BODY at all — no duff pad, no soil ellipse, no log, no mycelial fringe, no basal rooting — which is exactly what sibling s12 (blue puffball pair on a brown soil pad) and s17 (toothed caps on a log) supply and what makes them read as fungi. Do not 'fix the shadow'; add a substrate and a base.

CORRECTION 2 — the dark speckles are not craters and not warts. Each is a flat uniform-value filled circle with no rim, no cast shadow and no top-lit highlight; they carry zero relief in either direction. They read as pits only because a smooth sphere gives the eye nothing else to interpret them as. A wart pass needs a light-top/dark-bottom pair per bump plus a bumpy silhouette; a pore pass needs a rim. Currently it is neither.

NEW DEFECT the first judge did not name: the white crescent is not merely a rim light, it is MIS-REGISTERED. Zoomed 14x at the 3-4 o'clock position, the white stroke sits clearly OUTSIDE the body silhouette with a dark background gap of 1-2px between stroke and body, then terminates in a blunt flat cut end while the body edge continues on down-left. The arc runs from ~11 o'clock over the apex to ~4 o'clock and is an independent stroked path offset right of the body circle, not a highlight on it. It also fights the shading: the broad diffuse highlight is upper-LEFT, the specular limb is upper-RIGHT. Two light directions in one 150px object.

FUNGAL MUST-READS, checked one at a time: apical pore/ostiole — ABSENT; at 8x the apex is one unbroken smooth arc with no dimple, dot, star-split or peridium tear. Stipe/base/volva — ABSENT. Cap/hymenium separation — ABSENT (no gills, teeth, pores, tubes, margin or cap-edge anywhere). Warts/scurf/spines — ABSENT (see correction 2). Substrate contact — ABSENT (see correction 1). Irregular lumpy peridium outline — ABSENT; the silhouette is a machine-perfect circle, which is itself the single loudest wrong signal, since real puffballs are never circular.

BATCH CONTEXT, which makes this worse rather than excusable. This is NOT a shared-chassis failure — batch 011's fungi are genuinely diverse: s12 puffball pair on soil, s13 pink coral-fungus spike cluster, s14 classic reticulate cap on a white stipe, s16 fringed cup pair, s17 Hericium-like toothed caps on a log, s18 pink spiny spore-ball with a dark central pore, s19 particulate spore cloud. Every one of those is legible as a fungus in under a second. s15 is the one asset in the group that received the bare sphere primitive with no ornament pass at all. Critically, the puffball archetype it is presumably reaching for is already solved TWO CELLS AWAY in s12, which has the lumpy non-circular outline, the surface mottling, the reticulate cracking on the smaller ball and the soil pad. s15 has none of it. Its palette is also the coldest and least organic in the batch (blue-grey against the batch's ochres, creams and pinks), which pushes the read further toward rock.

VERDICT: the object reads as a moon or asteroid, or at best an inanimate marble. Not one feature on it is diagnostic of a fungus, or of a living thing. The first judge's headline read is correct; only the shadow-detachment and crater wording were wrong. FAIL stands. FIX ORDER: (1) break the circle — irregular lumpy peridium outline; (2) apical pore or peridium split at the apex; (3) real warts with per-bump light/shade instead of flat discs; (4) substrate pad plus basal rooting; (5) delete or re-register the offset white arc so the specular agrees with the upper-left key light.

Counting clockwise from top: ~11:30 short, ~1:30 long, ~3:00 long, ~4:30 medium, ~6:00 short (points down-left into the shadow), ~8:00 long, ~9:30 long. They are NOT at even angles — gaps run from roughly 35deg (1:30 to 3:00) to roughly 60deg (6:00 to 8:00), and the two left spikes sit almost parallel as a visible pair. Lengths are NOT uniform either: the 9:30 and 8:00 spikes run about 60px, the 11:30 and 6:00 spikes about 20px, a 3x spread. CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM:
1. 'Eight ... at even angles' is wrong twice — there are seven, at visibly irregular spacing with a bare arc on the lower-left and a near-parallel pair on the left.
2. 'Needle lances' with 'no organic base swelling' is wrong. At 8x the spikes are broad-based isoceles wedges: the 6:00 spike's base spans roughly 22px where it meets the sphere, wider than a fifth of the body radius. The base widening IS present. The real defect at the join is different and more fixable: the wedge edges are perfectly straight, hard-aliased polygon edges with zero taper curvature, the join is a hard silhouette corner with no fillet or gradient blend into the body, and every spike is filled with one flat lighter-teal value that ignores the body's upper-left key light — the 8:00 spike (facing away from the light) is the same brightness as the 1:30 spike (facing into it). So: not 'missing base swelling' but 'flat unlit polygons pasted onto a shaded sphere'.
3. 'The body touches no substrate' is FALSE. There is a cast shadow ellipse and the sphere's lower edge sits well inside its upper half; the 6:00 spike descends into it. Ground contact reads fine. What is genuinely absent is BASAL ATTACHMENT — no stipe, no volva, no mycelial skirt, no rooting cord, no substrate texture. The sphere meets the ground on a single tangent point like a dropped ball, which is the fungally-wrong part.
4. 'Detonator port' overstates it. The dark dot is a flat offset disc with no rim, and at this scale it reads as a single cyclops EYE more than a fuze. It is also the one element that could have been saved: a puffball's apical ostiole would be exactly a central pore, but it needs to be ON the apex (this one is off-centre and on the upper-left face), and it needs a raised rim or an inset shadow to read as a hole rather than a pupil.

WHY IT STILL FAILS: the judge is right about the gestalt. Sphere plus seven long radiating lances is a naval contact mine / caltrop / sea urchin / virus-icon silhouette. Nothing in the asset carries a fungal must-read: no cap, no gill or pore underside, no stipe, no annulus, no volva, no spore texture, no clustering, no decaying substrate. Spiny puffballs (Lycoperdon echinatum, Sclerodermataceae) do exist, but their spines are DENSE, SHORT and SOFT and cover the whole surface — the opposite of seven sparse hard lances. Cross-checked against the batch: fungi-h1-s6 is this identical chassis recoloured cream (same sphere, same seven-spike arrangement, same offset dark dot), and fungi-h1-s4 is the same sphere with the spikes swapped for grey speckles. This is one generic procedural primitive — sphere + optional radiating spikes + optional dot — not a fungal form language, which is the batch-level 'do these share one body?' failure as well. The fix is structural (silhouette and basal attachment), not polish.

WHAT I SAW. Packet reference row for fungi-h1-s6 is 'reference row: **NONE** (procedural or unlisted - judge coherence, and judge it against the others in this batch)', so there is no mustRead list; the batch header's own primary question governs: 'DO THESE SHARE ONE BODY?'. The asset is a glossy bone-white sphere, ball radius 44.0 px centred about (220,208) in a 440x440 frame, pierced by seven straight needle-sharp lances, with one small grey dot on the ball face and a soft black ground ellipse beneath. I read the full-size PNG, then re-cropped the ball region (x120-320, y140-290) at 3x with 1.6 gain and read that too, and additionally decoded the PNG in node to measure radial profiles, spike peaks, dot geometry and shadow extent at three independent luminance thresholds.

CORRECTION 1 - IT IS SEVEN LANCES, NOT EIGHT. Both s5 and s6 have exactly seven. Confirmed by eye at 3x (up-slightly-left, upper-right, long right horizontal, lower-right, small bottom, long left horizontal, long lower-left) and by radial peak detection, which returned 7 at thresholds 30, 55 and 90 and at a peak-normalised threshold. Anyone fixing this on the assumption of an eight-fold radial array will be editing the wrong loop.

CORRECTION 2 - THE ANGLES ARE THE DUPLICATE; THE LENGTHS ARE NOT. This is the load-bearing correction. Spike bearings (screen degrees, 0 = right, positive = downward): s5 = [0, 32, 114, 166, 193, 246, 328]; s6 = [0, 32, 115, 167, 193, 246, 328]. Identical to within 1 degree on all seven, across every threshold I tried - the angular skeleton is effectively locked between the two species. Ball radius 44.8 (s5) vs 44.0 (s6). BUT the lengths do vary: normalised to 22% of each image's own peak luminance, spike radii are s5 = [86.3, 70.0, 57.8, 90.3, 87.8, 51.5, 77.0] and s6 = [90.0, 74.3, 51.8, 83.3, 85.0, 56.8, 67.3] - differences of 3 to 10 px, up to 13%, and signed in both directions (+3.7, +4.3, -6.0, -7.0, -2.8, +5.3, -9.7), so this is real per-species jitter and not a thresholding artefact of teal-vs-white. The generator is already varying lance LENGTH per seed and is NOT varying lance ANGLE at all. The defect lives in the angle seed, not in a global 'make them different' knob.

CORRECTION 3 - NOT A PALETTE SWAP; TWO INDEPENDENT RENDERS THAT COLLIDED. The bright-pixel masks have IoU of only 0.80 at threshold 55 (0.84 at 60, 0.70 at 150) - a literal recolour of one bitmap would be 1.00. Beyond the length jitter, the two differ in lighting: s5 emits a broad teal ambient bloom that lifts the whole background field and washes out its own cast shadow (against a per-row local background reference my detector found 0 shadow pixels in s5 and 4,890 in s6), while s6 has a neutral warm vignette and a crisp black ellipse measuring 194 x 34 px, bbox [123,247] to [316,280], widest row y=263. s6 also carries a hotter specular, peak luminance 255 vs s5's 205, with 0.3% of the ball fully saturated. Diffing the two as colours would understate the bug: two separately rendered species landed on the same skeleton.

WHAT THE CLAIM GOT RIGHT AND SHOULD BE KEPT. The centre dot really is present in both, at the same place and the same size - s5's darkest in-ball pixel is at (222,196) rgb 56,144,146; s6's is at (220,197) rgb 124,123,120; measured dot diameters 10.4 px vs 11.0 px. It is not an s5-only feature and must not be 'restored' to s6, which already has it. One refinement: the dot sits about 11 px ABOVE the ball's geometric centre, not dead centre. The ground ellipses are also both centred on x=220 at comparable scale (s6 194 px wide; s5's edges read at x=130 and x=310, so about 180 px).

WRONG-ORGANISM CALL - SUSTAINED. A smooth glossy sphere with rigid, glass-straight radiating lances, a single dark sensor-like dot high on the face, and a cast-shadow ellipse reads as a naval contact mine, or secondarily a sea urchin or caltrop. There is no fungal cue anywhere on it: no cap, no stipe, no gills or pores, no bracket, no hyphae, no spore texture, no substrate attachment. The dot is a large part of why it reads as ordnance - it functions as an eye or a detonator. This is not a ceiling imposed by the generator: within this same batch, fungi-h2-s0 renders a convincing branching mycelial/coral canopy on stipes, fungi-h1-s8 a clump of pointed fruiting bodies, and fungi-h1-s4 a speckled puffball. So the family is not one chassis - s8 has 5 spikes at [34,149,233,283,314] with ball radius 89.5, s9 has 3 at [36,54,145], h2-s0 has 4 at [12,67,112,163] with ball radius 107.3, all genuinely distinct. The duplication is scoped precisely to the adjacent s5/s6 pair, which is where the fix belongs.

BAND. FAIL on two independent grounds, either of which is sufficient under this packet's stated criterion: (a) s6 is silhouette-indistinguishable from its immediate neighbour s5 - same seven bearings, same ball radius, same dot position and size, same ellipse - which is exactly the shared-body failure the batch header asks to be named; and (b) it does not read as a fungus at all.

The yellow mass occupies x=169-305, y=208-306 (a 136x98 box, ~31% of frame width) and is built from ~7-10 overlapping soft lobes with visible fold seams, four distinct specular gloss caps (peak values 248,231,168) and dark lobe-to-lobe creases (down to 111,89,37). At 3x it unmistakably reads as glossy, wet, brain-folded witch's-butter — the correct organism, in the correct colour, with the gloss the code comment calls 'half the read'. The wood substrate is present too: a bark-brown bough (#2a1d15 core rendering at 51,36,26) arcing x=23-417, y=132-188 visible, with its rgba(0,0,0,0.38) underside stroke reaching y~199 (black on a near-black field, so effectively invisible). Nothing here reads as the wrong kingdom or the wrong family.

WHERE THE FAIL IS RIGHT. The mass is genuinely NOT attached. Minimum visible brown-bottom-to-yellow-top gap measured across x=150-320 is 21 px at x=207 (brown ends y=187, yellow begins y=208); at the frame centre (x=237) it is 27 px. Everything in that band is plain background (11-21 luminance). Code confirms the intent it misses: the branch is stroked along 0.30->0.44->0.34 of S while the mass is centred at cy = S*0.56 with lobe radii of only 0.055-0.11 S, so the two shapes cannot overlap by construction. A mass described as 'welded' and 'gripping' floats clear of its branch. That is a real composition defect and worth fixing.

WHERE THE FAIL IS WRONG — three corrections the fix must not be made against.
1. 'Stranded in empty space WELL ABOVE' overstates it by an order of magnitude. The gap is 21-27 px in a 440 px frame — 5-6% of frame height, about a fifth of the body's own height. It is a hairline void, not a stranded element in a different part of the canvas. The branch sits directly over the mass, correctly centred on it; the arc even dips toward the mass at centre. The fix is to close ~25 px, not to relocate anything.
2. 'Spanning the full frame width' is factually true (x=23-417, 89% of frame) but is not a defect and should not be 'fixed'. A branch crossing the frame edge-to-edge is the intended composition for a tremelloid and matches fungiTooth's bough in the same file. Do not shorten it.
3. 'The body itself has no ground shadow and floats too' — the absence is real (fungiJelly is the one fungal family in this file that never calls ground(); I confirmed there is no dark ellipse anywhere below y=306, only a smooth warm ambient glow rising from 9,9,11 to 15,13,10), but the prescription is WRONG. A jelly fungus hanging off a bough is not standing on soil; adding ground() at S*0.84 would put a floor shadow under an epiphyte and make the render less correct, not more. What is missing is CONTACT shading against the branch, not a ground shadow.

CORRECT FIX. Raise the mass (cy from S*0.56 to roughly S*0.47-0.50) and/or drop the branch, so the upper lobes overlap the bough by ~15-20 px; draw the topmost one or two lobes before the branch stroke so the bark edge clips over them and they read as gripping; then add a small dark occlusion smear on the branch underside where the lobes meet it, in place of a ground ellipse.

BAND. Both identity elements — glossy lobed jelly mass and wood substrate — are present, large and readable; nothing defining is absent and it does not read as another organism. A 21 px attachment gap is a positional polish, not a broken render. POLISH, FAIL not upheld.

THE FAIL STANDS. No fungal must-read is present at any scale. There is no cap (no pileus dome distinct from anything below it, no margin, no incurved edge, no umbo). There is no stipe: I zoomed the base band 4x at 3.2x gain and the left sphere's lower contour is a clean unbroken circular arc that terminates at y=276 and touches nothing — no stalk, no volva, no basal mycelium, no substrate attachment. The spheres float clear of the shadow ellipse. There is no hymenium cue: no gills, no radial lines, no pore field, no warts, no annulus, no veil remnant. The top band at 4x is featureless smooth curvature. It reads as two boulders / a contact-binary asteroid, exactly as claimed.

I DELIBERATELY TRIED THE CHARITABLE READING AND IT FAILS. A pair of spheres could legitimately be a puffball cluster (Lycoperdon/Bovista are genuinely stipeless spheres), which would rescue the 'no cap, no stipe' objection. It does not survive inspection: puffballs need a warty/spiny/granular or areolate skin, an apical ostiole, and a tapered sterile base sunk into the substrate. Here the skin is perfectly smooth, the dots are RECESSED (flat dark fill, no highlight rim, no cast shadow) so they read as craters not warts, the apex is completely blank, and there is no base and no substrate contact.

CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM (fix against these, not the original wording):
1. 'Matte' is WRONG and this matters most. The render is not matte — the highest-contrast element in the entire image is a hard bright specular rim arc, one per sphere. Peak rim luminance is L=146 (at x230,y169) sitting on a body whose core samples are RGB(43,45,59) on the left sphere and RGB(51,53,70) on the right, i.e. L~45-60. The rim is a 2-3px near-white hard-edged crescent running roughly 10 to 12 o'clock on the left sphere (x123-183, y140-165) and 12 o'clock down the right flank to about 4 o'clock on the right sphere (x230 to x328, y150-227). That glossy hard edge-light is a large part of what makes this read mineral/ceramic rather than organic. Killing or softening it is a required part of any fix.
2. 'Slate' understates how dark this is. At true exposure the body is near-black blue-violet; nothing but the two rim arcs clears L=70. Under-exposure is an independent defect the original judge did not flag — even if the morphology were corrected, the asset would still barely read on a dark card.

The fix is to raise interior value and lower stroke contrast, NOT to "add a fill" — the fill exists. 2) "Radial hairs" is wrong — the ribs are not radial and are not hairs. They are all parallel and vertical regardless of where they sit on the ellipse, so they are not normal to the membrane, they never break the silhouette, and their length is set purely by where the chord meets the outline. That geometry is exactly why the thing reads as hatch marks / scale ticks on a gauge. Cilia on a ciliate must leave the body outline, follow the membrane normal, and vary in length and phase. 3) "One dotted horizontal axis line" is correct and is the single most damaging element: a perfectly straight pole-to-pole bar with a dot at each end and one in the middle is the visual grammar of a dimension line or an axle, and it is what pushes the read from "cell" to "CAD diagram".

ON "no volume or shading" — half right. There IS shading: the radial gradient plus the specular arc. But the gradient is perfectly symmetric top-to-bottom (y=169 reads 91, y=273 reads 88 on the same column), so it carries no light direction; there is no terminator, no bounce/rim on the lower edge, and no cytoplasm texture or organelle. The lone arc highlight is also the wrong hue — a grey-white that does not belong to the orange palette. So the form is lit like a glow, not like a body.

Siblings show what the family can do: microbe-h1-s10 is a cluster of flagellates with real modelled volume and long trailing flagella; microbe-h1-s12 is a coccus with a proper specular, terminator and settled interior. Against those, s11 is the outlier — it is the only member that resolves to a geometric primitive with tick marks. No shared-chassis problem here; the problem is the opposite, s11 does not belong to the same rendering standard.

WHY FAIL AND NOT POLISH. The identity is not readable: nothing in the image says single-celled organism. Perfect ellipse, perfect bilateral AND vertical mirror symmetry, uniform ticks, ruler bar with end caps — a viewer names this a stadium plan, a turbine hub or a measurement gauge before they name it a microbe. The defining must-read for the ciliate archetype (cilia that project past the membrane) is absent, not merely small or misplaced: I checked the rows just outside the silhouette (y=120, y=290, and the columns beyond x=69/370) and they are pure background, so nothing protrudes anywhere. This needs a re-draw of the ciliary fringe and removal of the axial bar, not a polish pass.

I ran the real selector over the real genomes (hashInt(0xF00D, ki*100+heat*25+s, 7) -> makeGenome): microbe-h1-s2 form=7 -> microAlgaeCell, and s7 (form=12), s8 (form=0) and h2-s0 (form=1) ALL resolve to microAlgaeCell too. It fails not by absence but by character: a constant-width 2px crisp pale hairline with no thickness modulation, no texture and no break reads as moulded glass, not as a lipid bilayer. Fix is to vary the stroke width around the circumference and soften it, not to add a rim.

2. WRONG: 'No ... organelle is drawn anywhere.' The green bottom mass IS the chloroplast (line 347, commented 'the cup-shaped chloroplast - the defining organelle'), and the five pale specks are the coded granules (line 348, five arcs of r=2 in rgba(200,240,180,0.5)). Nothing is missing there; everything drawn reads as the wrong thing.

3. WRONG: 'ten-o'clock specular blob.' It is coded as the PYRENOID (line 349, '/* pyrenoid glint */'), a real organelle of a green alga. Measured centre (193,190) vs cell centre (220,220), so ~10:30 not 10:00, diameter ~18px. It fails on PLACEMENT, not existence: it is drawn at (cx-0.35rr, cy-0.4rr) - upper-LEFT, entirely OUTSIDE the chloroplast, which occupies the bottom half. A pyrenoid sits INSIDE the chloroplast. Put a flat 50%-white disc at the canonical specular position of a sphere and it will read as a specular every time. Moving it into the green mass and dropping it to a dull starch-white would fix the read on its own.

4. RIGHT, AND I MEASURED IT. 'Dead-flat horizontal fluid chord.' I ran a per-column max-gradient edge detector on green-dominance: the chloroplast top edge sits at y=248 for essentially every column from x=171 to x=279 (the only outliers are the columns crossing the pyrenoid blob and the specks). That is ~110px of a 152px cell, flat to the pixel. CAUSE: line 347 is c.beginPath(); c.arc(cx, cy+rr*0.15, rr*(0.58+cz()*0.30), 0.3, Math.PI-0.3); c.fill(). Both endpoint angles (0.3 and PI-0.3) have equal sine, so filling the arc closes it with a straight HORIZONTAL chord. The result is a half-disc, flat side up - a fluid line, not a cup. A cup chloroplast needs a concave top (outer arc out, inner arc back) and should be clipped to the cell ellipse.

What does not vary is the SCHEMA - flat chord, five specks, one 10:30 blob, one hairline rim - which is why they still read as one drawing. Family-level: 4 of the 14 assets in batch-016 (s2, s7, s8, h2-s0) are this one painter, and 8 of 50 across h1+h2 vs 3.8 expected for a flat 1-in-13 pick.

The three siblings on the same painter sample (105,118,72) g-b=46, (109,158,122) g-b=36, (102,151,118) g-b=33. The 62% green bias failed to dominate an unusually blue incoming palette on this seed alone. For a GREEN ALGA, whose whole identity is that the cell is green because the chloroplast fills it, a slate-blue cell body is a primary identity failure - and it is precisely what makes the 'glass jar of green liquid' reading strongest on s2 specifically. Raise k, or clamp a minimum g-b separation.

7. CONFIRMED ABSENT: no nucleus is drawn - the function has no nucleus call at all, and the judge is right. Flagellum absence is defensible (a coccoid green alga such as Chlorella has none), so the nucleus is the real missing must-read, not the flagellum.

VERDICT: FAIL stands. The identity 'single algal cell, cup chloroplast, pyrenoid' is attempted in code but not one of its parts survives to the eye - the membrane reads as glass, the chloroplast reads as settled liquid because its top is a straight chord, the pyrenoid reads as a specular because it is outside the chloroplast at the highlight position, the granules read as bubbles because they float above the fluid line, the nucleus is genuinely absent, and on this seed the cell is not even green.

WHAT I ACTUALLY SAW (440x440 png, read at native size then cropped 130,120 190x190 and upscaled 4x nearest-neighbour). Packet row for this species is 'reference row: NONE' — no mustRead/aspect exists, so this is a coherence + against-batch judgement.

The asset is a near-perfect closed disc, measured body bbox (144,141)-(295,298), w=152 h=158, aspect 0.962. On it: (a) a 1px pale grey rim stroke running the ENTIRE perimeter, unbroken; (b) a large soft radial specular hotspot at upper-left, centred approx (200,190), ~40px across, near-white at its core; (c) a DEAD-FLAT horizontal chord at y=243 separating a mid-green upper field (sampled 97,143,112) from a darker green lower field (sampled 46,70,61) — I probed the surface at x=190, 205 and 250 and got y=243 at all three, zero meniscus, zero curvature, zero irregularity; the lower field's bottom follows the disc arc, producing a filled bowl; (d) six small uniform pale dots — four in a diagonal chain rising from the chord toward the hotspot at roughly (198,213),(206,222),(232,240) plus one higher, and two more inside the dark field near (222,272). Dots are 4-8px, all the same tint, no size or shape hierarchy.

WHY IT FAILS: that composite — smooth ellipse + rim highlight + gravity-levelled flat liquid line + rising bubbles — is the universal visual grammar of fluid in glassware. Biology produces no dead-flat horizontal internal boundary; gravity in a container does. The silhouette edge is a mathematically smooth ellipse with ZERO ruffle, notch, bud, lobe or protrusion anywhere on its perimeter. There is no cilium or flagellum breaking the outline, no pseudopod, no nucleus or discrete organelle (the dots have no size hierarchy so they read as bubbles/specks, not nucleus+vacuole+mitochondria), no cytoplasmic granulation, no cell-wall banding, no division furrow. The identity read is a petri dish / half-filled vial. The judge's headline is correct: container, not microbe.

CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM — 'distinguished from s2 and h2-s0 only by saturation' is factually wrong on three counts:
1. SILHOUETTES ARE NOT IDENTICAL. Measured body aspects: s8 = 0.962 (true circle), s2 = 1.034 (slightly squat/wide), h2-s0 = 0.895 (a visibly taller vertical egg/ovoid). That is a ~15% spread and h2-s0 plainly does not read as a sphere. (Note: the OUTER glow bbox IS pixel-identical across all three — (127,107)-(311,323) — which is the real shared-chassis evidence the judge should have cited.)
2. s2 DIFFERS BY HUE SPLIT, NOT SATURATION. s2's upper field is cool blue-grey slate (90,118,120) against a warm olive fluid (34,75,48) — a deliberate two-hue composition. s8 (97,143,112 over 46,70,61) and h2-s0 (91,137,109 over 36,82,48) are monochrome green top-to-bottom and are the pair that are genuinely near-identical in colour. So the judge paired the wrong assets: the colour-clone is s8-vs-h2-s0 (which differ by silhouette), while s2 shares s8's roundness but not its palette.
3. FILL LEVEL AND DOT LAYOUT DIFFER. s8's liquid chord sits at 0.65 of body height (a shallow ~35% fill); s2 and h2-s0 both sit at ~0.38-0.40 (~60% fill). So s8 is the emptiest of the three. Dot arrangement also differs: s8 a diagonal chain of 4 plus 2 submerged, s2 a wide scattered arc of 5, h2-s0 a loose cluster of ~6.

SO: the three are NOT distinguished only by saturation — they vary in aspect, hue split, fill level and dot layout. But every one of those variations is surface decoration painted onto one shared primitive (ellipse + rim + hotspot + flat chord + dots), and none of them is a cellular feature. The judge reached the right band by the wrong route. FIX BRIEF: the flat horizontal chord is the single load-bearing defect — no fluid-level line belongs on a cell. Replace it with cytoplasmic structure, deform the perimeter (ruffle/bud/lobe or a flagellum breaking the outline), and give the internal bodies a size and shape hierarchy so a nucleus reads as a nucleus. Re-tinting will not move this asset out of FAIL.

No membrane, nucleus, organelle or motility structure is present, so nothing in the image names a microbe.

rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 PNG at native size, at 4x nearest-neighbour zoom on the body, and again at gamma 0.28 (a huge exposure lift) to hunt for faint appendages. Nothing is hiding. WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: one closed ellipse, bbox (143,134)-(296,305), w=154 h=172, aspect 1.117, dead-centre on canvas. Its edge is a single uniform ~1.5px pale grey-green stroke of constant width the whole way round -- no undulation, no crenulation, no thickening anywhere. Outside that stroke the canvas is empty even under the gamma lift: NO flagellum, NO cilia fringe, NO pili, NO pseudopod, NO stalk, NO trailing filament, no glow other than the vignette. Inside: (a) a soft radial cytoplasm gradient brightest upper-left; (b) one hard-edged white specular disc at roughly 33%/32% of the body box, with a crisp circular boundary -- a lens/glass highlight, not a nucleus (it has no membrane, no nucleolus, no shading); (c) five tiny flat pale-green dots, all of them ABOVE the fill line, each a plain disc with no rim and no internal shading; (d) a perfectly HORIZONTAL straight line at ~62% of body height, below which a flat, untextured mid-green mass is clipped to the ellipse. That horizontal line is the fatal element. Cytoplasm does not settle to a level; only a liquid in a rigid vessel does. Combined with the hard specular and the clean glass rim, the read is unmistakably a snow globe / half-filled bottle, not a cell. The judge is right on every structural point.

CHASSIS CHECK (the packet's headline question -- reference row for this species is explicitly NONE, so the bar is coherence plus family distinctness). I built a 14-up contact sheet of batch-016. Four of the fourteen are this identical marble: microbe-h1-s2, microbe-h1-s7, microbe-h1-s8 and this one. I measured all four: widths 150 / 146 / 152 / 154 px -- effectively identical -- and heights 144 / 136 / 158 / 172, i.e. aspect 0.960 / 0.932 / 1.039 / 1.117. The ONLY parameters that move across the four instances are vertical stretch and hue. Same centre, same width, same rim stroke, same upper-left specular, same speck field, same horizontal fill line. So 'fourth copy of the glass-marble chassis' is literally correct, and the confirmed generator behaviour is: fixed-width ellipse, height jittered ~+/-13%, hue rotated. Worse than the judge stated -- h1-s8 is not merely the nearest sibling in silhouette, it is also the SAME GREEN, so h2-s0 and h1-s8 differ only by an 8% aspect change and nothing else legible.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM, neither of which rescues it. (1) 'Same speck-bubbles' is loose: h1-s8 carries three specks plus a small comma/streak mark BELOW its fill line, whereas h2-s0 has five specks and all five sit ABOVE the line, with nothing in the settled region. (2) 'Stretched into a slight oval' understates it slightly -- the ellipse is 12% taller than wide (h1-s8 is 4%), which is the largest deviation of the four, but it is still the only axis of variation, so the point stands.

WHY THIS IS FAIL AND NOT POLISH. There is no reference row, so no named must-read is absent; the failure is the other kind the brief calls out -- the asset reads as the wrong object. Set against its own batch-mates, which are genuinely specific organisms (h1-s19 magenta spirochetes with tapering terminal flagella, h1-s3 a teal tardigrade with segmented cuticle, stubby legs and eye spots, h1-s5 a heliozoan with radiating axopods, h1-s6 purple filaments with terminal bulbs, h2-s11 discrete bacilli rods, h2-s10 a swarm cloud), this marble carries zero organism vocabulary: no nucleus, no organelles, no membrane texture, no granularity, no locomotion structure, no polarity, no size cue. Nothing in the image names a living thing. Fix direction: kill the horizontal meniscus outright (it is the single strongest anti-life signal), replace the hard specular disc with a soft off-axis sheen, give the rim a variable-width lipid-bilayer read with a slight lobed/amoeboid deviation from the perfect ellipse, and add at least one interior structure with actual form -- a shaded nucleus with a nucleolus, contractile vacuoles with rims, or chloroplast bands -- plus a per-seed appendage (cilia band, one or two flagella, or pseudopods) so the four marbles stop being one object in four hues.

rows.verifyWhy:
Verdict upheld, but THREE of the four stated causes are factually wrong and must not be used as the fix brief.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY IN THE FRAME (440x440, background 5,6,12): a soft-edged green haze occupying the middle of the canvas, carrying ~250 small pale-mint rod strokes, ~10 translucent grey discs, and ~8 long curved filaments streaming off the right side.

CORRECTION 1 -- "runs off all four edges / clipped on every side" is FALSE, measured. I scanned every border pixel: on rows 0, 3, 10, h-11, h-4, h-1 and cols 0, 3, 10, w-11, w-4, w-1 the count of pixels above a background threshold is ZERO on every one, and the peak border value is 31/765 (i.e. plain vignette, not content). The content bounding box is x 25..417, y 73..365 -- margins of 25px left, 23px right, 73px top, 75px bottom. The mass is fully contained; the bottom crop shows a distinctly hard, almost horizontal lower silhouette edge with two lobes hanging below it, and the left crop shows a lobed, cauliflower-like colony margin. There IS a boundary; it is soft and unmembraned, not absent.

CORRECTION 2 -- "the only concrete forms are tick-marks and grey circles" misses the flagella. There are roughly eight long, smoothly curved, tapering filaments sweeping off the right flank between y~110 and y~350, terminating around x=416. They are the clearest drawn forms in the picture and they establish a left-to-right axis. Any fix brief that omits them will delete the one good element.

CORRECTION 3 -- "tick-marks" undersells them. At 3x magnification they are unambiguous bacilli: capsule-ended rods ~10-14px long, many bent into V/chevron pairs in a convincing corynebacterial 'chinese-letter' arrangement. The microbe identity reads. Nobody would call this smoke or a nebula once they look at the rods.

WHERE THE JUDGE IS RIGHT. (a) The grey discs really do read as lens dirt. I scanned one at (266,120): interior is a near-uniform 60,80,75 varying by ~5 levels across its whole 16px width, with only a 1-2px top rim at 72,87,85. They are flat neutral-grey semi-transparent fills with no volume, no rim light, no internal structure, and no hue relationship to the green -- exactly the signature of dust on a sensor. (b) There is no scale cue and no subject.

WHY IT STILL FAILS -- and the real reason. Judged against its own batch, which the packet explicitly instructs (reference row is NONE). Siblings s1, s11, s14 and s5 all render the same family as a SMALL NUMBER OF DISCRETE, VOLUMETRICALLY SHADED ORGANISMS on dark ground: s11 is eight 100px+ bacilli with a clear top-left key light and a shadow side; s1 and s14 are streptococcus chains of fully modelled spheres; s5 is a lit tardigrade. Every one of them has a protagonist and a lighting model. s10 has neither. Its rods are flat unlit fills at a tenth the sibling scale, its discs are flat fills, and its body is an unlit fog -- so the card depicts a substrate, a petri-dish field or biofilm mat, rather than a creature. That is a whole-idiom mismatch, not a cleanup: the fix is to re-author it as a few large, painterly, lit cells (keep the flagella, keep the chevron rod pairs as the identity, drop or re-light the grey discs), not to crop, re-frame, or add a membrane.

rows.readsAs: scattered rods — but the pearly plastic value reads as medicine capsules more than as bacilli

At lower right one rod passes straight through another to form a hard T with no depth separation, which reads as a render glitch. The rods are also uniform in length and thickness.

rows.readsAs: an out-of-focus photograph of dust motes, or smoke with confetti in it

rows.readsAs: a bicycle wheel, a dartboard, or a radar sweep dial - not a living thing

rows.verifyWhy: UPHELD, with three factual corrections to the stated cause. WHAT I SAW at full size and again at 6x nearest-neighbour zoom on the upper-right quadrant: a 440x440 canvas, near-black navy field, and one centred disc of radius 132px (30% of canvas). The disc is a radial gradient, brightest at the exact centre and falling off monotonically to near-black at the margin. Over it sit exactly four circles and a fan of straight radial spokes. Nothing else is on the canvas. CORRECTION 1 - the spoke count is 17, not 16. I sampled 2000 points around a circle at r=115 (between the outermost interior ring and the rim) and counted 17 threshold crossings at 0, 21.1, 42.2, 63.6, 85.0, 106.1, 127.5, 148.6, 169.6, 190.9, 211.8, 233.0, 253.9, 274.9, 296.2, 317.2, 338.4 degrees - a perfectly even 21.2-degree pitch with zero jitter. CORRECTION 2 - s13 and s19 are NOT geometrically identical. The same sweep on microbe-h2-s19 returns 15 spokes at a 24.0-degree pitch. Everything else does match exactly (same rim radius, same three interior rings, same hub radius, same gradient, differing only in hue: s13 is cold blue-grey, s19 is violet). So the pair is not literally the same file; it is the same construction with two spokes' difference and a hue swap, which is indistinguishable to a player and still a real repetition defect - the judge's conclusion survives, the word 'identical' does not. CORRECTION 3 - the stroke is 1.6px, not 1px, and the outer rim is drawn TWICE at full alpha while the spokes and interior rings are at ~0.5 alpha. That is why the rim is the loudest mark on the canvas (I measured luminance-sum 637 at the rim versus ~349 peak on an interior ring), and it is the single biggest driver of the bicycle-wheel read: the brightest thing in the picture is a geometrically perfect circle. THE CORE OF THE CLAIM IS CONFIRMED AND IS WORSE THAN STATED. I sampled a radial luminance profile along a ray at 10.5 degrees, deliberately threaded between two spokes, from r=0 to r=160. It reads 386 at centre and decays by 1-3 units per pixel, monotonically, all the way out - interrupted only by three narrow ring spikes at r=33, r=65 and r=98, and the rim at r=131. Between those spikes there is not one pixel of high-frequency variation. That is proof, not impression: there are zero areolae, zero punctae, zero costae shading, zero silica grain, no central annulus, no rimoportulae, no cingulum, no cell contents (no plastids, no nucleus, no cytoplasm) anywhere inside the valve. A centric diatom's entire visual identity is the hexagonal/radial pore array in the silica; this asset draws the scaffolding those pores would sit on and then leaves every sector empty. On volume: the judge said 'no volume', which is right in effect but slightly wrong in description - there IS a radial gradient, but it is centre-bright and perfectly axisymmetric with no directional light and no offset specular, so it reads as a backlit radar screen or a lens flare, not as a glass frustule with thickness. Note the spokes stop short at r=26 (0.06 of canvas) and just end in mid-air around a bare gradient blob, leaving 17 raw stub-ends at the hub - there is no central area to terminate into. ROOT CAUSE, for whoever fixes this: packages/art/src/speciesoverrides.ts, function microbeDiatom (~line 280). The function forks on 'const radial = r() < 0.5'. The PENNATE branch was rebuilt in Wave 20 and now has a raphe, three nodules, striae that fan and stop at the valve curve, and a white lens highlight along the upper face. The RADIAL branch below it was never touched - it is still the original wireframe, and it even contains a copy-paste bug: 'c.beginPath(); c.arc(...); c.stroke();' for the outer circle appears twice in a row, which is exactly the double-bright rim I measured. s13 and s19 both landed on the radial branch. The fix is to give the radial branch the same treatment the pennate branch already got. BATCH CONTEXT: the packet has no reference row for this species and asks for coherence against its 13 batch-mates. I looked at three - s12 is a soft volumetric biofilm colony with hundreds of bacilli and flagella, s14 is a rendered pink streptococcus chain with per-coccus specular highlights, s17 is a fully shaded tardigrade with segmented cuticle, eight clawed legs and a cast ground shadow. So the batch is NOT one chassis (that specific packet worry does not apply here). But it means s13 sits beside genuinely painted organisms as the only flat vector diagram in the set, which also puts it in direct conflict with the HD engine law that forbids flat primitives. FAIL is the correct band.

rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, but three parts of the stated cause are wrong and one real defect was missed. WHAT I SAW (440x440, centre 220,220): a violet radially-spoked, concentrically-ringed disc on the dark vignette field, nothing else in frame -- no flagella, no cilia, no fringe, no organelles, no nucleus, no debris.

MEASURED (PNG decoded and radially profiled, not eyeballed):
- Ring radii are IDENTICAL to s13. Luminance peaks along +x land at r=33/65/99/131 in s19 and r=32/65/99/131 in s13; the outer edge measures 132.0-133.5 px at all eight compass angles in BOTH files. So 'same radius, same three rings' is exactly correct and is the strongest part of the claim -- three inner annuli plus the rim, same construction, same size.
- 'Same sixteen spokes' is WRONG on both counts. Angular peak detection at r=50/80/115 gives s19 = 15 costae at 24.0 deg pitch (peaks 23.8, 47.8, 72.6 ... 335.3) and s13 = 17 costae at 21.2 deg pitch (20.6, 42.3, 63.8 ... 338.4). Neither is 16 and they are not the same. So it is not literally a pure hue swap -- it is hue plus a +/-1 spoke setting, a difference nobody can perceive, which arguably makes the redundancy point worse rather than rescuing it. Do not tell the fixer 'the spoke count is shared'; it is not, and the generator clearly already varies it.
- 'Flat disc' is imprecise. The interior is a strong radial vignette: mean ring luminance 116 at centre, 107 at r=20, 97 at r=40, 67 at r=80, 34 at r=120, 23 at r=128, then a single bright stroke at r=132 (154) and straight to background (13) at r=136. So the body FADES OUT into the backdrop before its own rim, and the rim is one hairline. That is why it reads as an empty wire wheel or a tilted dish rather than a filled cell -- not because the fill is flat, but because the fill is dark exactly where the silhouette needs to be legible. There is no glow, no soft membrane edge, no rim thickness; the organism ends in one anti-aliased pixel.
- 'Wagon wheel rather than a cell' is the part I want to correct in spirit even though the band stands. The SCHEMA is legitimate biology: a radially costate, concentrically annulate disc is precisely a centric diatom valve (Arachnoidiscus, literally nicknamed 'wheel of glass'; Actinoptychus). This is not the wrong organism. What is absent is every rendering cue that would sell a silica frustule -- areolae/punctae (the pore field), any variation in costa weight from hub to margin, a thickened or beaded marginal ring, a defined hyaline central area, and any specular value break. The fix is 'render the valve', NOT 'redesign the organism'. A fixer told to abandon the wheel would throw away the one correct thing here.

DEFECT THE JUDGE MISSED: at 4x on the centre, the costae have ragged, uneven inner terminations. They stop at scattered radii around the r=33 annulus -- several as short stubs ending well outside it, several crossing inside it -- so the hub is a scruffy corona of unfinished line ends instead of a central area. At the margin at least one costa stops roughly 15 px short of the outer arc. This is unfinished geometry, visible and fixable independently of the texture problem.

BATCH COHERENCE (the packet has no reference row and directs judging against the batch): the family is NOT one chassis -- s12 and s16 are granular colony clouds with punctate granules and trailing flagella, s4 is a cluster of rendered teardrop flagellates with sheen and red nuclei, s18 is a teal ciliate with a full cilia fringe, membrane and internal vacuoles. Against those, s19 is the only member drawn in bare uniform-width hairline vector over a gradient, with zero surface texture at any radius. It is the rendering outlier of the batch and violates the HD engine law's no-flat-primitives rule, and its only true twin is s13. FAIL stands on rendering fidelity and on carrying no information s13 does not.

rows.readsAs: a tardigrade / water bear - specifically, the exact same one as microbe-h2-s17

rows.readsAs: a green marble, or a jar half full of liquid

It is a single flat-shaded green sphere with one hard specular blob at upper-left, three tiny white dots, and a dead-straight horizontal chord slicing across the lower third in darker green - that chord reads unmistakably as a liquid fill line in a container, which kills any cell read. No membrane, no wall, no organelles, no cilia or flagella, no texture, nothing that distinguishes it from a rendered ball.

What is actually on canvas (440x440, verified by pixel scan and by 5x nearest-neighbour + gamma-0.42 crops): a mathematically perfect circle, bbox 145,147-294,292 = 150x146 px, centre ~(220,220), r~75. There IS a continuous membrane/wall stroke: a ~2px pale grey-green rim running the full circumference, brightest on the upper-left arc and still legible at the bottom. It is thin and generic but it is present, so 'add a membrane' is not the fix. CORRECTION 2 - 'flat-shaded' is false and this matters. Removing the sphere-volume lighting in favour of translucent cytoplasm is part of the fix; adding shading is not. CORRECTION 3 - 'three tiny dots' undercounts; there are FIVE. Separately from the specular blob (a hard-edged near-white disc r~9px centred about (194,190)), five flat uniform pale-green discs of r~4px are scattered with no pattern down the middle-right of the body, at source coords approx (212,204), (229,215), (248,232), (204,240) and (230,255). They read as flat stickers, not organelles - no rim, no nucleolus, no shadow, no depth cue, and they do not scale or dim as they cross into the darker lower zone. CORRECTION 4 - the horizontal chord is correctly identified and is worse than described. It is a dead-straight, perfectly horizontal line at y~245 (about 28% up from the bottom of the circle). The region below it is a SINGLE FLAT GREEN with literally no gradient - it does not participate in the sphere's lighting at all, it is not darkened at the left or right limb, and it terminates hard against the rim stroke on both sides. Gamma-boosting the shadows to 0.42 confirms there is nothing hidden in it. The result is unmistakably a meniscus - a half-filled jar or a lava-lamp fluid line. One of the five dots floats below the line inside the flat zone, which reinforces the 'sediment in liquid' read. Whatever this element is meant to be (a vacuole? a basal body? a pigment cup?), a horizontal chord is the one shape it must never be: it must curve, follow the body's lighting, or be replaced. CORRECTION 5 - there is no interior structure of any kind besides the five dots and the fill line. Gamma boost shows no nucleus, no cytoplasmic granulation, no vacuole outlines, no cell-wall texture. BATCH CONTEXT (the packet gives no reference row: 'procedural or unlisted - judge coherence, and judge it against the others in this batch'). Judged against its own batch this is far below the bar. microbe-h2-s5 is a legible tardigrade - segmented cuticle ribs, eight clawed stub legs, a distinct head lobe with two eye spots, contact shadow. microbe-h2-s7 is a legible flagellate - two tapered lobes, two long curling flagella, two red eyespots. s6 is not the same class of drawing; it would be indistinguishable from a decorative planet or bauble if dropped into any other set. FAIL stands on the absent identity, not on absent shading.

The head is an undifferentiated bump with no mouth cone or stylet, just two dark dots stacked vertically that read as one eye plus a nostril.

The legs read a little better here only because they are tonally darker. Nothing distinguishes it as a separate organism, and the head still has no mouth or terminal claw pair.
